a17_0062706.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 27 minutes. Booster systems engineer has just reported to the Flight Director that the S-IVB stage is in good shape, with 14 hours life time remaining. The limiting factor on the S-IVB is the battery life. Fourteen hours of battery life remaining on the S-IVB.

a17_0062706.speaker: Cernan
a17_0062706.text: Hello, Houston; how do you read CDR?

a17_0062706.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0062706.text: Read you loud and clear, Gene.

a17_0062706.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0062706.text: Bob, LMP's going off the air for a little while.

a17_0062706.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0062706.text: It sounded like a sigh of relief.

a17_0062706.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0062706.text: No, sir. Been enjoying listening to you; keeping - keep me awake down here.

a17_0062706.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0062706.text: Not as long as you've had.

a17_0062706.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0062706.text: I've just been lying around, floating around.

a17_0062706.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0062706.text: You make it sound so good.

a17_0062706.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0062706.text: Piece of cake. I'll talk to you in a little while.

a17_0063326.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 34 minutes. Apollo 17 now 26,553 nautical miles [49,176 km] from Earth; velocity, 11,606 feet per second [3,538 m/s].

a17_0063955.speaker: Evans
a17_0063955.text: Okay; we had another Master Alarm, and I just glanced up and it was the Main A Undervolt light that was on, just for a second. [Pause.]

a17_0063955.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0063955.text: Okay. Ron, we didn't see anything at all on Main A down here. We did have an Accumulator cycle again. Don't know if that ties in or not.

a17_0063955.speaker: Evans
a17_0063955.text: Well, the Main A Undervolt - I just happened to be looking right at the panel and the Main A Undervolt light blinked on for a second. [Pause.] And, of course, obviously, Main A is up now.

a17_0063955.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0063955.text: Ron, Houston here. We've checked the back room and the high-speed charts and that and don't see any glitch on Main A at all on our data down here.

a17_0064859.text: This is Apollo Control. It's 6 hours, 49 minutes. Apollo 17 is 28,232 nautical miles [52,286 km] from Earth; velocity, 11,291 feet per second [3,441 m/s]. We're continuing to operate at present on the normal GET of the Flight Plan, normal Ground Elapsed Time. Under that schedule the crew's rest period will begin about 9 hours and 15 minutes into the mission. If, however, the crew completes the activities that are scheduled in the Flight Plan early, the rest period will probably begin early if they so desire. However, at the present time we are continuing to operate on the GET of the Flight Pla

a17_0070658.text: This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 7 minutes. Apollo 17 has just passed the 30,000-[nautical-]mile [55,560-km] mark on its journey to the Moon. Now, at 30,039 nautical miles [55,632 km], velocity continuing to decrease. Now at 10,932 feet per second [3,332 m/s].

a17_0071010.speaker: Evans
a17_0071010.text: Houston, 17. That was O 2 Flow, High.

a17_0071010.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0071010.text: Roger. We copied that one. We saw it. Just about ready to call you when you called us just now.

a17_0071451.text: This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 15 minutes. Astronaut Bob Parker is now relieving Astronaut Bob Overmyer at the CapCom console and the commander of the backup crew, Captain John Young, has just left the control room. He has been sitting at the CapCom console with Overmyer since returning from the Cape early this morning. So the next CapCom voice you will hear will be that of Bob Parker.

a17_0073401.text: This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 34 minutes. Apollo 17 now 32,697 nautical miles [60,555 km] from Earth; velocity, 10,457 feet per second [3,187 m/s]. The crew a little over midway in the scheduled meal period in the Flight Plan.

a17_0074958.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0074958.text: That little Master Alarm there, I can't be absolutely positive, but out of the corner of my eye, I think it was the Suit Compressor light that glitched.

a17_0074958.speaker: Parker
a17_0074958.text: Okay. We copy that. You - we believe down here it was the High O 2 Flow.

a17_0074958.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0074958.text: Well, they're pretty close. I thought it was red and I thought, okay; that's good. That's the right time, I guess.

a17_0074958.speaker: Parker
a17_0074958.text: Okay; because we'd just called it out. I was just ready for you 5 seconds before you called me.

a17_0074958.speaker: Parker
a17_0074958.text: Roger. And Stoney is back in Houston on the console.

a17_0074958.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0074958.text: That's hard to believe. What are you doing back here? We're - we haven't even had time to go to sleep.

a17_0074958.speaker: Parker
a17_0074958.text: Well, I tell you, it's a tale that's hard to believe. It's almost as miraculous as your escape from the pad tonight. [Pause.]

a17_0074958.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0074958.text: You've seen one night launch, you've seen them all. Huh, Parker? [Long pause.]

a17_0074958.speaker: Evans
a17_0074958.text: We go to SCS. Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0074958.speaker: Evans
a17_0074958.text: Never know if this is it or not but we'll try it. [Long pause.]

a17_0074958.speaker: Evans
a17_0074958.text: Dust whipping all over the place. The stars in there...

a17_0075421.speaker: Evans
a17_0075421.text: Do good. [Pause.] Oh? Yeah, let's do it a little better now.

a17_0075644.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0075644.text: [Garble] Bob, mag November November is 130 now. And I just took another set of Earth pictures.

a17_0075644.speaker: Parker
a17_0075644.text: Okay. Copy that. November November at 130. [Pause.]

a17_0075644.speaker: Evans
a17_0075644.text: And, Houston, 17. You copying the torquing angles now? [Pause.]

a17_0075644.speaker: Parker
a17_0075644.text: Okay. We have them, and you're Go to torque them.

a17_0075644.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0075644.text: 007:57:58 - This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 58 minutes. Ron Evans is realigning the inertial platform that was scheduled on the Flight Plan for 8 hours, 15 minutes. That indicates that they are running 15 to 20 minutes ahead of the Flight Plan. Jack Schmitt is obviously taking some pictures. He gave Bob Parker a report on a film magazine that he was using.

This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 58 minutes. Ron Evans is realigning the inertial platform that was scheduled on the Flight Plan for 8 hours, 15 minutes. That indicates that they are running 15 to 20 minutes ahead of the Flight Plan. Jack Schmitt is obviously taking some pictures. He gave Bob Parker a report on a film magazine that he was using.

a17_0075644.speaker: Parker
a17_0075644.text: And, 17, we have a preferred REFSMMAT standing by if you want to give us Accept, and we'll send it up before you do your second P52.

a17_0075644.speaker: Evans
a17_0075644.text: Okay, you have P00 and Accept now.

a17_0075644.speaker: Parker
a17_0075644.text: Roger. Understand we have updata. It's coming at you. [Pause.] And, Ron, while we're sending it up to you, we'll also send you an update on the zero trunnion bias, as per the Flight Plan.

a17_0080236.speaker: Parker
a17_0080236.text: Okay, 17 - Ron, you can go to Block now. You've got your PTC REFSMMAT. You're free to do a P52 option 1 if you want. And, be advised we are suspicious from time to time you may have an open mike there.

a17_0081005.speaker: Evans
a17_0081005.text: Okay, Houston. Those are the differences in the gyro torque and I'll torque it - oh, 11, I guess. Eight [garble] 11.

a17_0081207.text: This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 12 minutes. Apollo 17 now 36,353 nautical miles [67,326 km] from Earth; velocity, 9,878 feet per second [3,011 m/s].

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Apollo 17, Houston. Over.

a17_0081332.speaker: Cernan
a17_0081332.text: Go ahead.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Rog. We've been discussing the question of what your sleep configuration is going to be in terms of headsets or not, particularly with reference to all of these various Master Alarms. And I guess we'd feel better if one of you guys slept with his headset on. We were curious as to what your plans are. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Cernan
a17_0081332.text: Bob, since I've got to wear the biomed anyway, I might just as well go ahead and keep it on.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. The other option is for us, if we were trying to get hold of you, is to put the Klaxon up. But we're a little - un-in-favor of that, because of the possibility of one of these spurious things waking everybody up that way.

a17_0081332.speaker: Cernan
a17_0081332.text: Yeah, I'll go ahead and keep it on and see how it works out for a while.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. We copy that. And, when you guys are ready, we have a couple of - we have three items to read up to you for the updates in the Flight Plan. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Go ahead, Bob.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. The first's in the Flight Plan itself, and it's the quads for the PTC spinup, and they'll be Alpha and Bravo. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay. For PTC spinup, quads Alpha and Bravo.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: All right, we just took that back. It should be Bravo and Delta for spinup; Alpha and Bravo only for damping. Copy Bravo and Delta for spinup; Alpha and Bravo for damping.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: And, 17, if you have that, I have two others. One's the Flight Plan Supplement Book, and the other one is in the G&C Checklist.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Go with the Supplement.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. In the Flight Plan Supplement, we have an E-Load update on page 1-43. Say; 1-43 - can give me a call when you get to that page? [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay, Bob. I'm there.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Under line - it's 30704, column Bravo - you'll find currently 33550. And let me give you a word of warning. When we change this, we'll be changing it again around 67 hours. These are primarily due to the launch delay. And we'll give you another GET update of this sort later on. The new number to replace 3...

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Bob...

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Go ahead.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Let me get a pencil, please.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: I'll use that instead of a pen.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Go ahead.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Under - Again, I remind you, 30704 column Bravo, which was 33550, is now 34761. The line just below it, which is 05, also in column Bravo, is 15403. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay, Bob. For 30704 Bravo, 34761; and for 31005 Bravo, 15403.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Very good. And the next one is in the G&C Checklist under the P37 block data. [Pause.] And to help you find it, that's on page 4-23. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Evans
a17_0081332.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. On the lift-off plus 15, be the first block. It's 01500, 3893, minus 174, 05756. The second block for lift-off plus 25 is 05 - Pardon me, start over again there; 02500, 6651, minus 175, 05725. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Evans
a17_0081332.text: Okay, Houston; Apollo 17. First one would be 01500, a Delta-V of 3893, minus 174, and GET 400K is 05756. The other one is T IG of 02500, Delta-V of 6651, longitude of minus 175. GET of 400K is 05725.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Roger. Good readback. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay, Bob. [Clears throat.] It's Jack. I'm going to be moving into the pre-sleep checklist here. Are there any things you want to change or alter in that? And are you ready for the waste - Waste Stowage vent to be closed?

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Roger, 17. We're ready for the vent valve to go closed. Waste Stowage Vent to Closed. And we have no anticipated changes, at the present time, in the Flight Plan, Jack.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay, I'm just looking at 1-29 in the pre-sleep checklist and - wondering if there was anything there. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Stand by, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay, 17. For antenna management tonight we'd like you to select Omni Bravo at the current time, and stow the High Gain Antenna. And we'll take care of managing our antennas from here on.

a17_0081332.speaker: Evans
a17_0081332.text: Okay. We'll give you Omni Bravo and stow the High Gain.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: And, Jack, we indeed do not have anything to add to the presleep checklist tonight. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: And - with your concurrence, I'll take the H 2 Fans all to Auto now.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Stand by.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Roger. We're ready for that. All to Auto.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Okay, Jack. I guess that you - we're not quite sure what you said or meant there - or what - what it is. In the Flight Plan itself, we want H 2 Heaters 1 and 2 to Auto, and we want H 2 Fans, on tank 3 only, to Auto. The three there is for H 2 tank 3. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: Okay. You're teaching me to read carefully early, aren't you?

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: We're trying. The 1 and 2 Heaters will be in Auto and 3 Fan will be in Auto.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: That's the way it is now, and consider the fans have been cycled.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Roger.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: According to the checklist. [Long pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: You might look at the third line on 1-29, and look at the H 2 line on the Flight Plan, and see why I was confused.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Roger. We were just discussing whether or not there was a fan or fans in each tank.

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: That ought to keep you awake this morning.

a17_0081332.speaker: Parker
a17_0081332.text: Going to take something. [Pause.]

a17_0081332.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0081332.text: What I was really trying to do, Bob, was get out of chlorinating the potable water, but you wouldn't bite.

This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 28 minutes. Apollo 17 now 37,832 nautical miles [70,065 km] from Earth; velocity, 9,667 feet per second [2,947 m/s]. Apollo 17 crew in the period now in the Flight Plan where they're making preparations for their rest period. Getting the systems in the proper configuration for a sleep period. The spacecraft has been maneuvered to the Passive Thermal Control or PTC mode - attitude, rather. And just prior to the rest period, the crew will spin up the spacecraft for thermal control during the rest period. The spin rate will be slow or approximately 3 revolutions

a17_0083043.speaker: Parker
a17_0083043.text: Okay. We're going to give you a little High Gain Antenna practice here. We'd like to pick up with the High Gain Antenna again so that we can get your PTC or can watch your PTC develop. We'd like you to go to a Pitch of 40 and Yaw of 275 on the High Gain. That's 40, Pitch: 275, Yaw; and Manual and Wide. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: And you want the High Gain selected, I presume.

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: Oh, I don't expect that'll be the last time you have to apologize. I think we're running about even now. [Long pause.]

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: You're missing quite a view, Bob. Sorry you're not here.

a17_0083043.speaker: Parker
a17_0083043.text: That makes two of us. [Pause.] Weitz just said, 'That makes three of us'. [Pause.]

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: What are you trying to tell me?

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: Who's your friend off on your right, tonight?

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: Oh, a Moon, huh? [Pause.] Why don't you ask him what he's reading at H 2 tank 3 quantity?

a17_0083043.speaker: Parker
a17_0083043.text: Okay, 17. On tanks 3 of H 2 , we're reading 84.38.

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: Okay, it looks like we're reading almost the same nowadays. [Pause.]

a17_0083043.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083043.text: I thought we launched a little bias, but I guess that's gone now. We're a little higher than that.

a17_0083527.speaker: Parker
a17_0083527.text: And, 17, Houston. We're seeing your rates are quite low enough to start the spinup to PTC. [Long pause.]

a17_0083527.speaker: Evans
a17_0083527.text: Okay. We'll see if we can't get it right this time.

a17_0083835.speaker: Evans
a17_0083835.text: Does it make any difference with the plus or minus roll there with the - now that you're going to use the High Gain? [Pause.]

a17_0083835.speaker: Parker
a17_0083835.text: Okay. Well, the Flight Plan says minus roll, why don't we do it that way? [Pause.]

a17_0083835.speaker: Parker
a17_0083835.text: And after you start the roll, 17, we'd like to go back to Omni Bravo and stow the High Gain.

a17_0083835.speaker: Parker
a17_0083835.text: We only needed the High Gain to just keep a good check on your rates. [Long pause.]

a17_0083835.speaker: Parker
a17_0083835.text: And, 17, that means stow the High Gain after you - after the startup. We'd like to watch the startup itself.

a17_0083835.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0083835.text: Okay. I was just going to ask you when.

a17_0084220.speaker: Parker
a17_0084220.text: Okay, 17 - We're ready for High Gain to stow and select Omni Bravo.

a17_0084935.speaker: Parker
a17_0084935.text: 17, Houston. We gather you're ready for sleep, almost. One thing we'd like to check at the end here is your O 2 heater configuration. Over.

a17_0084935.speaker: Parker
a17_0084935.text: Roger. Can you give us your O 2 heater configuration?

a17_0084935.speaker: Cernan
a17_0084935.text: Okay. We've got 1 and 2 in Auto, and 3 is Off.

a17_0084935.speaker: Parker
a17_0084935.text: Okay. We'd like those per the Flight Plan; 1 and 2 to Off, and 3 to Auto. [Pause.]

a17_0084935.speaker: Cernan
a17_0084935.text: Okay; 1 and 2 to Off and 3 to Auto.

a17_0084935.speaker: Parker
a17_0084935.text: Okay. And do you have a final change or update on the film status - beyond that 130 that Jack gave us?

a17_0085505.text: This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 55 minutes. As the crew of Apollo 17 prepares for a 5¾-hour rest period, the spacecraft is 40,165 nautical miles [74,386 km] from Earth; velocity, 9,349 feet per second [2,850 m/s].

a17_0085804.speaker: Parker
a17_0085804.text: And, 17, your PTC is looking real good so far.

a17_0085804.speaker: Cernan
a17_0085804.text: Okay. That number on that mag is still 130, Bob.

a17_0085804.speaker: Evans
a17_0085804.text: And Alpha Alpha, that 16-millimeter mag, is about 25 per cent left.

a17_0085804.speaker: Parker
a17_0085804.text: And I guess as soon as you've change the LiOH canister, if you have or haven't, and charged Battery Bravo, then we're ready for you to go to sleep at your leisure. Configuring your comm, remember the Squelch, Enable, and the Voice, Off, when you get ready to go to sleep. [Long pause.]

a17_0085804.speaker: Parker
a17_0085804.text: Roger, Apollo 17. We copy the film update, and we're ready for you to go to sleep once you've got the LiOH canister changed, if you haven't. And remember also the charge on brady - Battery Bravo. After that, it's just the comm configuration, Squelch, Enable, and Voice, Off, when you get ready to go to sleep.

a17_0085804.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0085804.text: Bob, You're cut in and out. Stand by. We'll talk to you in a minute.

a17_0085804.speaker: Parker
a17_0085804.text: Okay, I think we're losing an Omni here.

a17_0091233.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 12 minutes. Apollo 17 now 41,677 nautical miles [77,186 km] from Earth; velocity, 9,159 feet per second [2,792 m/s]. The spacecraft has stabilized into a Passive Thermal Control mode now. It's completing one revolution every 18 minutes.

a17_0092558.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 26 minutes. The Booster systems engineer has advised Flight Director Pete Frank that a second midcourse correction for the S-IVB, the third stage of the launch vehicle will be required. This maneuver is performed with the Auxiliary Propulsion System of the S-IVB, and the Booster Systems Engineer will command this burn at 11 hours, 15 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The magnitude of the burn is not known at this time. That will be determined shortly before the midcourse is performed. The purpose is to tune up the trajectory to more precisely target the S-IVB stag

a17_0093044.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 30 minutes. We have had no voice communications with the crew for some time now. But we do have indications that they have not yet fully configured the spacecraft for their rest period. Normally the voice switch is turned off the last step before the rest period. That voice switch is still on. Apollo 17 now 43,261 nautical miles [80,119 km] away from Earth; velocity, 8,964 feet per second [2,732 m/s].

a17_0094802.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 48 minutes. From the data that he is receiving, the Flight Surgeon, Dr. Sam Pool, reports that he believes the spacecraft Commander Gene Cernan is asleep. Cernan is the only member of the crew who is wearing the biomedical harness during the rest period, and therefore, is the only one that the Flight Surgeon is getting measurements on. But the indications are that - that Cernan is asleep and apparently the entire crew has gone to sleep. Apollo 17 now 44,749 nautical miles [82,875 km] from Earth; velocity, 8,794 feet per second [2,680 m/s]. The awake clock as

a17_0095855.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 59 minutes. The Flight Dynamics Officer, Bill Boone, has computed the half way marks for the spacecraft in both time and distance. We'll give those to you now. Apollo 17 will reach the halfway point in distance at a Ground Elapsed Time of 30 hours, 3 minutes. Its distance from both the Moon and the Earth at that time will be 114,787 nautical miles [212,586 km]. Its velocity, referenced to the Earth, will be 4,522 feet per second [1,378 m/s]; referenced to the Moon, 3,826 feet per second [1,166 m/s]. The halfway mark in time will be reached at a Ground Elapsed

a17_0102937.text: This is Apollo Control at 10 hours, 29 minutes. Apollo 17 now 48,070 nautical miles [89,026 km] from Earth; velocity, 8,434 feet per second [2,571 m/s]. Pete Frank and the Orange Team of flight controllers getting ready to hand over to Gerry Griffin and his Gold team of flight controllers at this time. Astronaut Bob Parker will remain as the CapCom for a good deal of this next shift. Several spurious master alarms that were seen while the spacecraft was still in Earth orbit are as yet unexplained. There are no obvious reasons for them. The spacecraft experts in the back rooms, the support room

a17_0112700.text: This is Apollo Control at 11 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. Approximately 11 minutes ago - as you were - 6 minutes ago, the S-IVB corrective burn was performed; roughly 14.2 feet per second [4.3 m/s] to modify the trajectory of the S-IVB third stage in the Saturn V, targeting for impact just weighted west of the crater Ptolemaeus at latitude 7 degrees south by longitude 8 degrees west. However, the actual impact location and the time of impact will be forthcoming after some additional hours of tracking of the stage has been gathered. We're looking now at a

a17_0122700.text: This is Apollo Control; 12 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. And Apollo 17 at the present time is 56,948 nautical miles [105,468 km] out from Earth at a velocity of 7,609 feet per second [2,319 m/s]. A short time ago, the Booster systems engineer Frank Van Rensselaer reported that after the final APS burn in the S-IVB stage, which is targeting the stage to impact on the Moon, he reported that the S-IVB stage was tumbling intentionally, after that burn, and as he gathered up all his documents and packed his briefcase, he, on the Flight Director loop, he said,

a17_0132700.text: This is Apollo Control; 13 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. The spacecraft presently is 61,186 nautical miles [113,316 km] out from the Earth. Decelerating slightly in its velocity, now 7,272 feet per second [2,217 m/s]. Crew has another hour and a half of sleep period remaining. They'll be awakened about 2:30 Central Time. This is a rather short sleep period, slightly under 6 hours, the object being to get the crew back onto Houston time day-night cycle eventually. The cycle is disturbed somewhat by the - initially what would have been a night launch, and e

a17_0142700.text: This is Apollo Control at 14 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. Slightly more than a half hour remaining until spacecraft communicator, Robert Parker, wakes the crew of Apollo 17 up, after a brief 6-hour rest period. Apollo 17 presently 65,273 nautical miles [120,886 km] out from Earth, velocity now 6,974 feet per second [2,126 m/s]. And getting back on schedule with Apollo 17 because of the late lift-off and the hold situation early this morning. The Translunar Injection burn was targeted to get the spacecraft at the Moon or into lunar orbit at about the same

a17_0145723.text: This is Apollo Control; 14 hours, 57 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. A 2-minutes mark remaining in the crew waken peri - wake period before - or sleep period before the crew is wakened. Spacecraft communicator Bob Parker should be calling them shortly and we'll stand by for that first wake up call. Rather slack day as far as crew activity today after their post-sleep checklist and checking over the systems. The Flight Director just advised the CapCom to hold off on the wake call until they switch antennas. There's some P23 navigation sightings that will be run today,

a17_0150245.speaker: Parker
a17_0150245.text: Glad to have you with us again. You guys got a good night's sleep, we think.

a17_0150245.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150245.text: Well, I'll tell you, it was [laughter] looked forward to. [Long pause.]

a17_0150245.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150245.text: Give us a few minutes here and we'll - get operational. [Pause.]

a17_0150245.speaker: Parker
a17_0150245.text: Roger. Give us a call when you're ready to talk to people. [Pause.]

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: Yeah, from the looks of things, Bob, down there, it looks like getting off last night was a good idea.

a17_0150944.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0150944.text: Got a new CapCom now, Geno. Why? Looks kind of cloudy down there?

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: Yeah. Hello, Gordo. How you doing? Yeah, I'm looking - oh, we're probably directly over - just west of the - out in the Pacific, but abeam of the bottom third of South America, I suppose. And I've got North America, Mexico, and the U.S. on the top third - the top 25 per cent of the Earth. And it looks like you've got cloud cover from somewhere where the coast bends around Corpus right on north into the Great Lakes and is completely out into the Atlantic, including covering Florida out there.

a17_0150944.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0150944.text: Roger. I can verify the part between the Cape and Houston, anyway. [Pause.]

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: Yeah, the Gulf looks like it's pretty well filled with clouds. Looks pretty thick from here.

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: However, if you're interested in going to South America, the whole continent looks - looks pretty good. A few clouds; but, for the most part, you can see the entire continent.

a17_0150944.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0150944.text: Rog. Guess it's summertime down there. [Pause.]

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: Okay, Gordo. We're - we're stirring slowly. We'll get back with you here.

a17_0150944.speaker: Cernan
a17_0150944.text: Gordo, one question. How does the spacecraft look to you? I didn't hear anything all night long as far as any Master Alarms or anything.

a17_0150944.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0150944.text: I'm getting the word that nothing was seen here either. It looks absolutely super.

a17_0151525.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151525.text: Okay, Bob, I've - or Gordo, I've got H 2 Heaters 1 and 2, Off now.

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Hello, Houston; America. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Go ahead, America.

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Okay, Gordo. I'm looking over the Flight Plan today. We'll be with you with the postsleep checklist, and primarily it looks like a P23 day for Ron and what we'd primarily like to do is spend a good part of that time getting the spacecraft cleaned up, reshuffled, restowed a little bit, and get it in order for the next few days ahead. It doesn't look like today's that big of a day.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay. [Pause.] Geno, I might give you some words on what we have in mind to get the GET back in sync here, if - if you want to hear those while you're looking through the upcoming hours.

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Yeah, why don't you - why don't you pass a few words on that?

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay. The plan we're considering, and we're offering it to you now for your opinion, is at 65 hours GET, we'll update, and at the time the clock goes to 65, we'll update it 2 hours and 40 minutes to 67:40. And we're shaping your trajectory such that you'll arrive at the Moon at the same time, GMT, as you would have, had you launched on time. In other words, your translunar time is 2 hours and 40 minutes less. So once we do that, we'll be back with all the right times in the Flight Plan without any updating. And the one thing we think of is that your next day will, which is now a 16-hour day, w

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Yeah, we - we'll get to the Moon, you say, the same GMT, so all our sunrise, sunset, lunar-orbit activities, and Sun angle at landing will be the same. And let me - I'll - it sounds pretty good, Gordo. I just want to take a look at that day that you're shortening and see what we're doing in there.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay. It doesn't cut out anything. In fact, we picked a time that's pretty much dead time as far as the Flight Plan goes. Take a look, and we'll talk about it later.

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Good morning, Gordy. This is Jack.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Good morning, Jack. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Let me fill my square on the postsleep checklist. I've got 24030, PRD.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay.

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: And I slept in and out - probably totaled about 4 hours in that last period. But I feel pretty good in spite of that, and expect now that I've educated myself on how to sleep, that it'll pick up the next time around.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: No medication yet, but I'm considering a couple of aspirin. I'll let you know if I take them.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Roger.

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: And, fluids? Let's see, I guess I've had two of your little water-measurement-containers full so far, plus the meal I had in my pocket. And I'll catch up on - I think I'm a little dehydrated. I'll catch up on fluids with breakfast.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay.

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: And my meal yesterday was the meal B in the pocket.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Roger. Meal B. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: And I guess consumables update. That's mainly yours.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Rog...

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: There's plenty there. And I'll wait for your words on that. And the watch is wound.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Roger. [Pause.] Okay. Got the consumables update numbers, if you're ready to copy.

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: No, not quite, Gordy. I'll give you a buzz.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay. No hurry. [Long pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Okay. The CMPs rad's 1509.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Gordy, this is Jack. How do you want to send the consumable - consumables information?

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: We were just discussing that here. Used to - in flights gone by, there was a place in the Flight Plan, a little form to fill out. But we're trying to figure out if there is such a place in the current data file. Do you know of one?

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Well, I'll tell you what I've got. I've got the consumables curves, and if there are any major changes to those curves, I guess you could give them to me, and I'll put them on as points.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: There's no...

a17_0151652.speaker: Cernan
a17_0151652.text: Page...

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: ...changes at all.

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Okay. And why don't we just do it that way in the future in case there is anything. And that's on page 1-45 and subsequent in the Flight Plan Supplement.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a17_0151652.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0151652.text: Looks like you took good care of my space - my systems last night.

a17_0151652.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0151652.text: No troubles at all.

a17_0153059.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0153059.text: Okay, Gordy. Your friendly medical officer up here has some more information for you. CMP, continuing, had about 3 hours of sleep, had - three cans of fluid, of water that is. And he ate everything in meal B but the fruitcake, and he didn't use the brownies and the beverage in meal C.

a17_0153059.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0153059.text: Okay. And continuing, the CDRs PD - PRD is 17019. He had 3 hours of fair sleep, no medication, and 1½ cans of water, and one-half a sandwich. The CMP's sleep was 3 hours. And I'll try to get more systematic as we go along here.

a17_0153059.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0153059.text: Jack, we're assuming no - no medication on the CMP. is that right?

a17_0153059.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0153059.text: That's affirm. We haven't gotten that kit out yet

a17_0160055.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0160055.text: Gordy, it's Jack. Looks like the windows have cleared up pretty well in PTC from the - ice crystals, anyway, that were on window - window 1. The hatch window still seems to have a film of something on it. But, otherwise, they look pretty good.

a17_0160055.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0160055.text: Okay, sounds good. [Pause.] Jack, while you're there, I might try - we've been talking about consumable updates and what would be the most meaningful way to give you the information. As a trial, for 14 hours, with reference to the charts in the back of the book, which in the case of - in case of all of them, are listed in percentages except the RCS, which is in pounds. On the cryo quantities, when I take all the tank percentages and plot them, it turns out that there's no real significant difference from the lines that are plotted on either hydrogen or oxygen. On RCS, you're running about 3 pe

a17_0161220.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0161220.text: Mark. Two aspirin for the LMP.

a17_0161220.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0161220.text: Jack, next time the Surgeon would like a mark on each individual aspirin. [Pause.]

a17_0161220.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0161220.text: Well, I gave it to you since I swallowed them both simultaneously.

a17_0161220.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0161220.text: I knew they wanted that, Gordy, and that's why I only gave you one.

a17_0161220.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0161220.text: Would they rather have them go down one at a time? [Pause.]

a17_0161220.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0161220.text: I'll have to go back to the backroom on that.

a17_0162506.text: This is Apollo Control; 16 hours, 25 minutes. Crew of Apollo 17 presently in a meal period. A little bit of levity a short time ago when Jack Schmitt, Lunar Module Pilot, called down to say: "This is LMP, Mark, 2 aspirin." He had mentioned earlier in his post-sleep checklist that he was considering taking two aspirins. Apollo 17 is presently 72,843 nautical miles [134,905 km] out from Earth; velocity, 6,477 feet per second [1,974 m/s]. We're continuing to stand by on the air-ground circuit for further conversation as the crew finishes up their meal period and gets what few Flight Plan updates

a17_0164444.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0164444.text: 17, Houston. We see the optic starting to stir there, you can go ahead with a P52, but before you do the P23, we have some updates to it.

a17_0164444.speaker: Evans
a17_0164444.text: Hey, okay, Gordo. We'll do that. [Long pause.]

a17_0164444.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0164444.text: 17, Houston. Can you confirm that you did change the LiOH canister before going to sleep last night?

a17_0164444.speaker: Evans
a17_0164444.text: Well, we can confirm that we didn't. How about that?

a17_0164444.speaker: Evans
a17_0164444.text: We'll - Thanks - thanks for reminding us. We'll try that first thing this morning. I was just getting too tired, and the CO 2 didn't look quite that high last night, so...

a17_0164444.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0164444.text: Okay, that's - that's fine. We're not concerned about being late with it.

a17_0165305.speaker: Evans
a17_0165305.text: Okay, Houston. That looked like a pretty good one that time. You note the star angle difference?

a17_0165305.speaker: Evans
a17_0165305.text: Okay [chuckle]. I can't see squat out through that telescope. I just hope it lines it up and does the right things. [Pause.] Okay. Those are the torquing angles, and you can let me know when you have them.

a17_0165305.speaker: Evans
a17_0165305.text: The telescope's no different than any other time. There's just a lot of reflection from the Lunar Module. And even though everybody said that before, you don't quite believe it until you see it yourself. [Long pause.]

a17_0165305.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0165305.text: Okay, Ron. You're clear to torque it.

a17_0165305.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0165305.text: 17, Houston. When you - if you can find a stenographer, I got some dictation, some PADs for you and also a Flight Plan update. [Long pause.]

a17_0165738.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0165738.text: Oh, okay. Stand by. [Pause.] Okay, Ron's ready to copy.

a17_0165738.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0165738.text: Okay. [Pause.] Okay, the P37 block data for 35 hours. Well, we've got 35, 45, 55 and 65. GET ignition of 035:00. Delta-V T is 5326, minus 175, 081:39. For a GET of 045:00, 7728, minus 177, 081:18. For a GET of 055:00, 5859, minus 175, 105:30. GET of 065:00, 4703, minus 175, 129:40. [Pause.]

a17_0165738.speaker: Evans
a17_0165738.text: Okay, I'll read that. Let's see, 35:00 at 5326, minus 175, and 81:39. At 45:00, 7728, minus 177, and 81:18. At 55:00, it's 5859, minus 175, 105:30. At 65:00, it's 4703, minus 175, and 129:40.

a17_0165738.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0165738.text: Okay, that's correct. I've got a maneuver PAD for you. It's a flyby maneuver at a time of 81 hours, which is 5 hours prior to LOI, This is required because you're presently on an impacting trajectory. And this is assuming you wouldn't do midcourse 2. Midcourse 2 will put you on a - on the proper trajectory. If you can get a maneuver PAD out, I'll give it to you.

a17_0170211.speaker: Evans
a17_0170211.text: Okay, Houston. This is 17. Ready for the flyby PAD. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay, Ron. We're just watching your roll angle. You're going to - we're going to be updating the optics cal attitude. And the roll will be 164, and you're coming up on that so maybe you want to stop the PTC near that roll angle first.

a17_0170211.speaker: Evans
a17_0170211.text: Hey, that's a good idea. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Gordy [garble]. [Long pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Gordy, did you read Jack?

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Loud and clear, Jack.

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: I can take the PAD, if you want to while Ron stops PTC.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. Why don't I give you the update to the Flight Plan, since that'll give you the new attitude and also the - a change in the star for the P23. And then Ron can get on with that. The PAD we can get after that.

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Go ahead.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. Turn to 17 hours in the Flight Plan, page 18. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Go ahead.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. The "Verb 49 maneuver to optics cal attitude" right at the top of the page. Cross out the attitude numbers and replace them with "Roll, 164; pitch, 301; and yaw, 348; at a High Gain pitch angle of minus 48 and a yaw of 315." Over. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: That's correct. Now go down a few lines to the sighting attitude at - one's at 17 hours and 15 minutes. And cross out that attitude and the High Gain pitch angle and change to a roll of 196; pitch, 304; and yaw, 348. High Gain pitch is a minus 61, and the yaw remains the same, 357. Over.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: That's correct. And now, on the first star of P23, we're going to change the star, so cross out - replace the Noun 70 numbers with star 21. That would be three balls 21. And delete the Noun 88 and the vector numbers there. [Long pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay, star 21 and no Noun 88s.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Right. And over on the right where it says "Merak," you can write in "Alphard." That's what 21 is. [Long pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. Now down on the next page; at 18 hours and 20 minutes; where it says "Optics calibration attitude." We got to put in the same thing as - the same change as above. We want, instead of 175, 298, 330, change that to 164, 301, and 348. High Gain of minus 48 and 315. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. [Pause.] Now, about 10 lines down, delete "Charge battery A." We're going to leave battery A [means B] charged for a while longer, since we used up so much of it on the pad last night.

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay. Delete "Battery charge A," and you want to leave it on B.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Yes. Right. Flip the page. Might as well clean up all of these checklist changes. At 19 hours and 40 minutes; change "Magazine Kilo Kilo" to "Magazine November November". [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay. That's done.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: And then skip a few pages to 24 hours and 30 minutes. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Go ahead.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: And at just above the "CSM Systems Checklist" callout there, write in "Charge battery A". [Long pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay, I got you.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: And we'll be leaving it on battery A all night long. Okay, that's all the - the Flight Plan changes. I've got that flyby PAD when you're ready. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay, I'm all set.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. Purpose is flyby, SPS/G&N. The weight is 66839; plus 1.21, minus .02 - correction, the yaw trim is a minus 0.12. Ignition time is 081:17:21.03. Noun 81 is a plus 0091.1, plus 0204.1, plus 0459.3. Attitude is 121, 153, and 321, Apogee is NA; perigee, plus 0021.2. Delta-V total of 0510.8, 1:17, 0506.3. Sextant star: 26, 096.5, 33.9. Boresight star is NA; Noun 61, plus 15.57, minus 175.00; 1099.9, 36243; and GET of 0.05g is 153:24:11. GDC Align stars are Sirius and Rigel; 256, 152, 069 - Ullage is none. And for remarks: number 1 is "Burn docked." number 2 assumes PTC REFSMMAT: number 3; LM

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay, Gordy. Do you read that?

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: I haven't heard anything since I finished the PAD, Jack.

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay. I'll push the other button then. [Long pause.] Okay, your readback: Flyby, SPS/G&N; 66839; plus 1.21, minus 0.12; 081:17:21.03; plus 0091.1, plus 0204.1, plus 0459.3; 121, 153, 321; H A is NA, plus 0021.0; 0510.8, 1:17, 0506.3; 26, 096.5, 33.9. Boresight star is NA; plus 15.57; minus 175.00; 1099.9, 36243; 153:24:11. Sirius and Rigel; 256, 152, 069. No ullage. Remarks: 1, burn docked; 2, PTC REFSMMAT assumed; 3, LM weight, 36281; and 4, assumes no midcourse 2.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. One correction on perigee of Noun 44. That's a plus 0021.2. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay; 0021.2 plus.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: And one additional remark. This results in a 187-mile perigee - perilune. [Long pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay. I got that.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Okay. For general information, we're planning midcourse 2 tomorrow at about 35:30, and it should be about 10 feet per second [3 m/s]. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Okay. [Long pause.] Strange enough, that's even scheduled at 35:30.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: I have one reminder to open the Waste Stowage Vent valve as shown on the - at 17 hours there.

a17_0170211.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0170211.text: Oh, okay. We were just going back to clean up. I think we owe you a LiOH canister change, too.

a17_0170211.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0170211.text: Rog. We concur with changing it.

a17_0171957.speaker: Evans
a17_0171957.text: And Houston, Apollo 17. We'll maneuver to the optics calibration attitude now.

a17_0171957.speaker: Evans
a17_0171957.text: It's funny eating potato soup, and all the soup is all around the outside of the bag. And you get a little hole right down through the middle of it. [Pause.]

a17_0171957.speaker: Evans
a17_0171957.text: It's just like in one g. The spoon isn't quite long enough to reach the bottom without getting your fingers on the side of the bowl.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: Gordy, I don't know what your weather is like down there, but from here it looks like you're probably overcast today. Might even have a pretty good storm going.

a17_0172353.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0172353.text: Well, it's gray and cold and a little rain, so your - your call is correct.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: Yeah, it looks like Mexico, in general, is pretty nice, although there is a band of east-west trending clouds that start from the - from the Gulf of California, across Sonora and probably up through New Mexico, and over into Texas as far around as I can see. Southern California looks like it's in pretty good shape today, but northern California looks like it's probably overcast. And a major system probably associated with that, that stretches into the northern western United States. [Pause.] But a band of clear weather looks like it stretches from Arizona right on up through, I would guess it

a17_0172353.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0172353.text: Rog. You're a regular human weather satellite.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: If Ron would just stop his maneuvers I'd tell you some more, but the Earth just set behind the LM.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: More specifically, it set behind the Rover, which may be a space first. [Long pause.] Pretty impressive storm system down off the west coast of Antarctica.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: And, Houston. The canister has been changed. Number 3 is in A as per the earlier Flight Plan instructions.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: Sorry we were late, but we got a little tired last night.

a17_0172353.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0172353.text: Jack, Houston. We'd like you to go ahead and get that Waste Stowage Vent open now, so we can keep to the schedule on cabin enrichment.

a17_0172353.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0172353.text: Okay; Ron's getting that. Keep nagging.

a17_0173528.speaker: Evans
a17_0173528.text: That the same as I had before? Ahh. [Long pause.]

a17_0173528.speaker: Evans
a17_0173528.text: Hey, that looks like a pretty good optics cal right there. That's three times. [Pause.] Okay. [Pause.] No, that's not very good. [Pause.]

a17_0173528.speaker: Evans
a17_0173528.text: Okay. Think we'll use that one there for the optics cal.

a17_0173528.speaker: Evans

a17_0200715.text: Well, if you saw my hands right now [laughter], you'd know why I said wait 1.

a17_0200715.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0200715.text: Understand. I'm just - just waiting for your call. Just didn't want you to think we're going to give you a whole rafter of it.

a17_0200715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0200715.text: Oh, we know you wouldn't do that. [Long pause.]

a17_0200715.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0200715.text: If you're eating, Jack, just go ahead and eat. This is nothing that can - we can just wait, and any time, just go ahead.

a17_0200715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0200715.text: Okay, Bob. Go with the update, and LM/CM Delta-P at 20 plus 09 [garble].

a17_0200715.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0200715.text: Want you to know, Jack, we just cut out by the antenna switching. Say again the LM/CM Delta-P.

a17_0200715.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0200715.text: Roger. Okay. My update is just simply on the bottom of page 3-23 at 2300 hours in the Flight Plan or 23 hours in the Flight Plan. "Waste Stowage Vent valve, Closed." Just delete that one, and move it over to 24:30, That's because you got started late on that.

a17_0200715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0200715.text: Okay. You could've just said, move it.

a17_0200715.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0200715.text: Okay. Just change it down to 24:30.

a17_0201200.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201200.text: Okay. Bob - about revision one on my previous discussion of the weather around Australia. That front does cross - probably Brisbane is probably cloudy. It does cross about that area, and - however, there is a bank of clouds that runs off of it down the coastline. So Sydney is either cloudy or has some pretty nice clouds off - off shore. And the remnants of the front as it dissipates in the hinterland of Australia dies out at about the Great Sandy Desert, and there is not a good indication that it crosses into the Ind - Indian Ocean. But we're getting over near the LM, and that's a little hard

a17_0201200.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201200.text: Now, it - more - looks more and more like the cyclone circulation developing right over the top of New Zealand; the South island, I think. And now I'm looking with the binoc, and as much - that anticyclone circulation is centered on the ice shelf. And I think that - well, I just don't know - I think that's the Ross Ice Shelf, but I'm not sure, off Antarctica. And the clouds from that circulation do extend over the ice shelf and barely onto the Antarctic con - continent.

a17_0201200.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201200.text: Now to the north of Antarctica. [Pause.] Let's see now. I ought to give you a better orientation than that. But, anyway, there is a large cyclone circulation pattern that has its southern extremity right on the edge of the ice shelf. And that - that is east by 20 or 30 degrees of longitude of the front that I just was discussing. By the way, that front intersects Antarctica.

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: Between New Zealand and Australia, the front I was discussing previously has some fairly strong transverse cloud patterns. It's hard to say whether they're high cirrus or not. But the clear area to the south of the front suggests that maybe the jet stream is roughly paralleling that front in that area. [Pause.]

a17_0201622.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0201622.text: Roger. [Pause.]I'd have to look up and see...

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: If I had to guess, I'd...

a17_0201622.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0201622.text: ...if they do have any jet stream down there right now.

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: I - if I had to guess, if you were flying - west from Sydney this afternoon, you'd have a pretty strong tailwind behind you, Bob.

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: Let's see, did I get that right? [Pause.]

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: But the bulk of Australia is very clear, all the south and the north. It's just that one line of - of cloud that crosses the center section.

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: That put all the major cities of the south, Perth and Adelaide, at least, and Melbourne, certainly in the clear. And in the north, Darwin, in those areas, are very nicely clear today.

a17_0201622.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0201622.text: Roger. [Pause.] I hope we can get this out to them and let them know that you're watching and tell them how good the weather is.

a17_0201622.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0201622.text: Oh, that's all right. I'm just having fun, Bob,

a17_0201622.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0201622.text: Understand. I imagine they'd appreciate it though.

a17_0203518.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0203518.text: Bob, I tried to pick out the Hawaiian islands on that last little turn here through window 5. And I can't say that I did. I think I've got them - the area spotted. It looks like they might be under some fairly heavy cloud cover today. I do not see the islands. I'm not sure I could, if it was clear.

a17_0203518.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0203518.text: Roger. Hey, Jack, I got some answers to your question from last night on where Little America is with respect to - on Antarctica.

a17_0203518.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0203518.text: There's a - inden - indentation that looks like a gulf that's called the Ross Sea, and on the northwest edge of the Ross Sea is Little America, That's the location of it.

a17_0203518.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0203518.text: Okay. And that would be the coast of Antarctica that sort of faces New Zealand and Australia. Is that correct?

a17_0203518.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0203518.text: Negative. According to the map I've got, it's - the Ross Sea looks like it would be more facing up towards the South America area. [Pause.] It's actually kind of facing up sort of the middle between Australia and South America, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0203518.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0203518.text: Okay, Bob. You cut out, and I presume you meant that - the Ross Sea was facing north - sort of the Pacific between South America and Australia?

a17_0203518.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0203518.text: That's affirmative, Jack. It's a very sharp indentation or sea or gulf onto the Antarctica. [Pause.]

a17_0203518.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0203518.text: Okay. I think I know the area you mean, and I'll check it out again when it comes by.

a17_0203518.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0203518.text: Okay. That's Little America on that west-northwest edge of that Ross Sea. That's where Little America is.

a17_0203518.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0203518.text: Yeah, all that - those names are familiar. I just had forgotten my geography. I'll see if I can recognize them.

a17_0204511.text: This is Apollo Control at 20 hours, 45 minutes. We're occasionally picking up a bit of noise on the Air-to-Ground circuit. This is due to the fact that the spacecraft is in the Passive Thermal Control mode. As it rotates, we're gradually losing contact through one of the Omni antennas and re-establishing adequate signal strength on another one. And as it moves from antenna to antenna on our coverage, we get the noise. This is a characteristic that becomes more pronounced as the spacecraft gets farther and farther from Earth. Here in Mission Control, the Flight Activities Officer has been activ

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Okay, Bob, checking on the Ross Sea, and if I've got her pegged right, it's got a fair amount of open water in it this time of year.

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: Roger.

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Although it's completely surrounded, I think, completely surrounded, I think by portions of the icepack. And off to the west of there, it looks like there's an area that might be - clear of snow, and - does my memory serve me correctly, that that's where McMurdo Sound is, and some of the dry valleys?

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: I believe so. That's the Little America area right now, all that general vicinity, Jack. [Pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Okay. It looks like the prime recovery area and the Samoa island region is clear, and my guess would be, from the fairly subdued zero phase point, that they might have fairly nice seas out there. The boys on the Ticonderoga are probably enjoying themselves immensely, I hope.

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Indonesia looks like it's having a nice day, with the possible exception of the region over just north of Australia. New Guinea and that area they - some clouds in there. I can't tell whether they're high or low clouds though. They look like they're probably fairly high clouds. But north of New Guinea, there's a strong concentration of clouds. Although small, it looks fairly dense like there might be a little tropical depression in that area.

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: The folks in Carnarvon ought to be enjoying a very nice day. [Long pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: I've been trying to spot tropical storm Teresa, which is - a couple of days ago was in the Philippines. But I can't - I don't think I quite have that visible to me right now.

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: Roger, Jack. Say, you might want to put something in the back of your mind here a minute. We made a run of the DSE recording just now of the TLI to get an idea of the quality of the DSE recording, and Gene came through loud and clear. Ron was very weak and almost unreadable, and we never caught you, Jack, in there. We don't - maybe you weren't saying anything during TLI, but we never did catch anything you said.

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Okay. I don't recall talking too much during TLI.

a17_0204511.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0204511.text: Roger. Understand. Now Gene - Gene came through real loud and clear. So whatever technique he was using went on that tape real well. [Long pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: Hey, Jack; Houston. [Pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Hello.

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: Hey, Jack. Just a couple more comments on that DSE. I think, as you well know, it's very critical on the position of your - of your boom there, and those areas that you're critical in, why, make sure that you've - you've really got those beauties up or you're talking right in - right into it. And this - this really makes a difference, because the DSE - The volume is - is fairly low, and if you're muddled just the least bit, why, it - it's going to be difficult to pick it up. So talk slow, and - and get right up next to the mike, because I know you - you're doing it. Just some voices come acros

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Roger, Stu. Thanks for the comments. As a matter of fact, you probably called it just right. I think during - once I got the helmet off, I loosened up my chinstrap, and my mike booms had moved away from my mouth some. And I'll keep that in mind. Thanks for the reminder.

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: Yeah. It's - that's probably the most critical item is that - is the position of those, and this has been true of - in the past, and it just really makes a difference in - in that - being able to pick up the data off the voice.

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Roger. I've - Ron and I did some experimentation with that in the chamber, and couldn't agree more. But I sometimes don't remember it. Thank you.

a17_0204511.speaker: Cernan
a17_0204511.text: Well, Stu, I just...

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: I - I

a17_0204511.speaker: Cernan
a17_0204511.text: ...thought I'd...

a17_0204511.speaker: Cernan
a17_0204511.text: Okay. Go ahead, Stu.

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: No, I was saying I was - I'm sure you - you're aware of that, but I think the fact that the volume is - is down just accentuates the - the problem. [Pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0204511.text: Okay. Gene had something he wanted to ask you.

a17_0204511.speaker: Cernan
a17_0204511.text: Stu, I - I just thought you'd like to be aware of it, as much time as we've all spent down at the Cape, probably May is one of the nicest months down there. However, having had the opportunity to - to be up here during May, I find out that it's not nearly as nice up here.

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a17_0204511.speaker: Cernan
a17_0204511.text: And I'd like to - to thank all my friends for that

a17_0204511.speaker: Roosa
a17_0204511.text: Okay.

a17_0210321.text: This is Apollo Control at 21 hours, 3 minutes. Things continuing to progress smoothly and very quietly here in Mission Control and aboard the spacecraft. And we'd like to have a bit more discussion of the Ground Elapsed Time update after first making the disclaimer that GET clock updates are not done for the purpose of confusing people; although, I'm sure it seems that way at times. And, by way of clarifying the previous description of this GET update we should - should point out that the amount of time that the clocks are changed both here and Mission Control and aboard the spacecraft will be

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Bob, you with me? [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger. We wouldn't go away, Jack. We're listening. Did you call?

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Well, I just - I'm - Yeah, I almost lost a pass here, and just a couple more words about Australia. As a - as a general landmass, it's red. Very strong red hues, except for the north and eastern coasts, where that red gradually merges into a greenish-gray. It's as - as red as portions of - of northern Africa appeared to be yesterday.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Very striking color. It would be more of an orange-red, really, with brown subduing it. It's not - obviously not crimson or anything like that.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: You think it's a function of Sun angle, Jack? Or is it just - just the red like we see out in New Mexico area sometimes - some of the areas?

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Yeah. No, it's not Sun angle, because that'll hold a good red color right - right in towards sunset or sunrise. It's - it's due primarily, I'm sure, like most desert areas, to the oxidation of the iron-bearing minerals in the sands and rocks in those regions.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Getting limonite and hematite. Little geology thrown in there, Bob. Sorry.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: That's all right. [Pause.] Got to keep you warmed up for the next couple of days. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Well, I think the Flight Plan will probably keep me warmed up, too.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger. We thought that time around T&D was just outstanding.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Hey, Bob. We - I think we've pretty well got impressions from you down there on that - on that night launch. I might give you a few of mine.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Go ahead, Gene. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: 17, Houston. Are you there? [Pause.] You're right - right on the edge, if you read me. We're getting a lot of static. If you'll just hang on a minute, we'll be in - back into some comm here. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Gene, Houston. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: 17, Houston.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Go ahead.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: We're just standing by for your comments you wanted to make. I think we lost comm there a minute. We're back with you.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Okay, Bob. The entire boost itself was not unlike what you've heard and what Stu down there understands from the physical cues, and what have you. But the significant part of going at night is that as soon as we did have ignition down there in the bottom of the S-IC stack - even though I only have a little slit out of - out of the rendezvous window here, and Ron doesn't have much of a hole in the boost protective cover out of the hatch window, we could definitely confirm ignition because we could see the reflected light on out through in front of us. It was by no means blinding, of course; we

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger, Gene. Any comment you might make on the possibility of picking up your yaw, if you'd lost your platform at that time - remember the discussion we had about the yaw in the late - like a Mode IV or something like that?

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Yeah, Bob. I not only will comment - I was aware of it, and I was looking for it. And during parts of the S-II and parts of the S-IVB burn, I even turned the lights down in the cockpit - in hopes that I could see stars out there; but I could not make out a one. Ron, I think, may have saw Saturn out the overhead hatch; but looking through the rendezvous window, during a boost phase and during a time-critical phase like a Mode II or Mode IV, I am very much afraid that we would not have been able to pick up that reference.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: As I remember it, as low as I had the interior lights there for a period of time - and I didn't want to keep them that low, of course - to see if I could get adapted very fast because we were in a dynamic phase of the burn. But my window just gave me a very deep purplish hue, a hue of which I could not, literally, see through to look to see any stars at all. Now, that may have been due to the very low intensity of our interior flood lights.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger, Gene. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Bob, this is Jack. A little lay impression there. I think I - saw just about everything Gene was talking about - as far as his description - and felt like it was - although everything was an amazing experience, each one in itself, after each one was over, you could think back and say, "Yeah, that's what other guys said it was like." The old Saturn V has got to be a pretty consistently performing vehicle. But - with the added night-time contrast, I think it made it probably the best ride any three guys have ever had.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Bob, I might add, that the S-I was, as usual, pretty shakey on lift-off. I saw all the maneuvers as I called them out - the yaw and small reverse roll. Going through Max Q, I got up to 25 per cent; but my yaw attitude error was zero and my pitch attitude error probably wasn't even at - oh, certainly less than 2 degrees. After Max Q, she smoothed out by comparison quite a bit; and the S-II was a very quiet ride, a very smooth ride. However, you are always aware, due to just a little rumbling out in the S-IVB, that she was still burning for you. The S-IVB, I think, was just a continually - rumbl

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: Gene I think one of the big things that impressed me was the - how instantaneous the decelerations were of each one of the boosters when they cut off. That included the S-IV TLI cut-off. No physical appreciation of tail-off at all. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: And, Bob, from my rendez - from the right-hand rendezvous window when the tower jett occurred, there seemed to be a lot of burning particles streaming away from it. I could not see - did not notice or remember seeing the actual cover or tower itself; but I - we were inside the cone of the burn and with a lot of streaming. It looked very much like a sky rocket - portion of one at any rate. Reminded me of the Fourth of July out in Silver City a few years ago.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger. Say, any time you got your Flight Plan handy, I've got a discussion here I'd like to run through with you on the - how we're going to recover those 2 hours and 40 minutes from the launch delay - and you'll need to copy it into the Flight Plan. And then just wanted - want you to be advised, we're not happy with the PTC. We get a half angle of about 17 degrees; and so sometime after the P52 coming up at 23:00, we'll want to do another PTC, or initiate PTC again. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Well, that was the commander who initiated PTC, and I've already heard about that.

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: [Laughter.] You bet he has. Okay. We've got the Flight Plan here, Bob. Which part of it are you talking about [garble]?

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Well, let's just talk some words here for a minute, and then I'll go through some specifics that you can just write down on a page because you don't want to do it until a little later. Okay, what we're going to set up here - You will arrive at lunar orbit at the same GMT time. The landing Sun angle - Sun elevation angle - and the camera settings and everything will be unchanged when you get to lunar orbit. To compensate for the 2 hour, 40 minute late launch, we're going to hack 2 hours and 40 minutes out of the timeline. And we're going to - They'll be out of the TLC timeline - and we're going

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: Okay, Bob, looks like we delete 1 hour from 46 to 47 hours. And then the activities that are at 46:30, we'll do those at 45:00.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger, Ron. And then starting at 47, just take - just scratch 1 hour off of each time, just subtract 1 hour from each of those times up through 66 hours. Just subtract 1 hour from 47 up through 66. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: Okay, we can do that. Subtract 1 hour from 47 through 66 hours.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Okay. And then just for your information - you won't have to do it - but we're going to play the old simulator step-ahead game at 66 hours of the old time, which will be 65 hours of the new time. So however you want to call it, we'll call you; and we're going to sync you up at 67:40 at that point. We'll play the old step-ahead game there.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Okay, Bob. That means that you're not going to actually do any clock updates or syncs until - until somewhere in the 60's there and not in the 40's.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger. It'll be 65 hours of the new time or 66 hours under the old time; depends on how you want to look at it. But that's when we'll sync you up.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Okay.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: You'll be in sync all the way out to that time; just - we're just going to delete and jump you to 67:40.

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Okay.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: And just another note of interest - You don't have to write this down - what - let's see; I'll read it to you. The awake periods will be - on day 3, you'll be 15 hours, 8 hours sleep starting at 11:33 CST; then at day 4, you'll be 14 and 20 hours, with 8 hours sleep. So - it actually just shortens a couple days there. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: Okay. Mighty fine. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: The beauty of that - that Tommy came up with on that, Ron - is that all you have to do is go subtract those 1 hours and no more reading or anything else; just subtract them and we're in business.

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: Yeah, it looks real fine.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: We're going to give Tommy a gold star for that one.

a17_0211018.speaker: Evans
a17_0211018.text: [Laughter.] You bet. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0211018.text: [Cough] Bob, this is Jack. I'm going to try and get a little exercise. I'd be interested to know how high I can get my heart rate just fooling around up here.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Okay, if we can [pause]. We'll keep you posted, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: Bob, just to keep you and the people there thinking a little bit, today is a relatively short day; but it is a good day because it gives us a chance to again get acclimated, finish our stowage and just generally go through all the things that have to be gone through for the rest of the mission. We've got 3 eating days today, and judging from what we're thinking and talking about now - that the last two are going to be sort of stretched into one eating period because three meals on this particular day just is not really going to be stomachable. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger. We understand that. [Pause.]

a17_0211018.speaker: Cernan
a17_0211018.text: I think you'll find out that our eating and drinking, for the most part, is starting off relatively slow; but - I think we'll pick it up here by tomorrow.

a17_0211018.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0211018.text: Roger.

a17_0213304.speaker: Cernan
a17_0213304.text: Bob, one other thing while I'm thinking about it. The PU shifts were - were all noticeable, but probably the one that really caught me a little bit by surprise was the PU shift on the S-IVB during - during TLI.

a17_0213304.speaker: Cernan
a17_0213304.text: It just felt like you lit in the other burner.

a17_0213304.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0213304.text: Just for Jack's information, you're running in the 80s on your heartbeat. We saw a 91 or 2 there for a few minutes. Are you working - still working out?

a17_0213304.speaker: Cernan
a17_0213304.text: Hey, Bob, what was Jack running before he started that? [Pause.]

a17_0213304.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0213304.text: He was running in the 60s; a constant somewhere in the mid 60s.

a17_0213304.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0213304.text: Okay, Jack. You're running about 105 and 103 right now. [Long pause.]

a17_0213304.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0213304.text: Kind of interesting, Jack. You slowed down, and then you're back up to 105 right now. Now you're slowing down again. [Long pause.]

Flight surgeon John Zieglschmid is watching the heart rates of Jack Schmitt, as Jack exercises aboard the spacecraft using a modified exerciser, that consists primarily of a cylinder and a cord that comes out of it. Allows him to adjust the amount of tension or resistance to pull that the device has, and there are a variety of ways in which it can be used, allowing him to pull against the adjustable tension - this bungee like device. And he's gotten his heart rate up somewhat in excess of 100 beats per minute .

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Go ahead, 17; this is Houston.

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Hello, Houston; this is 17.

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Roger. Go ahead. [Pause.]

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: 17, Houston. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Hello, Houston; this is 17.

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Roger, 17. Go ahead. Roger, 17. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Hello, 17; Houston. Do you read?

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Honeysuckle Comm Tech, Houston Comm Tech, Net 1. Goddard voice, Houston Comm Tech, Net 1.

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Goddard voice.

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Roger, Goddard. I'm reading you loud and clear, Honeysuckle. I'm not getting to him.

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Hello, Houston; this is America. Over.

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: America, Houston. Stand by. If you read us, don't change anything in the cockpit yet.

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: 17, Honeysuckle.

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Roger, Honeysuckle. I read you...

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Hello, Honeysuckle. 17's reading you loud and clear.

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Roger. We have a comm outage and I'll be right with you.

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Okay. Very fine. How are things down there today?

a17_0214030.speaker: Comm Tech
a17_0214030.text: Fine, your weather report was beautiful. [Garble.]

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Oh, your country looks beautiful from here. [Long pause.]

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Okay, 17; Houston. How do you read now?

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: We got you, Bob.

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Okay. That was our network problem, not your problem onboard.

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214030.text: Okay thank you, I just figured out what happened on my PTC. Here - with his exercises, Jack is shaking all of America in all three axes, here.

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Roger. He finally got to 115 on the heart rate.

a17_0214030.speaker: Cernan
