a17_0214030.text: Yeah, my rate needles are bouncing back and forth a half a degree [laughter].

a17_0214030.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214030.text: Roger. Got to find something to pin it on. [Long pause.]

a17_0214455.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214455.text: Jack. Surgeon over here says you got a 120 on the heartbeat for a moment there - 122 right now. [Long pause.] Okay, 130, Jack. 130. [Long pause.] 140, Jack, 140.

a17_0214455.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0214455.text: 021:46:16 - The numbers reported to Jack Schmitt by CapCom are his heart rate. And you heard him report a heart rate up to about 140 beats per minute as Jack is apparently continuing to exercise vigorously with the onboard exerciser. This is aimed, among other things, at keeping the cardiovascular system which tends to get lazy in zero gravity in condition.

The numbers reported to Jack Schmitt by CapCom are his heart rate. And you heard him report a heart rate up to about 140 beats per minute as Jack is apparently continuing to exercise vigorously with the onboard exerciser. This is aimed, among other things, at keeping the cardiovascular system which tends to get lazy in zero gravity in condition.

a17_0214455.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214455.text: 17, we've got a serious one here. You might be interested. All that exercise banging around in there destratified tank 3 O 2 , so it stirred it all up good.

a17_0214455.speaker: Cernan
a17_0214455.text: Yeah, glad we brought him along then. We found some use for him.

a17_0214455.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0214455.text: Once an EECOM, always an EECOM. [Pause.] I have to cre - create my own G in order to run in place.

a17_0214455.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0214455.text: How high up did the heart rate get, Bob?

a17_0214455.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214455.text: We got you at 140, Jack. Were you running in place? is that...

a17_0214455.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0214455.text: 140 was - Yes, I was - I'm underneath the right-hand couch holding on to the main Y-Y strut with my hands and running against the LEB.

a17_0214455.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0214455.text: Roger. It worked real well. 140 and you were running in the mid-60's, so you picked up about - almost 70 beats there, no problem. Surgeon is very happy.

a17_0214455.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0214455.text: Roger. [Laughter.] Well, I'm happy too. You know, it took a while to find a technique I was - initially, I got up to 90 with just isometrics - pushing against the couch, and the running is obviously what it takes.

a17_0214455.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0214455.text: But I don't - Bob, I don't I really don't feel - I guess I lost you.

a17_0215138.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215138.text: Roger. We're with you. We had a little comm problem there as - you know, coning on this - as we were changing on the antenna - but we're with you.

a17_0215138.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215138.text: Okay. What's the heartrate right now?

a17_0215138.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215138.text: Right at - Stand by. [Pause.] We had a data dropout, Jack, that's why I'm holding up. And it just came on and we'll tell you in a second here. [Pause.] About 60, Jack. Right about 60 even.

a17_0215138.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215138.text: Okay. That's where I was when I started, so that's - you certainly recover fast. And I don't know whether that's faster than in one g or not.

a17_0215138.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215138.text: Well, we're happy with it - the Surgeon is happy with it, so it's good.

a17_0215138.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215138.text: Well, I just - How does that compare - do they have any data on how that compares with the recovery - say, the 5-minute recovery time on the ergometer?

a17_0215138.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215138.text: We can look it up, Jack, if you're interested. We do - we'll have to check your records, they don't have it right in front of us.

a17_0215138.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215138.text: Well, no big deal, just curious.

a17_0215550.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215550.text: Jack, just for your information - the Surgeon's pulled out the recovery rate data and it's the same with our data, which is a little rough here. It's the same for zero-g as your one-g ergometer data. [Long pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Bob, since we've got a few moments to talk - which I know we won't have later in the mission. Something I don't ever remember happening, but it's happening now in the windows. That's the 1, 3, and 5, but not 2 and 4, is that in the center of the window about 6 or 8 inches in diameter, as you come through the night side of the rotation, you pick up a very light - oh, you'd might call it even a frost. Very light frost on the window - more like a - a moisture frost, film of moisture, or film of frost - not very thick like crystals at all. As you come through the sunlight, it tends to sublime away

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger. We copy that.

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Bob, I don't know whether you were copying Honeysuckle's call to us, while you lost comm there for a while.

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger. We copy.

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: But they said that they had [hearing Overmyer] - Okay. [Pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: They kind of concurred with your...

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Okay...

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: ...weather report there, Jack.

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Oh, lucky guess. I might say that the sub - the zero phase point that we're looking at is right at the northeast coast of Australia, and it's much brighter. It's very - it's a very bright point now - oh, it's hard to say how far across. But, quite unlike what I mentioned being in the vicinity of the Samoan islands earlier. And it's right at the shore, and it could be just that the shore area has somewhat choppier seas. So maybe - maybe the brightness of that point is a function of sea state, although I don't know exactly what type of seas it would take to brighten it up. I suspect choppy seas

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: That front is - seems to have slowed down its progress. It's about in the same position, possibly slightly farther north than when I started talking about it this morning. The wave that has - seems to be developing off the - now off the southwest coast of New Zealand is much more pronounced than it was. Definitely seems to now have a slight cyclonic pattern - clockwise pattern. And I wouldn't be surprised if the next couple of days that moves along the front over towards Sydney. And maybe a little farther north than that might - Brisbane is probably more likely.

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger, Jack. [Pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Except I got the movement wrong again. Although it does seem to have progressed west from - from New Zealand. [Pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger.

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: I take back what I said about forecasting Sydney's weather. I think that'll - I would suspect that would move to the northeast like - now that I look - it seems like an earlier front, which is partly dissipated, had the same kind of motion, and now lies considerably north and east of the one I've been talking about.

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: Thinking back on some weather briefings we had last week, Bob - Are you there?

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: That's affirmative.

a17_0215946.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0215946.text: I'll talk to you later. I think you're - We're losing you for a little bit here.

a17_0215946.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0215946.text: Okay, Jack. We're reading you loud and clear right now. Oh, you're going out a little bit now.

a17_0221033.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0221033.text: You back with us, Bob?

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: That's affirmative. [Pause.]

a17_0221033.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0221033.text: Okay, I was going to try to recover there from that last few statements. As I recall, the weather briefings that we had at the Cape last week, that - talking with Ken Nabor and Jim Nicholson down there, that the patterns we were seeing from the satellite pictures in their forecast - or analysis anyway, charts in the New Zealand part of the Pacific, those waves formed along the front would move north and then curve east. And that appears to be the pattern that was visible in one of the older fronts. And I suspect if that pattern would hold with the wave that's developed off the co - right on th

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: Roger, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: Houston, how are you reading now?

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: Reading you loud and clear.

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: Okay, Bob. As I look at the clock, we're - just 24 hours ago we were about within our hold somewhere. For this period yesterday we were in our hold, and I think it goes without saying; but we'd sure like to pass on our debt of gratitude and thanks for the response that the people down at the Cape came up with. And particularly at Marshall. I think we all knew no one would be going anywhere unless everyone was satisfied that we were going all the way. And that's certainly the way we felt, but we do want to thank everybody who had a part in making that come true.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: Roger, Gene. I think it was a superb show between the Cape and Marshall and Houston and probably even Goddard, with the Network and just about everybody concerned, really, had to do some work there to bring it off. It went off real smoothly.

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: Yeah. After flying with Stafford a couple of times and having that happen a few times back, I thought maybe he was aboard.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: [Laughter.] Okay. [Pause.] I think that was a first for getting a Saturn V to 30 seconds before ignition and - or rather actually 30 seconds before lift-off and holding there.

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: It got mighty quiet onboard about 30 seconds.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: I sure imagine.

a17_0221033.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0221033.text: We all felt like old hands the second time around, though.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: Roger.

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: Bob, I've been at that 30-second count one other time and it's no different the second time around.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: Roger.

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: But we - we do appreciate the work, and I think it's typical of - of what made this manned space program such a super program. The response of people like that.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: We concur with that, Gene, wholeheartedly. [Long pause.]

a17_0221033.speaker: Cernan
a17_0221033.text: And with that in mind, tell everyone to stick around because there's a lot yet to be done.

a17_0221033.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0221033.text: You better believe it.

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: The old accumulator cycle again, I guess, gang.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. We're seeing it. [Pause.] Looks like you got a Master Alarm. is that affirm?

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: Yes, sir. That's how we tell these days. Although it doesn't happen all the time, and I guess as long as - Whenever we have that Waste Vent, Closed, we probably wouldn't be bothered by it at night.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. That's - that's our feelings here, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Say, Gene and Ron, I talked to your fraus on the phone here a little while ago, and they gave me a very interesting observation you might appreciate. They were standing close to some water when launch and they noticed that when the booster lit up, something scared all the fish because the water literally began to boil with fish jumping from the light, I guess, or from the shock wave or something. It was - made a very distinct impression because that's the first thing both of them told me about.

a17_0222020.speaker: Evans
a17_0222020.text: That's pretty neat.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: It's a neat way to go scare up the fish, I guess.

a17_0222020.speaker: Evans
a17_0222020.text: [Laughter.] Right [Long pause.].

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: How are they doing today, Bob?

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Really fine, really fine. They're just - like I said, they're just really tickled pink, and Barbara said that she wants you to know she's going into quarantine until after the weekend here, until after landing.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: If she goes into quarantine, it'll be a space first.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: You got to be careful about all this.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: Well, you know what to tell them...

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: Go ahead, Bob.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: You got to be careful now - The hotboxes are open - the hotlines are open at the houses there, so everything you say is being listened to. [Pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: Yeah; okay. In that case, just want to say hello and we're having a super good time looking forward to what's coming, and we thank you for the news, Robert.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: And my impression of the world, philosophically, I suppose you'll be getting from time to time, but it sure hasn't changed.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger, Gene.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: It's sure beautiful. It's sure beautiful and, looking back at it, there's several billion people who have got a lot to work for because it's one of the most beautiful sights we've ever seen here.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger, Gene. You guys are sounding great and doing real great. We're pressing right on here.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: I just want to emphasize, Bob, that these first 2 days - of course, yesterday was a pretty good day, but today we're catching up and - and, as I say, on the food consumption, don't be expecting too much.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: Acclimation and familiarity, and stowage, and preparation, and enjoyment and relaxation - are ready to call it a day today, which is probably the most ideal day in the Flight Plan to put it, because it's probably the only one we'll have.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger.

a17_0222020.speaker: Cernan
a17_0222020.text: Not that they aren't all going to be enjoyable.

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: Hey, Bob, your hourly weather report is due and - I'll wait awhile [laughter]. I keep losing your comm.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: Bob, you there?

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger, Jack. We're standing by.

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: Okay, I had a quick - quick look and just to bring you up to date, we're starting to be able to see the coast of Asia. The Philippines are wide open today. And the - that tropical storm Theresa that I mentioned I thought I could see - indeed, I'm sure that's what that little concentrated mass of clouds was north of New Guinea. And, I suspect, although I didn't get a good fix on it, that the folks in Guam may be in for some heavy weather. [Pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: Oh, and, Bob, I got another pair of pictures. And that would be up to 134.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. That's on November November, is that affirm?

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: That's affirm.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Real - Good show. [Pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0222020.text: And that was taken - the last pass, about 10 minutes ago, if you want to keep track of GET.

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Roger. Thanks, Jack; I'm doing that. [Long pause.]

a17_0222020.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0222020.text: Just for some information for Ron, in particular. We've evaluated the data from the mapping camera and the pan camera cycling there and it looks real good. Everything looks right normal.

a17_0222020.speaker: Evans
a17_0222020.text: Hey, that's outstanding. Good deal.

a17_0223447.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223447.text: That's the strangest sounding Bob I ever heard.

a17_0223447.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223447.text: Okay. Good. Nice to talk with you. Hey, I don't know whether you were around, Gene, the other day when I was talking about the circulation patterns around Antarctica. We were looking then at the Indian Ocean - actually, South Atlantic in the Indian Ocean region. And you see the same pattern at about the same latitude, say 60 degrees south, where all the linear cloud patterns which presumably are - reflect the various cold fronts have - are arcuate with their convex sides, or more actually, almost pointed sides are all lined up in a west-to-east direction around that latitude. It's quite a spec

a17_0223447.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223447.text: That would make four of those major convex fronts that I can see from this view crossing - south of Australia up into the South Pacific.

a17_0223447.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223447.text: On - on that tropical storm that was Theresa, I don't know whether they're still calling it now - that now, but I'm not sure, it may be a little south of Guam. Guam may not be in trouble with that one.

a17_0223447.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223447.text: It looks like it's just a bit to the west of Manila there - about 5 or 6 degrees, no more than that about. [Long pause.] Looks like it's about 5 degrees west of Manila and about 5 degrees south. And it is still called Theresa.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Okay, Gene, if you're still there, I don't like to argue with you but I think our analysis chart's a little more up to date.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: That center - that area that you just mentioned is very clear now - east of the Philippines. Did you say west or east of the Philippines?

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Okay, that area that you mentioned, 5 degrees east, is very clear and the center of the - what appears to be the storm that I'm speaking of, would be about 142 longitude and maybe 8 degrees north latitude.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Which would put it south of Guam.

a17_0223937.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223937.text: Okay, yeah, you're over in the area between Guam and the Carolines, then.

a17_0223937.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223937.text: You're over in the area between Guam and the Carolines, then. You're saying it would be just about due west of the Carolines, then. Okay.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Yeah, you're probably looking at a - oh, I don't know - maybe a what - a 12-hour old prog, or something?

a17_0223937.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223937.text: Yeah, that's the one I had for launch day.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Okay. Well, it's - it's - moved quite a bit now, and I guess it's the same storm; still - still seems to be very well organized but quite concentrated and small. [Pause.]

a17_0223937.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223937.text: Okay. I'll get a new prog in and compare your estimate there.

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Okay. I think that's pretty good - those - 142 and 8 degrees would be pretty good center of that storm. I've got some pretty good coor - I can see Mindanao, and I can see the - let's see - just a second - what is that on Australia? [Long pause.]

a17_0223937.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0223937.text: Yeah, of course, that is Port Moresby. I can see that point there, and between those two - I can pin that one down probably within a couple of degrees.

a17_0223937.speaker: Kranz
a17_0223937.text: Okay. We'll get a satellite photo and bring it in here in just a bit.

The conversation over the past few minutes has been between Flight Director Gene Kranz and Jack Schmitt. Apollo 17 at this time, almost directly above the northeast coast of Australia, some 94,000 nautical miles [174,000 km] from Earth.

a17_0225000.speaker: Evans
a17_0225000.text: Houston, canister number 4 is in Bravo now.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Houston, 17. [Long pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Go ahead, 17. [Pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Okay, Bob. That storm off the - just off the southwest coast of New Zealand is still intensifying and has both high and low level clouds as you can see by shadow lines. It looks like it may grow into pretty - pretty fair storm system. Borneo is very clear today; and, as is the Philippines. And I mentioned, there's a - looks like a very strong frontal system that stretches from, oh, let's say, the south coast of - or southeast coast of Vietnam up - up between and across Tai - between the Philippines and Taiwan and across Taiwan. And right along, and I can't tell, I think, just off - just south

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Roger.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Probably south - probably southeast. I hadn't noticed it before, but it's extremely concentrated northern hemisphere cycl - cyclone pattern. I don't know whether that's on your prog or not. That's not what's left of Sally, is it?

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Stand by. Let me look at the prog over here a sec. Okay. We - it doesn't show on the old one; the new one is coming in there shortly, Jack.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Okay. If that is a developing depression, it's approaching Luzon and not very far away - 2 or 3 degrees of longitude now, although Luzon is clear.

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: I can see Korea quite well, Bob. It's clear today.

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Yeah, we - we've got the fronts. The leading edge of the front on our prog was past Korea and on Japan, and you've got it moving quite a bit further east there.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Well, I'm not absolutely sure...

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Master Alarm on the accumulator.

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Roger. We copy.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: I can't make out Japan spe - specifically yet; but it's clearly past Korea, and, by - by inspection, it looks like it would be also past Japan by now, the trailing edge of the front. However, the circulation center on farther northeast may be affecting Hokkaido, as I said.

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Roger. Like I said, the front on the old prog for yesterday showed that front on the other side of Japan, so it's moved across pretty well.[Long pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: As I recall, they had a tropical storm called Sally that went into - [garble] a few days ago, and so I suspect this new one that seems - that I think I see between Borneo and Vietnam may be something else; a new depression or I may be - be fooled by it.[Long pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Mainland China, Bob, was the last pass here. I can't see the Ear - see the Earth now, but Mainland China looked like it was clear as far as I could see. There might be another front quite a ways inland, but that gets right at the LM, and I can't tell. But Korea, Yellow Sea, and the regions of China south of there - Shanghai, Nanking and those places are - look as if they are quite clear today. I'll check that again next time around.

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0225611.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0225611.text: And, Jack, we're ready to terminate the charge on Battery B and start the charge on Battery A.

a17_0225611.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0225611.text: Okay. That's in work.

a17_0230355.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230355.text: Houston, for your information, System Test 7A is about 0.6.

a17_0230355.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230355.text: Say that again, Jack. I missed that. 0.6 on system test 7A?

a17_0230355.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230355.text: Okay, Bob. Battery A is being charged now.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Bob, you got any of the LMies in there today?

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Any of the LMies? Rog. They're all sitting by. Just gave me a big thumbs up, Jack.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. Give them a thumbs up on the Rendezvous Radar antenna. It looks real good. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: I'm nose-to-nose with it practically here at about 2 feet, and it's extremely clean. And I see absolutely no sign of any - anything abnormal with it. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Matter of fact, compared to some of the flaking problems and things like that we've heard about in the past, I never saw a cleaner piece of hardware than that LM looks right now.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Appropriately, finally we're getting - we're starting to use it during the Christmas season. It sure looks like a Christmas package with all the orange tape on it.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Ron, we got your Noun - Noun 05.

a17_0230630.speaker: Evans
a17_0230630.text: Okay. I'll go ahead and accept that one this time. [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: We got the 9 degrees, Ron. You can torque. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Evans
a17_0230630.text: Okay. I'll torque at 940. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Okay. We got it. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: And, Jack, we've been looking at our records. We don't have a previous Systems Test reading for 7 Alpha. Do you recall any previous readings on that one? [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay, that looks like another accumulator cycle - got a Master Alarm. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: We dropped data just then, Jack, so we can't concur or confirm it. That is exactly the right time...

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: [Garble] all right. [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Bob, you cut out about your Systems Test meter discussion.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger, Jack. Do you have any previous 7 Alpha readings? We don't have any in our log here written. We're just wondering what the past readings on that was.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: No, I think that was the first one we would have been called to make after a battery charge, right?

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: That's affirm, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Go ahead, Jack. I - you're coming in very weak.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Well, I didn't intend to be transmitting. We were just discussing the battery vent and things. We may have missed something in the dump checklist. We'll check it out.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: No, sir. We don't think so. We just thought may you might have read it earlier.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Oh, yeah, you want the battery vent - it should be closed now, right?

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Stand by, Jack.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. Ron says it ought to be open.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: That - that's affirm...

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: [Garble] So let me check the checklist.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: ...it should be open. That - there's no question about that. It should be open.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. It's open.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Really, there's no problem, Jack. It should be open, but the value appears a bit low to us, and we'd like to read it again before you go to sleep. We may want to close it. [Pause.] And a nominal reading would be 1.7...

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. We - we closed it when we were doing all our dumping some time back and neglected to open it again. So, it was closed when I gave you the reading, and it has been closed during some 2 hours, anyway. I'll - you can figure out how long.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Okay. We - we copy that. [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Jack, would you mind opening the vent and watching the system meter concurrently with it? [Pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Stand by.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Well, it's - it's Closed now, and it's still reading what it - 0.6. Do you want us to open it again?

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Rog. Open the Vent and...

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: I mean, it's open now. I'm - I'm sorry, Bob. It is now open and reading 0.6. It read 0.6 when it was Closed.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Okay. Just leave it open now.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: And we will want to still check it prior to your sleep period.

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay, Bob, a little update on the coast of Asia. It looks like some residual cloudiness would be affecting the Pusan region of Korea. And, also, that's residual after the frontal passage. And it looks like maybe Shanghai, after all, may have some storms associated with it, but it's really hard to pick out exactly - the exact coast line of Asia, but I - there are some clouds in the Yellow Sea, behind the front, Look like they might be possibly some high cirrus is all.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Jack, do you still see that storm that you said was sitting between Guam and - Borneo in that area?

a17_0230630.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0230630.text: Okay. I see there is this cloud concentration between New Guinea and Guam. The more I look at it the less well developed it appears to me compared to some of the other circulation patterns. It could be just a residual depression from Theresa that has moved out into that area. It is an isolated, a relatively isolated cloud pattern, fairly small, but apparently fairly dense. But has - does not have a strong cyclonic pattern to it. Nothing at all like the pattern that now exists above Borneo and seems to be moving towards Luzon.

a17_0230630.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0230630.text: Roger. We copy.

a17_0232133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232133.text: Okay, Houston. We're moving in the pieces of a Presleep Checklist. Here's some onboard read-outs for you. Battery C is 37.0; Pyro Bat A, 37.2; Pyro Bat B, 37.2; RCS A, 95; Bravo, 94; Charlie, 94; Delta is 96. [Pause.]

a17_0232133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0232133.text: Roger. We copy that. And if you've started it, we don't want you to reinitialize the PTC until about 24:00 on the timeline.

a17_0232133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232133.text: Okay. We're - we're just getting a little ahead - we - took us longer last night on the presleep than we expected. We're trying to work it out again.

a17_0232133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0232133.text: Yeah. We don't to - we want to terminate the waste stowage vent at that time, because we think that that vent is what's contributing to our PTC coning.

a17_0232133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232133.text: Okay. We're - we're not - we're not really ready to go to sleep yet, but we're just moving ahead.

a17_0232133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232133.text: And if it's okay, I'll cycle the H 2 fans.

a17_0232416.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0232416.text: 023:24:36 - This is Apollo Control at 23 hours, 25 minutes. The crew has completed realigning the inertial measurement platform, the platform used as a stable reference. The spacecraft Guidance and Control system uses it as a reference in determining its own attitude. They've also been charging the two entry batteries that are used during peak electrical loads of lift-off, and then are recharged during the translunar coast when the fuel cells are producing a surplus of electrical energy. They've recharged one of those two batteries and are in the process of recharging the second one at this ti

This is Apollo Control at 23 hours, 25 minutes. The crew has completed realigning the inertial measurement platform, the platform used as a stable reference. The spacecraft Guidance and Control system uses it as a reference in determining its own attitude. They've also been charging the two entry batteries that are used during peak electrical loads of lift-off, and then are recharged during the translunar coast when the fuel cells are producing a surplus of electrical energy. They've recharged one of those two batteries and are in the process of recharging the second one at this time. And you

a17_0232827.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0232827.text: Say, Jack, we got a request in here from our ARIA friends. [Pause.]

a17_0232827.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0232827.text: They're just wondering if your looking out that way, if you could give them some sort of update of what the weather in the Wake island - Kwajalein - the south of the Wake area looks like.

a17_0232827.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232827.text: Okay. Let me work on that one.

a17_0232827.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0232827.text: Okay. You're going to mearn - earn your American Meteorological Society badge here pretty quick.

a17_0232827.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0232827.text: Okay. Let me get the monocular, and we'll look at Wake island. [Pause.] I miss having all those nice latitude and longitude lines on the globe.

a17_0232827.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0232827.text: 023:29:43 - The ARIA friends that CapCom, Robert Overmeyer, was refering to, are the crews of the Apollo Range Instrumented Aircraft, used in supplementing the Manned Space Flight Network coverage. They'll be leaving from Patrick Airforce Base prior to the end of the mission and flying into the Wake island area to be on station during Apollo 17's reentry and splashdown.

The ARIA friends that CapCom, Robert Overmeyer, was refering to, are the crews of the Apollo Range Instrumented Aircraft, used in supplementing the Manned Space Flight Network coverage. They'll be leaving from Patrick Airforce Base prior to the end of the mission and flying into the Wake island area to be on station during Apollo 17's reentry and splashdown.

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Okay, Bob. I'll probably have to work on this one a little more, but - but it looks like around Wake, or in the vicinity of the Kwajaleins and north to Wake, about all you have is a lot of cloudiness although - and in a generally - over a wide part of that Pacific, I'm talking about 15 or 20 degrees of longitude and latitude, there's a - roughly a clock - a clockwise circulation pattern. But the clouds do not look very dense or concentrated in any one area. And at leading off to the southeast from that general cloud mass, there're cyclonic - anticyclonic cloud mass is a - is one of the old fro

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Roger, Jack. I'm sure that the ARIA troops are listening down at Patrick and caught all that.

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Well, my guess is, Bob, and it's purely a guess, is that there - probably - if they were out there right now, would be experiencing an intermediate layer of clouds with scattered showers. And a not too strongly developed circulation system, so I can't predict the winds. But I wouldn't expect them to be anything - anything what might be down - associated with the remnants of the tropical depression Theresa. Now that Theresa - what's left of it, if I'm correct in - in picking it out there, probably is - is moving in that direction, although it looks weak enough that, right now I don't think it w

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Roger. The prog I got in my hand for 3-hour-old weather has Theresa located just about in the Manila area. Did you concur with that, or do you think it passed the - the Philippines?

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Well, I don't - Manila's clear. The only thing approaching near Manila is - is this other storm center that now is north of Borneo. And to the east of Manila, it's clear all the way over to this little cloud mass that I was guessing might be Theresa.

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Roger. All I say, this is 3 hours old so...

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: ...And that's about - I gave Gene Kranz some coordinates on it. You can look it up. Those were pretty good coordinates for that cloud mass. Now whether that's really Theresa or not, I don't know. [Pause.]

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: We got one thing with - for the last couple of hours here, we've been getting high-bit-rate data through our new facility - a new facility at Tidbinbilla, Tidbinbilla is through a 210 [-foot, 64-metre] dish, and they're covering the first...

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: ...between Wake in the Kwajaleins, Marshall islands, in that area, it doesn't look like a very concentrated weather pattern, although it looks like you'll have ceilings in that region. And they're overcast ceilings rather than broken. Except around the fringes of it.

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Roger.

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: We'll keep an eye on it of course. [Long pause.]

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Jack, how do you read us now?

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: You're loud and clear.

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Okay, 17, for the last 2 hours, we've been getting high-bit-rate data from a new facility, the facility at Tidbinbilla and they're working their first Apollo flight ever, you might give them a cheery hello. [Pause.]

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Tidbinbilla, is that correct?

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: That's affirmative. It's very close to the Honeysuckle base...

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Where is that?

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Very close to Honeysuckle.

a17_0233344.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0233344.text: Well, how you doing - how you doing mates? We certainly appreciate you guys being on the loop for this one.

That new 210-foot dish antenna at Tidbinbilla, which is near Honeysuckle Creek, which in turn is near Canberra, now online and accounting for our excellent signal strength from the spacecraft. Apollo 17 at this time is 96,958 nautical miles [179,566 km] from Earth. The speed is 5,233 feet per second [1,595 m/s].

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: 17, Houston. We'd like Accept, and we'll update your gyro drift, the pitch, roll, and yaw drifts. [Pause.]

a17_0233344.speaker: Cernan
a17_0233344.text: Okay, got Accept and P00.

a17_0233344.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0233344.text: Roger.

a17_0234512.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0234512.text: 17, Houston. The computer is yours. And you can go back to attitude and reinitialize PTC whenever you want to.

a17_0234512.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0234512.text: You can go to attitude and reinitialize PTC whenever you want to.

a17_0234512.speaker: Cernan
a17_0234512.text: Okay. Did you mean to leave the computer with Verb 21 Noun 01 up?

a17_0234512.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0234512.text: Roger. That's your computer with that - as you got it.

a17_0235009.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235009.text: Rog. We've got a recommended configuration for your H 2 fans and H 2 heaters. We would like the H 2 Heaters 1 and 2 to Auto and H 2 Fans 1 and 2, Off; 3 to Auto. Your O 2 heaters look good. [Long pause.]

a17_0235009.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0235009.text: Okay. Let me verify that I've got these right. H 2 Heaters 1, 2, Auto. O 2 Heaters, 1 Off; 2, Off; 3, Auto. H 2 Fans - H 2 Fans, you want Off; Off; and Auto. is that correct?

a17_0235009.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235009.text: That's what we wanted on the H 2 Fans. And the O 2 is fine, as you've got it.

a17_0235009.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0235009.text: Okay. They're Off, Off - Okay; H 2 Fans: Off, Off, and Auto.

a17_0235009.speaker: Cernan
a17_0235009.text: Okay, Bob. I just cleaned the suit circuit return valve screen, here. It was probably, as expected, a little crud on it. A few things have collected, but really not too bad.

a17_0235009.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0235009.text: Bob, a little more about Wake and the Marshalls and Kwajalein. That large pattern of what appear to be broken overcast clouds in a - a clockwise circulation pattern - crosses the equator region now that I've tried to project that through.

a17_0235725.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235725.text: Roger, Ron. When you stop the present roll on the PTC to reinitialize, pick a roll angle of 315 or 130 for stopping, so that we have good comm during the damping period.

a17_0235725.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235725.text: Roger. That'll give us good comm to watch the data on the damping.

a17_0235725.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0235725.text: 023:59:35 - This is Apollo Control, now 24 hours after lift-off and Apollo 17, 97,917 nautical miles [181,342 km] from Earth. The crew, at the present time, is stopping the Passive Thermal Control mode. They'll be reestablishing it. It had begun to diverge a little bit - begun to wobble about the axis, and the concern in going to sleep with that sort of situation is that it will wobble through the point at which they would have gimbal lock and of course we would wake them up before then but in order to avoid having to disturb the crew's sleep they'd like to get the Passive Thermal Control very

This is Apollo Control, now 24 hours after lift-off and Apollo 17, 97,917 nautical miles [181,342 km] from Earth. The crew, at the present time, is stopping the Passive Thermal Control mode. They'll be reestablishing it. It had begun to diverge a little bit - begun to wobble about the axis, and the concern in going to sleep with that sort of situation is that it will wobble through the point at which they would have gimbal lock and of course we would wake them up before then but in order to avoid having to disturb the crew's sleep they'd like to get the Passive Thermal Control very stable, so

a17_0235725.speaker: Cernan
a17_0235725.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read?

a17_0235725.speaker: Cernan
a17_0235725.text: Okay. We're at 300. Do you want us to go to 315 yet, or is 300 going to be okay?

a17_0235725.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235725.text: That's good enough, Gene. And we'd like you to close your waste vent at this time, please. [Pause.]

a17_0235725.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0235725.text: And, 17, Houston. We've got the same recommendation. We recommend Alpha and Bravo for damping; Bravo and Delta for spinup. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0235725.speaker: Cernan
a17_0235725.text: That was Alpha and Bravo for damping and Bravo and Delta for spinup.

a17_0240451.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0240451.text: If one of you want to break out the Flight Plan Supplement, we have a change to the E-Loads on page 143 due to the change of gyro-compensation parameters. If you want to copy them down when you get the Supplement out.

a17_0240451.speaker: Cernan
a17_0240451.text: Okay. We'll give you a call.

a17_0240451.speaker: Cernan
a17_0240451.text: Okay, Bob. We're in our - we're on our damping cycle now.

a17_0240816.text: This is Apollo Control. We're in the midst of turning over the shift now to Mission Control, to the team of Flight Director Pete Frank. Gene Kranz and his team will be going off shift in about 25 minutes. We do not plan to have a change of shift press briefing. The crew aboard Apollo 17, scheduled to begin an 8-hour sleep period in a little less than one hour at a Ground Elapsed Time of 25 hours. And we have no major activities in the Flight Plan before that time. At 24 hours, 9 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a17_0241213.speaker: Cernan
a17_0241213.text: Bob, I just hit the control stick. It's locked again in roll; it may have bumped it a little bit.

a17_0241715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0241715.text: Houston, 17. Okay if we close the waste stowage vent now? Oh, okay. I'm sorry. It's closed.

a17_0241715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0241715.text: Forget it. We got it, I - I was left out. [Long pause.]

a17_0241715.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0241715.text: Okay, Bob. On the film status, we're still where we were, November-November, 134. And I'll probably take two more pictures before we go to sleep.

a17_0241938.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0241938.text: And, 17, if one of you are down in the LEB, could you give us a read-out on Systems Test 7 Alpha?

a17_0242251.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0242251.text: Okay, Houston; 17. Are we configured properly now for comm? [Pause.]

a17_0242251.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0242251.text: Stand by, Gor - stand by, Jack.

a17_0242251.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0242251.text: Okay. I've got - I'm on Omni Bravo right now. [Pause.]

a17_0242251.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0242251.text: We're in good shape on the comm, and we'll be controlling the Omnis. [Long pause.]

a17_0242251.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0242251.text: 17, the rates look great. We're ready to initialize PTC. [Pause.]

a17_0242714.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0242714.text: Roger, Gene. We copy, and we watch the roll start.

a17_0243303.speaker: Cernan
a17_0243303.text: Hello, Houston. I think we've got everything done on the checklist. The chlorine has been - water has been chlorinated, we're in PTC, and I think Jack picked up everything else. How does it look to you?

a17_0243303.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0243303.text: Roger, Gene. Let's - let us make a check through the room here, and then just a reminder that I've got that addition on the E-Loads for the - in the Flight Plan Supplement. [Pause.]

a17_0243303.speaker: Cernan
a17_0243303.text: Yeah. Stand by. Jack's going to keep the headset on and the biomed, and he'll close you out with that, and if there's nothing else, I'm going to go off the air.

a17_0243303.speaker: Cernan
a17_0243303.text: Okay, say goodnight to my friends back there.

a17_0243303.speaker: Cernan
a17_0243303.text: Hey, just so that we know, it is about midnight, right?

a17_0243303.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0243303.text: It's about 7 minutes after midnight, Gene.

a17_0243303.speaker: Cernan
a17_0243303.text: Okay, just didn't want - wanted to make sure it wasn't noon.

a17_0243555.text: This is Apollo Control at 24 hours, 36 minutes. As Gene Cernan says goodnight, Apollo 17 is 99,714 nautical miles [184,670 km] from Earth; velocity, 5,114 feet per second [1,559 m/s]. The Lunar Module Pilot, Jack Schmitt, will be wearing the communications headset and the biomedical harness for the sleep period tonight.

a17_0243555.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0243555.text: Bob? This is Jack. Your last report for the day as the Earth goes past window 5. The first thing I noticed was that our zero phase point is not nearly as bright on the west coast of Australia as it is on the - was on the east. And it's looking right at the coastline now and see no bright spot in the center. Also, that circulation pattern or tropical depression possibly that I saw earlier north of Borneo is now even more strongly developed at the tail end of the front that stretches up toward Japan. And it - it really looks like a humdinger from here. Beautiful circulation pattern and very conc

a17_0243555.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0243555.text: And I'd be very - be very curious to know tomorrow morning if you - you people are carrying that one on their progs or on their analysis chart.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay, Bob. You want me to erase something on page 1-43 and insert something else?

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: That's affirmative, Jack. On 1-43 under column A, down at line 11 and 12 and 13. Just to make sure you're at the right spot, the line 11 old data is 00115. Do you copy that? Do you see that?

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: I'm with you.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Okay. Change that line to 00377. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Go ahead.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Change line 12 to 00050. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Go ahead.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: And line 13, 00523. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay, I got that and [laughter] as you might imagine, when I said erase, I did. And do you have the 04 and the 05 again, please? [Pause.] That is, if they're pertinent.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Stand by, Jack. I'm lost myself here a second.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: He gave me an update on 30704 and 31005, and I just erased it.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Okay, The 04 under column B is 34761, and the 05 line under column B is 15403. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay. Here we go. In line Alpha; 31411, 00377; 31512, 00050; 31613, 00523. In line Bravo, 30704 is 34761; 31005 is 15403. Over.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger. We copy, Jack. Just a reminder to be sure and configure the comm for the presleep checklist. And, just for your information, Jack, I - I hold you at 100,116 miles. I was going to give you a call at 100,000 even, and then I got talking to you. So you've crossed the 100,000 mark right now. Tomorrow, you're probably not going to be giving us our weather report, You'll be too far out, but we'll probably be starting to hear from the Moon, huh?

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: We're not going to see much of the Moon, you know. It's going to be pretty dark, so I'll have to keep looking at the Earth.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Pretty good - pretty interesting place. Very interesting place.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: I'm real sure.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: And I guess - I guess, maybe, I - 100,000 miles. My goodness gracious. That's impressive.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Yes, sir. You're slowing down all the way, Jack. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Well, it's sure downhill all - all the way back, isn't it?

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: That's for sure. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Jack, did the CMP get off the line, and is he sacked out now, too?

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Yeah, I lost both those guys. They - they decided they wanted to sleep, and I may be rumbling around here for a while but I took - we all three took Seconal, so I think we'll get to sleep before long.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger. Just give us a call if you need anything, and we'll be watching everything there, and pleasant dreams. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Now, you don't really mean that, do you?

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Well, I can't come up and tuck you in so - hope you have a good sleep. You need lots of rest up there, gang. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: I'll tell you, Bob, about halfway though this day, I think I acclimated. And I really feel good. I've been eating a lot better, and I'm not - the only thing I ever really felt was a slight headache. It really - not the fullness of the head that people described, I guess, but just a little headache. I could have been looking at the Earth too much. I don't know.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger, Jack. You've been sounding good.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Oh, actually, I feel - I've been feeling fine. Just - none of us have felt like eating. And that's probably normal, and everybody's eating more now, and we'll start getting to sleep, I think.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger. [Long pause.] Jack, just a reminder on that comm for the presleep checklist. It's important to us because we can get the - we can get high-bit-rate data more. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Bob, you cut out, but I'm in the comm sleep configuration now. I'm working that way.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Okay. Ed Fendell was shaking his head for a minute. Now he says as long as you're working that way. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Bob, you still cut out. Let's try it again.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: No - no problem, Jack, Just a reminder on the comm; that's all. We're watching you go through the checklist here.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay, I'm on High Gain now, and Omni Bravo selected. [Long Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: How do you read, Bob, on the High Gain?

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Read you loud and clear, Jack.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay. And it's in Reacq and Narrow.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Stand by. Stand by on that, Jack. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Say, Jack, can we refer you to the checklist on S/1-27, a sleep configuration there, where you S-Band Squelch, Enable, et cetera? [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Roger. I'm Enabled. [Pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Oh, et cetera. Yes.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Okay. I'll get to that in a minute, Bob. Who knows, I might have something else to say.

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Bob, I just probably ought to qualify all those remarks about the Earth's weather. It's purely a novice talking about something he is very unfamiliar with, except for having a longstanding interest in it. And I think the one philosophical point, if any, that comes out of it is that somebody, probably 3½ billion years ago or so, could have looked at the Earth and described patterns not too dissimilar. And it was within those patterns that life developed, and now you see, I think, and obvious to everybody, what that life has progressed to doing. And I certainly think all of us feel that i

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger, Jack. We concur.

a17_0244133.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0244133.text: Bob, you always wished that you had a poet onboard one of these missions, so he could describe things that we're seeing and looking at and feeling in terms that might - might transmit at least a part of that feeling to everybody in the world. Unfortunately, that's not the case. But he certainly couldn't look at that fragile blue globe and not think about the ancient sails of life that are crossing its paths and wonder ahead to the - up to the present, to the modern sails of life that are represented by the men that developed out of that life that are sitting there next to you and that are the

a17_0244133.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0244133.text: Roger, Jack. You're doing a pretty good job expressing them.

a17_0245825.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0245825.text: Roger, Jack. We'd like to go to select Omni Bravo, and stow the High Gain in the the normal stowage. It's customary we do not use the High Gain for PTC going TLC. [Long pause.]

a17_0245825.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0245825.text: Okay, Bob. I'm sorry, but the checklist indicated that you do. I'll go back to Omni Bravo.

a17_0245825.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0245825.text: Rog. It's probably ambiguous. If you end up going up on the checklist, up to the top of 1-28, it shows you where you want Omni Bravo. [Long pause.]

a17_0245825.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0245825.text: Ambiguous is the best word I can think of for it.

a17_0245825.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0245825.text: Ambiguous is the best word I can think of for it.

a17_0245825.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0245825.text: Rog. We - I concur. I should have probably called you earlier and just pointed out on the Flight Plan where it says presleep checklist. And then there's the word "comm," and it says "Omni," and that leads you into the checklist and makes sure you use the Omni setup for - for the sleep configuration.

a17_0245825.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0245825.text: Ho, ho, ho. Tricky fellows. I guess you're right.

a17_0245825.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0245825.text: Yeah, it's something we don't - we don't - sim PTCs, TLCs, and TECs very often. That's for sure. [Pause.]

a17_0245825.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0245825.text: Well, that's because we have a whole day to learn out here.

a17_0245825.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0245825.text: 025:01:16 - This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 1 minute into the mission. Apollo 17 is 100,953 nautical miles [186,965 km] from Earth. Velocity, 5,062 feet per second [1,543 m/s].
This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 1 minute into the mission. Apollo 17 is 100,953 nautical miles [186,965 km] from Earth. Velocity, 5,062 feet per second [1,543 m/s].

a17_0252240.text: This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 22 minutes. We haven't heard from Jack Schmitt recently, however, the Flight Surgeon reports that his data indicates he's not yet asleep. Apollo 17 now at 102,000 [nautical] miles [188,900 km] from Earth. Velocity, 5,018 feet per second [1,529 m/s]. We'll continue to leave this line up until we get an indication that the Lunar Module Pilot is asleep. The other 2 crewmen are asleep at this time. At 25 hours, 23 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a17_0252537.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0252537.text: Okay, Bob. I think I'll hit the hay. How does everything look to you? [Pause.]

a17_0252537.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0252537.text: Looking pretty good, Jack. We'd like the S-Band Normal Voice to Off, and S-Band Squelch Enable, please.

a17_0252537.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0252537.text: Yeah, I'll get that. I just want to make sure that PTC and everything looks good.

a17_0252537.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0252537.text: Okay, talk to you in the morning - or to somebody anyway.

a17_0252537.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0252537.text: Roger. Parker will wake you up - I think. Have a good sleep.

a17_0252537.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0252537.text: 025:26:52 - This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 27 minutes. Jack Schmitt has said 'goodnight'. We'll take the line down now and come back up with Mission Control reports hourly. Apollo 17 now 102,202 nautical miles [189,278 km] from Earth. Velocity, 5,010 feet per second [1,527 m/s].

This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 27 minutes. Jack Schmitt has said 'goodnight'. We'll take the line down now and come back up with Mission Control reports hourly. Apollo 17 now 102,202 nautical miles [189,278 km] from Earth. Velocity, 5,010 feet per second [1,527 m/s].

a17_0262701.text: This is Apollo Control at 26 hours, 27 minutes. The crew has completed the first hour and a half of an 8-hour rest period. Here in Mission Control, flight controllers are monitoring spacecraft's systems while the crew sleeps. All goes well with Apollo 17. Spacecraft is 105,060 nautical miles [194,571 km] from Earth. Its velocity is 4,893 feet per second [1,491 m/s]. This is Mission Control, Houston.

a17_0272711.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 27 minutes. 5½ hours remain in the crew's rest period. All spacecraft systems continue to operate normally. Apollo 17 is now 107,835 nautical miles [199,710 km] from Earth, velocity 4,784 feet per second [1,458 km].

a17_0282702.text: This is Apollo Control at 28 hours, 27 minutes. Everything continues to go well with Apollo 17. Astronaut Bob Parker has come on duty at the CapCom console now, and he will send a wakeup call to the crew in 4 hours and 32 minutes. Apollo 17 is 110,561 nautical miles [204,759 km] from Earth. Velocity, 4,679 feet per second [1,426 m/s].

a17_0292701.text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 27 minutes. Apollo 17 is 113,208 nautical miles [209,661 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed at 4,579 feet per second [1,396 m/s]. In 36 minutes, Apollo 17 will reach the half-way point to the Moon in terms of distance, at a Ground Elapsed Time of 30 hours, 3 minutes, no seconds. Apollo 17 will be 114,787 nautical miles [212,586 km] from both the Moon and the Earth. 3 hours, 32 minutes remaining in the crew's sleep period. At 29 hours, 27 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a17_0302702.text: This is Apollo Control at 30 hours, 27 minutes. 24 minutes ago, Apollo 17 did reach the half-way point in distance in its journey to the Moon. At that time, in the elapsed time of 30 hours, 3 minutes, it was 114,787 nautical miles [212,586 km] from both the Earth and the Moon. Its velocity at that time was 4,522 feet per second [1,378 m/s]. At this time, Apollo 17's distance is 115,842 nautical miles [214,539 km] from the Earth. Velocity is 4,483 feet per second [1,366 m/s]. Midcourse correction number 2 will be performed at an elapsed time of 35 hours, 30 minutes. That's 5 hours, 1 minute fro

a17_0311210.text: This is Apollo Control at 31 hours, 12 minutes. Apollo 17 is now 117,746 nautical miles [218,066 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 4,415 feet per second [1,346 m/s]. Flight Director Pete Frank and his Orange team of flight controllers will hand over Mission Control duties to Gerry Griffin's Gold team of flight controllers in about 15 minutes at 7 am Central Standard Time. Each of the departing controllers is now briefing his relief. There will be no change of shift news conference. The Orange team will double back after 1 shift, returning to the Control Center at 5 pm today to get back o

a17_0322707.text: This is Apollo Control at 32 hours, 27 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The mission of Apollo 17, which at this moment is 120,887 nautical miles [223,883 km] out from Earth. Velocity has continued to decrease to 4,305 feet per second [1,312 m/s]. Slightly over half hour remaining until spacecraft communicator Robert Parker gives the crew a wakeup call. And a relatively busy day ahead with the midcourse correction - midcourse correction maneuver number 2 at 35:30 Ground Elapsed Time, a 10½-foot-per-second posigrade maneuver which will raise the trajectory slightly from an impact trajectory w

a17_0325802.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0325802.text: Is that the best you could do?

a17_0325802.speaker: Parker
a17_0325802.text: That's not very good either. Give us a call when you want to talk to us.

a17_0325802.speaker: Parker
a17_0325802.text: You guys look absolutely super. No problem at all.

a17_0325802.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0325802.text: Nice way to wake up. Maybe we'll just sleep in for a few more hours.

a17_0325802.speaker: Parker
a17_0325802.text: Stand by. I'll check on that.

a17_0332109.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0332109.text: 17, this is Gordo. Bob just finished up his workday with that last call, and I'll be on now.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Houston, 17. How do you read?

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Loud and clear, Jack.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Good morning, Gordy. How you doing?

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Real good. How about you?

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: We all feel pretty good this morning. Got some reports for you.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Okay. Ready to copy.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Okay, on the CDR. PRD is 17025; 6½ hours good sleep. One Seconal, which is the one I reported last night, so that's just one now. Had a - yesterday, midday or so - he had a nausea pill for gas. And we hadn't found the other gas pill, so he tried that one. And he drank, since I last reported, two and a half containers of water.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Roger.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: The CDR food intake, as with all of us, is a little bit random, and I don't know exactly the best way to report it, unless you want it all in detail.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Let me check while you go on, and I'll see if they want a detailed description of the food or not. [Long pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Okay. LMP medical. PRD 24036; 5½ to 6 hours good sleep, 1 intermittent. Again, I had a Seconal but that's the same Seconal I mentioned last night. And since last report [pause] I guess one - 2½ containers of fluid. Water. [Pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Okay.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: And just for checking on the water intake, you should have me down for six containers of water.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Roger. Six total.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: That's affirm. [Pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: CMP medical. PRD is 15023; 7½ hours very good sleep. He had the same Seconal we had. And, since last report, has three water containers for a total of six now.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Jack, I guess we do want an accounting of all the food. Whatever you think is the best way to report it. [Long pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Okay, Gordy. Back on the CDR, and I'll just tell you what we ate. For the day 2. CDR: mixed fruit, that's the can, instant breakfast, one vitamin pill, a bag of tea, turkey and gravy, and the wet pack, and orange juice. [Long pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Okay, The LMP: cinnamon toast bread, mixed fruit, instant breakfast, coffee, lemonade, peach ambrosia, one vitamin, one slice of bread, grapefruit drink, gingerbread, orange drink. And I have one complaint: somebody slighted me on a caramel candy in meal C.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Rog. [Pause.] We'll start an investigation.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Yes, it was not there. Okay. CMP: the spiced oat cereal, mixed fruit, instant breakfast, and coffee, potato soup, and peach ambrosia. That's all for breakfast. And then later on, he had chocolate pudding and a grape drink. And let's see - we all - You might log him for a vitamin pill and me for a vitamin pill.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Okay.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: Oh, yes, I forgot. It's here; one frankfurter, for lunch.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: And we just changed LiOH canister as per the Flight Plan.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Okay.

a17_0333124.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0333124.text: And in a minute, I'll have weather report for you.

a17_0333124.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0333124.text: Very well.

a17_0334059.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334059.text: Gordy, the null bias check. Plus 0.9 in 100 seconds.

a17_0334059.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334059.text: Okay, one question G&C had. Do you do that null bias at a plus 100 or a minus 100 on the EMS counter?

a17_0334059.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334059.text: Okay, and it's increased up to 101.9, right?

a17_0334059.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334059.text: Roger. Miscopied you; 0.9. Okay; thank you.

a17_0334059.speaker: Evans
a17_0334059.text: Yeah, okay. Seems to me like last night it was 100.7.

a17_0334059.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334059.text: And for our part of the postsleep checklist, I have the consumables status, if you'd care to listen. [Long pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Gordy, [we'll] take your consumables in a second. Let me bring you up to date on the weather around the world, if you're interested.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Yes, we are; go ahead.

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Africa, looks in pretty good shape. There's a - except for an area probably around Zambia and Rhodesia in the tropical convergence zone there, where it looks pretty cloudy and probably quite rainy. There's a very strong circulation pattern and presumably a storm off - just off the coast of northwest Africa. Very spectacular spiral formation of clouds in a cyclone development. It looks like there are probably two fairly weak cyclones - southern hemisphere cyclones in the South Atlantic. One, southwest of Cape of Good Hope, and the other about due west of - of the Falkland Islands, maybe a littl

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: [Garble.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Okay, Jack. We got all that up to Argentina, then the Omni switch kind of cut you off. [Long pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Jack, we got the - at least the first part of your weather report fine up through the clouds in northern Argentina, and then the switch in Omnis cut you out.

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Okay, that was about it, Gordy. That's - I'll talk to you some more later about it. I guess the main thing I need now is your - are your consumables.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Okay. By the way, you were looking back from more than halfway to the Moon. You're about 125,000 [nautical miles, 230,000 km] out now. On the consumables, the RCS is running at 1.3 percent over the Flight Plan line. On the O 2 , tanks 2 and 3 are right on the lines, and tank 1 is about 4 percent below the line. But it's been there all the way since launch, that same bias on tank 1. On the hydrogen: tanks 1 and 3 are right on the lines, tank 2 is about 3 percent above the line. All in all, you're looking real good consumablewise. [Pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Okay. That's hardly worth writing down, I guess.

a17_0334517.speaker: Evans
a17_0334517.text: That's the way we like to see it.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Same here. [Pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Oh, the only other thing I have in the way of updates is a PIPA bias update. You can load it yourself, or we can load it when we come up with the uplink prior to the burn. Your choice. And then we'll have an update to the erasable load update and a supplement to correspond with that bias update.

a17_0334517.speaker: Cernan
a17_0334517.text: Gordy, why don't you go ahead and load it yourself when you send up the vector?

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Okay, and I'll give you that update for the supplement. It's on 1-43 whenever you're - whenever it's convenient. [Pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Cernan
a17_0334517.text: Okay, Jack's getting that out. I ran another PIPA bias at minus 100, and it confirmed the first one. It ended up at 99.2.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Go ahead with your update on 1-43, Gordy.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: Okay. It's in the load A of the octal ID of 03, which now reads 77252. Change that to 77655. [Long pause.]

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Did you copy, Gordy?

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: I didn't copy your readback; no.

a17_0334517.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0334517.text: Okay, 306 03 and Alpha 77655.

a17_0334517.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0334517.text: That's right.

a17_0340319.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0340319.text: Okay. For the reference on - on those menus, at least for the LMP, I think I'm probably putting 8 or 9 ounces of water in the citrus drinks and those kind of things, rather than 7, which has probably upped my water intake some.

a17_0340319.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0340319.text: And I think that probably goes for everybody. That probably goes for - it goes for Ron and probably Gene also.

a17_0341007.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0341007.text: 17, Houston. I have a little synopsis of the news here, if you'd like to listen during breakfast. Let me know.

a17_0341007.speaker: Evans
a17_0341007.text: Okay, mighty fine. Send it up.

a17_0341007.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0341007.text: Okay, front page first. In Paris, Henry Kissinger met for 30 minutes this morning with French President George Pompidou at the Elysee Palace just hours before his scheduled conference with North Vietnamese Politburo member Le Duc Tho - Tho, that is. North Vietnamese spokesmen accused Kissinger of attempting to force a peace settlement by threatening further escalation of the war. As both US and North Vietnamese negotiators expressed disappointment at the continued deadlock, Chief American delegate William J. Porter traveled to Brussels to brief Secretary of State William B. Rogers. Rogers will

a17_0342928.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0342928.text: Gordy, film update on mag November November. I'm on frame 138, and that includes a couple of pictures I mentioned to Bob I took just before I went to sleep. And also, two pictures this morning at about 33:30. Those are the Earth.

a17_0343520.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0343520.text: 17, Houston. A reminder. We need the H 2 Purge Line Heaters, On, now. And I do have a maneuver PAD for the midcourse when you're ready to copy. Over.

a17_0343520.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0343520.text: Okay. I've already got the Heater, On. And give me about 5 minutes, and I'll get the PAD.

a17_0343520.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0343520.text: Okay. And if you'll give us Accept and P00, we'll get the up-link started just after the next antenna switch. We want to catch it between switches. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0343520.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0343520.text: Okay. You got P00 and Accept.

a17_0344949.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0344949.text: Believe it or not, Gordy, I'm ready for your PAD.

a17_0344949.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0344949.text: Okay, Jack. It's a midcourse 2, SPS/G&N; the weight is 66786; plus 1.21, minus 0.13; ignition time is 035:29:59.09; minus 0003.4, plus 0002.1, minus 0009.8; attitude is 132, 194, 343; H A and H P are NA; Delta-V T 0010.6, burn time is 0:02, 0006.5; sextant star is 25, 233.7, 16.4; rest of the PAD is NA. Ullage, none. Other remarks; LM weight, 36281. High Gain angles: Pitch, minus 21; Yaw, 181. And this will give you a perilune of 53.1. Should make everybody onboard feel a little more comfortable. Over. [Pause.]

a17_0344949.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0344949.text: Okay, Gordy. We haven't felt particularly uncomfortable, but knowing no way we would hit the Moon. Here's MCC-2, 7 - SPS/G&N; 66786; plus 1.21, minus 0.13; 035:29:59.09; minus 0003.4, plus 0002.1 And you cut out on Delta-V Z . Give me that again, please.

a17_0344949.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0344949.text: Okay. Delta-V Z is a minus 0009.8. [Pause.]

a17_0344949.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0344949.text: Okay. Delta-V Z , minus 0009.8; 132, 194, 343; Noun 44 is NA; 0010.6, 0:02, 0006.5; 25, 233.7, 16.4; rest of PAD is NA. No ullage. LM weight, 36281. High Gain Pitch, minus 21; Yaw, 181. Perilune, 53.1.

a17_0344949.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0344949.text: Okay. That's a good readback. [Long pause.]

a17_0344949.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0344949.text: 17, Houston. You can go back to Block now. [Long pause.]

a17_0344949.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0344949.text: Jack, a couple of quick items. We'd like for you to terminate the Battery A charge now, and also turn the H 2 tank Heaters for tanks 1 and 2, Off. [Pause.]

a17_0344949.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0344949.text: Okay. H 2 tank Heaters 1 and 2 are Off, and I'll terminate the charge.

a17_0345816.text: This is Apollo Control; 34 hours, 58 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 17 spacecraft should, at this time, be coming out of the Passive Thermal Control mode and getting into the proper attitude for the midcourse correction burn number 2, which is some 31 minutes and 23 seconds from now. Apollo 17 presently 126,988 [nautical] miles [235,182 km] from the Earth, traveling at velocity of 4,098 feet per second [1,249 m/s]. The midcourse correction burn number 2, with an ignition time 35:29:59.1, has a velocity change in the posigrade direction of 10.6 feet per second [3.2 m/s], which for the Serv

a17_0350254.speaker: Cernan
a17_0350254.text: Okay, Gordo, there's all balls and 05 on that P52. [Pause.]

a17_0350254.speaker: Cernan
a17_0350254.text: And you're looking at Noun 93. Okay, you're looking at Noun 93. [Long pause.]

a17_0350254.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0350254.text: Okay, and we Go to torque it. [Long pause.]

a17_0350254.speaker: Evans
a17_0350254.text: Houston, Apollo 17. When we ran the Delta-V test, we - we're reading minus 22.2 and I'm having a little trouble finding the SPS cue card. Wonder if FAO know exactly - knows exactly where that is?

a17_0350709.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0350709.text: Houston, if you saw a Master Alarm, it was the Power SCE Normal switch getting hooked to Off. [Pause.]

a17_0350709.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0350709.text: As far as we know, the SPS burn card ought to be in with the rest of the cards in R-2.

a17_0350709.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0350709.text: Gordy, we finally found that thing. It was way back in the back; sorry.

a17_0351451.speaker: Evans
a17_0351451.text: Okay, Houston, We'll get to the attitude in about another 4 minutes or so. Then we'll whip in the P30 and go right into P40. We're doing a waste water dump, urine dump, and - man, the sky is just full of little bitty particles.

a17_0351451.speaker: Evans
a17_0351451.text: Hey, I doubt if we can get the star sextant check, but you can try it.

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
a17_0351847.text: Just the burn time's good. [Long pause.]

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
a17_0351847.text: Okay. We'll see if we can get the DET started here. [Long pause.]

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
a17_0351847.text: Okay; got the DET started.

a17_0351847.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0351847.text: Jack, you can bring up the High Gain any time now.

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
a17_0351847.text: In 10 minutes, Jack so we're in good shape. Okay, got the DET. [Garble.]

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
a17_0351847.text: Yeah, he's dumping waste water. It's about 15. [Pause.] Yeah. Yeah, straight up to Relief, Jack.

a17_0351847.speaker: Fullerton
a17_0351847.text: And, Jack, also we're showing 10 percent on waste water, now.

a17_0351847.speaker: Evans
