a17_0972125.text: This is Apollo control at 97 hours, 21 minutes. We're 50 seconds away from the time Apollo 17 should be within communications range on it's fifth revolution of the Moon. We'll stand by for first contact.

a17_0972125.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972125.text: Roger. We're just about ready to finish up here. I have a couple of questions. Do you want us to cycle the cryo fans or just leave them alone now? [Pause.]

a17_0972125.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0972125.text: We'd like them just left alone, left in your configuration you are now, Jack.

a17_0972125.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972125.text: Okay, there will be no cycling then.

a17_0972125.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0972125.text: Roger. We have one question. Who's got the duty tonight or will he be wearing a headset? [Pause.]

a17_0972125.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972125.text: Yeah, he - Ron has the duty. He will be wearing a headset, but I will be on the biomed underneath.

a17_0972125.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0972125.text: Understand that. And one note for Gene. It's an addition to that Flight Surgeon's note. When you rehydrate your food, make sure that you go the - let it rehydrate for the maximum amount of time. I know you miss it on this one, but the next - like tomorrow morning, make sure it rehydrates the maximum amount of time.

a17_0972125.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972125.text: And we got the star crater stereo trio.

a17_0972125.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972125.text: And that - we're - mag - Oscar Oscar is on 93 now. The last three pictures were that trio.

a17_0972125.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0972125.text: 097:28:20 - This is Apollo control at 97 hours, 28 minutes. We're showing...

a17_0972820.text: This is Apollo control at 97 hours, 28 minutes. We're showing...

a17_0972820.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972820.text: Bob, we're essentially complete on the presleep checklist. And except for computing communications configuration and Ron will take care of that.

a17_0972820.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972820.text: And, Bob, while we're gradually getting in configuration here, let me reiterate something that I've been watching this rev as we did a lot of other things. And that was this relationship of the light-colored or light gray swirl patterns on the surface to patterns - associated pattern - parallel patterns that are darker than the average of the surrounding area. And this is true both in Mare Marginis and in most cases on the back side. [Pause.]

a17_0972820.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0972820.text: Roger, Jack. We'll get that to the PI.

a17_0972820.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972820.text: Roughly, although they're very irregular patterns - roughly it's concentric zoning of dark to light within a intermediate albedo surface. Now there are variations on that theme; sometimes you don't get the symmetry quite as good, but it's common enough that I think it's worth noting.

a17_0972820.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972820.text: Also, there's a sequence of different kinds of crater filling on the far side, and I think that, as the orbital stay progresses, we may be able to pin down the relative age relationships and the characteristics of those crater fill - filling episodes. Whether they are single episodes that happen in a variety of crater or they're a function of the age and characteristics of the craters in which you find them is not clear right now, but the - they seem to form fairly distinct groupings of crater-fill material.

a17_0972820.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0972820.text: One of those crater-fill materials that you also see in other kinds of depressions other than craters is a very smooth, light, plains-forming material. And it is, although cratered, when you see it at the terminator, it is smoother than the mare; that is, it does not seem to have the swell, the sea swell characteristics or ridges or any other features other than the crater's superimposed on it.

a17_0972820.speaker: Mission Control
a17_0972820.text: 097:33:12 - Apollo 17's orbit now 59.2 by 13.7 nautical miles [109.6 by 25.4 km]. The present altitude, 17.8 nautical miles [33.0 km].
Apollo 17's orbit now 59.2 by 13.7 nautical miles [109.6 by 25.4 km]. The present altitude, 17.8 nautical miles [33.0 km].

a17_0973520.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0973520.text: 17, Houston. You can go ahead and close the UV cover. We'd like to hold off 1 minute before you turn the UV off. We want to look at 1 minute of data with the cover closed. [Long pause.]

a17_0973520.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0973520.text: Oh, okay. Roger. A walk-on. I see it now. [Long pause.]

a17_0973520.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0973520.text: Okay, We'll give you a cue when you go UV, Off, and INCO would like to know what you've got on your High Gain pitch and yaw knobs. Not the dials but the knobs. [Pause.]

a17_0973520.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0973520.text: All right. The knobs are - about plus 20 and 185.

a17_0973520.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0973520.text: A Pitch of plus 20 and 185 on the Yaw. [Pause.]

a17_0973520.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0973520.text: And, Jack, you can turn the UV off now. [Long pause.]

a17_0974154.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974154.text: Okay, I got the landing site. We're right over the top of it, and the scarp is fantastically detailed at this - Can you see in there, Gene? Right down, right down, straight down there.

a17_0974154.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974154.text: Okay, well, the sli - the light mantle is ob - very obviously mantling the area. The scarp was very detailed, and, so far, could not see any structure in the massifs at all, but I haven't had any - didn't have much time to watch it on that pass. [Pause.]

a17_0974154.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974154.text: The slide very definitely subdued the general detail in the plains area - or the light mantle, if you will, rather than slide. [Pause.] MOCR Crater was finally out of the dark.

a17_0974154.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974154.text: Jack, we'd like to know if you think you can adjust the High Gain as close to plus 15 and Yaw 190 as possible? [Long pause.]

a17_0974154.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974154.text: Okay, Bob, that's adjusted plus 15 and 190, and I suspect I was a little closer to 15 than 20 when I called you before.

a17_0974154.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974154.text: I'll tell you, from this altitude and with that low Sun, there's no question of the sharpness of the topographic features in the landing area. The - the scarp, and even some of the apparent back - pardon - backflow features - and Parker will know what I'm talking about - that is apparent flows to the west in the light mantle area were extremely sharp, even those fronts going west were sharp. It looked even more like a mare ridge than it ever did before.

a17_0974602.speaker: Cernan
a17_0974602.text: Okay, Bob, this is Gene. I had a - just a quick view of the site, and if we're anywhere near it, we'll recognize it, I think, without question. And, I think with that, we'll bid farewell and good night.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: Okay, gang. And looking for a busy day tomorrow - -

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: Never fear. Your old CM...

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: Go ahead; I cut you out.

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: I say never fear, your CMP is watching.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: Roger. And, just a reminder S-Band...

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: He's got the watch tonight.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: ...Normal Voice to Off tonight, please? [Pause.]

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: Okay, okay, as soon as I get bedded down, I'll do that.

a17_0974602.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974602.text: Don't worry, he's got a batch of guys up here reminding him of that one.

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: And I've checked out the little whistle, and it works like a charm.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: Roger. I was betting on...

a17_0974602.speaker: Evans
a17_0974602.text: Just to make sure, I'm going to check it again.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: ...you guys to get that switch last night, and I lost my bet. [Pause.]

a17_0974602.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974602.text: And, Robert, good night to all.

a17_0974602.speaker: Overmyer
a17_0974602.text: Good night up there.

a17_0974602.speaker: Schmitt
a17_0974602.text: And that is a test. This is a test, test, test.

a17_0974602.speaker: Cernan
a17_0974602.text: Good night, babe.

Shortly before losing radio contact, Gene Kranz checked with each of his flight controllers, got a report that everything was in order, no problems as Apollo 17 went behind the Moon.

We're about 5 minutes away now from putting in a call to the crew, getting them up for breakfast, and ready to start a day that will culminate with landing on the lunar surface and the first EVA at the Taurus Mountain site, Taurus-Littrow, near the Sea of Serenity. CapCom Joe Allen, will be putting in a call to the crew in about 4½ minutes from now. We'll stand by for that wakeup call to the crew of Apollo 17. a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: (Music) "Good Morning America, How Are You"

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Good morning, America. How are you? [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: This is America. That's a good way to wake up.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Good morning, America. How are you? you'll be gone a million miles before the mission's done.

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: [Laughter] Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: Houston, America. Are you reading okay now?

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: You're loud and clear, Ron. How are we?

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: Okay; mighty fine, Joe. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Let's hear it again, Joe. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Are you serious?

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Well, I just got on a headset. You never had a chance to...

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Stand by. Here it comes.

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: ...wake me up before. [Laughter] [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: It's coming at you, America. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: (Music: City of New Orleans by John Denver)

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: How about that?

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Thank you, Joe. That's great. We're moving on.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Don't you know?

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: And a big eight-wheeler. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: And, America, you're 10 minutes from LOS, and the spacecraft looks great. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Okay, Joe. That's good to hear. And we're starting to move now, and we'll be ready for you when we come around.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: All righty. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: How long are you with us this morning?

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Oh, not too many more minutes. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Hope we didn't keep you up last night.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: The pleasure was ours, Jack. [Pause.] We devoted our 8 hours to selecting your wakeup call this morning and got a little help from the news room pool on that suggestion.

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Well, that was a good suggestion. I had forgotten all about that song. That's a good one. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: You ought to find the 'Golden Rockets' for us some morning.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: You'll wish you hadn't asked. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: 17, this is Houston. You'll be pleased to hear that the IR in the SIM bay is returning some beautiful data to us here.

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: Hey; great, Joe. That's good to hear, by gosh.

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: What are you learning, Joe?

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Hotspots on the Moon, Jack. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Well, we know we had one going around it. We didn't know we had any on it. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Evans
a17_1054500.text: Houston, the LM/CM Delta-P is 0.4.

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Copy that. [Pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Where - where's your big anomalies, Joe? Can you summarize quickly?

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Jack, we'll get - get that for you next pass.

a17_1054500.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1054500.text: Well, don't worry about it. I think we're going to have a lot of things on our mind the next pass. But we're just passing over Orientale again, Joe, and in Earthlight, it's probably one of the most spectacular sights in nature. [Long pause.]

a17_1054500.speaker: Allen
a17_1054500.text: Copy that, Jack. And I can imagine.

a17_1060039.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1060039.text: Joe, can you imagine waking up anywhere else? [Long pause.]

a17_1060039.speaker: Allen
a17_1060039.text: 17, we'll think about that 'til you go LOS. [Pause.]

a17_1060039.speaker: Allen
a17_1060039.text: 17, about 30 seconds to LOS. We'll see you on the other side. It's going to be a good day.

a17_1060039.speaker: Cernan
a17_1060039.text: No, unfortunately. It doesn't mean we can't have any, though.

a17_1065046.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1065046.text: Okay, Houston. We're with you and we're in the process of getting the tunnel pressurized and moving right towards probe and drogue removal.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Okay, Jack. Good morning.

a17_1065046.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1065046.text: Good morning, Gordy. Welcome aboard.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a17_1065046.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1065046.text: I take it you're going to pick up the - the reports - post-sleep reports later. Is that correct? From Ron?

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Any way it's convenient to you.

a17_1065046.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1065046.text: Well, we're moving towards getting the suits on. Unless you want me to take 5 minutes here, we'll leave it alone and let Ron give it to you.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: That'll be fine.

a17_1065046.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1065046.text: Everybody ate and drank and slept just about like last night.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1065046.speaker: Cernan
a17_1065046.text: Good morning, Gordy.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Good morning, Commander.

a17_1065046.speaker: Cernan
a17_1065046.text: Tell Joe I'm sorry I didn't get a chance to say hello to him, but I did hear his presence being evident.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Okay. We'll pass it along. [Long pause.]

a17_1065046.speaker: Evans
a17_1065046.text: Houston, America. The tunnel hatch is out.

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Okeydoke, Ron. [Long pause.]

a17_1065046.speaker: Cernan
a17_1065046.text: Gordy, how does America look to you this morning?

a17_1065046.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1065046.text: Beautiful, as it has all the way to date. [Pause.]

a17_1065046.speaker: Cernan
a17_1065046.text: Okay.

a17_1070040.speaker: Evans
a17_1070040.text: Okay, Houston; America. The old probe is underneath the couch.

a17_1070348.speaker: Evans
a17_1070348.text: Okay. How are Jack's EKGs and stuff. He's going to tape them now.

a17_1070348.speaker: Evans
a17_1070348.text: [Chuckle] Wait a minute, he's not plugged in. But, you know, he's had them on all night. Were they good?

a17_1070348.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1070348.text: Yes, when he was plugged in we had good signals.

a17_1070804.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1070804.text: America, Houston. If someone's near the telemetry switch, if you go to Accept, we'll give you a state vector. [Pause.]

a17_1070804.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1070804.text: Okay. And as we're supposed to update your trajectory, which is looking good - predicted perilune at PDI without DOI-2 would be 11.9 [nautical miles], a little lower. So that means that DOI-2 will be a little less, in terms of Delta-V, than nominal. But, otherwise, looking good.

a17_1070804.speaker: Evans
a17_1070804.text: Okay. Did you say 11.2 for perigee, now - without DOI-2?

a17_1070804.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1070804.text: I might have said that. It's 11.9 predicted at PDI time without DOI-2.

a17_1070804.speaker: Evans
a17_1070804.text: Oh okay, 11.9 predicted without - at PDI time without DOI-2.

a17_1070804.speaker: Evans
a17_1070804.text: Okay, so DOI-2 will be a little less than predicted.

a17_1070804.speaker: Evans
a17_1070804.text: I'm repeating it to these guys that are getting suited here, see.

a17_1070804.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1070804.text: Okay. I have your vector now. You can go back to Block.

a17_1071311.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071311.text: America, Houston. You owe us a reverification of the docking tunnel index angle. [Pause.]

a17_1071311.speaker: Evans
a17_1071311.text: Well, I kept [garble] thinking it might move back to zero, but it hasn't moved - plus 1.2.

a17_1071311.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071311.text: Okay; plus 1.2. For your information, Ron, on consumables this morning, we're running 6 percent above the Flight Plan line on RCS. On the hydrogen, we're about 8 percent above the line on Tank 2; right on the lines on the other two hydrogen tanks. And on the O 2 , we're running our standard 4 to 5 percent below the line on oxygen Tank 1; Tank 2 is right on; and Tank 3 has now gained to about 3 percent above the line. All looking good.

a17_1071311.speaker: Evans
a17_1071311.text: Okay, Houston. Hey, that's mighty fine.

a17_1071950.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1071950.text: Houston, America.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Go ahead.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay, I'll give you the Commander's food from yesterday.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: All right. Ready to copy. [Pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Four bacon squares, cornflakes, orange beverage, two sips of coffee, a vitamin. Okay, Meal B: chicken and rice soup, meatballs and sauce, orange PA drink, and caramel stick - one caramel stick. Okay, Meal C: potato soup, beef and gravy, citrus beverage, a chocolate bar, a package of pecans. [Pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay. We're with you so far. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay; Commander's medical log: PRD 17036, 6½ hours of good sleep, one Seconal last night, three bags of fluid.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Roger.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Three bags of water, let's - I better put it that way, I guess. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. Here we go on the LMPs food.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay; two bacon squares, scrambled eggs, two apricots, cocoa, and a coffee. Meal B: fruitcake, cit - citrus beverage, hamburger, and a coffee. Meal C: lemonade, beef and gravy, ambrosia, cereal bar, and tea. [Pause.] I guess that's it.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Hey, Houston. Why don't I give you LMPs menu this morning too - day 5?

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Then I won't have to get back in their pages. Okay. It's a sausage patty for the LMP - sausage patties, cinnamon-toasted bread, instant breakfast, coffee with K, and a grape drink, and a vitamin. [Pause.] Okay, for the Commander on day 5: spiced oat cereal, sausage patties, instant breakfast, and vitamins.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay; for the LMPs medical log: PRD 24108, 7¼ hours very good, one Seconal last night, 3½ cans of water.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay. We're ready to go on Command Module Pilot of the spaceship America and his [garble] menu.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Go ahead, captain.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay, bacon squares, scrambled eggs, cornflakes, orange juice, [pause.] two coffee, three caramel candies - that's three sticks of caramel candy. Meal B: chicken and rice, meatballs, butterscotch pudding, orange PA drink. I missed the vitamins up there in A, too. Okay, Meal C: potato soup, beef and gravy, chicken stew, orange GF drink, tea, chocolate bar, and a package of pecans. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay; CMP medical log: PRD 15034, and about 5½ of good sleep; a little trouble getting to sleep last night, and I woke up early this morning. I took a Seconal; didn't seem to have much good - much effect, and I had four cans of water.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: I think I was on the biomed all the time last night, too, so you can check out that sleep.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay, Ron, While you've got that book with you, I can give you a one-line change to the E-memory load as a result of our changing the short-burn constant.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. Stand by 1 here.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay, Houston; America. I've got the right page now.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay. It's page 1-43. It's load Delta. Identifier number 5; the old value is 01606. Change that to 01637. [Pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. It'll be load Delta, and the octal identifier 05, and its new value is 01637.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: That's correct. [Long pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. The LMP has got his suit on. They're connecting up the LCG water connection, and he's still unzipped.

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: Okay, Ron. In the Flight Plan, you're coming up on a Verb 45 and then going to P00 prior to the P52. After going to P00, we'd like you to change to B/D Roll from A/C. Over.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. We'll change the B/D Roll. Looks like we're going to run into a problem on our P52 down here, with these guys getting suited. Is it really necessary now? [Pause.]

a17_1071950.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1071950.text: There's no time criticality on that. When they're out of the way, go ahead with it.

a17_1071950.speaker: Evans
a17_1071950.text: Okay. Good.

a17_1074244.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074244.text: Okay, Houston, how do you read the LMP?

a17_1074244.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074244.text: Okay, Gordy, I'm opening the hatch.

a17_1074244.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074244.text: Okay, Gordy. Index 1 plus - or plus 1.2.

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Okay, Houston, I'm going to skip the P52 here for a while and maneuver to the docking attitude - undock attitude, that is.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Roger. [Pause.] Stand by on that one, Ron. [Pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Wilco.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: We want to be sure we can get some stars - good stars in the undock attitude. [Long pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Ron, this is Houston. We didn't see you do a Verb 45. Over. [Pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: You're right. Good one.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: And if there's any - if you - if there's no reason why not, we'd just as soon you go ahead and do the P52 now. Finish that off and then start the maneuver. Over.

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Okay. The big reason is that Gene's getting into his suit right now.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Okay.

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: As soon as he gets out and gets in his suit, well, I'll do a P52 maneuver.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Ron, Houston. Can you give us Auto on the High Gain? [Pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Okay. Just a second, Houston. [Long pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074549.text: We're transferring to LM Power, Houston.

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Okay; Off, Reset, back to Off.

a17_1074549.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074549.text: Okay. We have LM Power.

a17_1074549.speaker: Evans
a17_1074549.text: Okay. That was 107:49:28.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074549.text: LM Water's Open, and O 2 's Open.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_1074549.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1074549.text: Okay; 3-4, Houston, in the LM. And step 1 is good.

a17_1074549.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1074549.text: Okay.

a17_1075231.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1075231.text: And I'm going off of CSM comm, and I'll be coming at you before long on - on S-Band, if I can.

a17_1075615.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1075615.text: Ron, Houston. We've taken a look at stars available in the undock attitude, and they don't look too good. We suggest you use the present attitude for your 52 and then maneuver. Over.

a17_1075615.speaker: Evans
a17_1075615.text: Okay. I'm just about to get Gene out of the way here, and then I will.

a17_1075615.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1075615.text: Okay, and we're less than 3 minutes to LOS now. So when you finish that 52, we'd like you to copy down the Noun 5 and 93s for us.

a17_1075823.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1075823.text: America, Houston. About 1 minute to LOS. Nothing further for you. We'll see you on the other side. [Pause.]

a17_1075823.speaker: Evans
a17_1075823.text: Okay, Gordo. We're hustling like hell. We might make it. [Laughter]

a17_1075823.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1075823.text: 107:59:32 - This is Apollo Control, 107:59 Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. We've had Loss of Signal at this time as Apollo 17 coasted behind the Moon on the tenth lunar orbit. Approximately 47 minutes until the spacecraft both come around the far side as the crew prepares to transfer into the Lunar Module; that is, Cernan and Schmitt prepare to transfer into the Lunar Module. Get it powered up in preparation for today's activities of the Descent Orbit Insertion maneuver number 2 and ultimately the landing at Taurus-Littrow and the first extravehicular activity. As they come

a17_10850xxcsm.speaker: Evans
a17_10850xxcsm.text: Okay. We're finally going to maneuver to the attitude.

a17_1084456.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1084456.text: There we go. Should have done that in the first place. [Long pause.]

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1084757csm.text: Challenger, this is Houston. How do you read?

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1084757csm.text: Hello, Gordy, this is Challenger, we're reading you loud and clear.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay. You're readable. Lots of background noise at the moment. [Pause.]

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay. We'll update you in just a minute.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay. Another one is verify locked. The band was up. So you're locked here; the red thing is in.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay, and I got it over here.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1084757csm.text: Let me give them an E-memory dump. I can press on. Gordy, Jack'll update you in just a second. And I've got some words for you, but I'd like to give you an E-memory dump as soon as you get the steerable.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1084757csm.text: Hey, Houston; America. Man, you wouldn't believe it. I finally got my suit on.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay, Gordy. How do you read the LMP? This is your S-Band T/R in secondary power amp check.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay, LMP. You're clear. Lots of background noise though.

a17_1084757csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1084757csm.text: Okay. I'm going to bring up the steerable.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Hello, Houston. I'm ready to give you an E-memory dump.

a17_1085510.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1085510.text: Okay. We're ready to take it. Go ahead.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Ron, how do you - Ron, how do you read on Simplex Bravo?

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: I do not read you. Coming at you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I don't read you at all, Jack.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Hey, Ron, I do not read you. Check your VHF switch.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I'm down to Simplex Bravo. [Pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Yeah; go ahead.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: I'm talking on B now. How do you read?

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: I do not read you. Do you read me?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: No, I don't read you at all either, Jack.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: No, I don't read you. [Long pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: No, I don't read you!

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I've got everything on in my Auto panel. Let me try the other one for backup. [Long pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Yep, I'm on Left. I'm on Left? Let me go to Backup.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I've got you; I got you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: I don't have you, yet.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. How do you read on VHF Bravo? You're loud and clear.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Hey, I finally got you!

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: That was my fault, Ron.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. You were kind of clipping there for a little bit. I got the last part of your transmission.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. It was just warming up. You're loud and clear now.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I heard that it was just - I missed the just - It was just warming up, but I got the loud and clear.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Houston. I've got a couple I want to pass on to you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1085510.text: Go ahead, Gene. [Pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay. When I first put in the...

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Ron, how do you read now?

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: ...LGC breaker...

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I read you loud and clear; that's VHF B.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Stand by, Houston.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Am I clipping now, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Yeah, I didn't hear you at all that time.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Am I clipping now?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Yeah, you're still clipping. All I got was "now."

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. How do you read now?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. "How do you read now?" I got that.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I guess we're okay. It was the squelch.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: [Laughter] Then I missed that part of it. [Pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: [Laughter] Then I missed that part of it.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Ron, how do you hear, Gene?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. Loud and clear, Gene.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay; very good.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: How do you read the LMP now, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Now, you're still clipping, Jack. Can you move your mike a little bit closer or something?

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. How do you read now?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: No, I didn't read you at all that time.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: How do you read now?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Not clear.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I've got the Squelch to full decrease.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Well, you're going to have to yell or something. I still - you're still clipping yourself out, Jack.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. Do you read Gene, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: No, I didn't read you that time.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay. We're going to press on and get these VHF checks Go. We can cut them.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. Okay; switching to Alpha.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Bravo is off; Simplex Alpha is on. [Pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Bravo is Off; Simplex Alpha is On.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Ron. How do you read on Alpha?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Don't read you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: How do you read on Alpha, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Don't read you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: How do you read the LMP on Alpha, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I don't read you guys at all, except through the tunnel. [Pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I don't read you guys at all, except through the tunnel.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: How do you read on Alpha, Ron?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. Got you loud and clear that time. And, Gene, can you verify the capture latches are all engaged?

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay. How do you read me?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: I didn't read you at all, Jack.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: This is Gene. How do you read me on Alpha?

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Didn't read you.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay. Let's press on. You're getting us intermittent. We can get it.

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay. I got you that time, and check the capture latches.

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Houston. I'm pretty sure the VHF...

a17_1085510.speaker: Evans
a17_1085510.text: Okay?

a17_1085510.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1085510.text: ...is all right. It seems to have something to do with the Squelch setting, and it's probably because we're so close.

a17_1085510.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1085510.text: Okay. We concur. We'd like you to press on and not worry about the VHF any more for now.

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Gordo. We are. Here's a couple of quick ones. When I pushed the LGC DSKY breaker, In, I did not get a restart light. The keyboard came up with 400 in R-2. The LGC light was already on, and it went off as prescribed. When I did a Verb 35, I got all the proper lights except when the LGC and ISS lights came on, the entire Caution and Warning dimmed. One more item. In our DAP setting, we are reading in our checklist for R-1 plus 645 and for R-2 plus 641. The DSKY DAP came up plus 641 and plus 645. It just reversed those numbers. And I'm going to deploy the landing gear.

a17_1085510.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1085510.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1085510.speaker: Cernan
a17_1085510.text: Okay, Houston. Master Arm is on, and B light is on.

a17_1085510.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1085510.text: Roger.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1090157csm.text: Roger. Are you ready for a landing gear?

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1090157csm.text: Yeah, I'm up in the tunnel, but go ahead. [Pause.]

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1090157csm.text: Yeah, I'm up in the tunnel, but go ahead.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1090157csm.text: Ron, if you read, the landing gear is coming on my Mark.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1090157csm.text: Okay. I read you. Go ahead.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1090157csm.text: Mark.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1090157csm.text: Hey, Houston. We got a good one out front.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1090157csm.text: Sounds good.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1090157csm.text: [Laughter]

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1090157csm.text: We show them all deployed.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1090157csm.text: And the flag is gray. Okay. The flag is gray.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1090157csm.text: Roger.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1090157csm.text: Okay, Houston. The Primary Evap Flow time, 108 - Evap Flow time 108:16:55. And I'm ready to copy your abort constants and a DOI-2 pad.

a17_1090157csm.speaker: Fullerton

a17_1123500csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1123500csm.text: And do you have a 231 update?

a17_1123500csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1123500csm.text: Stand by. Negative. No change, Jack.

a17_1123500csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1123500csm.text: Also, Houston, I lost the landmark at 24:01 instead of 24:19.

a17_1124612csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1124612csm.text: And, America; Houston. We haven't watched you load P24 yet.

a17_1124612csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1124612csm.text: Hello, America. Do you read Challenger?

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: One minute, Houston, and we're standing by. We're Go for PDI.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. You're looking good here. (Long Pause) SASS Node.js

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, approaching 30 seconds. Blank DSKY. [Gene uses the Display and Keyboard Assembly ( DSKY ) to enter data and commands into the PGNS. It is located at his right hand, over the hatch. Jack uses the Data Entry and Display Assembly (DEDA) to monitor the AGS and, later in the descent, to enter trajectory corrections.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: DSKY blank. (Pause) Average G . [Cernan - "When you go into something as dynamic as an engine burn, you get major fluctuations in the accelerometers and, to navigate effectively, you have to average the accelerations over a finite period of time."] [In February 2009, Journal Contributor Paul Fjeld pointed out that Gene was mistaken about average g. See the discussion linked here .]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Got two lights.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Engine Arm is Descent. I think the tapemeter drove. I'm not sure. (Pause) Confirm the ullage. [In other contexts, "ullage" is the empty portion of a cask. Here, the word is used to describe a 7.5 second firing of the Reaction Control System (RCS) in order to settle fuel in the tanks prior to ignition.] [Cernan - "At ignition, the tanks were about three quarters full of fuel and one quarter pressurized helium. The trouble was that, in zero gravity, you didn't know where the fuel was in the tank. Therefore, you had to apply a little acceleration and drive the heavy (that is, denser) fuel d

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Standing by for ullage. (Pause) Ten seconds. (Pause) Fuel ullage. We've got ullage.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Proceed on 99. It took. 2, 1, 0... [Schmitt - "Having gotten ullage, we pushed the computer's Proceed button which told it to continue with engine ignition."] [Journal Contributor David Woods writes, "The software was written such that if the computer needed an input from the crew to allow it to proceed with its next function, it flashed a '99' in the display. The crew pressed the 'Proceed' button and the computer continued. This was usually used in the context of an engine ignition, as in 'Do you really want me to go ahead and light this thing?'."] [Gene is prepared to do a manual backup of t

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...Ignition.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Ignition, Houston. Attitude looks good. Engine Override is On, Master Arm is Off. We got a Descent Quantity Light On at ignition, just prior to ignition. [The Descent Quantity Light is an indication of an inadequate fuel supply. In this case, it is a false warning. Gene discusses his reaction to the warning at 113:11:55, after the landing.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: DPC tank's good. RCS is good at 15 seconds.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. [We have been unable to translate "DPC" or find it in any list of Apollo acronyms. Undoubtedly, "DP" is "Descent Propulsion" and it is entirely possible that Jack got momentarily tongue-tied as he checked the propellant tanks and meant to say DPS for Descent Propulsion System.] [Schmitt - "Probably, I was doing a quick check to make sure the tank pressures were okay. Evidently, the Quantity Light was giving a false warning."]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: RCS is golden. Should be stable throttle up. (Pause) [For the first 26 seconds of the burn, the engine is fired at minimum thrust - about 10% of full thrust - so that the engine gimbal can be adjusted to put the thrust axis directly through the center of gravity. At throttle up, the engine is switched to full thrust, where it will remain until the last couple of minutes of the descent.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Stand by. There's...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Throttle-up's on time, Houston.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...throttle up.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: And the computer likes it.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. [Cernan - "Once you get into the computers, it's like riding a bicycle. Maybe you change to a different kind of bicycle, but it's still easy enough to learn. Long before we flew Apollo 17, I had gotten very comfortable with all of the computer systems. I had flown on Apollo 10 as Lunar Module Pilot and, on that mission, was responsible for a lot of things as far as computers were concerned, especially the AGS . Along with Tom Stafford, I also got to know the main computer to the point that I could sleep with it. After that flight I backed up Apollo 14. The morning of the Apollo 14 launc

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: (To Houston) Still got the Quantity Light on. (Pause) Okay, attitude looks good, Jack.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. At 30 seconds (after ignition). Should have about 108 (degrees of pitch). (Pause) [They are flying with their backs parallel to the lunar surface below them and their feet pointing in the direction of motion. Attitudes are being measured relative to the landing site. At the landing site, pitch is zero when the spacecraft is oriented vertically and would be 90 degrees if they were flying over the site parallel to the surface with their feet forward. At PDI, they are about 18 degrees east of the landing site and the local horizontal plane is tipped down 18 degrees to the east compared with

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: (Marveling at the experience) Oh, boy!

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: AGS and PGNS are close. [Schmitt - "The two, separate guidance systems had been initialized to the same data at some point prior to ignition. The AGS had some strapped-down gyros and wasn't as accurate as the PGNS; but, if the primary system failed, the AGS was certainly accurate enough to get us back to orbit. Here, I am checking to see that the two systems are in satisfactory agreement. Sometime prior to the mission I had worked out a way to update the AGS's knowledge of altitude by inputting a value from the radar data as soon as that became available. We'll see that later. LMPs were always

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay; 3400. I confirm. (Pause) Audio Clip  [This clip was prepared by Colin Mackellar from recordings made at Honeysuckle Creek from Net 1 and provided by HSK Receiver Operator Alan Foster. The audio quaility is a bit better than the digitizations done from audio cassettes provided in 1989 by NASA Johnson.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, you're Go for Enter.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. Go for Enter. [Cernan - "The ground couldn't fly the spacecraft or do anything with it, but they could read a lot of the data out. While I keyed the new data into the computer and Jack verified it on-board, they could also read it and verify it on the ground. Normally, they'd look at it and verify it before we'd go ahead and actually execute whatever command or (enter) whatever data they'd given us."]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: 1:30. We're Go coming through 57K. [They are one minute and thirty seconds into the burn and are at an altitude of 57 thousand feet, or about 17 kilometers, above the lunar surface.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, the altitude's high and the H-dot is high. At least...That's right. (Pause) Okay, at one...(Correcting himself) At 2 minutes, you ought to have 89 on the ball. [Cernan - "We had an inertial attitude gyro, like in an airplane, which we called the "eight ball" or simply the "ball". It was essentially fixed in space and we would rotate the spacecraft around it. With the LM sitting on the lunar surface, the ball would have shown a pitch of zero degrees; and, while we were in the initial descent and lying on our backs with our feet forward, looking up at the sky and slowing down, it would sho

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: We're still 30 feet per second high in H-dot. But we're about 8000 feet high...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, Houston,...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...(make that) 7000 (in altitude).

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...we'd like you to cycle the PQGS switch Off and then back On. [PQGS is the Propellant Quantity Gauging System. Cycling the switch will let them see if the quantity warning light is real.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Houston. Coming up on 2 minutes. (Pause as he listens to Fullerton) Okay. It (meaning the switch)'s Off. And it's back On. Quantity Light is out.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. That should be good now.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: And, Houston, we...(Hearing Fullerton) Okay. We have Engine Thrust and Commanded Thrust, full-scale high.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Man, that looks good.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, babe, let's check them at 02:30.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: RCS looks good.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: 02:30, I'm about 89 degrees...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Cabin looks great...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...coming through 51.5 thousand feet.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: 89 is great. We're catching up on our altitude. We should start dropping H-dot here a little bit. AGS and PGNS are together. AGS has us a little bit out of plane. And we're north; (AGS) has us north of track. [That is, the AGS is showing them north of the planned ground track. Jack will ask the question again in about 2 minutes.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, Houston...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Gordo; coming up on 3 minutes, we're Go and...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...you're Go at 3.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ...we're out of 49K. (Hearing Fullerton) Roger. Understand we're Go.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. At 3 minutes. 82's your ball number. We're still looking for (that is, coming down to) the right altitude. So H-dot is high.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. (Pause) The day of reckoning comes at 4 minutes, Jack. (Pause) Thrust-to-weight (ratio) building up, looking good. Attitudes are good.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, at 03:30, you ought to have 79...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, it's right on.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: We're still a little high, about 2500 feet (high). H-dot is still high. (Long Pause) [In the last two minutes, the altitude error has decreased from 7000 feet to 2500 feet and has closed, therefore, at a rate of 40 feet per second. At PDI, they were about 30 degrees of longitude east of what would have been the closest approach to the surface (perilune) of their pre-PDI orbit. Being east of the perilune, they were already descending toward the surface at a rate of about 67 fps - a rate which would have slowed in the absence of the burn - and they had planned to maintain that rate of 67 fps for

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. The tapemeter moves in spurts and jerks, both on altitude and altitude rate (in response to the first radar returns from the surface).

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Yeah. [Schmitt - "There was a tapemeter display for showing the radar data - altitude and altitude rate (H-dot) - when that became available. Physically, it was a pair of tapes with numbers on them which moved up and down behind a needle."] [Cernan - "We had so many rate needles that it's a little hard to remember; but we could change them to show a lot of things like altitude and altitude rates. I think we could change this particular tapemeter (which was next to the " 8-ball " attitude indicator on Gene's side of the spacecraft) showed either the radar data or the computer's best guess about

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, Houston. You're Go at 4 minutes.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ED Batts are 37.2 (volts). [These are batteries that supply electricity to the explosive devices which would separate the Ascent Stage from the Descent Stage in the event of an aborted landing attempt using the ascent stage to return to orbit. Jack will check the batteries periodically.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. ED Batts.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: ED Batts are 3...(Listening) Okay.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Gordo, yaw's coming at 340.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Roger. [See Gene's comment at 112:56:33. This yaw maneuver - a rotation around the thrust axis - is designed to put the landing radar in optimum position. Prior to ignition, they had the spacecraft yawed left by 70 degrees for optimum communications with Earth and are now reducing that to 20 degrees left. Once they get down to an altitude of 30,000 feet, they will go to a zero-yaw, windows-up attitude for the landing.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: And the radar lights are out! Beautiful. [The radar has acquired the lunar surface.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, sounds great. Both (Nav) systems are Go...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: You're looking at Delta-H.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. You're looking at Delta-H. [Schmitt - "This was the difference between the radar altitude and the PGNS calculated altitude"]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: And you're Go for a Verb 57.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Verb 57 is in. [Schmitt - "Verb 57 allowed the radar data to be incorporated into the computer."]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Hey, Houston, is the AGS (indication that they are) out-of-plane correct?

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Cernan - "We had gone into lunar orbit in the CSM on a path that went from northeast to southwest across the front face of the Moon. That track took the Command Module over the landing site but wasn't exactly the right path for the final approach. So we flew the LM a little south out of the CSM orbital plane so that we could line up with our runway, so to speak, down the axis of the valley."]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, coming up on 5 minutes, Jack. Let's take a check at it. About 74 degrees (of pitch).

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: That's good. 70 feet per second (descent rate); we're coming down. 36...You're still (garbled, either "two" or "three") thousand feet high;

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, you're Go at 5 minutes...

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay, Houston; we're now out of thirty...(Stops to listen)

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Okay. Go at 5. We're out of 36.5 (thousand feet) now. We've got the Earth right out the front window. (Pause) [Cernan - "We landed so far east and north that the Earth was in the southwestern sky above the mountains. Every other flight landed where the Earth was essentially overhead; so ours was unique in that, during our descent, we were looking right at the Earth as we were coming down in the valley. As those mountains rose above us, we were looking at the Earth - I mean - right smack in front of us! We didn't have to look up at it; it was right there. Can you imagine coming down, thirty-six

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Fullerton
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Challenger, Houston. Battery 3, On, at your convenience.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: Battery 3 is On. [They are about fifty miles from the landing site.]

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: 05:30, Gordo. We're Go. We're out of 34K.

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Schmitt
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: 73 (degrees), 34 (thousand feet). We're right on altitude. The H-dot ought to start dropping off. Except that we want to keep it high. [Their average descent rate during these 5.5 minutes has been 100 fps, with about 30 fps of the total due to the descent to the planned trajectory. If this is a reference to the chart, he may be saying t

a17a_1124856_to_1130348.speaker: Cernan
a17a_1124856_to_1130348.text: (With a slight tone of authority, to Jack) You're allowed two quick looks out the window, one now and one when we pitchover.

a17_1125041csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1125041csm.text: One minute. You ought to have 98 (degrees of pitch). Okay, H-dot is high right now. [H-dot is the descent rate, the time derivative of the altitude. They are descending faster than planned; hence, H-dot is high. The reason for this is that they are above the planned trajectory and the computer is bringing them down to it.]
