A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Man, that looks good.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, babe, let's check them at 02:30.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: RCS looks good.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: 02:30, I'm about 89 degrees...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Cabin looks great...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ...coming through 51.5 thousand feet.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: 89 is great. We're catching up on our altitude. We should start dropping H-dot here a little bit. AGS and PGNS are together. AGS has us a little bit out of plane. And we're north; (AGS) has us north of track. [That is, the AGS is showing them north of the planned ground track. Jack will ask the question again in about 2 minutes.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Challenger, Houston...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, Gordo; coming up on 3 minutes, we're Go and...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ...you're Go at 3.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ...we're out of 49K. (Hearing Fullerton) Roger. Understand we're Go.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay. At 3 minutes. 82's your ball number. We're still looking for (that is, coming down to) the right altitude. So H-dot is high.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay. (Pause) The day of reckoning comes at 4 minutes, Jack. (Pause) Thrust-to-weight (ratio) building up, looking good. Attitudes are good.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, at 03:30, you ought to have 79...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, it's right on.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: We're still a little high, about 2500 feet (high). H-dot is still high. (Long Pause) [In the last two minutes, the altitude error has decreased from 7000 feet to 2500 feet and has closed, therefore, at a rate of 40 feet per second. At PDI, they were about 30 degrees of longitude east of what would have been the closest approach to the surface (perilune) of their pre-PDI orbit. Being east of the perilune, they were already descending toward the surface at a rate of about 67 fps - a rate which would have slowed in the absence of the burn - and they had planned to maintain that rate of 67 fps for

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay. The tapemeter moves in spurts and jerks, both on altitude and altitude rate (in response to the first radar returns from the surface).

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Yeah. [Schmitt - "There was a tapemeter display for showing the radar data - altitude and altitude rate (H-dot) - when that became available. Physically, it was a pair of tapes with numbers on them which moved up and down behind a needle."] [Cernan - "We had so many rate needles that it's a little hard to remember; but we could change them to show a lot of things like altitude and altitude rates. I think we could change this particular tapemeter (which was next to the " 8-ball " attitude indicator on Gene's side of the spacecraft) showed either the radar data or the computer's best guess about

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Challenger, Houston. You're Go at 4 minutes.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ED Batts are 37.2 (volts). [These are batteries that supply electricity to the explosive devices which would separate the Ascent Stage from the Descent Stage in the event of an aborted landing attempt using the ascent stage to return to orbit. Jack will check the batteries periodically.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Roger. ED Batts.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ED Batts are 3...(Listening) Okay.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, Gordo, yaw's coming at 340.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Roger. [See Gene's comment at 112:56:33. This yaw maneuver - a rotation around the thrust axis - is designed to put the landing radar in optimum position. Prior to ignition, they had the spacecraft yawed left by 70 degrees for optimum communications with Earth and are now reducing that to 20 degrees left. Once they get down to an altitude of 30,000 feet, they will go to a zero-yaw, windows-up attitude for the landing.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: And the radar lights are out! Beautiful. [The radar has acquired the lunar surface.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, sounds great. Both (Nav) systems are Go...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: You're looking at Delta-H.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ...right on the line.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay. You're looking at Delta-H. [Schmitt - "This was the difference between the radar altitude and the PGNS calculated altitude"]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: And you're Go for a Verb 57.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, Verb 57 is in. [Schmitt - "Verb 57 allowed the radar data to be incorporated into the computer."]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Hey, Houston, is the AGS (indication that they are) out-of-plane correct?

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Cernan - "We had gone into lunar orbit in the CSM on a path that went from northeast to southwest across the front face of the Moon. That track took the Command Module over the landing site but wasn't exactly the right path for the final approach. So we flew the LM a little south out of the CSM orbital plane so that we could line up with our runway, so to speak, down the axis of the valley."]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, coming up on 5 minutes, Jack. Let's take a check at it. About 74 degrees (of pitch).

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: That's good. 70 feet per second (descent rate); we're coming down. 36...You're still (garbled, either "two" or "three") thousand feet high;

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Challenger, you're Go at 5 minutes...

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay, Houston; we're now out of thirty...(Stops to listen)

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: ...the AGS out-of-plane looks okay to us. (Pause) [Fullerton will give them a fuller explanation of the out-of-plane indication at 187:40:10 , just prior to launch.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Okay. Go at 5. We're out of 36.5 (thousand feet) now. We've got the Earth right out the front window. (Pause) [Cernan - "We landed so far east and north that the Earth was in the southwestern sky above the mountains. Every other flight landed where the Earth was essentially overhead; so ours was unique in that, during our descent, we were looking right at the Earth as we were coming down in the valley. As those mountains rose above us, we were looking at the Earth - I mean - right smack in front of us! We didn't have to look up at it; it was right there. Can you imagine coming down, thirty-six

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Fullerton
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Challenger, Houston. Battery 3, On, at your convenience.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: Battery 3 is On. [They are about fifty miles from the landing site.]

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: 05:30, Gordo. We're Go. We're out of 34K.

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Schmitt
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: 73 (degrees), 34 (thousand feet). We're right on altitude. The H-dot ought to start dropping off. Except that we want to keep it high. [Their average descent rate during these 5.5 minutes has been 100 fps, with about 30 fps of the total due to the descent to the planned trajectory. Now, they are on the nominal flight path and Jack's "we want to keep it high" may be a reference either to the fact that the rate will start to increase again once they get down to about 32,000 feet or to the altitude/altitude rate chart he has been consulting. If this is a reference to the chart, he may be saying t

A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.speaker: Cernan
A17_landing_rec_from_Net_1_at_HSK.text: (With a slight tone of authority, to Jack) You're allowed two quick looks out the window, one now and one when we pitchover.

a17_1125539csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1125539csm.text: I can't see a thing except the Earth.

a17_1125539csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1125539csm.text: That's what I'm telling you to look at.

a17_1125539csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1125539csm.text: (Laughs) Oh! There's the old Earth! [Cernan - "Jack couldn't spend much time looking out the window. He went through the whole landing and hardly had a chance to see where we were going, because he was looking at fuel and oxidizer gauges, looking at battery currents, updating the AGS computer, verifying my entries in the PGNS, and writing things down. So he was very busy inside the cockpit and probably stole a glance or two outside. I had to look outside. Actually, I had to look both places - inside and outside - but my primary focus was out the window and on all of the attitude and rate indic

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1130256csm.text: Hey, Challenger; this is America. I heard you all the way down. That's great. Beautiful.

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1130256csm.text: Hey, Challenger; this is America. I heard you all the way down.

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1130256csm.text: (To Evans) Ron, I had the meatball all the way.

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1130256csm.text: That's great! Beautiful. [Cernan - "When you land on a carrier, you've got a mirror and you've got an orange light that reflects in the mirror. On the carrier you've got a row of green lights that also reflect in that mirror and if the meatball - the orange light - is below the green lights, then you are low, below the glide slope; and if the meatball's above the green lights, you are high. So what you do is fly your carrier approach so that the meatball is right in line with the green lights. So I was telling Ron that I had it 'locked' all the way in."]

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1130256csm.text: Jack, are we going to have some nice boulders in this area.

a17_1130256csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1130256csm.text: Okay. The old (16-mm sequence) camera's off.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Where'd you land? (Joking) You never let me look outside at all. Hey, you can see the boulder tracks (on the North Massif)! [During the 3.9 billion years since the Massifs were raised, boulders have been dislodged occasionally from outcroppings high on the mountains. As they tumbled down toward the valley floor, the boulders carved grooves where they rolled or slid, and cut strings of craters where they bounced. The resulting tracks erode only slowly because of countless small impacts and the downslope movement of soil. AS17-144- 21991 , which Jack will take from the cabin after EVA-1, shows t

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Okay, Gordy. We're standing by for your Go. We look good. We're looking good onboard. [In this case, "Go" is permission to stay.]

A17A1130349.speaker: Fullerton
A17A1130349.text: Okay. You're looking great here so far.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: There are boulders all over those massifs.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: God, look at that propellant. We could have gone all around and looked around. [As mentioned previously, at touchdown they had fuel enough left for about 117 seconds of hovering.]

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: We should have hovered around a little bit; gone and looked at the Scarp.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: No, thank you. (Jack laughs) I like it right where we are. [Cernan - "From about a thousand feet down, the planned landing site looked good. So I was just concerned about spacecraft attitude and spacecraft motion during the final approach. I was not concerned about the terrain we were landing on. It was real nice to be down with lots of propellant left but, while it would have been fun to fly around the valley a little and then land, the important thing was to get the spacecraft down safely. It would have been like flying through a thunderstorm and making a safe landing, and having somebody sa

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Okay, Gordy. While you're waiting on that Go, I shot for a spot, around 2 o'clock from Poppie. There's a number of boulders out at 12 o'clock from Poppie, and I really think I'm probably not more than about 100 meters out in front of it, and slightly to the north. Actually, I may be a little bit closer to Trident than I expected Poppie to be. I think I've got Trident right out the left window. And our first cut at the mobility around here in the Rover (is that) it ought to be super. [Here, Gene is using clock positions, centered on Poppie, with 12 o'clock being west. As Gene remarks at 113:05:

A17A1130349.speaker: Fullerton
A17A1130349.text: Okay. Sounds good. (Pause)

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: But I tell you, the Massifs and Bear Mountain are two different products. (Pause)

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Sure look it, don't they? (Pause) Of course, they're different slopes, too. [Unlike either of the Massifs, Bear Mountain has a distinctly wrinkled, hummocky appearance. Jack is reminding Gene that the apparent difference may, in part, be due to lighting effects.]

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: I think you're looking, probably...That may be Rudolph, right there, Jack, out your window. [Again, Gene is mistaken. Rudolph is actually about 200 meters west and 150 meters north of the LM. The crater visible out Jack's window is unnamed.]

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: I was looking more at those boulders and trying to stay in the spots in between them than I was...

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Yeah, you did great, Gene.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: ...relationship to that crater. 113:05:26 Schmitt: Man, there was practically no dust, just a little bit of a film. You had the ground all the way to the ground.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Yeah. I could call touchdown on the shadow. Look at that. (Pause) Really here. (Jack laughs) [Once they start to deploy the ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package), Gene and Jack will have another discussion about the superb visibility they had during the final phase of the landing. The experiences of other crews are summarized after 121:04:14 .]

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Okay, Gordy. We're hanging in for your Go. [Cernan - "The ground wasn't about to commit to a three-day stay when we'd only been there ten minutes. They wanted a chance to look at all the spacecraft systems. This initial post-landing phase was the critical one. Did you bust a tank? Was there any helium or fuel leaking? How was the battery power holding up? During these first few minutes, we were ready to launch immediately. They were taking a quick look and, if things looked okay, they would then let us go ahead and reconfigure the computers and the navigation system for a non-emergency lift-of

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: (Relishing the thought of doing geology at this magnificent site) It better be a Go!

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Check everything again. Let's just double check.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Okay.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: That hasn't changed.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Okay, that's good.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: The manifold (pressure) hasn't changed. The RCS hasn't changed. Ascent water hasn't changed. The batteries haven't changed.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: Oh, my golly!

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Only we have changed.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: You know, you can't see into Camelot, Jack; that rim is Camelot out in front of us.

A17A1130349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1130349.text: Yeah.

A17A1130349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1130349.text: You (garbled under Fullerton)...

A17A1130349.speaker: Fullerton
A17A1130349.text: Challenger, you'll be glad to hear you're Stay for T-1.

a17_1130621csm.speaker: Mattingly
a17_1130621csm.text: And, America; we have a Stay for T-1.

a17_1130621csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1130621csm.text: Gordy, you're a smooth talker, you know it? We are Stay for T-1. (Pause) (To Jack) Okay. You can forget all I told you about Verb 22 Noun 46. [T-1 is a pre-programmed opportunity to launch and catch up with the CSM on this orbit. If, during these first minutes, Houston had decided that something was wrong with the spacecraft they would have told the crew to launch at T-1 or even sooner. With the Stay, they will now prepare for T-2, the next pre-programmed launch opportunity.]

a17_1130621csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1130621csm.text: Challenger, understand stay for T-1. Good.

a17_1130621csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1130621csm.text: What was that? (Jack laughs) [Ron is congratulating the Challenger crew. Apparently, Jack was surprised to hear him. My thanks to Journal Contributor Jack A. Kozak, who brought the Evans transmission to my attention.]

a17_1131117csm.speaker: Mattingly
a17_1131117csm.text: And, America, I have a Pan Camera photo PAD whenever you're ready for it. It'll go on page 129.

a17_1131117csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1131117csm.text: That's right. [Schmitt - "We had done one of our field tests near Sunset Crater, partly because it was volcanic terrain."] [Cernan - "We didn't use a Rover at Sunset, but we had something that allowed us to be mobile. We did a 'typical' lunar traverse that sort of simulated, out in the field, the kind of traverse we would run through on the Moon. It was all pre-planned, of course; so we had an EVA-1, 2, and 3 where we were to do different things. At stop 1 on EVA-1 we were going to do this, take a sample of the soil, and then do that. Now, that doesn't mean that we were doing an exact replica

a17_1131117csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1131117csm.text: Okay. Let's see what we're doing. We got 3 minutes for T-2. Let's take another check.

a17_1131333csm.speaker: Mattingly
a17_1131333csm.text: America, Houston. The LM has a Stay for T-2.

a17_1131333csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1131333csm.text: Okay. You can unzap that water, if you'd like. And let's go off VOX. Let's go on PTT. Tape recorder, Off. [Comm Break. VOX is the voice-actuated mode of communications. PTT or "Push-to-Talk" is the alternative. In the PTT mode, astronauts can only talk to Houston by manually activating the microphones that were part of the "Snoopy" helmets that they each wore. The tape recorder has only a limited amount of tape available and has been on since before undocking. They will turn the recorder on at about 116:23:07 during the preparations for EVA-1.] [Schmitt - "The key for the microphone was a big

a17_1131333csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1131333csm.text: Okay. Regulator 1 is Closed, Houston; Oxidizer (and) Fuel Vents coming Open.

a17_1131333csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1131333csm.text: Master Arm, On. Master Arm's coming On.

A17A1131520.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1131520.text: (Reading from the checklist as they reconfigure the LM) Okay. Master Arm, Off. Okay. We'll monitor oxidizer pressure until 20 to 40 (psi), and then Ox Vent, Closed; fuel pressure to less than 8 (psi). Fuel Vent. (Pause) Descent Quantity light...(correcting himself) Reg light. Excuse me. (Pause) Okay. Mode Control, two to Att Hold. Well, we just keep going, I guess. (Pause) Yeah. Hey, we can press on. (Pause) Okay. (Pause) Okay. Now wait a minute. Here we go. Let's get that. Go up here first. (Pause) Because I haven't selected it. (Pause)

A17A1131520.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1131520.text: (Gene is now reading from the checklist as Jack sets controls on his side of the spacecraft) Okay. ECA Control is Closed. (Pause) (Battery) 3 is back on. Battery 5 is Off/Reset, and it's off the line. Battery 6, Off/Reset, and it's off the line. (Pause) Inverter number 2 breaker is In. Inverter 2. Let me check the voltage. Voltage is great. (Pause) Okay. Keep going. (Pause) Descent Engine Override's Open. (Pause) Ascent ECA Control's Open. (Pause) CWEA (Caution and Warning Electronics Assembly, pronounced "seewee") cycling, cycled; both lights are out. Okay. Cabin pressure is good. Okay.

A17A1131520.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1131520.text: And then, (Pressure Regulators) A and B going to Cabin. (Pause) A is to Cabin. B is to Cabin. Pull-Egress. (Pause) (Cabin Gas) Return (Valve) is Egress. (Pause) (Cabin) Repress (valve) going to Auto. (Pause) Stand by for a noise. There you go. It's in Auto. Okay. Now it's your turn. Verify...(Pause) Wonder where it's going? (Laughs) Out, I guess. (Pause) [Schmitt - "When you go to Repress, Auto, you get a little bit of gas flow across the valve; maybe we saw something that it ejected. Or maybe I was just wondering where the gas was going."] [Details of the LM Environmental Control System ( ECS

A17A1131520.speaker: Cernan
A17A1131520.text: Gordy, let me comment about the handling of the bird. After you once fly it (the LM) around in orbit a little bit, you get accustomed to the thrusters, and it came back to me quite a bit from (Apollo) 10, anyway. And you get a feel for acceleration and deceleration as well as the attitude-hold capability. And, really, the response, even with a heavy descent stage near the surface, is phenomenal. Responded exactly in the direction I wanted, held attitude very good. And, let me tell you, the LLTV (Lunar Landing Training Vehicle) played no small part in this landing as far as I'm concerned.

A17A1131520.speaker: Mattingly
A17A1131520.text: Okay, America. We're about 3 minutes from LOS. All systems look good. And GNC has noticed that you've got the Optics not in Zero, and next time you're down that way, it would make everybody feel better if you'd put it there. It's not - not something that you have to do right away.

A17A1131520.speaker: Cernan
A17A1131520.text: Okay. Noun 22 again. I'll go ahead and torque them. 113:43:49 Fullerton: Okay. Go ahead. [Long Comm Break] [Jack and Gene and I then had an extended discussion of LLTV training .] [Gene has been making a new gravity measurement during the Comm Break.]

A17A1131520.speaker: Mission Control
A17A1131520.text: 113:44:26 - This is Apollo Control at 113 hours, 44 minutes Ground Elapsed Time in the mission of Apollo 17. Some refined numbers on the landing site for Challenger: In degrees, minutes and seconds, the latitude has been pinned down to 20 degrees, 9 minutes, 50.5 seconds north; longitude 30 degrees, 46 minutes, 19.3 minutes - or seconds east, which is about 639 meters east of the designated landing point - the premission landing point. For those newsmen who have the landing site with the grid coordinates on it, that corresponds to DN.0 by 84.2. At 113:45 Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Con

A17A1131520.speaker: Mission Control
A17A1131520.text: 113:48:59 - This is Apollo Control at 113 hours, 48 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We're estimating a change of shift, if you will Press Conference, with the landing team flight director, Gerry Griffin, in the small briefing room at 3:00 pm. To repeat, estimated Press Conference in about 20 minutes, approximately, 18 minutes to be exact, in the small Briefing Room in Building 1. Some 42 minutes away from acquisition as the Command Module, America, comes around on revolution 14. Meanwhile on the surface, to repeat the estimated landing site. It is right down the line on the Ground Track. However

A17A1131520.speaker: Mission Control
A17A1131520.text: 114:11:10 - This is Apollo control at 114 hours, 11 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the mission of Apollo 17. Commander Gene Cernan's heart rate during the descent and landing ranged from 102 average during the descent portion of the landing to 128 at actual touchdown. There's a change of shift briefing that will start momentarily in the small briefing room in building 1. We'll take down the broadcast line at this time, tape any conversation during that period and play it back at the conclusion of the briefing which starts now. This is Apollo Control out.

a17_1131705csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1131705csm.text: Yeah. It's a good thing it's in the sextant because you can't see it in the telescope. Because the Earth is in the field of view.

a17_1131705csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1131705csm.text: Inverter 2 is selected. (Pause) Okay. And DECA Power, Open. (Pause) And guess what? Take your helmet and gloves off. [Comm Break]

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1132518csm.text: Okay, Houston; this is America. I think I'll go ahead and use a shaft to 00.12, and a 57.470.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1132518csm.text: The visibility prior to pitchover was such that I could see Nansen. I could see the Scarp. I could see Lara. I could not see Camelot until after pitchover. However, once I had pitchover, if I could have froze(n) it right there like we do in the simulator occasionally, I could have picked out everything there was to see. Even at 6000 feet, the small triangle with Frosty and Rudolph and Punk were visible to me. I had Poppie from orbit, as a matter of fact, so it was easy to see. Barjea was a very sharp, round crater just as depicted on the L&A. The thing I really didn't get a good look at, becau

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1132518csm.text: Gordy, this is the LMP. Let me say that the inside of the spacecraft looked just like the simulator.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1132518csm.text: Very good, Jack. (Pause) [Once again, Jack is lamenting that, rather than get a chance to look at the Moon during the descent, he'd had his eyes glued to the instruments.]

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1132518csm.text: Another interesting thing, Gordy. All the way through PDI prior to pitchover, Jack and I had the real America - or the other America - right smack out the front window all the way down, which was pretty spectacular. [Cernan - "Because we were landing early in the morning at a site so far east, we landed at a very early phase of the Moon and almost the entire Earth was sunlit. We took the picture of the fullest Earth that any crew saw because we left Earth almost at the New Moon. As we stayed there, the fraction of the Earth that was sunlit got less and less and it got to be a three-quarters Ea

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1132518csm.text: I bet it was. And you can consider yourself Stay for T-3.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1132518csm.text: Thank you, sir. You're getting smoother (that is, becoming a smoother talker) all the time. If you're happy with Noun 22, I'll Pro(ceed).

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1132518csm.text: Stand by one. (Pause) You're clear to Pro. [Cernan - "You could align the inertial platform either with the stars or with gravity. Here, we were gravity aligning. I think Noun 22 showed you the new alignment angles (in yaw, pitch and roll, in tenths of a degree), and it gave you a chance to look at it and say 'Yes, I want it; I'll accept it,' or 'No, I'll keep my old alignment.' The fact that we were still aligning the platform means that we were still in a mode to leave the lunar surface on a contingent basis. We'd taken our helmets and gloves off, but still hadn't really powered down for a l

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1132518csm.text: Okay. Go on the H 2 tank, thanks.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1132518csm.text: Okay, Gordy. I had the angles matched on the steerable high-gain antenna and went to Slew, and it (the signal strength) held for a few seconds and then dropped off.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1132518csm.text: Okay. It looks pretty good (his tone of voice suggests "but not optimal"). You might try to peak it up just a little more. [Fullerton is suggesting that Jack adjust the antenna pointing for a maximum signal strength from Earth.]

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Mattingly
a17_1132518csm.text: Okay. It's all - it looks good, Ron.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1132518csm.text: No, we're on an omni(-directional antenna) now.

a17_1132518csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1132518csm.text: I'll try the steerable one more time here. (Pause)

a17_1134101csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1134101csm.text: Okay. The old lithium hydroxide canister's changed.

a17_1134101csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1134101csm.text: Jack, this is Houston. We do have the pre-PDI AGS cal numbers. You won't need to read them to us. [That is, Jack can skip the readout called for in the checklist at the bottom, right-hand column, of page 1-2 .]

a17_1134101csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1134101csm.text: Gordy, you going to want a recycle on this gravity measurement? I doubt if it (the computer) will need it.

a17_1134101csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1134101csm.text: Stand by. (Pause) No; no recycle necessary this time through.

a17_1134101csm.speaker: Mattingly
a17_1134101csm.text: Okay. I'll give you Houston time. It's 14:35:21 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5.

A17A1134232.speaker: Cernan
A17A1134232.text: Gordy, let me comment about the handling of the bird. After you once fly it (the LM) around in orbit a little bit, you get accustomed to the thrusters, and it came back to me quite a bit from (Apollo) 10, anyway. And you get a feel for acceleration and deceleration as well as the attitude-hold capability. And, really, the response, even with a heavy descent stage near the surface, is phenomenal. Responded exactly in the direction I wanted, held attitude very good. And, let me tell you, the LLTV (Lunar Landing Training Vehicle) played no small part in this landing as far as I'm concerned.

A17A1134232.speaker: Mattingly
A17A1134232.text: Okay, America. We're about 3 minutes from LOS. All systems look good. And GNC has noticed that you've got the Optics not in Zero, and next time you're down that way, it would make everybody feel better if you'd put it there. It's not - not something that you have to do right away.

A17A1134232.speaker: Cernan
A17A1134232.text: Okay. Noun 22 again. I'll go ahead and torque them. 113:43:49 Fullerton: Okay. Go ahead. [Long Comm Break] [Jack and Gene and I then had an extended discussion of LLTV training .] [Gene has been making a new gravity measurement during the Comm Break.]

a17_1134859.speaker: Cernan
a17_1134859.text: Okay, Gordy. It's a little better.

a17_1141110.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1141110.text: Okay, Houston. We're at the bottom of (page) 1-8 , and I'm standing by for your lift-off times. [Checklist page 1-8 gives the configuration of the Environmental Control system ( ECS ).] 114:xx:xx Fullerton: Okay, Jack. Lift-off time for rev 15 is 116:55:51; 16 is 118:54:28; 120:53:04; 122:51:40; 124:50:17; 126:48:53. Over. 114:xx:xx Schmitt: Okay. Starting with rev 15, 116:55:51; 118:54:28; 120:53:04; 122:51:40; 124:50:17; 126:48:53. 114:xx:xx Fullerton: That's a good readback. [Comm Break. These are nominal lift-off times for upcoming orbits. Jack is entering the numbers in the on-board fligh

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: Bob, we'll give you a call in a minute. We just made a couple of suit adjustments.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay. Copy that. [Gene and Jack donned their suits at about 107:40, prior to undocking, and then donned their helmets and gloves at about 10 minutes prior to PDI. After the landing and once they were sure that the LM was in good shape, they took the helmets off at about 113:18, about 16 minutes after touchdown. However, since they plan to make a full EVA during this first day on the Moon, they have left their suits on and, as they will tell Houston in a couple of minutes, they are now adjusting drink bags and food sticks inside their neckrings for use once they get outside.] [Comm Break.]
It's estimated that the Lunar Module Challenger is on the planned north south line and approximately 1 to 200 meters east of the planned landing point.

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: 17:40, went to Operate.

This is Apollo Control at 115 hours, 18 minutes. We want to distinguish between the targeted landing point and the planned landing point. It had been the crew's intention all along to land approximately 200 meters east or short of the targeted landing point, the point at which the computer was targeting the Challenger. So, we believe that Challenger is approximately 300 meters east of the targeted landing point, which would put it about 100 to 200 meters east of the planned landing point.

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: 18:40. Lunar Sounder, Standby.

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Okay; we're maneuvering to VHF test attitude.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Apollo 17, Houston.

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: Go ahead, Bob.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay, Challenger; we've just lost about 16 dB (decibels) on your high-gain signal strength there. We're wondering if you happened to hit the switch there, has it moved, or could you give us a check on it?

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: We're nowhere near it. Stand by one. (Long Pause)

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay. And, Challenger, that should be a Pitch of 21 and a Yaw of minus 45. [Cernan - "The high gain (antenna) had a pitch axis and yaw axis. I don't think it had a roll axis. I don't think they were particularly related to the inertial axes of the spacecraft."] [Gene's memory is correct. From the LM, Earth is at an elevation of 45 degrees and at a bearing 30 degrees south of west; therefore, these pitch and yaw numbers are not simply related to the direction of Earth in the local sky.]

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: Plus 21 and minus 45; Rog. (Pause) Bob, (give us) about 2 minutes here.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay [Long Comm Break. Based on Jack's mention of the Buddy SLSS (Secondary Life Support System), or BSLSS, at 115:27:18 and Bob's comment at 115:29:10, they are in the middle of the left-hand column of checklist page Surface 2-1 . On this page they are stowing loose items, putting a 500mm lens on a Hasselblad camera, stowing film magazines and other gear in the Equipment Transfer Bag (ETB) which they will take outside with them, propping up a pair of cue cards for their pre- and post-EVA equipment procedures on the panel in front of them, turning on a heater for the urine disposal line - they

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Okay, Houston. I'm about ready to press ahead, if you all are?

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: Bob, this is Jack. On that high-gain (antenna pointing), I'm up close to 3.9 (signal strength) now, which is better than when we landed. Do you want me to do anything to it?

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Stand by on that. (Pause) Leave it alone. It seems to have gone away, Jack. It may have been a ground problem. (Pause) Did you guys adjust it, Jack?

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Okay. High Gain Antenna Power is On. We go to Manual and Wide. Minus about 12, and Yaw about 21 or something, 211. [Garble] on the High Gain. Ah-ha, Auto. Looks like it worked pretty good. Okay. Mode to VHF. Find it - there it is. Mode to VHF.

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: Yeah, Bob. (Mis-understanding the question) We had to fix the drink bags and a couple other things.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: No. Did you guys adjust the high-gain antenna?

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: No. I didn't touch it.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay. Copy that. [For the next few seconds, Jack thinks he is in the Push-to-Talk mode of communication but actually has a live microphone. Bob will call his attention to the fact in about a half minute.]

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: Buddy SLSS's in there? No. That's over there. [The Buddy SLSS (Secondary Life Support System) is an apparatus which would allow the crew to share PLSS feedwater in the event that one of the PLSSs failed. The apparatus consisted of a hose to provide feedwater from the astronaut with the working PLSS to the astronaut with a failed PLSS. The apparatus also included a tether to couple the two suits together to avoid pulling loose the connection to either suit. See Gene's comments starting the the third paragraph below 115:44:19 .]

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: Oh, did they?

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: (Garbled) in there?

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: I thought it was over on your side. (Pause) Okay? (Pause) Okay, that's over there. Bigger than it used to.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: And, Challenger, we have you hot miked.

A17A1151712.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1151712.text: Well, because ...(Hearing Bob) Huh? [Comm Break]

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Operate.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Challenger, Houston. Over.

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: Go ahead, Bob.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay. When you guys get to the top of page 2-5 ...And I assume you're down still in the ETB, from what your comments were on the hot mike there. When you get to the top of page 2-5, we'd like you to put both Demand Reg's to Egress. Over. [They are loading cameras, film, and other gear for the EVA into the ETB. By putting the oxygen demand regulators in the Egress position, they will cut off any addition of oxygen to the cabin except through the suit circuit. This is not a standard procedure at this point in the mission and Houston's request suggests they are checking some aspect of the ECS ope

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: Okay, Bob. Will do. We'll give you a call as we go along.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Roger. Thank you. [Comm Break] 115:30:55 Cernan: Hey, Bob, while I'm thinking of it, we're working with one pair of scissors down here. We're going to take them out with us in the ETB. You might make a point of reminding us to bring them back.
This is Apollo Control at 115 hours, 30 minutes. Ron Evans in America has about 14½ minutes left before Loss of Signal on the 14th revolution. He's...

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Okay. It went to Standby at 30.

A17A1151712.speaker: Mission Control
A17A1151712.text: 115:29:36 - This is Apollo Control at 115 hours, 30 minutes. Ron Evans in America has about 14½ minutes left before Loss of Signal on the 14th revolution. He's...

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Mode is gone to HF. Recorder is Off. Lose a little comm here, huh? Maybe. Okay; there's Bravo. Select Omni. The High Gain at minus - Manual, Wide. Minus 10 and 25 for AOS.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Okay. I copy that. Never did find Ron's, huh?

A17A1151712.speaker: Evans
A17A1151712.text: Okay; good. And High Gain Antenna Power is going Off.

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: No, sir, and I couldn't just leave him up there starving to death.

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Roger on that. [This suggests that they are in the middle of the right-hand column of page 2-1 .] [Schmitt - "Each of us had a pair of scissors which normally traveled with us, but Ron lost his on the trip out from Earth. We had a lot of fun kidding him on the way out and all the way back about losing his scissors in a spacecraft which was, after all, not very big. But the complication was that the whole timeline on the surface was geared to having two pairs of scissors. With two pairs, Gene and I could leave one pair in the cabin and take the other pair outside - probably as a contingency too

A17A1151712.speaker: Cernan
A17A1151712.text: By the way, how's he doing?

A17A1151712.speaker: Parker
A17A1151712.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Bob consults with Bob Overmyer, the Command Module CapCom.]

A17A1161017.speaker: Cernan
A17A1161017.text: Okay. The LMP has got the RCU connected to the PLSS.

A17A1161017.speaker: Parker
A17A1161017.text: (Making a mis-identification) Copy that, Jack. [Comm Break. They are near the top of the right-hand column of page 2-6 . They have mounted a Remote Control Unit on Jack's suit chest and are making connections to the PLSS. The top surface of the RCU has an oxygen quantity gauge, an oxygen fan switch, and a variety of warning flags. Communications switches are located on the bottom and the switch which controls the flow of PLSS water through the Liquid-Cooled Garment is on the left side. Once outside the LM, Gene and Jack can mount their 70 mm cameras on brackets attached to the front of the RCU

A17A1161017.speaker: Cernan
A17A1161017.text: Okay, Bob, I'm going to get on a PLSS (meaning Gene's), now.

A17A1161017.speaker: Parker
A17A1161017.text: Okay, Geno. Copy that. [They will now repeat the PLSS donning procedures for Gene.] [Cernan - "Getting the PLSSs on was very difficult. It was a two-man operation. The PLSSs were strapped to the side walls, at working height, and you had to back up against yours and the other guy would then unhook it from the wall and help you get it strapped to your back. The LM was so small that it was a very difficult operation, even in soft (unpressurized) suits."] [Gene is partly mistaken. While his PLSS was stowed on the wall behind his station, until they started EVA-1 preps, Jack's PLSS was secured to

A17A1161017.speaker: Cernan
A17A1161017.text: (Unintentional key) Sublimator is (garbled). [They are checking to make sure that Gene's PLSS sublimator exhaust is clear. The sublimator, which provides suit cooling, is described in more detail at 116:52.] [Very Long Comm Break] [Gene's next transmission is not present on the PAO tape used to generate the audio clip.]

A17A1161017.speaker: Cernan
A17A1161017.text: Okay, Bob. I've got my PLSS on. We're picking it up with verifying the powerdown configuration on the upper, right-hand corner of the EVA prep checklist. [Note that this is a separate checklist from the Lunar Surface Checklist which has been in use up to this point. Both contain the same EVA prep information but the EVA prep list is printed on stiff cards which are much easier to handle than the relatively bulky book which contains the full list of procedures to be followed while the crew is in the cabin. In the Surface Checklist, they are starting the section labeled " PLSS Comm Check " on pa

A17A1161017.speaker: Parker
A17A1161017.text: Houston copies. [Comm Break. Once they have verified the circuit breakers, they start the comm check, beginning with Jack. We don't hear any of this activity until they get to the section labeled "Audio (CDR)" in the middle of the left-hand column of page 2-7 .]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: (I've) had enough water today (that) you could say you discovered me. I'm "water on the Moon". Okay. Let's turn the descent water off, and let's stow this ( water gun (photo by Mick Hyde) and hose). [One of the important discoveries made from the Apollo samples was that the lunar rocks and soils are extraordinarily dry, lacking even water locked up in mineral structures that one almost always finds in Earth rocks. Because a local source of water would be very useful in the operation of a permanent lunar base, discovery of water of any kind would have been of great interest.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. (Descent) water's going Off. Descent Water's Off. [Jack is closing the valve on the Descent Stage water tank.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. And it's...Man, is it...(Pause) Okay. Position your mike.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay; mikes are good.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Top of the page. [They are starting the top right-hand column on the cue card. In the Surface checklist, which contains the same information, they are starting the section labeled "Helmet/Glove donning" at the bottom of the left-hand column of 2-9 .]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Before we turn the (PLSS) fans on, let's make sure we've got...All I've got hooked here is the (LM) water. Those cables are all stowed. They're not in your way, are they?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: No, not in my way.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Pretty good. Let's...

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: (Garbled) though. Do you want to put this (garbled)?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yeah. (Pause) That's probably a little bit better.

A17A1163809.speaker: Parker
A17A1163809.text: 17, Houston. Over.

A17A1163809.speaker: LM Crew
A17A1163809.text: (Garbled)

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Go ahead, Houston.

A17A1163809.speaker: Parker
A17A1163809.text: Roger. We're still seeing the commander's Suit Disconnect valve's in Connect. (Pause) [Houston has noticed that the valve setting is incorrect. There is some telemetry from the ECS but very little from the suits: water and oxygen quantities and water temperature, only.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: (Responding to Houston after changing Gene's Suit Isolation Valve ) How's that? (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Parker
A17A1163809.text: Yep, there it goes. We got it. Thank you.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay, Bob. (Pause) (To Jack) Okay. We got to get the PLSS fan on. Don't forget that's (operating on PLSS) battery power. (Reading) We can don our helmets, check our drink bags , don our LEVAs , protective visors (down), secure our tool harness. (Pause) Our O2 umbilicals are already stowed. CDR's under the handhold. Verify the following. Now, where we pick up our...(Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Evans
A17A1163809.text: Okay, I've got to switch to window number 3 for end of target. Say again, the target number.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Have to put the helmets on, I think. [Schmitt - "The helmet itself was a clear plastic bubble with a padded head rest inside at the back. The Lunar Extravehicular Visor Assembly ( LEVA ) was everything else that sat on top on the helmet. It contained the sun visors and also passive thermal protection."]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay, yep. Then we pick up our gloves.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: I reckon.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yep, there it is. Okay. Well, let's do one at a time here.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: That's mine.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: That's yours. Okay. Do you want to turn your (PLSS) fan on for circulation (in the suit)?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Well, I guess I better. Fan's on.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: I'll pull this out just to get it out of your way.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. (Pause) 116:40:24 Cernan: Okay. Okay. All your candy bars and lemonade, and all that jazz are all clear. Water, I should say. (Pause) [Cernan - "We were going to be locked in the suit for maybe nine hours and we had a little water bag that we suspended from the inside rim of the suit. The bag hung on your chest and had a little one-way valve on the top of it so that you could turn your head and take a drink. It was like sucking on a nipple. And then we also had one of these high protein or high calorie sticks shaped like a ruler. It was a soft stick and you could chew it. We had it insid

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Mmm. That sounded good. [There is a solid, audible click as Jack's helmet locks into place.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Try it. Okay. It looks good here, Jack. (Pause) Okay. (Do you) want your LEVA ?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Guess so.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Enjoy it in there; you're going to be in there for a few hours.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Can't think of any place I'd rather be right now.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Sounds like you're in there, too. Oh, too far back. Okay, that's better. (Pause) I'm freezing my "you-know-what" off.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Me, too. (Both laugh) [They are still pre-cooling themselves with spacecraft water.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Does that look lined up to you?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Looks pretty good.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Let me...

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Wait a minute. (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: (Grunting) Let me get this down around. Okay. That's around behind you; thermally protected back there. That's below the OPS hose. [Gene is adjusting the back flap of Jack's LEVA .]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Right now, I'm hoping to get out of this warm. (Laughs)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. You're thermally...Let me double check that. The helmet is locked. Your visor is locked. It's one thing you don't want to lose among some others. (Pause) Okay. Okay, you want to give me a hand?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Not particularly. (Laughs)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: (Possibly referring to something that's blocking the neck ring) Oh, man. Where did that come from?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Watch your nose, drink bag, candy bars , popcorn! (Pause) Click, click, click.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Squeeze hard back there.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Want your fan (on)?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yep.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Looks good.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. I can hear the fan running. Oh, man. Whew! (Long Pause) Looks good here.

A17A1163809.speaker: Evans
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yeah. That's all right.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: There you go.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: It's new. Never been used before!

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Make sure that ( LEVA ) flap in back goes below that OPS hose. (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Want to put your protective visor down? (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yeah, if you got that thing all...You got it all down?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yep. 116:43:49 Cernan: You happy with it (the LEVA flaps) back there?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yes, sir. You're nice and protected.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Good Velcro. Okay. You're all covered here.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Not my other one is it? No.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: No.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Ohhh! (Pause) I think we've got to get tool harnesses here. "Don LEVAs ." Look at that scratch right in the middle of that thing. Okay. "Don LEVAs and lower protective visor."

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. [They are near the bottom of the lefthand column on page 2-9 .]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: "Secure harness and self-doff straps." (Pause) Okay. Stay where you are. (Pause) Can't miss it. (Pause) Okay. "Stow the LM O2 (hoses). And comm (cable)." Okay. They're all stowed; everything except (LM) water (hoses), right? [The self-doffing straps are secured to the side of the visor assembly and can be used to release the tool harness.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Verify the following. "Check your helmet and visor."

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. You check me. I'll read them. "Helmet and visor, aligned and locked."

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. That's locked.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. O2 cover's all locked. There's a peek at them.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: That's locked.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: "Purge valve"; everything down there.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: That's locked; that's locked.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: "Comm carrier."

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Stand by. That's locked.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. "Diverter Valve is vertical."

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Comm is that way. Diverter Valve is vertical. [With the selector in the vertical position, Gene is getting all of his oxygen flow into his helmet. With the valve in the horizontal position, he would direct part of the air flow into the torso.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: (Checking Jack's suit) Okay. One more time. Your helmet is locked; purge valve, locked. Yep. That (meaning the O2 connector)'s locked; that's locked; that's locked. And, let me see (the comm connector). Let me see! Yes sir, and that's locked. Don't let anything to chance (pause) today. And the Diverter Valve is vertical.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Comm; you checked, too.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Verify your old white dots.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Old white dots. My old white dots (pause) look good to me. [Cernan - "I think that, in order to make things easier and save time, all of the circuit breakers that had to be opened for an EVA were indicated with a white dot (on checklist pages 1-4 and 1-5 ). That way we could just go down the panel and shut off all of the things that we didn't want running while we were out on the surface. And all the switches that had to be changed had decals on them to show the proper EVA positions. It not only saved time, but it also cut down on mistakes; it was a lot riskier to read down a list of bre

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: (Can you) move a little?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yeah, I'll move.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. [Jack needs to turn so that he can look at his circuit breaker panel. With both of them in suits and wearing PLSSs, there isn't much room to spare and Jack needs to have Gene change his position slightly so that he can turn.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Got it. (Pause) I'm going to miss Danny being out there to hand us those light PLSSs.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: That's right. (Pause) [This is a reference to training exercises. They had practiced donning full-sized PLSSs inside the LM and then trade those for smaller, lightweight units once they were outside. Danny Schaiewitz was the engineer who handed them in. He worked for the manufacturer, Hamilton-Standard. According to Ed Brisson, who headed up the Hamilton-Standard operation at the Cape, Schaiewitz was well liked by the crews and socialized with many of them. Some of the other suit techs and engineers who were involved in Apollo 17 were Hamilton-Standard employees Jeff Robert, Ray Arnold, Gerry

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: You want it?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. I want the EVA decals, also, Jack.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yup.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: White dots plus decals.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Rog.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay, Bob, we're turning the page (that is, turning the cue card over).

A17A1163809.speaker: Parker
A17A1163809.text: Roger. We're right with you. (Long Pause) [In the Surface Checklist , they are in the middle of the right-hand column of 2-9 .]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. "Don EV gloves".

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay; on...

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Is that it?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: That's it. "Don EV gloves." Doing a little greasing in here. [Gene used lubricants on both the wrist rings and on his hands to protect them from abrasion. Here, he is probably greasing one of his hands. Jack used nylon glove liners in an effort to protect his hands. Note that Gene and Jack have taken care of all of the circuit breakers and switches prior to donning the bulky gloves.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: (Reading) And make sure your "wrist locks are locked. Glove straps adjusted and cover the wrist rings!" Golly. (Long Pause) I sure missed hearing it click, but they are locked. One of them is, anyway. (Pause) Okay, Jack. I verify...

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: (Laughs)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: What?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Guess what?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: They don't go on any easier in one-sixth g, do they?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: They break just as easily, too. [One of the glove tie-straps may have broken. If so, it is a matter of no great importance.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay, I've got my one glove locked. One of the old dust covers.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: I never had that happen in training; you did.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: It's locked. That's about as locked as it can go. Boy, I'd hate like the devil to have that (glove lock ring) pop open. Okay; that's very good. You want me to help you with one, or can you get it?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Well, I don't know. I've only worked on one so far.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: I've got a free hand before I grease it up. [Cernan - "I'd gotten one of my gloves on at this point, so this was my last chance to help Jack with an ungloved hand."]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: (Referring to the broken glove strap) I broke that one. (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: I'm telling you, from the looks of that soil out there, that drill may have a job ahead of it.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yeah, I didn't have a chance to mention that. I don't think the regolith is very thick, and I think you've got rocks below it. (Pause) [During this EVA, Gene will drill three 2.5-meter-deep holes, two for a heat flow experiment and one for a deep core. If the soil layer had been thinner than 2.5 meters, Gene would have had a difficult drilling task ahead of him. However, as Gene's drilling and other bits of information will show, the soil is actually about 5 meters deep and he will have relatively little difficulty.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: You got that?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Well, how does it look?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Let me take a look. (Pause) No.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Didn't make it, huh?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Yeah, well, let me...Hold your hand up here. Hold it up here. [Gene is helping Jack don his glove.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Looks good on my side. How is your side?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Good over here.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Thank you.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Get the old other hand. (Long Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. That's locked. (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Let me pull this (wrist cover) down for you. (Pause) Okay?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: And my other glove is locked. (Pause) Now for the fun in back. (Laughing) Oh, me; oh, my. (Pause) [Gene may be having trouble with one of his own glove straps.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: I think I got it! I think I got it. (Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Pull it and let go. Isn't that the word?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: That's what they tell me. Want me to get it?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: I got mine...No, I got it. (Have you) verified yours (is) locked?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Both my gloves are verified locked. (Pause) How does that grab you?

A17A1163809.speaker: Evans
A17A1163809.text: You know you look at - next to Macrobius A, there is a kind of a dark halo-type crater there. Very small one. And it doesn't have the appearance of a hummocky crater rim to it, at all. It looks like the material just kind of spreads out all over the area, but it doesn't have a hummocky appearance to it. I'm going to take a look at that again when I come back - on back around on the other side. There's a small mound down in the bottom of the crater, also. It's a domical-shaped structure in the bottom of that small crater. It's right next to J3. North of J3.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay; feels good.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Is your mirror on tight enough? Checklist on tight enough. (Pause) That's the best I can do; I guess. [Here, Gene is referring both to a small mirror that Jack has strapped to his left wrist (along with a watch) and to the cuff checklist on his other arm. As Gene mentions in a comment that follows 163:19:53 during preparations for EVA-3, the wrist mirror could be used to examine the front of the suit. However, on the landing missions, wrist mirrors were only flown on Apollo 16 and 17, primarily for reading the frame counter on the right-hand side of each Hasselblad magazine. On those two fligh

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Now what?

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Wrist rings are covered. "Note if PGA biting." No, mine's all right. Your's okay?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: No; it's fine. [They are both now sealed inside their suits but have not yet pressurized their suits with PLSS oxygen. The PLSS fans are on and, as air moves through the backpacks and carbon dioxide is removed by the LiOH canisters, the suit pressure decreases and the suits can slowly collapse around them and "bite". The Apollo 12 crew experienced some discomfort at this stage and suggested that, if other crews had the same problem, they briefly turn the PLSS oxygen on to partially inflate the suits and alleviate the biting.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. "LGC (Liquid Cooled Garment) cold as required." We been on cold all this time, right?

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Yes. [Cernan - "During my Gemini flight we had tried to use the flow of oxygen through the suit for cooling but decided that that wasn't adequate. So we developed the liquid-cooled garment. The way it worked was that the PLSS had two separate supplies of water. One was a closed-loop supply which was moved by a pump through the liquid-cooled garment. Then you had a sublimator which had another, physically-separate, open-loop supply of water. There was a cooling coil in the sublimator where the water in the closed loop could transfer heat to the open-loop supply and a diverter valve that determi

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Guess you can open that breaker, and I'll stop shivering. (Laughs)

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. [Jack is turning off the flow of LM water by pulling the LCG circuit breaker open.]

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: And, we can disconnect the LM water hoses. Let's help each other with those, so we don't screw up the other hoses.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay; breaker's open.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Let me turn around this way.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. Go ahead and I'll...(Pause)

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay. You want to get mine or you...

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: No, I'll get yours.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: Okay. First of all I'm going to take that (LM water hose) off. (Pause) (Connecting Jack's PLSS water hose) Okay. Now let me get your other one. There it is. Okay. We did this before. Stand right there. (Pause) It's locked, Jack.

A17A1163809.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1163809.text: Okay.

A17A1163809.speaker: Cernan
A17A1163809.text: It is locked. (I'll) get the (dust) cover on. (Pause) Okay. The cover is on. Okay. Yours off?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Hang on.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I'll push towards you. Make sure that thing falls in the hole, because yours didn't right away. (Pause) Did it fall in?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yeah. Yeah, it's in the hole. Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Dust cover on?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Dust cover's on.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: And my PGA is going to start biting here if we don't get going. (Pause) Okay. "PLSS diverter..." I've got to turn my oxygen on a second, Jack.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yeah, so do I. (Pause) [They are adding a little oxygen from the PLSS tanks to slightly inflate the suits.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: (Feeling the PLSS controls) That. That. There it is. Okay. It's on. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: A little hard to get it off, isn't it.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yeah. Okay. Mine is back off.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yeah, mine is (too).

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. "PLSS Diverter Valve, Min; verify."

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Mine's Min. [They are making sure they are in the minimum cooling setting.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. "PLSS Pump, On." That's to the right. [The pump moves the closed-loop supply of PLSS water through the Liquid-Cooled Garment.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: " Pressure Regs A and B , Egress." [Cernan - "We were telling the spacecraft ECS system that we were going into an Egress mode and are about to depressurize the cabin on purpose."]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: I think we're already at Egress. [Houston had requested the changed setting at 115:29:10.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Pump's on. We're in Egress.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, my pump's on. I can feel it running.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Keep talking. [They are now finished with 2-9 and are about to start a suit pressure integrity check at the top of 2-10 .]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Pressure integrity check. Okay. "PLSS O2, On." You ready for this? [They will inflate the suits so that they can check for leaks while the cabin is still pressurized.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: I hope so. 116:55:20 Cernan: Okay. PLSS O2 On. Mine's on. "Pres(sure) Flag and O2 Flag (will) clear, 3.1 to 3.4 (psi)." (Pause) Okay. I'm coming up. I know that. (Looking at his watch) Gee, it's 10 minutes to 6 at home. [That is, it's 5:50 PM Central Standard Time on 11 December 1972 in Houston. Gene and Jack are probably getting ready to start the stopwatch function on their Omega Speedmaster Professional wristwatches. The cuff checklist indicates planned EVA elapsed times at which various activities are to start and, by setting their watches, they will not have to depend on Houston to know w

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I'm still coming up (in pressure).

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Keep coming up. Just got mine on.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Oh, okay. Well, I'm ahead of you then. (Pause) Okay. The Press Flag will clear 3.7 - correction - 3.1 to 3.4 (psi).

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: What do you want me to do when I'm pressurized?

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Well, we want to make an integrity check.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yeah; but then what?

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Can you reach those (LM) water hoses right there? By chance? Before you get too hard? [The suits get relatively inflexible once they are inflated, making it even more difficult to turn or bend.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Stow them out of the way. Okay. When you get...When you get up...Okay. Press Flag cleared on the commander. (Pause) Okay. The O2 Flag did not clear. I'm at 3.8...Okay. O2 Flag cleared on the commander.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Still got an O2 Flag on the LMP.

A17A1165349.speaker: Evans
A17A1165349.text: No, it still looks like that area that's blown away there is Dog November - between Dog November and Dog Papa. And about 83.4 or something like that.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, you're not up (to 3.1 to 3.4 psi) yet; I suppose.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: No.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I'm going to take my PLSS O2 Off for one (minute). Counting 1 minute; 57. Let me know when you're up, Jack, and I'll give you a minute hack. [They will turn off the PLSS oxygen supply and spend a minute looking for indications of suit leaks.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1165349.text: Copy.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I'm clear.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. You up?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yep.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: You can turn your PLSS O2 off any time. Let me know when. Can you reach it? If you can't, I'll get it for you. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Why don't you get it.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay; Mark it.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: You're on the 30-second mark, and I'm on the minute mark. [The second hand on Gene's watch was at 0 when he started his integrity check and at 30 seconds when Jack's started.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay, and I'm at 3.8.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I'll give you a hack when...(Pause) Okay. I'm coming up on 45 seconds. (Pause) Okay. I'm one minute; I'm going back on. Okay, Houston. Commander went from 3.8 to about 3.67. I'll get yours on when you need it on, Jack. [This slight decrease in suit pressure is normal and indicates good suit integrity. The decay is due partly to the fact that it takes the oxygen a while to fill all the nooks and crannies, and partly to breathe-down. Once they start a continuous flow of oxygen, the PLSS will maintain a pressure of about 3.8 psi.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: I copy that, Commander. [They are still only 20 minutes behind schedule.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. And we'll pick Jack up here in about 10 more seconds.

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, Jack. I'm turning on. Did you mark it?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay, Houston; 3.8 to 3.6. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Hello, Houston; you copy the LMP?

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: Roger. Copy the LMP. Okay; and Challenger...

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Standing by for your Go for depress.

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: (Already prepared to give permission) You'll be glad to know you are Go for depress.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Thank you, Robert. I understand we are Go for depress.

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: That's affirm. [A little formality in the proceedings, the only one after the permission to stay for T-2.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, Jack. Can you reach the front (dump) valve, or do you want me to (get the overhead dump valve )?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Well, let me turn around here.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, on (circuit breaker panel) 16...First, around on 16. Cabin Repress, Open. [They are pulling a circuit breaker on panel 16 so that the LM's oxygen system won't try to repressurize the cabin when they open the dump valves in the forward and overhead hatches.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay; 16...

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Cabin Repress, Open.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Circuit breaker is coming open.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay, and Cabin Repress valve , Closed on the panel. [The repress valve is behind Jack's station on the right side of the cabin.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. The valve is closed.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. If you can't reach it (the dump valve on the forward hatch), I guess I can.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. I just had a momentary tone.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: So did I. I got it, too.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: I think it was when you closed the Repress valve. (Pause) Can you reach it (the forward dump valve )? If not, I'll reach the overhead one.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: I think you better reach the overhead one. [Opening the dump valve in the forward hatch requires bending over slightly against suit pressure. Reaching the overhead valve requires raising an arm and can be a less difficult maneuver in the cramped confines of the LM, especially for a six-footer like Gene. Training photo KSC-72PC-540 shows the overhead valve at the upper right.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Slip over to your right. Some more. Let me turn here. (Pause) Wait a minute, I got to turn (to reach the overhead valve). [Jack must be facing inboard. Gene wants him to lean toward the window so that Gene can reach behind him to get the overhead valve. In order to reach up with his right arm, Gene must also be facing inboard.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. How far down are we going to take it? 3.5 (psi), right?

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yeah, wait a minute. I'm not there yet.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Well, I just want to make sure that I'm watching (the cabin pressure gauge). [While Jack watches the cabin pressure gauge, Gene will open the overhead valve and let the pressure decrease from 5 psi to 3.5 psi. At that point, he will reclose the valve by putting it in the Auto position. In Auto, the dump valve will open only if the cabin pressure exceeds 5.4 psi. The suit pressure regulators will try to track the decreasing cabin pressure, and keep the difference at 3.9 psi. Because of a finite response time, the relative suit pressure will go up initially - to about 5.3 psi - and then decay. T

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay; now. Okay, coming open. You ready? You reading the checklist?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Stand by Auto. (Cabin) Repress (valve) is Closed.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Say when.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: You ready?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute, wait a minute.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Got the wrong place (in the checklist). "Open, then Auto at 3.5." Okay; go ahead.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Here it comes. I can see daylight through it. [Cernan - "The valve, as I recall, was just a little circular disk that was held against a seal by the pressure in the cabin. It had a little lever and I could get enough mechanical advantage to crack it a little bit and vent some of the air. I want to remember that we had some screw-type vents on the hatch of the Command Module; but I'm sure that this LM valve wasn't like that. Nothing in the LM was very fancy unless it absolutely had to be. Everything had to be as lightweight as possible, and that usually meant very unsophisticated designs.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay, it's coming down. Okay. That's four (psi). Stand by.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Mark. 3.5.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. It (meaning the overhead valve)'s off.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. And your cuff gauge should not be below 4.6, and mine's at...

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Mine's at 5.0.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: 5.1. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. The suit circuit is locked up at 4.5. [The Suit Circuit Relief (Valve) is in the Auto position and will open only if the suit circuit pressure is greater than about 4.3 psi. Note that the suits were disconnected from the suit circuit when Jack closed the Suit Isolation Valves at 116:33:21 and 116:39:14.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: We're at 3.5 (psi cabin pressure) and holding. And I'm decaying. I'm below 5.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
