A17A1165349.text: So am I. [Pressure regulators on the suits are gradually reducing the pressure difference to 3.8 psi.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Verify that; okay. 117:01:31 Cernan: Okay. I'll start my watch. [The are starting the stopwatch function on their Omega Speedmaster watches as per the comment following 116:55:20 .]

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: Okay. We verify and we're counting.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Watches started.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. "Overhead or Forward Dump Valve , Open". [They will now reopen the dump valve and let the cabin pressure fall to zero. This is the start of the EVA.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Here it comes.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: And it's going down.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: You going to want me to put this in Auto afterwards or not? So, I can turn around, Jack.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Stand by.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: (Garbled) Open...

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: (Garbled)...

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: ...leave it Open.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Leave it Open.

A17A1165349.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1165349.text: At your convenience, High Gain to Auto.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: No, we don't (put it in Auto), because then we don't want that hatch to get closed. (Pause) [Cernan - "We wanted to leave the dump valve s open because we were going to close the hatch for thermal reasons while we were outside. By leaving the dump valves open, we were making sure that, if any air bled into the cabin for any reason, then pressure couldn't build up inside the LM and make it tough to get that hatch open. Now, I also think that we did have an ability to open the dump valve (in the forward hatch) from the outside. I really believe we did, as I remember. But it was obviously still s

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: I got to turn around here. Oh, boy! (Long Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Boy, you sure get heavy (meaning "stiff") at 5 (psi), don't you? [As the cabin pressure drops, the relative suit pressure increases for a while.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Where are we (in the checklist)? (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: We're right here, huh? (Pause) [They are at the top of the right-hand column on 2-10 , waiting for the cabin pressure to drop low enough - to about 0.2 psi - that Gene can open the hatch.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: What that was...(Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: What's cabin (pressure), Jack? (No answer) Do you read, Jack?

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: Jack, this is Houston.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Wait a minute.

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: CDR, we're not reading the LMP either.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Now, how do you read, Jack?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. You're loud and clear.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: We got a switch in the wrong place as usual, Bob.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: I just hit the Mode Select; that's all.

A17A1165349.speaker: Parker
A17A1165349.text: Okay. We copy.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. "Partially open the forward hatch", when we can.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Can you zap over to the left as much as you can?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: To the right, you mean?

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yeah. To the north. [Jack must be facing forward now.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: To the north.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: The north.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: The north. (Both laugh) Okay, it's about 0.2 (psi), Gene. [Fully open, either the forward or overhead dump valve will reduce the cabin pressure from 5 psi to 0.08 psi in 180 seconds. With both valves open, the time would be 90 seconds. Including the 17 seconds used to bleed the cabin to 3.5 psi, they are now 141 seconds into the depress.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Let me...

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: You going to be able to get to it?

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yep. (Pause) You betcha. I've come this far. I'm not going to miss getting that hatch open. (Pause) [Cernan - "The lunar module, in contrast to the command module, was nothing but a tin can that buckled when you pressurized it; a lightweight tin can just strong enough to hold the pressure we needed. When we depressurized the LM, all the skin surfaces relaxed; and when we got back in and pressurized, the hatch would bow out and you could sort of feel and see the panels bow out. The hatch was nothing but a flimsy little piece of metal with a seal on it. And it didn't have a big fancy lock. It ju

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Hey, something just flew out (the hatch). [Jack is probably looking out his window and has seen a bit of debris and/or ice expelled by the escaping air. They are about 153 seconds into the depress.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: It's open now.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Gosh, look at those trajectories. (Laughs)

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yeah. Put just enough air in here, we're...Okay; it's open, babe.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. [Gene has pulled the hatch open against about 0.2 psi of cabin pressure, and that is enough of a pressure difference to create a noticeable wind blowing out the hatch. The flow of air is visible because the moisture in it turns to ice crystals as it expands, and also because the wind picks up stray bits of paper and/or other debris.]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: It is open. (Pause)

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. "Final prep, PLSS (sublimator) primary H2O." I've got to figure out how to open that now.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. (Pause) When you're at 5 psi, it's (hard to reach the PLSS controls)...

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: We never did really train for this in the right way.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Yeah, we did. [Schmitt - " I know I had done this once in the KC-135 aircraft, but I don't remember whether or not that was an actual training exercise. We only got about 20 seconds at a time of one-sixth g in the airplane. And maybe we never even tried to open the PLSS (sublimator) water valve for lack of time. It was certainly harder on the Moon."] [Cernan - "Another explanation is that we may not have trained with a 3.5 psi pressure difference. If not, then we wouldn't have had 5 psi suit pressures at this point in training."]

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Okay. My water is Open.

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: And my water is Open. (Pause; breathing heavily) Okay. Well, let's see; "Rest until cooling sufficient; 3.7 to 4.6 (psi)." I'm to 4.9; coming down.

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: Yeah, I am, too. Coming down. [Cernan - "When you moved around, like we were here, inside the lunar module, and then when we were getting out and going down the ladder, it was work even in one-sixth gravity. We had heart rates going up at times, on the lunar surface, to 140 beats a minute. And I think probably through most of the EVA that I did breathe heavy because I've got a fairly good lung capacity - I've never smoked - and I tend to do that. Throughout many of these tapes on the lunar surface activity, you'll find me taking deep breaths and sounding like I'm "breathing heavily". But it re

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: CWEA (Caution and Warning Electronics Assembly) status. PREAMPS and ECS. Can you see that?

A17A1165349.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1165349.text: See a PREAMPS, and I see ECS. Barely. [Schmitt - "The ECS light came on in response to cabin depressurization. The fact that it came on confirmed that we were depressurizing; and showed that the warning system was working properly."]

A17A1165349.speaker: Cernan
A17A1165349.text: Okay. Water Sep Component Light, On.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well, the next thing it says is that Gene gets out.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I don't see that.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: That's what it says on my (cuff) checklist. (Pause) [They have completed all the steps on the EVA Prep cue card. Their EVA checklists are quite different, reflecting the division of tasks. Gene and Jack are on EVA-1 cuff checklist pages CDR-6 and LMP-6. Jack is joking, of course. The first items on LMP-6 after "Cabin Depress" are "CDR Egress" and "Assist CDR".] [The small area available to the crew at the front of the cabin is best illustrated by images taken during final Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 LM close-out on the pad at the Cape prior to launch.] [An Apollo 16 view from above shows the LMP's

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Good heavens!

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: That means you got to get out of the way so I can open the hatch.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, I'm going to have to turn around a little, I think, so I can help you. [Jack will turn from facing forward to facing left so that he can reach over the open hatch (the top is waist high) and help push Gene down below the instrument panel.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. (Pause) Boy, beware of that corner.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: This high pressure...(Laughs)

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yeah. I tell you at 4-1/2 (psi), you're really pretty heavy (means "stiff").

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: What was that that came shooting up here? A piece of bread? (Laughs) Would you believe that?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yeah, I'd believe it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Why is our hatch open? Somebody opened our hatch. Are you getting cooling?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I'm beginning to, I think. I still got a Water Flag. (But I'm) not hot.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Stand by. Okay. (Long Pause) How does the water pressure look, Houston? [The cooling system is not yet up-to-speed; hence the warning flag.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Evans
A17A1170525.text: Okay.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Challenger, they're looking just a little bit low. We're still expecting them to build up. It's going to take a little while. [In order to get out of the spacecraft, Gene has to face left and get down on his knees. He then maneuvers himself to his left to get his feet pointing out the hatch. He will then move his legs out, gradually lowering his torso toward the floor so that he can crawl out backwards. There isn't much room - fore and aft - and it takes patient effort to get out.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. I'm getting down on my knees out here. How am I looking, Jack?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You're just fine. I'm holding you away from the DEDA...(correcting himself) the DSKY.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. I'm going to put this visor down now, I think. (Pause) How does that look to you?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: What?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: How are my legs? Am I getting out?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, I don't know. I can't see your legs.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh, okay. (Laughs)

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I think you're getting out though, because there's not as much of you in here as there used to be. Oh, hey, Gene, when I get down there, I got to fix your tool harness (on the PLSS). Hold it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Can you reach it?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: It's come off the bottom again.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Can you reach it?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, I can't do it now, because it's come off from the bottom. I'll have to...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh, the bottom of the PLSS, huh?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Yeah.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Well, my legs are out. Keep that hatch open.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Can you squat down any further, because you're hooked on...(Pause) You're making it worse. Okay.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: How's that?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Now, be careful because you might hook it on something down there.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh, the tool harness?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Yeah. The back. It's loose on your back; on the back of the PLSS.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh, man, I don't like that. Okay. I'll watch it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, I'll fix it when I get out there.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (To himself) Okay. I'm still reading 4.0 (psi). Houston, the Commander is on the porch of Challenger.

A17A1170525.speaker: Evans
A17A1170525.text: Okay, Pan Camera Power - Let's see. Pan Camera Power is Off.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Roger. We copy you, Commander, and your feedwater pressure is looking much better...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: How am I...(Stops to listen to Bob)

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: ...now, and you're probably getting cooling.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Everything else look good to you?

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: That's affirmative. [In reviewing tapes for all of the missions, it seemed as though the LMPs had an easier time getting in and out of the cabin; or, at least, didn't talk about their struggles as much.] [Schmitt - "Most of the LMPs were smaller than the Commanders; that might have something to do with it. And you could open the door a bit more without someone standing behind it. And mostly, if somebody's there to help you, he's going to help you. And, if they're not there, you're not going to have all this conversation."] [Cernan - "I think the main reason that the Commanders had a bit more t

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay, Jack. I'm going to get the MESA (Modular Equipment Stowage Assembly). [As per CDR-6 , Gene is reaching for the D-ring to release the MESA, a table-like structure containing tools, replacement batteries, food, etc. When Gene pulls the lanyard, the MESA will fold outward about 120 degrees from the northwest face of the LM. Later, Jack will pivot the MESA back up to a comfortable working height. By allowing the MESA to pivot beyond 90 degrees, the designers have made it possible for the crew to use the MESA even if there happens to be a small crater right where they need to stand.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay. And I'll have an ETB ready for you (as per LMP-6 ). [The Equipment Transfer Bag (ETB) is a soft-sided, padded bag about the size of a piece of luggage big enough to fit under an airline seat, being about 2 feet long and about one foot in each of the other dimensions. On Apollos 11 through 15, a TV camera had been mounted on the MESA so that the Commander's climb down the ladder could be watched. On Apollo 16, TV coverage of John Young's first step was eliminated because of the need to conserve LM battery power after the six-hour landing delay. For Apollo 17, the camera is stowed and ther

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (Reaching for the D-ring) Oh, man; oh, man; oh, man.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Deploy, MESA!

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (Chuckling) Okay. Here it comes. (Pause) There she goes, Babe.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Hey, hey! [The MESA is located below Jack's station, to the right of the ladder from his perspective in the cabin, and he can watch the MESA deployment out his window.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: There she is. All the way down; it looks like. Okay. I jettisoned...Oh, you want an ETB?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: That's up to you.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yeah.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You're the commander.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I got it! I got it. And, the (suit) pressure looks like it's started to stabilize at 3.8. I don't know whether I'm getting cooler or not, but I feel pretty good.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Okay. We copy that.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: How about a jett(ison) bag, too?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. (Pause) [This is a bag containing the day's accumulation of empty food bags and other trash. Later, Gene will get the jett bag out of the way by kicking it under the descent stage.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (Using the lanyard to lower the ETB to the ground) Oh, Jack, I could swing it over the - it won't be any problem - over the strut. Okay; and the jett bag is swinging free.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You mean the ETB.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: ETB. Oh, man. This looks like a Santa Claus bag.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: It is. [Gene is using a lanyard rather than the clothesline-like Lunar Equipment Conveyor ( LEC ) used on Apollos 11 through 15. Jack recalls that the LEC was "just another case of somebody looking for spiders under rocks", assuming that things were going to be harder to do than they actually were. Gene is using the lanyard to lower the ETB because it contains the cameras and, therefore, he doesn't want to risk dropping it.] [Cernan - " I think that when I was backup for Apollo 14 we had some kind of conveyor belt that we would use shipping things up and down. Quite frankly, as I recall, it wa

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh, boy. There it goes. The Rover looks in good shape. ETB is down there. Okay. I've got all my visors down. Jack, I wouldn't lower your gold visor until after you get on the porch, because it's plenty dark out here. [As on all Apollo missions, the LM was landed to the west, early in the local lunar morning. The ladder is on the forward, west-pointing strut and, therefore, will be in the LM shadow throughout the mission. As Gene stands at the top of the ladder, the Rover is stowed to his right, in the southwest sector of the descent stage. The Rover is stowed in a folded configuration. There i

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (Going down the items on cuff checklist page LMP-6 ) Tape recorder...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: ...I'm on my way (down the ladder).

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: ...is off. Sensitivity, max and max. [Jack is turning off on-board recorder to conserve tape during the EVA. It won't be turned on again until about 140:04:26 during EVA-2 Preps. Jack is also setting voice sensitivity controls on the comm system. On Apollo 11, Buzz Aldrin did not set his sensitivity quite to maximum and, as a result, his transmissions were broken throughout the EVA.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay, Houston. The Commander is about three quarters of the way down. (Pause) [Cernan - " Getting down the ladder in the suit wasn't any particular problem. It would have been a lot easier without a suit; but, of course, we wouldn't have been going outside without them and they performed just tremendously, admirably. There had been a tremendous amount of technological development in the suit between my EVA on Gemini IX and Apollo 17. I mean, walking on the surface with the mobility of a Gemini EVA suit would have been damn near impossible. It was just an order of magnitude difference in techno

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Jack, I'm out here. Oh, my golly! Unbelievable! Unbelievable; but is it bright in the Sun. (Pause) Okay! We landed in a very shallow depression. That's why we've got a slight pitch-up angle. (It's a) very shallow, dinner-plate-like, dish crater just about the width of the struts (meaning the total span of the landing gear). How you doing, Jack?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Fine. Getting the circuit breakers verified (as per LMP-6 ).

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: The LM looks beautiful. (Pause) Oh, do we have boulder tracks coming down (the side of North Massif). Let me see exactly where we are. I think I may be just in front of Punk.

A17A1170525.speaker: Evans
A17A1170525.text: You know, it's funny. It wasn't as bright - That pass over - This last pass - as it was the time before.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Okay. We copy that, Gene; and are the boulder tracks...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I'm beginning to...

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: ...to both the north and south?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (Responding to Bob's question) Okay. On the North Massif we've got very obvious boulder tracks. A couple of large boulders come within 20 or 30 feet of the (break in slope)...Looks like where we can get to them; there's a couple I know we can get to. Well, the Sun angle is such that, what I saw on the South Massif earlier, I can't see very well. But, I know there were boulder tracks over there. Bear Mountain...Boy, it's hard to look to the east (toward the Sculptured Hills). Bear Mountain and the Sculptured Hills have a very, very similar texture on the surface. The Sculptured Hills' (texture)

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Okay. We copy that, Gene. Have you got an LMP with you yet?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well, here come his feet. Jack, let me make sure...We didn't have an awful lot of dust on landing; but I can dig my foot in 8 or 10 inches, and I know we're at least that thick. [That is, the regolith is at least 8 to 10 inches deep.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: There's a small little 1-meter crater right in front of us with a whole mess of glass right in the middle. That's right in front of the MESA, as a matter of fact. Right where I want to park the Rover. Jack, you're looking good.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Beautiful, guys; beautiful. 117:14:42 Cernan: (Gene is walking around the LM to get his bearings) I'm going to take a quick look back. I think this is Poppie, and I can give you a real better idea where we are. [There is a 20-meter-diameter, sharp-rimmed crater about 30 meters east of the LM. Gene may be thinking this is Poppie and is probably walking over to it at this point. At 117:45:45, Jack will take a color pan from behind the LM and a little north. Frame AS17-147- 22511 shows the crater east of the LM and a set of footprints going out to it. Close examination of the foreground prints sh

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (As per LMP-6 ) Hatch is closed, barely.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Hey, Jack, don't lock it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I'm not going to lock it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: We've got to go back there. You lose the key, and we're in trouble. [By now, this was an old Apollo joke, having been used in some form by the 11, 12, 15, and 16 crews.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Oh, I'm on the porch!

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Who said this place was smooth? Oh, boy! There's a lot of local depressions here I didn't figure existed.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Hey, who's been tracking up my lunar surface?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Hey, Bob, I'm east of the LM now. I'm east of the LM, and the back strut of the LM is...Well, the LM straddles this crater I talked about, and that's where we get the pitch angle; the back strut is probably right down in the eastern one-third of that crater. Just a very subtle crater.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Hey, man; you had some forward velocity.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: That's what I wanted to have. (Pause) [The footpad imprints indicate a little forward motion at touchdown.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Boy, I look at some of these rocks that are filleted here, Jack, and there sure are a lot of sparklies in them. Awful lot of sparklies. [Cernan -"Fillets were not a surprise. We expected to see fillets on some sides of a boulder and not on others and saw fillets almost everywhere we went. On some of them, you could almost draw lines in the direction that the stuff had come from. We had a good background from training and knew where to look and how to interpret what we saw."]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You landed in a crater! 117:16:11 Cernan: That's a pretty good shot. [Schmitt - "At some point, and maybe it's here, I stepped down off the ladder onto the sloping side of a boulder which had little balls of glass and debris that made it very slick. And I slipped and my left leg went out from under me. Fortunately, I was still hanging onto the ladder."] 117:16:15 Cernan: Okay. I'm going to get to work in a minute, just as soon as I take a look at Trident (actually Poppie).

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Why don't you come over here and let me deploy your (PLSS/OPS) antenna (as per CDR-6 and LMP-6).

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Just walk around for one second. [Gene is suggesting that Jack take a moment for familiarization, as per LMP-7 .] [Cernan - "You adapt very, very quickly. You very quickly realize, probably in the first couple of minutes, that you don't need to take baby steps or regular steps to get anywhere. Somehow your brain and your body coordinate your movements and, if you're going to go any distance - 10 or 12 or 15 feet or further away - you start skipping or hop-skipping to get where you're going. And it's not like you start running. It's just that you move with such ease. Later on, when you st

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (Laughs) Hey, man, put your visor down.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: And, I'll be over there, and you can fix my tool harness. I don't like that thing loose.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I don't like it loose, either. What are you doing over there (by Poppie)? We're supposed to be working.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I was just going to give them a fix (meaning another estimate of where they landed). All these little craters, Jack, have got glass in the bottom of them. Here's another one. [Gene remembers that they trained to recognize glass, an indication of very fresh impacts.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (To Houston) There's very clear sweeping of the surface by the descent plume out, oh, about 10 meters. No, 15 meters. (Pause) (To Gene) Come over here, and I'll fix your antenna.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Hey, Bob, how big is Poppie supposed to be?

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Gene has probably started back to the LM. Frames AS17-147- 22513 and 22514 show two sets of footprints. Both were made by Gene - one on the way out, one on the way back.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: It looks on the map...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I didn't hear you. You cut out.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Okay. It looks on the map like it's about 75 meters in diameter. Fairly subtle.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Okay, I tell you where I think I landed...Oh, about 100 meters from Poppie at 10 o'clock. [Gene may be referring to an unnamed, 200-meter-diameter crater NNE of the LM. The near rim is about 150 meters from the LM. An alternative interpretation is that Gene is referring to the crater he just walked to, which is Poppie. This interpretation would seem to require that Gene has mis-spoken. They are about 100 meters NNW of the center of Poppie or, roughly, at 2 o'clock. I am inclined to believe that Gene has mis-spoken and has, for the moment, correctly identified Poppie. However, at no time

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You think that's Poppie, huh?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: I think so. I think...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: That's an awful big hole. 117:17:42 Cernan: (Letting himself be talked out of it) Well, I know. I got to look around a little more. It sure is not Trident. Bend over and I'll...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: It might be part of Trident.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: ...get your antenna. Get your antenna. Oh, a little more. (Pause) God, it's beautiful out here.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, hang on.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yep. (Pause) [Jack probably has his knees bent but would not be kneeling.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (To Bob) Okay. The immediate surf(ace)...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Not yet. Yeah, you talk to them. I don't want you to stand up yet.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: The surface is moderately cohesive, which holds a pretty good bootprint. Very fine-grained. Gene's (garbled) looks very much like previous soils (that is, soils at other Apollo landing sites). (To Gene) You got it?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yeah.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: You got a hole behind you now.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well, I'll stand in it, and you can get at it better. [Jack is now releasing Gene's antenna, held down by a loop of Velcro on the top of the OPS to keep it out of the way as they go through the hatch.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, you got me right in (that is, facing) the Sun. Can you come around this way? Ho-ho. (Laughs) I'm going to have to get upstream of you.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Look, you get up on the hill, and I'll get in the hole.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Yeah. There you go. Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Don't move too fast. Boy, your feet look like you just...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: (Finishing the thought) Walked on the Moon, huh? Well, I tell you Gene, I think the next generation ought to accept this as a challenge. (Pause) Let's see them leave footsteps like these someday. Got another...Well, that'll be all right. 117:19:12 Cernan: Okay. What did you do with my tool harness?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I'm going to work on it; that's what I'm going to do. (Pause) Whoa; hold still.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. (Pause) Boy, I tell you, looking to the east, you might just as well forget it. (Pause)

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Well, let's see. How's this thing...I'm going to have to loosen it.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well, if you could just stretch it around.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: I can't.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: You can't, huh?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: But I will be in a minute.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Don't loosen it to the point where you can't get it back on.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Won't. (Pause) Okay. You're almost reconfigured.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay. (Pause) Somebody tied you on wrong, too. They've got the strap reversed for the Velcro. Okay, Gene. I think that'll hold.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay, and I'm going to...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: If it doesn't, I'll fix you again.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Man, there's sparklies in the soil, Jack. You can just look at it. See them all over? Very fine-grained. It's sparkly, that's all. Bob, I'm going to Min cooling...(correcting himself) or, intermediate cooling .

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Boy, that sure...

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: See the soil sparkle?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Yeah, I think that's little (pieces of) glass.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Let's go back here and get to work, and I'll show you that crater that's got nothing but glass in the bottom.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: That's a vesicular rock of some kind there, Geno. It almost looks like a Mono Craters (California) pumice, but don't quote me. [Jack hasn't had a good enough a look to make any confident statements about the rock and doesn't want anyone - the press in particular - to jump to any conclusions.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Bob, I have to reiterate. Even the small, even the very small - the 1- and 2-inch, 3-inch - fragments that are laying around here - have been dusted and filleted...

A17A1170525.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1170525.text: I hope you haven't - I hope you haven't spilled any; and, by the way, LMP is on the surface now, too.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Do-tu-doo!

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: ...with the dark mantle. 117:21:16 Schmitt: And that sweeping by the descent stage goes all the way out there, Houston, to where we were; which was about 50 meters, I guess. Hey, man...(Jack stumbles) Whuh, whuh, whuh, whuh. Hey, these rocks, they almost have a very light pinkish hue to them, and they're not obviously breccia. Now, that's like a breccia there. But this is something else again.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yeah. I don't think there is any place you could land around here where you wouldn't have one foot(pad) in a crater.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Looks like a vesicular, very-light-colored porphyry of some kind; it's about 10 or 15 percent vesicles. I'm right in front (that is, west) of the LM. Quite a few of the rocks look of that type. Sort of a pinkish hue to them. The texture is coarse, but I'm not sure how crystalline they are, yet. [A porphyry is a rock composed of two different sizes of crystals, usually large crystals imbedded in a matrix of small crystals. Vesicles are spherical imprints of gas bubbles trapped in a solidifying rock. The vesicle may be glass-lined if the rock cooled quickly, or lined with crystals if the cooling

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay; back to work. Jack, when you put up the ETB (on the MESA), check down there below it. [Apparently, the scissors fell out of the ETB as Gene was lowering it. He may have seen them fall, or he may have noticed them on the ground when he got to the bottom of the ladder.]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Oh-ho-ho. (Laughs)

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Okay, let me take a look at the Rover. [As per CDR-7 , Gene will examine the Rover before pulling off the protective thermal blanket that covered it on the way out from Earth and, finally, preparing for the actual deployment. In the meantime, Jack will adjust the MESA height and then take care of the other MESA items on LMP-7 .]

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Let's don't forget those ( scissors ).

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Yep.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: That's my fault; I guess (for not packing the ETB carefully enough).

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well...

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Okay.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Oh man, I tell you, we came down at just a little forward velocity. Look at that, right there. About a (one)-foot slip on the pad. I tell you, there's craters all over here. Okay, baby. I'd sure like to think that that (Rover) wheel is where it's supposed to be. It looks good to me. (Pause) Our next little vehicle to work. (Long Pause while Gene examines the Rover, using cuff checklist page CDR-7 as a guide) Okay. Bob, so far, the Rover looks pretty good.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Roger; sounds good, Geno.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: (To Parker) Hey, let me ask you. When I was behind the LM, I could look right into an area and see the bell of the ascent stage. I never realized that before, but I guess that's normal, huh?

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Yeah; We saw it on the (launch) pad (at the Cape). Remember.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Barely.

A17A1170525.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1170525.text: Remember when we went out there?

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: The only reason I asked, Bob, I'm sure it's normal, and it doesn't look anything's missing, it's just right into the Sun.

A17A1170525.speaker: Parker
A17A1170525.text: Yeah, the consensus of opinion down here is that you can, also.

A17A1170525.speaker: Cernan
A17A1170525.text: Well, that's probably the best place in the world to get a consensus of opinion from. Okay, Jack, it's about work time. I've got this Rover about ready for your pull up there.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Hey, we have a picture, 17. We have a picture.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Jack? (Responsing to Bob) Ah, beautiful, babe. It's all yours. I hope it moves now. [The TV is being controlled from Houston by Ed Fendell . We are looking south toward Bear Mountain, which is the low, dark hill just left of center. Fendell starts a clockwise TV pan.] [The original, 1972 transcription of Gene's transmission at 118:14:25 is "You have? Ah, beautiful, babe. It's all yours. I hope it moves now." In April 2012, Journal Contributor Vlad Pustynski asked me to check the audio because he did not believe "You have?" is what Gene actually said. Listening to the audio, it was immediately

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: It does.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I hope it moves. You'll find out...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Noticing the TV in motion) Hey, it moves! It's alive! [Note that the MP3 clip includes a repetition of Gene's and Jack's transmissions at 14:31 and 14:35. It seems likely that the repetition is due to a switch in the signal handling configuration in Houston from audio-only to combined audio-video.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: And...

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, Bob, I'm going to get SRC 1. [Gene is starting checklist page CDR-12 . The Sample Return Containers (SRCs) or "rock boxes", are machined from solid pieces of aluminum and are designed to hold an internal vacuum in the interest of returning samples to Earth without contamination. The SRC seal mechanism consists of a strip of soft indium metal - a few millimeters wide - in the rim of the lid, a matching knife edge in rim of the body, and O-rings outside both the indium strip and the knife edge. Prior to the mission, each of the boxes was packed inside a vacuum chamber so that there is now

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay, could we have a EMU check on you fellows when convenient? [The Extravehicular Mobility Unit is the combination of the suit and the PLSS and as Gene says, it is a self-contained spacecraft. Here, Bob wants readings on oxygen quantity, pressure, and warning flag status. The oxygen gauge and warning flags are on the top surface of the RCU and can be read - as long as the lighting is adequate - merely by looking down. The pressure gauge is wrist-mounted. As Jack explains later, this request for an EMU check is also a disguised suggestion that they slow down.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Commander is 3.8 (psi) plus. I must be 80 percent (oxygen remaining) and no (warning) flags and no (warning) tones.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay, LMP is about 80...Let me see. (Counting marks on the gauge) 75...About 80 percent (oxygen), and no flags, no tones. (Pause) I got 83 percent. [Fendell reaches the clockwise pan limit and finds Jack working at the left side of the Rover. Jack is transfering film magazines from the ETB into the enclosed stowage space underneath the CDR seat, as per LMP-11 .] 118:15:22 Parker: Okay, copy that. And you've sure got a lot of stuff on the Rover already.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yeah, Mag Helen has just gone into (that is, under) the seat. [The magazines are labeled "AA", "BB" and so on and usually are referred to as "Alpha", "Bravo", etc. Here, Jack begins a verbal game of using female names and will do so throughout most of the mission.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that. (Pause) [Those listening to the audio track may have noticed a high-pitched beep at the start and end of each of Bob's transmissions. Markus Mehring has provided a discussion of these Quindar Tones .] 118:15:45 Schmitt: Mag Cynthia is in there. (Pause) [Fendell has started a counter clockwise pan and is looking west across the LMP seat and the right-rear Rover wheel toward the western entrance to the Valley of Taurus-Littrow.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, Bob, SRC-1 is open. [After opening the rock box, Gene is removing SCB-1 and, at 118:17:39, will hang the SCB from the tool gate. He is at the top of checklist page CDR-12.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Mag) Gail is in. (Pause) [Fendell is looking at the South Massif. Note the dark tracks just beyond the LM shadow.] 118:16:09 Cernan: Jack, watch these SRCs. They don't like to lock on this table very well.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: They never have. (Pause) [There is a small stand or table on the MESA big enough to hold one of the SRCs. There are locks on the table to hold the SRC still while it is being packed or unpacked.] [Fendell is looking at Bear Mountain.] 118:16:24 Parker: Okay, and Jack, did you get mag...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: ...Charlie as well?

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: That's affirm. [Fendell is looking toward the LM ladder with the heavily-shadowed East Massif in the background. The Rover is parked west of the ladder and slightly north of it.] 118:16:32 Parker: Okay. And we did not copy your cuff gauge reading (suit pressure) down here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Oh, you didn't? Well, maybe that's because I didn't give it to you. 3.9 (psi). No wonder that's so much work. [Nominal suit pressure is 3.8 psi. Anything higher makes the suit even stiffer and the work correspondingly more difficult. Here, however, Jack is joking; the difference between 3.8 and 3.9 would hardly be noticeable.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Go ahead. Copy that. (Pause) [Fendell finds Gene at the MESA. He has his back to us as he tries to get the rock box securely attached to the MESA table.] 118:16:53 Cernan: Okay, Bob, SRC 1 is...(Pause) She sure won't stay in the MESA very...(Pause) There, let me try that. Okay, that will stay there. Okay, Bob. It's closed. It sure doesn't seem like it wants to stay there, though. And the organic sample has been sealed.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that. [As on all of the missions except Apollo 11, each of the rock boxes contains an Organic Sample Monitor consisting of a small Teflon bag and, in the bag, rolls of very clean aluminum metal. At the top of the Teflon bag are two metal sealing strips, very similar to those in the individual sample bags described below. Here, Gene is sealing the bag by twisting the metal strips and folding tabs at either end. The aluminum will then be exposed to any contamination from the spacecraft and the PLSSs in much the same way that the lunar samples will be exposed, thereby allowing experimenters

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: (Seeing the TV move) I guess you believe we're here now, huh?

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Now we believe you're here. We see you in person. [Fendell finds Jack, who is still putting film magazines and other gear under Gene's seat as per LMP-11 . The North Massif is in the background.] 118:17:20 Cernan: Okay. Bob, the SRC cover will not stay closed. It just slowly springs up. There's nothing I can seem to do for it. I might be able to set something - a blanket - on top or something. [That is, a piece of the thermal blanket that Jack had previously removed from the MESA. The lid needs to be closed to keep the interior of the box from being heated by sunlight.] Video Clip ( 3 min 07 s

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay, stand by on that. We'll get back with you.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. I'm putting...(Responding to Bob) Yeah, it just flops open. I'm taking SCB-1 to the Tool Gate (as per CDR-12 ). [Gene goes to the rear of the Rover.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I'll get me a hammer and I'll give you a gravimeter reading.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: No, you won't. [The Traverse Gravimeter is sitting on the back of the Rover and needs to be still for three minutes to produce a good reading. Jack is mounting the Buddy SLSS (see below) behind Gene's seat; and, as he works, the Rover jiggles. Until he is done, the gravimeter measurement can not be started.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Not until you're done. I'll go get the (U.S.) flag (out of the MESA) then. Guess what? We're here again. (Pause) 118:18:06 Schmitt: The Buddy SLSS is on the Rover. (Pause) [Cernan - "I don't remember much about it, except that it was a buddy-breathing system - a set of hoses and stuff - that would let us share one of the oxygen supplies if the other one failed. It would have restricted our movements, but it also would have got us back to the LM."] [The Buddy SLSS was actually a set of hoses which would have allowed them to share cooling water rather than oxygen. It was intended for use in the

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that. [Fendell is looking at the North Massif.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (To Gene) If I get that camera (that is, Gene's camera, which is on his Rover seat), you can punch the gravimeter, I think. [Jack goes back to the Rover.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Get the camera, and I'll give them a gravimeter reading. (Pause) Is that all you need? Because I'll go get the (U.S.) flag (as per CDR-12 ).

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay, you'd better let that...Yeah, but why don't when you go...Let me get some tongs, too, (off the gate). We need to salvage those...

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: ... scissors . (Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Let me steady the Rover and punch (the gravimeter button). (Pause) [Jack takes Gene's camera to the MESA.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, Bob. Mark gravimeter and the light is flashing.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay. We copy that. (Pause) [Gene begins the measurement by pushing a button marked "GRAV". The gravimeter will work if the outer case is within about 15 degrees of vertical; however, the actual gravity-sensing assembly inside the case needs to be very level and, during the first stage of the measurement, a set of internal motors slowly rotates the assembly on three axes until leveling has been achieved. While this is going on, a light on the top flashes, warning the astronauts not to touch the gravimeter. Once the leveling is complete, the light stops flashing but then stays lit until the mea

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Singing) "Oh, bury me not on the lone prairie. Where the coyotes howl, and the wind blows free." Okay, where am I? (More to himself than to Gene) You're doing a gravimeter (and) getting the flag. I've got your camera. I'm going to salvage the scissors . [Jack takes the tongs toward the ladder. Gene is unstowing the U.S. flag. Once he retrieves the scissors, he will help Gene with the flag deployment that starts at the top of LMP-12 and Gene is in the middle of CDR-12 .] [Cernan - "The flag that we took to deploy was the one that had hung on the wall of the Mission Control Center during all th

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, get the scissors , and I'll be putting the flag in. And don't go near the Rover. 118:19:46 Schmitt: Don't go near the water. That reminds me of a good book. (Long Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Oh, boy. [Jack now has the scissors, but doesn't have a place to put them. He is referring to the comic novel "Don't Go Near the Water", written by William Brinkley and published in 1956. He turns to face the TV camera and has the tongs up at chest level.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I can't go near the Rover?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Let me tell you...No.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I can't go near the Rover.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Why don't you set them...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: How about you letting me stick these in your pocket with your (hammer)...

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: No. (Pointing into the MESA) Set them up there. Just set them in there. We'll get them when we come back in.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay. I'll tell you what I'm going to do.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Just set them inside the...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Put them in the...Gonna hang them here on the (ladder) hook.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, that's good.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Right there. Video Clip ( 4 min 30 sec 1.1 Mb RealVideo or 40 Mb MPEG )

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, Jack. How about the flag right over here in this little mound? [Jack returns to the MESA. Gene is moving north of the LM to deploy the flag. The checklist suggests 30 feet out at 2 o'clock]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Which mound?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, let me take a look over here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: How about right up there on that little high point?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Right up in here where I'm going.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yeah. Of course, your idea of a high point might be different than mine. I meant the North Massif! (Laughs)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: That's probably the best place in the world for the flag, is right up on the top.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay, let me come over and help you. Dum da dee. How about right...

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: (Laughing as he thinks about the possibility of hitting bedrock with the flag pole) (Garbled) how much regolith (soil) we've got in a minute.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Hey, you're in the edge of the crater though. That's no test. [It is a shallow, six-foot-diameter crater with a soft rim. Pushing the flag staff into the ground would be easy and would not tell them much about the depth or cohesiveness of the regolith.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, that's all right.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Move right over here near your tire tracks. [They move a few steps west.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Yeah. This is a high point right here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: That's good.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Right there. [Jack pushes the staff into the ground by hand. He has his back to the TV and we can't see how far he gets it in.] Movie Clip (2 min 07 sec; 1.4 Mb)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, that wasn't too bad. Okay, let me give it a few whacks. (Pause) Oh, baloney. [Gene is having trouble getting the hammer out of his shin pocket . After getting the hammer out, he turns it so he can use the flat to hit the top of the staff.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Watch your fingers. Now that wasn't too bad. Want to make sure it stands up. That's getting pretty...What we could do...I don't know how far we could drill... [Gene is thinking about the three holes he will have to drill at the ALSEP site. Gene only raises the hammer about 15-20 cm on each stroke. Sixteen strokes drives the staff about that many inches - about 40 cm.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Whang! I think we hit something solid with that one.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: No, it was still going. [Cernan - "I don't know how deep it went, but deep enough that it was very firmly planted. Obviously, we hit something hard, momentarily, and then went through. Nothing's going to blow that flag over."] [Indeed, the flagstaff was still standing after Gene and Jack launched back to orbit and, therefore, will remain standing until somebody goes back and moves it or there is an impact very close by. The flag can be seen in the post-launch TV at about 188:04:30 . Note that the flag is pointing north. Before the launch, as can be seen in Jack's post-EVA-3 picture AS17-143- 2

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yeah, but did you ever see it vibrate like that? [To the extent that the flag staff behaves like a pendulum between hammer blows, the frequency of oscillation is slower than it would be on Earth by a factor of 2.4, the square root of six. To the extent that it is behaving like a violin string - for which the frequency is determined by string tension rather than gravity - its behavior would be almost the same as it would be on Earth. Because Jack is still standing in the line of sight, we only get an occasional glimpse of the staff. The vibration isn't obvious in the TV picture.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: No, I've never put a flag up on the Moon before.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Incredulous) What!? [Cernan - "There were two sections to the pole: the bottom section which had a hardened top on it so that, when you banged it into the ground, you didn't smash it in. The top section just telescoped down inside the section you banged into the ground, and that held the flag. The flag was on a two-section, curtain-rod type thing that was folded up. You unwrapped the flag, swung this curtain rod up, latched it at roughly 90 degree angle to the pole, and then extended the outer part of it. The flag looked all wrinkled, because it was folded up all wrinkled."] [Details of the f

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Pull that end. [Jack jumps to grab the end of the flag.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Laughing) You're going to have to get it down to my level. You tall guys are all alike. (Pause) Wait, I'm not through. [Gene is 6'0" and Jack is 5'8".]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. How about getting it stretched out?

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I will. I just can't start forward as fast as I'd like to. (Pause) Hate to touch it, my hands are so dirty. (Pause) [Jack pulls the lower corner taut.] 118:22:37 Cernan: Okay?

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Well, it's going to want to curl. Maybe it'll...It sort of looks like it's waving in the breeze. [Gene puts the upper half of the staff into the section in the ground.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Yes, sir. How about right there? (Pause) (We'll) take a couple (of pictures) this way, and we'll take a couple that way. How's that? [Jack backs up, going south to take pictures as per LMP-12 .] [Schmitt - "You couldn't actually see your feet without bending over, but you could anticipate what was in front of you well enough. Going side-to-side or backwards, you just had to be sure there was nothing in the way."]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Oh, let me get over to the other side. [Jack changes his mind, goes east of the small crater and winds up north of the flag.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: We can get the Rover in the background.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yeah, and the LM. [Gene turns the flag so that it stretches out to the east.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: It does wave when you do that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: We've got a beautiful picture of you guys up (on the screen) down there (in the front of the Control Room).

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Let me tell you, Bob. This flag is a beautiful picture. You see that? 118:23:20 Schmitt: Okay, it's partially covering the Rover, but I think it's a pretty good shot. [ Gene has been west of the flag, holding the staff; he now moves to the east side. This sequence of photos of Gene includes AS17-134- 20377 , 20378 , 20379 , and 20380 . They show Gene's pockets, the hammer, his checklists, the dirt he has accumulated on his legs and, beyond the space between the LM and the Rover, Bear Mountain.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: How's that?

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Let me get the focus right. (Pause) [Jack probably means "f-stop", rather than "focus".] [Each of the film magazines has a decal (from the Lunar Surface Procedures volume) on the top which shows recommended f-stop settings for aiming directions relative to the Sun. The actual flight decals - such as the one on a B&W shown here - are slightly different in detail. Smithsonian Institution photo by Jim Remar.] Movie Clip (1.0Mb; mov)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I don't know how to put it. There you go. Wait a minute. [Jack takes AS17-134- 20378 .] 118:23:40 Schmitt: All right, I got you reaching for the flag. [Gene takes hold of the corner of the flag with his left hand and salutes with his right. Jack is partly hidden by the flag.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: How's that?

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: That's very good, Gene. Let me get it in stereo. [Jack takes a step to his right. This photo is AS17-134- 20379 .]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Houston...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: That's beautiful.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: ...this has got to be one of the most proud moments of my life. I guarantee you. (Pause) (To Jack) Why don't you get a close-in one and we'll trade cameras. [Gene steps to the west of the pole and salutes. Jack steps in to take a close-up, AS17-134- 20380 , then moves east, possibly to take a down-Sun, but does not do so. Finally, he gives Gene the camera and they trade places.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Houston, I don't know how many of you are aware of this, but this flag has flown in the MOCR (Mission Operations Control Room at the Johnson Space Center in Houston) since Apollo 11. And we very proudly deploy it on the Moon, to stay for as long as it can, in honor of all those people who have worked so hard to put us here and to put every other crew here and to make the country, United States, and mankind, something different than it was. Video Clip ( 3 min 02 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPEG )

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger, 17. And presuming to speak in behalf of some of those that work on the MOCR, we thank you very much. [Gene waves Jack closer to the flag.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Jack, right where you were. I'll step to the right. Right there. (Pause) [Jack salutes] 118:25:18 Schmitt: Well, that's all right. I'll keep it (his arm) down. (Pause) [Gene takes AS17-134- 20381 then moves to his right.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Stay there. (Takes AS17-134- 20382 ) Get closer (to the flag).

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I'm going to get on the other side. (Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, I want to get something here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: What's that?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I want to get the Earth.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Let me get over here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Get around on that side. [Jack had moved west of the pole, and now moves back. He overshoots his mark and sprays dust as he stops.] 118:25:54 Schmitt: I don't think it's going...You're a little close, maybe, to have them both in focus. That might do it. [Gene starts to bend his knees and, in an effort to get Earth in the picture along with Jack and the flag, almost gets down on his knees. His first effort, AS17-134- 20383 gets the flag but very little of Jack and the Earth, his second photo, AS17-134- 20384 , is much more successful. After he gets up, Gene gives Jack the camera and they trade

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Try that one time, then we'll give up and get to work. (Long Pause) [Jack holds the camera in his hand and gets it as low to the ground as he can without kneeling.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Point it up a little...Yeah. (Pause) [This is AS17-134- 20385 .] 118:26:32 Schmitt: Let me try it again.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. [This is AS17-134- 20386 . This photo shows the "red apple" actuator for the purge valve reasonably well.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I don't know, Geno.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. 118:26:38 Schmitt: Let me get over here closer to you. (Pause) [Once again, Jack almost goes to his knees.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay. That might have got it. [This photo is AS17-134- 20387 and, in addition to having Earth in the picture, it shows Gene's checklist and watch/mirror band on his left arm, the OPS actuator on the right side of his RCU , and the OPS antenna on the top of his PLSS. The red bands on the suit and helmet show that this is Gene and not Jack.] 118:26:45 Cernan: Okay, very good.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay. All right, let's do it. (Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: You think your gravimeter's ready so I can go back there? [They go back to the Rover, putting one foot in front of the other as they walk.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger, 17. The gravimeter's ready and a couple of words here. One, I presume you found the scissors , right? [They stop to listen.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Two...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Not Ron's, we found ours. [Jack moves toward the Rover again.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger. And the second thing is: we do want the SRC closed. And if you can partially latch it, I'm not sure that's easily done, that would be one solution. The other would be to put something on top of it to hold it closed.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: (Heading for the MESA) Okay, Bob. I'll find something

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay, copy that. One of the brackets off the MESA would be something, or a rock that's nearby; that's another possibility. [Jack consults his checklist, then turns to Gene. He is in the middle of LMP-12 and his next task is to perform an inspection of the LM.] Video Clip ( 3 min 26 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 31 Mb MPEG )

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Gene, what are you going to be up to now?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I'm going to go get the...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: The experiment pallet?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: ...pallet. [Gene is at the top of CDR-13 and, for his next task, he will go to the northeast LM quadrant and unstow a pallet containing hardware for the Surface Electrical Properties (SEP) Experiment.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (Starting toward the LM) Okay, why don't I give the old (LM) inspection bit here. (Goes back to the Rover) And I really ought to have my camera, shouldn't I?

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I need a...

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yeah.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger. That's affirmative.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: ...(garbled) on this (SRC lid).

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: What would you just...

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, I'll find something.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I'll take the old CDR's camera. Not a bad camera to take.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Jack, I'm going to take the old gunny sack here and put it over (the SRC). That'll hold it down.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: I presume you're talking about the big bag, Gene. 118:28:27 Cernan: Yeah, the big bag that was on the ladder hook. That's all it needs. It's just a little bit. There's just enough spring force in it. [A bag can be seen hanging from the ladder hook behind the lefthand side of the bottom rung in AS17-134- 20482 , which was taken at the end of EVA-3.] [Jack moves north of the LM to begin his inspection. In order to look up at the radio antennas and other gear mounted at the top of the spacecraft, he must bend his knees and thrust his hips as far forward as possible in order to get his center of m

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: How's that for coming down gentle? [Each strut contains a shock absorber which would partially crush during a less than soft landing and, among other things, leave the engine bell closer to the ground. Only on Apollo 15 did the bell touch, and then only because Dave Scott landed with one footpad in a moderately deep crater.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: That's what you call "Okay, Number Three Wire", Jack. [Cernan - "'O.K. Number Three Wire' is another naval-aviator, carrier-pilot's term. There's generally four wires on the flight deck and you can catch 1, 2, 3, or 4. Obviously, if you come out of a carrier landing alive, it's successful; but 'O.K., Three Wire' is a term the LSO (Landing Signal Officer) gives you if you just make a perfect, super landing aboard ship. He'll write down the wire he got; he might say, 'low in the groove, number one wire' or 'high and fast, number four wire' or 'slow at the ramp, number two wire' or 'FAB' - which

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Hey, we never heard what our landing parameters were.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: We'll worry about that later.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I don't really care, now that we're here.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Oh, but they always give them to us in the simulator. (Pause) [Gene has moved a step or two east of the North Strut and is removing the gold insulation blanket that covers the SEP pallet. He throws the blanket under the LM with an easy motion.] 118:29:51 Cernan: Hey, Bob, judging from what I see on my clock (the stopwatch function on his wristwatch), we're not but about 5 minutes behind. 118:29:57 Parker: That agrees more or less with the way we read it. [Cernan - "I had two watches: one inside my suit which I kept on Houston time, and the other on the outside which we started - probably at 12

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Gene had a little forward motion as I think you heard us call. And that shows up in the forward footpad at any rate, or did (before the EVA started and Gene and Jack scuffed up the mark). It looks like he may have hit tail first a little bit. That's embedded to the full pad depth. I see no...By George, Gene, you may have had a first. I think you stroked that thing.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Stroked what? [Gene pulls the SEP pallet out of its stowage position and tries to lean it against the strut. The pallet is about a meter long and about a third of a meter wide.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: The rear landing gear.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Well, we can measure it and find out. [This is a matter of principle, since none of the other commanders compressed a landing gear shock. There is no indication in the mission report that there was any compression.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I'll take a picture of it (and save time by letting the folks back in Houston settle the question after the mission.) 118:30:44 Schmitt: May have stroked it. The lower orange Mylar, is folded a little bit. [Gene is facing the TV camera, holding the SEP pallet.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger. There's word floating around down here about typical Navy landings, but I'm not sure whether we believe it or not. [This remark may be coming from Air Force pilot Charlie Duke who, with John Young, is probably sitting with Bob. Duke and Young were the Apollo 16 landing crew and are now serving as the Apollo 17 backup crew. Jack's picture of the rear landing gear is AS17-134- 20388 .]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: He caught his tail hook. Hey, Bob... Video Clip ( 3 min 40 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 33 Mb MPEG )

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: That's the best way. [Cernan - "I had a firm idea in my mind about how I wanted to land. I wanted to bring that thing down as quickly as possible and then, when we got down within the 50 or 60 feet range, slow down to two or three per second and maintain two or three feet per second and a little forward velocity of a foot or so per second forward. You learned very quickly in the LLTV that if you tried to get it down at about one foot per second, all of a sudden you started hovering, or maybe you put a little bit too much thrust in and you started going up a little. So I tried to keep going dow

A17A1181422.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1181422.text: America, Houston.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: (To Bob) Okay, I've got to give you a (gravimeter) reading, Bob, if you're ready.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Ready.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: You put the big bag up... [Busy as they are, Gene and Jack don't always hear what each other is saying or remember what was just said.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay. We copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Jack, I put that (big bag) there to hold the SRC down. 118:31:52 Schmitt: That's all right, I just put a sample in it. It's in the bottom of the bag. It's about 8 by 5 centimeters by 3 centimeters. Slightly tabular. [Jack goes to the Rover and, out of view of the TV, takes Gene's camera off and stows it under the CDR seat as per LMP-12 . He then leaves again. While at the Rover, he may have taken AS17-134- 20389 , which is a good picture of the front of the vehicle and the LCRU, the LCRU mirrors, the TV camera, the TCU, the big dustbrush , and some cup-type sample bags which, later, Jack will

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay. We copy that. It's in the big bag.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Yes, sir. [This is probably the rock that disappears sometime between now and the end of EVA-2. Jack makes brief references to the disappearance at 123:40:07 and 147:36:11.] [Jack turns to the east so he can get some light on his camera to check either the settings or the frame count.] 118:32:14 Cernan: Okay, Bob. A Mark on gravity. [Gene is now making a measurement with the TGE sitting on the ground.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: And the light's flashing.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that. (Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: I've got to tell you, Bob. I haven't done everything there is to do in the Navy, but deploying that flag has got to be the most proud thing I'll ever do in my life. If you could see you (the Earth), and you could see it (the flag) from where we are, I know you'd feel the same way.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger on that, Geno.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Whoo! (Laughs) [Jack has tripped.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: God, he's pretty up there. God, you're pretty up there over the South Massif. Beautiful! [Gene is looking at Earth.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Hope nobody saw that (trip).

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Beautiful.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Oh, they were watching me. (Laughs) Those finks. [Jack can see that the TV camera is pointed in his general direction; however, he was moving too quickly for Fendell to follow and wasn't actually in the field-of-view when he tripped.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: You weren't doing anything with the gravimeter on here (that is, on the Rover), I hope. [Jack may have just read the line "Note TGE Status" on LMP-12 . Note that Jack should have checked the TGE status before stowing Gene's camera at 118:31:52. If the TGE had been on the Rover with a measurement in progress, Jack would have disturbed it.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: No, it's on the deck (that is, on the ground).

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay.

A17A1181422.speaker: Evans
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Magazine SS is full.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay, you might grab me a frame count when you set it on there, Jack.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Too late, Bob.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Okay.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: I'll get that later.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: We'll get it later. No hurry. [Gene goes to the SEP pallet which is still leaning against the (north) strut; Jack goes to the MESA to deploy the Cosmic Ray experiment at per LMP-12 .]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay, now if I can figure how to get this off. [Gene is about to remove the SEP receiver package from the pallet.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: (To Bob) You've got to educate us again. We may not remember those. Oops. [Jack is asking for a future reminder about the frame count.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Bob, the SEP's in hand.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger on that. (Pause) [Fendell starts a TV pan. The SEP receiver/recorder is a box about one-foot on each side. Gene will mount the receiver on the inner surface of the geopallet and the extendible, three-section SEP receiving antenna on the geopost immediately behind Jack's Rover seat, as can be seen in training photos S72-50270 and S72-48890 . After the EVA-1 traverse, Gene and Jack will deploy a low-frequency (a few megahertz) radio transmitter about 150 meters east of the LM and then, during the EVA-2 and EVA-3 traverses will record signals which, having been altered by their passage thro

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Okay. I'll give you a (SEP) temperature. Let's see whether it fits. (Pause) I'll bet it does. (Pause) Come on; lock, baby. Okay, it's On... MP3 Audio Clip ( 14 min 56 sec )

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: ...It's locked.

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: Roger. [The SEP receiver is temperature sensitive. Later in the mission, the fasteners on the SEP receiver dust cover will fail, the radiator will get enough dust on it that Gene will never be able to get it properly cleaned, and the temperature will rise to the point that the instrument shuts itself off.] [Fendell is looking at the U.S. flag with the North Massif in the background.] 118:34:27 Cernan: Okay. Bob, here's a temperature for you. Forty degrees (Fahrenheit about 5 Celsius). Video Clip ( 3 min 04 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 28 Mb MPEG )

A17A1181422.text: Say again.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: Four-zero.

A17A1181422.text: Copy that.

A17A1181422.speaker: Cernan
A17A1181422.text: (Reading CDR-13 ) "Close (SEP dust) cover." Okay, number 1. Something over here. Never did figure out what. [Details of the SEP receiver antenna deployment are given on a decal.]

A17A1181422.speaker: Evans
A17A1181422.text: Okay. Good idea. Reacq and Narrow.

A17A1181422.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1181422.text: Okay, Bob, the "Shade" is deployed facing deep space. (Pause)

A17A1181422.speaker: Parker
A17A1181422.text: (Momentarily puzzled) Oh, copy. Roger. Understand the cosmic ray. Jack is using a strap to hang the "Shade" detector - in the shade, of course - from one of the plus-Z (west) strut supports. He will then hang the "Sun" detector - in full sunlight - from one of the minus-Z (east) support

A17A1183423.text: Copy that.

A17A1183423.text: ...It's locked.

A17A1183423.text: Say again.

A17A1183423.text: Four-zero.

A17A1183423.text: Copy that.

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: (Reading CDR-13 ) "Close (SEP dust) cover." Okay, number 1. Something over here. Never did figure out what. [Details of the SEP receiver antenna deployment are given on a decal.]

A17A1183423.speaker: Evans
A17A1183423.text: Okay. Good idea. Reacq and Narrow.

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: Okay, Bob, the "Shade" is deployed facing deep space. (Pause)

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: (Momentarily puzzled) Oh, copy. Roger. Understand the cosmic ray. [Jack is deploying the cosmic ray experiment as per LMP-12 , a cousin to the solar wind experiment flown on Apollos 11, 12 and 15.
