A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: Okay, Bob. The (SEP receiver) antenna is deployed. It's not on the post yet, but it's deployed. (Long Pause) [Note that, as indicated on CDR-13 details of the SEP Receiver Antenna deployment are listed on decals afixed to the instrument. At present, I do not have copies of those decals.]

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: (Talking to the antenna) Oh, oh. Come on. Don't get all caught on something. (Pause) That's better. That's better.

A17A1183423.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1183423.text: TEI-26, SPS/G&N; 37630; plus 0.53, plus 0.97; 139:41:14.32; Noun 81's plus 2450.7, minus 2097.8, minus 0807.1. Roll is 187; pitch, 104; yaw, 323; rest of the PAD is not applicable. Good old Sirius and Rigel for set stars; 133, 200, 030. Ullage, four jet, 12 seconds. Longitude of the Moon at T IG will be minus 160.39. Over.

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: Okay, Bob. I think (I've) just about got the "Sun" side deployed, just as perpendicular to the Sun as I think anybody could do.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Okay. Copy that. Good enough. 118:36:11 Schmitt: Okay, I don't have any pictures (of the cosmic ray experiment) yet (because Jack doesn't have a camera with him), so you might put that down as something to get later.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Yeah, we'll catch that in the pan(orama) next EVA or something like that. (Pause)

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: Boy, if that (SEP) antenna doesn't get some noise from outer space, I don't know what will. If they are out there, and they are I'm sure. They'll see that one. That is even weirder looking out here than it is in the high bay. [The "high bay" is in the Flight Crew Training Building at the Cape. Fendell finds Gene at the rear of the Rover, mounting the SEP.]

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: Hey, Bob? Before I leave (with) the ALSEP, remind me to check the cosmic ray. I might hit it here in the process of deployment. [Jack is about to remove the ALSEP from its storage compartment in the southeast quadrant of the LM, and is afraid that he might hit the "Sun" part of the cosmic ray experiment. He is at the top of LMP-13 and his first task is to open the doors of the Scientific Equipment (SEQ) Bay.] [The SEQ Bay has a small, vertically hinged door on the left, which Jack will open first. It also has a two-secton, horizontally hinged door that is opened by pulling on a lanyard. Diagra

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Okay, try not to.

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: I got a little close.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Okay.

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: (Responding to Bob's "Try not to") Oh, I will. (Pause)

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: Okay. The (SEQ Bay) doors are open!! Beautifully. I don't know what talent you have for landing in holes, Cernan, but once again I'll be doing all the ALSEP work in a hole. (Pause) Okay. [The repetition of Jack's 118:37:04 transmission in the MP3 file may be the result of a change of tapes by the audio technician at NASA Johnson who, in 1989, made the cassette copies used years later to make the MP3 file.] Video Clip ( 3 min 26 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 31 Mb MPEG )

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Are you saying we should have kept the pulleys there, Jack? [Cernan - "At one time, I think there was a pulley we could use to lower the ALSEP to the ground. We probably took them off. I didn't like all that extra garbage; I thought we could handle things quicker without all those crutches. It was just a matter of wanting fewer things to mess with. But Jack found himself, as he said, 'in the hole' and had to reach higher than he wanted."]

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: (Agreeing with Bob, but grudgingly) Yeah, I need the pulleys. [Schmitt - "There were some pulleys originally, but we had more problems with them than they were worth. As it turned out, I don't think we had a great deal of problems getting the packages out."]

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: You know, Bob, I've got a little bit of a problem here. I've got the SEP connector on. (Jack laughs) But...It'll slide down in, but the locking cover just won't go over. [As per CDR-13 Gene may be attaching the SEP Nav cable to the Rover. This cable probably carries information from the Rover Nav system to the SEP recorder.]

A17A1183423.speaker: Evans
A17A1183423.text: Okay. Readback. TEI-26, SPS/G&N; 37630; plus 0.53, plus 0.97; 139:41:14.32; and 81's plus 2450.7, minus 2097.8, minus 0807.1. Roll 187, 104, 323. Sirius and Rigel; 133, 200, 030. Four jet, 12 seconds. Lunar longitude at T IG is minus 160.39.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Roger, Geno. Understand. And it slides in far enough, and you think it's aligned, huh?

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: Yeah, I'm positive it's aligned. It just didn't appear to lock over, well not appear, it just won't lock over. I'm shoving it home. Okay, I got it.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: Okay. Copy.

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: I got it. Makes everyone happier.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: I'm glad we have the right solution to that one, Geno.

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: The right solution is the fact that you've got a man here doing it.

A17A1183423.speaker: Overmyer
A17A1183423.text: Good readback, Ron. And the Earthshine photo PAD is at 121:05 in the Flight Plan.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker
A17A1183423.text: (Laughs) [Cernan - "This is a response to "should you send man or machine into space?" We've had a lot of controversy and comment on that over the years, and this was just a subtle little comment to reinforce man's usefulness in space, even for a seemingly simple operation."]

A17A1183423.speaker: Cernan
A17A1183423.text: (Looking at his checklist) Okay.

A17A1183423.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1183423.text: Hey, Bob. The ECA Temp Monitor switch is On.

A17A1183423.speaker: Parker

A17A1184806.text: Okay, Bob. I think I'm going to move a little bit to the northwest of my present position in order to get a little farther away from that big rock (Geophone Rock).

A17A1184806.text: Okay, Jack.

A17A1184806.text: Roger.

Why we ever had them I'll never know; there were always plenty of rocks you could use. People working in a non-real e

A17A1184806.text: Or I'll retrace your steps.

A17A1184806.text: No sir, I got it on, but a little piece of the rail is cracked off. A17A1184806.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1184806.text: I've not seen any sign of layering in any of the craters. In their walls. [ Jack reappears. A17A1184806.text: Can you see me, Bob?

A17A1184806.text: Hey, leave me enough room to deploy the heat flow.

[Most of the experiments have constraints of one kind or another about proximity to rocks and/or craters and also to the Central Station, the RTG, and to each other. For example, the heat flow experiment is designed to measure temperature gradients in the soil down to a depth of about 2.5 meters. Craters and rocks, because they absorb and radiate heat differently than a flat surface, can influence the temperature gradients to depths equivalent to their own dimensions.]

A17A1184806.speaker: Cernan
A17A1184806.text: That's why I didn't land up there. (Pause) [Geophone Rock, which hadn't been noticed in the pre-mission photos, is about 70 to 80 meters northeast of the planned landing point.] [Fendell pans to Jack, who is resting with the ALSEP on the ground.]

A17A1184806.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1184806.text: Okay, I think I've got a place. And I think it'll also give you a spot for the neutron flux that's sheltered from the RTG. [The neutron probe is designed to measure the natural flux of neutrons due to the decay of radioactive elements in the soil and due to interactions between the soil and cosmic rays and the solar wind. Because the RTG is powered by a plutonium fuel element, it produces enough neutrons that the neutron flux experiment has to be shielded by placing it either in a depression or behind a rock or, preferably, both.]

A17A1184806.text: Okay. You say you have a place like that, Jack?

A17A1184806.text: Okay.

But it's one of those things that you can do fairly easily with enough practice that would also be tough to automate. The main problem with the ALSEP was that it took a lot of time to deploy. A17A1184806.text: Okay, stand by.

A17A1184806.text: That's okay, Jack.

A17A1184806.text: Okay.

A17A1184806.speaker: Parker
A17A1184806.text: Stay there.

A17A1184806.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1184806.text: All righty. It looks pretty good to me.

A17A1184806.text: Bob, it's really, in detail...The meter and half-meter scale relief is a little more than we can stand here for a good site. But I think this will be all right.

A17A1184806.text: Okay, copy that. We're ready to press on with ALSEP interconnect. [The ALSEP interconnect procedures start in the middle of LMP-14 .]

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: Pulled the pin at the wrong time. [In Houston, those who have been following what Jack has been doing in detail tell Flight Director Gerry Griffin that Jack has prematurely released the dust cover but that there will be no adverse effects.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay. The heat flow (electronics package) is level; the gnomon is good. And, Bob, I verified that that dirt is not on the mirror. It's on the white stuff that, you know, is horizontal to the (top) surface of the box. [Jack does a high, two-footed kangaroo hop over a cable and heads south. Note the reel at the center of the trailing cable.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Okay. Copy that, Gene; that's okay.

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: The mirror's clean.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Roger. Thank you.

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, I'll give you a TGE reading.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Roger. We're ready.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Okay. We copy that. [ Jack stops and, one at a time, takes five orange-colored, geophone flags out of the storage compartment on the top of the dust cover and sticks them in the ground. The flags will be used to make the geophone locations visible in the photographs and also to help Gene to keep from running over the geophones with the Rover. In addition, as Jack emplaces the four geophones at the ends of long N-S and E-W lines centered on the geophone module, he can sight across the central module to a flag at the opposite end of an arm and keep his lines straight.] [Gene is now at the bottom

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Bob, was that ( TGE measurement taken) with the (TV) camera running?

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Roger. The camera's been running all this time.

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: That's beautiful. [Again, there is some concern that movement of the TV camera might upset the TGE . The successful completion of this measurement indicates that there will be no problem.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay. Your temperatures are down to 100 and maybe a skosh under 120, so maybe those batteries are cooling off.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Okay; good. [If there has been any cooling, it has only been a fraction of a degree. By the end of the ALSEP deployment at 121:35:00, the temperatures will be down to 96 and 110 degrees.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: It's sure good. I don't want to walk on that third EVA. 119:26:59 Parker: Roger. [Schmitt - "I don't recall that we had developed any contingency plans for walking traverses. I think the idea was that, if it ever came to that, you'd develop plans in real-time, depending on what you'd gotten done before the Rover failed. With all the redundancy built into the Rover, and with two successful Rover missions completed, they figured that it wasn't much of a risk. If we'd had to, I think we could have probably gotten to our main objectives almost as fast loping as we could driving. You could move pre

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: I'm getting to like driving this machine. [Journal Contributor Jim Scotti notes that the "machine" is almost certainly the Rover. Although Gene is working with the drilling equipment, he probably hasn't left the Rover.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay, pull pin 2. Pin 2 always comes after...(fixing his joke) comes before pin 1.

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: I think that's in the NASA documents now. [Jack uses the UHT to lift off the geophone dust cover.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: What's that?

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: "Pin 2 comes before pin 1."

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: (Laughs) Okay.

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: "Reel 3 comes before reel 1 and 2", also. [Jack tosses the dust cover toward the trash pile.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: (Pause) I think I overdid that one.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Yeah, it went clean out of sight. [Fendell pans to follow the heat shield; only catches the shadow of it landing.] RealVideo File (25 min 38 sec)

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: But by all means, "watch reel 2". [This may have a private joke between Bob and Jack.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: (Laughing) Oh, you think you're so clever. (Pause) [Schmitt - "The Support Crew had all sorts of clever little sayings and pictures and stuff like that that they would put into the checklist. Bob's favorite, since our motto was 'the end of the beginning', was 'this is the end, not the beginning'. And he had some little pink patches he called "Rover patches" as distinct from the flight patches; and there may have been something like that in the checklist at this point. Some of it you couldn't repeat over the airway. Or maybe this was just another part of the private joke."] [Jack does not turn

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: Believe it or not, Bob, I'm anchoring the geophone module.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: Hey, Jack, it looks to us on the TV as though you're anchoring the geophone module with a flag.

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: Yeah, that's what I'm doing. (Pretending neither of them is hearing the other) I'm anchoring the geophone module with a flag. (Pause) Movie Clip (2 min 36 sec; 1.6Mb)

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay; one leg, two legs, three legs. And none of them (fell off)... [Gene is pulling out the three legs of a stand on which he will rest the drill stems and hang his wrench. He is at the top of CDR-18. Jack, who is still in the TV picture, has run back to the Central Station and is now releasing the Lunar Mass Spectrometer. This task is at the top of LMP-18 . The LMS will measure the density and composition of the very tenuous lunar atmosphere. Because the LM releases enough gases during depressurization and during launch to overwhelm the instrument, like many others of the ALSEP gear, except

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: Hey, Bob, remind me to police the garbage pile.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: All right.

A17A1192436.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1192436.text: The garbage pile is turning out to be just like every other ALSEP deployment. It's hard to control.

A17A1192436.speaker: Parker
A17A1192436.text: And I understand all your legs came out okay, Geno, or didn't come out.

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Okay. (Answering Bob) Yes, sir; they all came out okay. [Schmitt - "The legs on Gene's drill-stem rack were packed unextended and when you extended them, they popped out with a spring. In training, they may have actually fallen off."] [Bob agrees with Jack's recollection.] 119:28:51 Schmitt: Okay. LMS ring is pulled. [Jack frees the LMS and the Central Station jumps a little.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Oh, Manischewitz! (Putting the drill on the ground) I don't know where I picked that word up (Jack chuckles), but it's better than some (pause), I guess. Now if I can use my little lean-tool here. (Pause) [He leans on the drill to remove the wrench. Here, Gene is using "Manischewitz" instead of cursing.]

A17A1192436.speaker: Cernan
A17A1192436.text: Oh, man, that works great! That works great. Put this out of the way. (Pause; putting the drill about ten feet north) Bob, I'm into the white marks; it depends on what you want to call the surface. You know, give or take 6 or 8 inches. (Pause) [Gene tamps dirt around the stem with his boot, then hangs the wrench on the rack.]

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1192853csm.text: Okay, Ron. No [garble] for picture taking, but you need to select Omni A when you get a chance.

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1192853csm.text: Copy that. [Jack carries the LMS eastward.] 119:29:02 Cernan: Amazing. Amazing. (Long Pause) Okay, Bob. I've got my tools of the trade right here. I'm ready to go to work. Now, I put a mark in the deck...(Looking for a spot he scratched on the ground to show where he wanted to drill the first hole) There it is; right there. (Pause) [Fendell pans to Gene who is carrying a wrapped bundle of drill stems, a stem rack, and the drill. He positions the rack southwest of his mark. He is at the top of CDR-18 ] Video Clip ( 3 min 04 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPEG )

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1192853csm.text: Hey, Bob, what have I forgotten? The package won't rotate. [Jack is stumped by the fourth line on LMP-18 .] 119:29:53 Parker: Try rotating the UHT (Universal Handling Tool). [Gene is holding the drill by a loop handle which allows him to set it on the ground, handgrips down, without bending over very far.]

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1192853csm.text: No, I'm serious. (Pause) Oh, rotate the UHT, huh?

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1192853csm.text: No...That's right. I'm sorry. (Laughs) I knew it! I knew it would happen! [Schmitt - "I was probably supposed to put the UHT in a socket and rotate it; the instrument was probably locked unless you put the UHT in and rotate it. Obviously, I had forgotten to do that in training and had forgotten again on the Moon."]

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1192853csm.text: Where's your garbage pile, Jack? I can't find yours...

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1192853csm.text: Well, don't worry about my garbage pile. It turns out it looks very much like the ALSEP. [Gene removes and discards the top of the quiver-like drill stem bag; and then leans the bag on the rack.]

a17_1192853csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1192853csm.text: Okay. I made a mark over here that says that should be about cable length...

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1193405csm.text: Well, I didn't see any slices down there that time.

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1193405csm.text: Every once in a while she breaks through a soft spot.

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1193405csm.text: Good. (Long Pause) [Gene stops for a moment, releasing his grip, then drills a final few inches before going to the rack for the wrench. Jack is in the background, still trying to level the Central Station.] [Schmitt - "In drilling those holes, it was nice that fifty percent of the regolith is particles smaller than 100 microns. The chances of hitting a large rock were pretty small, in spite of what you see scattered around on the surface. Because you're looking across the surface at a very low angle, you get a distorted view of how many rocks there are."] Movie Clip (1 min 54 sec; 1.3 Mb)

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1193405csm.text: Bob, I'll tell you, this Central Station's a bear - a bear - to get level. (Pause) Well, I just got dust on it now. (Pause) It (meaning the ground)'s just too soft. [The process of getting the equipment level is a matter of finding a level position on the uneven ground, rather than smoothing and leveling the surface itself. The soil can be pushed out of the way or piled up with a boot, although care must be taken not to get any dust on thermally-sensitive surfaces. Here, Jack is leveling the base of the Central Station, prior to raising the top and the attached thermal curtains. Meanwhile, Gen

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1193405csm.text: Boy, that sure was drilling in hard stuff because it took a lot to get it (the drill) off (the stem). (Pause) [Gene takes the drill by the loop handle and sets it on the ground.]

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1193405csm.text: Okay, Jack. And we could certainly stand (tolerate) a little bit of dust, at least, on top of that Central Station sunshield.

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1193405csm.text: Yeah, I guess the level's important.

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1193405csm.text: Roger. [Schmitt - "By leveling the Central Station and getting it aligned relative to the Sun, I could then use pre-determined coordinates for pointing the antenna."] [The pre-determined antenna settings are printed on cuff checklist page LMP-20. Meanwhile, Gene does another deep knee bend, with his right hand on the detached drill to try to remove the wrench. However, the drill is to far away from the wrench and he doesn't get any support. He starts to lose his balance and has to scramble in the driection of the fall to regain is feet. In the process of recovering from the fall, he lifts the

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1193405csm.text: I can just see what John (Young)'s thinking right now. That's what makes the difference. That's where you expend your energy. (Pause) [Cernan - "We knew they were watching a lot of things on the television, so when we made a statement, we didn't necessarily make a complete statement because we knew they're looking at what we're talking about. In this case, I was talking about the difficulty of getting the wrench off."] [John Young had practised doing dynamic grabs in the 1/6th-g airplane before Apollo 16 and got quite good at it. Gene hasn't yet learned to do it efficiently.] [Gene gets a 71-c

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1193405csm.text: Bob, I don't know that I'm going to be able to do that without a lot of time. It (meaning the level bubble)'s hanging against the south edge.

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1193405csm.text: I don't know whether I'm going to be able to level the Central Station. (Pause)

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1193405csm.text: (Without looking) Anything I can do, Jack? (Pause) [Gene threads the second stem into the one in the ground. Behind him, Jack tries to free the bubble by jerking the Central Station to one side or the other every few seconds.]

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1193405csm.text: Okay. I got it off the edge. [Gene picks up the drill and hits it with his hand to knock some dust off.]

a17_1193405csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1193405csm.text: Okay; maybe we better just leave it there. (Pause)

a17_1194152csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1194152csm.text: Ron, you're about ready to go over the hill. You're looking really good.

a17_1194152csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1194152csm.text: Don't work too hard. [Gene stands motionless next to the drill rack, his arms out in front of him in the rest position, knees slightly bent.]

a17_1194152csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1194152csm.text: My fender's still on; which makes me happy. (Pause; then he starts working again)

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, Manischewitz! (Putting the drill on the ground) I don't know where I picked that word up (Jack chuckles), but it's better than some (pause), I guess. Now if I can use my little lean-tool here. (Pause) [He leans on the drill to remove the wrench. Here, Gene is using "Manischewitz" instead of cursing.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, man, that works great! That works great. Put this out of the way. (Pause; putting the drill about ten feet north) Bob, I'm into the white marks; it depends on what you want to call the surface. You know, give or take 6 or 8 inches. (Pause) [Gene tamps dirt around the stem with his boot, then hangs the wrench on the rack.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Yeah, something like that will do, Gene, I guess. We can measure it (garbled, but means "from the photos").

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Gene, is the stuff (the drill cuttings) coming up changing color on you at all?

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: No, Jack. It isn't changing color. I can't even tell where it's coming up. Video Clip ( 3 min 50 sec 1.0 Mb RealVideo or 34 Mb MPEG )

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: (Laughing as the top of the Central Station springs up; Gene turns to look) Ho ho. Ho ho.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: (Looking back at his work) I don't think it (the cuttings) is coming up. I think I'm just pushing it aside.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Boy, I'll tell you...

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: I saw something come up then just then, Jack.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: ...the old ALSEP Central Station. Yeah, it deploys itself; it turns out. [Checklist page LMP-19 contains the phrase "guide C/S up" which suggests that, in training, the Central Station raised itself reluctantly. Here, it sprang up to full height without any hesitation. Photo AS17-134- 20491 shows the raised Central Station from the east. Jack has not yet attached the antenna and gimbals that are shown in the photo, which was taken after the ALSEP deployment was complete. Note the attachment points on the top where the various experiment modules were mounted. The LSG is in the background at the

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Roger on that. That was...

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Bob...

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: ...pretty amazing.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Okay. I finally leveled it in the bull's eye. I don't know whether you heard me or not, but it was perfect. So it's okay. It's got about 20 percent dust cover on the top.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. (Pause) [Gene has picked up the heat flow probe and removes it from its protective bag. The bag has kept the probe clean, despite the amount of dust that he has kicked around while drilling the hole. He is at the middle of CDR-18 .]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Sure glad you've got that probe covered.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: And, Jack, ALSEP says that that's okay; that twenty percent's no problem. [Fendell starts to pans away from Gene; Experiments tell Flight they'd like to continue watching the heat flow deployment.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Okay. (Pause) I put a rock under the northwest corner. Oops. Guess what happened? (Laughs) Just like in training, Geno.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: What happened?

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: The old geophone cable caught on the corner. (Pause) Okay. Oops, I'm not ready.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: (To himself) That says F4B on that; that's an airplane! (Long Pause; he discards something) Houston, there's no dust on the (heat flow) probe except that which was on my hands. [Gene goes to the heat flow hole he just drilled.] [Jack's next task, on the bottom of LMP-19 , is to secure the thermal curtains that cover the east, west, and south faces. They are secured with patches of Velcro.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: That must be solar wind. (Pause)

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Sorry not to be more talkative, but this is taking all the concentration I got. 119:48:57 Cernan: I'm going to have to push this down, I can see that. [Gene has trouble getting the tip of the probe to go into the drill stem. After maneuvering it like a fishing line for a while, he finally does two quick knee bends so that he can push the probe in with his hand.] 119:49:04 Schmitt: You know, this Velcro doesn't hold any better here than it did in training. [Schmitt - "The four corners of the thermal curtain were sealed with Velcro, and it never worked very well. Because of the Apollo fire, we h

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: (Talking to himself as he reaches for something on the rack) Oh, don't lose that, Geno. Don't lose that. Don't lose that. Notice how you talk to yourself out here?

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: (Chuckling) Who, me? (Pause) "Help", I says. "You is getting farther and farther behind." [Gene does a discus throw of a bag or box from which he has just removed a rammer. He almost spins out of control and almost falls.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Well, I've had my "whoops" for today.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Your one what?

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Well, I just did my "whifferdill."

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Oh, did you fall?

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: No. It's funny how for every action there's an equal and opposite reaction, isn't it? [Gene telescopes the rammer from an 18-inch (0.5 m) length to about four feet (1.3 m).]

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Hey, I've heard that before. Okay. (Reading) "Secure thermal curtains". Thermal curtains are secured.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Copy that. Video Clip ( 4 min 01 sec 1.0 Mb RealVideo or 35 Mb MPEG )

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: How far behind am I, Bob?

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Stand by. (Pause) Roger. We're showing Gene just about 20 minutes; and Jack just about 25. Between 20 and 25 (minutes) for both of you.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Okay. (Pause) How are our consumables?

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Jack is concerned that they won't have much time to devote to geology. His next task, on LMP-20 , is to release the Central Station antenna gimbal assembly from the LEAM pallet and then mount it and the antenna on the Central Station. Meanwhile, Gene is having trouble getting the tip of the rammer in the hole. It seems to have a cable slot.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, if this thing isn't going to work better than that! (Long Pause) [Gene gets the rammer in the stem.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Bob, just like the book says, it's down to Papa 1; and it hooked.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: How about that. (Long Pause) [Papa 1 is a mark on the heat flow cable indicating how far the cable has gone into the drill stem. The bottom heat flow drill stem has a closed drill bit so that the stems would remain clear for insertion of the probes. The heat flow probe contains multiple sensors and Gene is emplacing thermal shields between them. He is in the bottom paragraph on CDR-18. Meanwhile, Jack polices the trash pile, moving outlying items onto the main part of the pile, and then returns to the Central Station.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, boy! The old fingers really suffer on these.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Take it easy. [Cernan - "I remember that, at the end of the day, my fingers and forearms were very tired. You were always moving your fingers against the pressure in the gloves."] [Gene removes the rammer from the hole, reattaches it to the cable at a higher position, and pushes it down the hole again. The cable has a number of sensors attached to it.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Now this one down to F1. Would you believe (it's down to) F1?

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: I believe you, Gene. (Pause)

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Bob, in this soil, best number I can give you is about an inch below the white spots, or Bravo 1. [Here, Gene is telling Houston how far the top drill stem is in the ground. This is the "Measure height of stem" task on CDR-18 . Fendell pans the TV, finds Jack, and zooms in.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Copy Bravo 1. (Pause)

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: I got a better way of putting that last thermal shield on, though. (Long Pause) RealVideo File (25 min 52 sec)

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Okay, Bob, you're looking at it coming out to the south, but I don't expect it'll stay that way unless I put some dirt over the cable. How's that grab you?

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Stand by, Gene. [The last thermal shield minimizes the amount of heat the cable carries into the hole. It is visible in AS17-134- 20497 . Note how Gene has positioned the cable so that it extends south from the hole for a foot or so before turning west toward the electronics package. The heat flow cables have retained some loops and waves from the days of storage in the LM. In the weak lunar gravity field, this "memory" is retained longer than it would on Earth. On Apollo 16, John Young caught a foot under a heat flow cable near the Central Station and tore it loose. Here, Gene wants to cover

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: You like that thermal shield the way it is? Okay. That's coming out south. That's in good shape. I'm pleased with that. Video Clip ( 3 min 15 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo clip or 29 Mb MPEG )

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Dirt's okay, if you want to put it on there, Gene.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: I'll tell you, I'm happy with it. I'm moving on.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Now, the thermal shield is on there, Bob. I got them all on there. [Fendell returns to Gene as he picks up the stem quiver and, in the process, knocks the wrench off the rack. He retrieves it relatively easily with the rammer.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: If you want to put some dirt on there to hold it down, that's okay.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, okay. Well, I got it down without the dirt.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Good enough.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: I'm just finding all sorts of good ways to make life easier out here. (Pause) [Gene picks up the rack and moves west and a little north. He is now at the top of CDR-19 and is about to drill the second heat flow hole.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: (To himself) Stay away from the cables. (To Bob) Bob, and I didn't forget the last measurement either.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Roger that. [Cernan - "One thing I ought to mention here, in case I forget it, is that on the first day you never felt any heat soak into your gloves. But I remember that on the third day you could feel the heat soaking in. That's because the Sun was 26 degrees higher than it was on the first day. You couldn't feel it on your body because you had the liquid-cooled garment; but your hands had no liquid cooling on them and, also, your hands were sitting out in the sunshine a lot of the time."]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Hey, can you see this big mound that's just...(correcting himself) not a mound but the depression that's just to the north of me?

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Roger, 17; Houston sees it.

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: It's probably behind the Rover. (Listens) Okay. Well, how's that look for the core? [Gene puts the drilling gear down.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Stand by. (Long Pause) Geno, can you give us a distance estimate to that? Does it look like it's 80 feet or so (from the RTG)?

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Yeah.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Then that sounds good. [After Gene drills and extracts the deep core, he will emplace the neutron flux experiment in the resulting hole. The experiment is designed to measure background levels of neutrons produced by the natural radioactivity of the soil and by cosmic rays. Gene needs to be at least 80 feet from the RTG so that the neutrons it emits will not overwhelm the "natural" signal.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Oh, shucks! [Gene has dropped the wrench again; he retrieves it with the rammer.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Hey, Bob, is there any way a level bubble can fail? (Gene laughs) [Jack is referring to one of two level bubbles on the Central Station antenna gimbal assembly. He is leveling the gimbal assembly as per LMP-20 ]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Hey, Jack, remember that's on top of those wobbly springs there. And with the thing not being straight, you shouldn't really expect the level bubble to be level after the thing's been deployed. That happened at the Cape a couple of times, remember? [Bob thinks that Jack is talking about the level bubble on the top of the Central Station, the one that Jack was using before he raised the top and curtains, rather than the ones on the gimbal assembly. Meanwhile, Gene goes to retrieve the drill from the first heat flow hole.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Yeah; but Bob, I've moved this practically all the way down the full throw and that bubble won't move, and I can't get it to move by tilting it; and I was leveled. And the bubble on the top of the Central Station is still level. [Gene has the drill in hand.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. You're talking about the level on your other one, huh? Stand by on that. 119:56:16 Schmitt: The gnomon, yeah...Both of them? (Pause) I can't get it to move to the other side of the fluid. [Gene is back at the second heat flow hole.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: Keep working. That thing shouldn't fail. (Pause) [Gene threads the 137-cm stem into the drill chuck.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Well, I've gone full throw. That's not level. That bubble's stuck in there, somehow. In both of them. That's not even pointing close to the Earth. Okay, I'm going to have to tweak it up...Let them see the signal strength and tweak it. [Gene picks up the drill.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Why don't you try and manually point it; try and level it and see what you can do toward getting it (pointed) towards the Earth. Video Clip ( 3 min 13 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 28 Mb MPEG )

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: I will, Bob. That bubble's just not working. I can't figure that one out. [Cernan - "With the station not level, you would just try to get the antenna pointed more or less in the right direction and see if you had an acceptable signal strength."] [Gene has to get on tiptoes, his hands above the top of his helmet, to get the stem vertical. He starts drilling.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Just go ahead and use the...

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Okay. Maybe I jarred it loose here.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay. MP3 Audio Clip ( 13 min 12 sec )

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: I think I jarred it loose.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: That's another first.

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Don't ask me how.

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Okay, we won't. (Long Pause)

A17A1194510.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1194510.text: Okay. And I got the other one loose. That's very strange! A sticky level bubble. (Laughing) Never heard of it. [Schmitt - "Whatever fluid they used evidently had surface tension in excess of the one-sixth g buoyant forces that were trying to move the bubble to the center, at least when the bubble was over at the edge. It took a jarring motion of some sort to break that surface tension."] [Unfortunately, we have been unable to identify the fluid in the bubble level. Gene stops drilling and looks at the TV camera.] 119:57:54 Cernan: Hey, Bob...

A17A1194510.speaker: Parker
A17A1194510.text: Go ahead, Jack...(correcting himself) Gene. [Gene gestures with his left hand, pointing north.]

A17A1194510.speaker: Cernan
A17A1194510.text: ...If you're looking at me, what I'm talking about is this depression in here for the core. Oh, maybe 15, 20 meters out in here. Jack, what did you have in mind for the neutron flux?

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: I think I jarred it loose.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: That's another first.

A17A1195720.text: Don't ask me how.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay, we won't. (Long Pause)

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Okay. And I got the other one loose. That's very strange! A sticky level bubble. (Laughing) Never heard of it. [Schmitt - "Whatever fluid they used evidently had surface tension in excess of the one-sixth g buoyant forces that were trying to move the bubble to the center, at least when the bubble was over at the edge. It took a jarring motion of some sort to break that surface tension."] [Unfortunately, we have been unable to identify the fluid in the bubble level. Gene stops drilling and looks at the TV camera.] 119:57:54 Cernan: Hey, Bob...

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Go ahead, Jack...(correcting himself) Gene. [Gene gestures with his left hand, pointing north.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: ...If you're looking at me, what I'm talking about is this depression in here for the core. Oh, maybe 15, 20 meters out in here. Jack, what did you have in mind for the neutron flux?

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Either the one you're down in, there; or next one over behind that rock in front of you over there. 119:58:15 Cernan: Oh yeah, I can go way over there. (Grasping the drill) That's not too far probably for...

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Well, either way I think is fine, Gene. But I would suggest behind the rock.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: For a neutron flux, huh? [By putting the detector in a depression and behind a rock, Gene will reduce the contaminating neutron flux from the RTG's plutonium source. Photo AS17-147- 22575 is one Jack will take after Gene has finished drilling the deep core hole. The picture is taken looking to the northeast and shows Gene at the Rover, with the east heat flow hole between the Rover and the place where Jack is standing. The rock in question is beyond the Rover to the left and the drill stem rack is just visible over the top of the rock. The RTG is behind Jack and this picture shows that the roc

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Yes, sir; and the core. [Schmitt - "In analyzing cores, people had looked for and found radioisotopes which had been formed by the absorption of cosmic-ray neutrons in the lunar soil. If you knew the neutron flux and spectrum, you could use the abundance of these isotopes to determine ages and turnover rates for the soil. There had been estimates made of the neutron flux and, and there were also a lot of arguments about the estimates. This experiment was designed to give a direct measurement."]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Well, I thought they wanted a core in that depression.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Well, there's also one over there.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay, and 17...

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: We can give them a choice.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: I'll go behind that rock; that looks good from here.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: And, 17, we think you guys are in by far the best position to judge that; far better than we are. You know what the requirements are on shielding and...

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Okay. [Gene stops drilling, looks at his watch on his left wrist, and then resumes.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: ...(you know that the distance from the RTG needs to be) greater than 50 meters...(Correcting himself) 25 meters. 119:58:54 Cernan: Okay, Bob. (Pause) [Gene completes the drilling and reaches for the wrench.] [Schmitt - "I suspect that we had practiced this specific ALSEP deployment a half dozen times. I had done the Apollo 15 deployment a few times as part of the backup crew training; and Gene had done the Apollo 14 deployment. You didn't want to train for it too much, because each situation was going to be different. You needed to know it just well enough to be able to be adaptable, and a ha

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Okay. The long bore is in.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. Copy that, Gene. Looked like that one went in fairly well. [Gene opens the wrench.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Well, probably about like the other one did. Not too bad.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. [Gene leans on the drill to attach the wrench.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Oh, I must be getting old. I expect the next two are going to be a little harder. (Pause) [Gene has the drill off.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Bob, I'm not very happy with this (antenna) level. But I'll turn it on. Have me come back a little bit later, when they've warmed up some more, and let's see what it looks like. [Schmitt - "The fluid surrounding the level bubbles was probably an oil that wouldn't freeze when it got cold in the LM Equipment Bay. We'd been in the barbecue mode on the way out, rotating the spacecraft to get uniform heating, but there wasn't any active heating in the Equipment Bay and it would have gotten pretty cold. I was probably thinking that the fluid was still a little viscous from having been cold. Maybe th

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. We'll do that. Give me a mark when you turn it on, and we'll see what kind of signals we get.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Okay. The gnomon (shadow) is aligned; I'm going to turn the shorting plug on.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Copy that. (Pause) [By turning the shorting plug "On", Jack is letting current flow from the RTG into the Central Station - rather than through the shorting plug itself. Jack notes that the phrase "turning the shorting plug on" is a misnomer.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: It's On. [Gene has the wrench off.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Roger. Video Clip ( 3 min 18 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 29 Mb MPEG )

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: And the needle is full scale left.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Copy that. (Long Pause) ["Full-scale left" usually means "off", and the needle is undoubtedly indicating that there is no current flowing through the shorting plug and, implicitly, that the current is now flowing into the Central Station.] [Gene has the second stem (71-cm) out of the rack and is bracing the one in the ground with his right foot, toes up and on the stem, heel down and on the ground. Next, he giggles and twists the stem with his right hand.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: I can't believe that.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: What's the problem?

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Well, that whole bore turns in the ground, it's so loose. You know how those threads sometimes stick on you a little bit. (Getting the wrench again) I got one stuck halfway down and the whole bore is turning, so now I've got to use a wrench on it. [Gene needs the wrench to hold the first stem still while he threads the second into it. He leans on the drill to attach the wrench.] [Jack is now at the top of LMP-21 and is about the deploy the LEAM (Lunar Ejecta and Meteorite experiment).]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay, Jack. And we have...

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Bob, I've got a rock about 10 feet southeast of my LEAM location. I can move a little more north and get, oh, 15 feet from that. That okay?

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: How big is the rock there, Jack?

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Oh, it stands...It's a meter wide and stands about a third of a meter high. [This is the rock beyond the garbage pile in AS17-147- 22584 . The RTG is in the foreground on the left side of the picture. Notice the deep shadows on the west face of the East Massif on the far horizon. Geophone Rock is at the right edge of the picture and the geophone module is in front of it. The large rock beyond and to the right of the LEAM is one that Jack will examine at 120:22:42, after deploying the east geophone. The planned LEAM deployment location relative to the Central Station is shown on LMP-15 .]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: About a third...about a foot high?

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Bob, how's that for...(Listens)

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: (Lecturing tone) A third of a meter.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. [The Lunar Ejecta and Meteoroid Experiment is designed to catch and count both small meteoroids and ejecta from lunar impacts. Ejecta from small, local impacts would tend to have rather flat trajectories and a nearby rock would "shadow" ejecta from beyond it. Jack wants to emplace the experiment far enough from the rock that it's shadow will be unimportant. AS17-134- 20500 is a good picture of the LEAM with the trash pile, the Central Station, and the LSG beyond it. The RTG is to the right of the Central Station and the white box beyond the RTG is the Heat Flow Experiment package.] [Gene

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Bob, how's that for soil mechanics? I pulled the first bore right on out trying to get this thing on right. [Fendell pans away from Gene, looking for Jack, who is southeast of the Central Station deploying the LEAM and apparently releasing the stool legs.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Well, put it in before your hole fills up there, Geno.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Yeah. Right now I'm interested in getting this second bore on. (Pause) Now, let's see if I can get it back in! (Pause) Well, not quite as far, but high enough for me to reach the (drill handle). It still feels, Bob, like there's a lot of fragmental material down there.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: I copy that, Geno. Good luck.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: That was an interesting little exercise. Well, I got the bore on right, anyway. (Pause) Video Clip ( 3 min 18 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 29 Mb MPEG )

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Well, shoot. (Pause)

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay, Jack. As long as it's only 1 foot high and 10 feet away, that's satisfactory.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [Jack sets the LEAM on the surface and rocks it with the attached UHT to find a level position.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Okay, Bob, the LEAM's deployed, aligned, and the level bubble is just touching the inner ring.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Copy that. [Having removed the UHT, Jack kicks the ribbon cable, perhaps to remove some dirt.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: (Wanting to know if Houston is getting data from the Central Station) Hey, Bob. Did you get anything from the ALSEP yet?

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Watch that cable, Jack. (To Gene) Roger. We started to tell you that when you had the question there, and we're getting a good lockup on the data.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Well, keep an eye on it (that is, on the signal from the Central Station), because I'm not happy with the level. [Jack is near the RTG and moves the LEAM cable a little with the UHT.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. We'll get back with you on that.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: I'll check. Make me check it. (Pause) I found a way to get over cables. (He makes a little jumping noise as he kangaroo-hops over the cable) Bee-doop! (Laughs) (Pause) [Jack uses the UHT to pick up the heat flow pallet for use as a base for the seismic array antenna. He is in the middle of LMP-21 ] 120:06:01 Cernan: Oh, Manischewitz. Whew!

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: There you go again.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: I know. Let me get this one off and take a bite of candy here. [The pallet falls off of Jack's UHT. Apparently, the UHT locking pins had not seated properly in the receptacle on the pallet.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: I'm kind of having trouble with UHTs today. They just don't want to lock in when you get dust in there. [Schmitt - "Anything that is not hermetically sealed is just not going to work very long."]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Hey, Jack. Be careful with that UHT on the heat flow because it was aligned, real good.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: It was what?

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: The heat flow electronics, when you go over there for that UHT, was aligned.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Oh, yeah. [Schmitt - "There were two UHTs. Gene had used his to carry the heat flow electronics box and align it; and then just left the UHT in the heat flow box. So he's warning me not to disturb the alignment when I go to get his UHT later on."] [After spending a short while trying to engage the UHT pins, Jack gives up on what we might call the high-tech end of the tool, turns the UHT end for end, and hooks the handle - which we can call the low-tech end - through the red handle which can be seen in NASA photo S72-37260 . He then lifts the heat flow pallet off the ground.] Video Clip ( 2 min

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Bob, I'm going to take a zap of cold (cooling) water.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. Sounds good to me.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Whee! Almost looks like it's getting dark out. Is it? Guess not.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: (Laughing and doing an Amos and Andy impression) Hope not, or "we is in trouble". [Cernan - "When you stop working and take a rest, you have a chance to look around. Earlier, when I was taking a rest from drilling the first heat flow hole, I had a chance to get ahead and talk to the ground about a place for the core hole, which I wasn't going to do for a long time yet. When you took a rest, that was the only chance you had to just look around; otherwise, you got so involved with what you were doing that you had tunnel vision and your perspective was very limited. So I looked around and said 'O

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: I think I may have gone the wrong way. I did. I went to Min instead of Max. Here it comes. (Pause) Oh, boy! Oh, boy. (To Jack) Man. Watch it. Okay, Jack. You're all right. Still deploying.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Huh? [Gene is telling him that he hasn't gotten to the end of the cable.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Still deploying. Nothing; you're all right. 120:07:24 Schmitt: It's coming out a little hard. (Pause) Wouldn't you know it?

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Okay. I'm back in Min, Bob.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: By any chance (do you) have any heat flow data yet?

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: No, Geno. We don't have the heat flow turned on yet. 120:08:01 Cernan: Oh, that's right. Okay. (Pause) I think that's right. Okay. I'm about to give you your number...Oh, God darn it! (Jack laughs) (Pause) [Gene knocks the drill over and then picks it up by going to one knee in a quick down-and-up motion.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: (To himself as he runs the drill for a second) Crank it a couple of times. (Pause) Clean as a whistle! Clean as a whistle.

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Well, just like I thought; the antenna doesn't want to go in. (Pause) [In order to keep the socket clean, it is covered with a piece of aluminum foil which, rather than tearing easily, is resisting Jack's efforts to push the antenna through. See Jack's debrief comment at 126:38:56 .]

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Is that the number 3 section there, Geno?

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: There, it's in. [Jack uses the UHT to push the antenna into the socket.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: (Responding to Bob) Yes, sir, Bob.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Roger. Beautiful. 120:09:02 Cernan: Well, it's the last one I got. (Chuckles) I guess we'll find out when I put the probe in. I think they're all in there. [Gene starts drilling. He is at the top of CDR-19 and is emplacing the second 71-cm stem in the second heat flow hole.] [Fendell pans to Jack who is now at the Central Station.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Okay. I'm about ready to deploy some geophones.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay, Jack. Did you get the antenna into that subpallet okay, eventually?

A17A1195720.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1195720.text: Yes. Video Clip ( 3 min 18 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 29 Mb MPEG )

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Good enough. [Jack picks up a piece of the Central Station pallet and drops it on the trash pile.]

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: Bob, I occasionally hit stuff and it spits this whole drill back at me. Knocks it back about a half an inch or so, and then it will bite through it.

A17A1195720.speaker: Parker
A17A1195720.text: Okay. MP3 Audio Clip ( 20 min 37 sec )

A17A1195720.speaker: Cernan
A17A1195720.text: My general impression is that there is an awful lot of fragments I'm busting up down there.

A17A1195720.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [Cernan - "When the drill's spinning and it hits something, it kicks the drill and spits it back at you. Not vertically, but rotationally. It was tough drilling. So, the drill turned backwards."] [Jack continues policing the trash pile, using the UHT to push things around.
