A17A1201037.text: Oops, there's a heat flow probe. [Jack does a high kangaroo hop to avoid the first heat flow hole.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: What happened?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: (Laughing) I messed up...

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Man, don't hit that. Give me heart failure after all that drilling.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: No, I just walked too close to it. I apologize for that.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: I don't care how close you walk to it...

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Well, Mark (Langseth) does.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Just don't step on it. (Pause) [Because of John Young's accident, no heat flow measurements were made on Apollo 16 and this is the last chance to confirm the Apollo 15 data. Marcus Langseth is the Principal Investigator.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: I do that (pause) in training, though. (Pause) [Gene is on CDR-19 and has just finished drilling the second heat flow hole. He has the wrench attached to the top stem and is trying to twist off the drill; but he has to get down to re-position the wrench. The TV jiggles as Jack works at the Rover. He is getting his camera and the gnomon so that he can document the geophones as he deploys them. He is at the top of LMP-22 .]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Ooh. (Grunting and breathing hard) Hey, Bob, just out of curiosity, what kind of heart rates has this drill been producing on me?

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Stand by. (Pause)

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay, you've been running at 120 flush, Gene, with peaks of 140 to 150 from time to time.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Okay. (Pause) [Gene has the drill off.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: And there goes the last heat flow hole on the Moon.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Oh...(Listens) [Gene positions the drill, leans on it, and removes the wrench.] Video Clip ( 3 min 06 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 29 Mb MPEG )

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Yes, sir. I tell you, if you learn how to use your instruments in this one-sixth g - you take your time and you get around - it's frankly phenomenal. But if you try and bend over without some help; (it's) not so phenomenal. (Long Pause) [Gene has the wrench off and hangs it on the rack. He moves the drill out of the way. The TV has stopped jiggling, so Jack is probably on his way to the geophone module.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Boy, what a ride that Challenger gave us coming down. What a ride. (Long Pause) [After a couple of unsuccessful attempts, Gene uses the wrench to pick up the heat flow probe. He removes the cover which he then drops accidentally.] Video Clip ( 3 min 15 sec 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 30 Mb MPEG ) Note that this clip includes audio from the Flight Director's loop.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: (Talking to himself) Oh, you dummy. You dummy. (Pause) Jack, you still with me?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Yeah.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Okay. [Gene now drops the wrench as he tries to hang it on the rack.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Boy, I'm getting dropsies now. Getting dropsies.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Don't push it.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Getting dropsies.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Take a rest. (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "Except for the little things, the ALSEP deployment went pretty much like training; and many, if not most, of the little problems had already happened in training. The only physically difficult part of the deployment was carrying the ALSEP out to the site, and then using your hands. All the manipulation just wore out the forearm muscles. You went slower and slower and slower, and then you got to the point where you started dropping things."] [Gene tosses something off to the north, and then comments on how far it's flying with so little effort.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Unbelievable. Unbelievable. (Long Pause)

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay, Geno. And the (first) heat flow (probe)'s on and looking good.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: That's good news, Bob. Let me give you another one here. (Pause) [The probe goes in fairly easily.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: While it's dirty, I'll tell you I'm in to the bottom of the white marks. (Pause) And that's, oh, about Bravo 1 again.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay, I copy. Papa 1, Foxtrot 1, and Bravo 1? [Papa 1 and Foxtrot 1 are the desired depths of the bottom and middle shields, as indicated on CDR-19 . Bravo 1 is the height of the top stem. Bob was talking to the Experiments people in Houston and didn't realized that Gene had only given the last of these readings.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: No, sir, Bob. No, the bore stem is in to the top of the white marks; I'm still putting the probe down.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay, copy that.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: And the top of the white marks is about Bravo 1.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Copy that. [Gene attaches the rammer to the cable.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: About Bravo 1. Okay. Here goes the probe. (Pause) Pick a number you'd like to hear. How about Papa 1? [This is the mark indicating the deepest and most desirable penetration.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: How about Papa 1 there, Geno.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Bingo, babe, you win; and it locked in.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger. I think Mark won on that one, too.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Papa 1. [Gene removes the rammer from the hole and re-attaches it to the next higher probe.] Video Clip ( 3 min 22 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 31 Mb MPEG )

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger. (Pause) And, Jack, I gather you are probably traipsing across the landscape with a geophone about now, right?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: That's affirm.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. And let me ask you...

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Good gravy! You know how big that (Geophone) rock...

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Stand by. Go ahead.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Go ahead, Bob. [ Fendell pans away from Gene. Jack is emplacing Geophone 3 eighty-eight feet south of the geophone module. Gene is looking in his direction and, with Jack in the foreground, is getting an appreciation for just how big Geophone Rock is. It is 3 meters tall, or about 10 feet. Jack is at the middle of LMP-22 .]

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: (To Jack) Okay. I gather...You said that the LEAM was leveled and aligned, and I gather that meant it was on the black decal on top. Do you happen to remember what a number was on that?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Well, I'll check it! But I think you know where that decal is.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Well, okay. Good enough. [Fendell finds Jack as he deploys Geophone 3. He is thirty meters south of the module and about 20 meters northeast of Geophone Rock. For future reference, the gnomon is visible in the TV picture. Frame AS17-147- 22549 is a documentation photo of geophone number 3, which Jack will take at about 120:38. Note the geophone flag and the gnomon at the left side, just in front of the partially buried boulder. Note, also, that Gene is at the Rover. Patrick Vantuyne has created a red-blue anaglyph from 22548 and 49 ( 435k ).] [Training photo 72-H-1412 show Jack deploying a geo

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Okay, Bob. The little thermal shield went to F-1.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Hey, that's another bingo.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: And it's coming out to the south. (Listens) I'm coming out to the south.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "By running the heat flow cable southward out of the hole, you got more uniform heating than you would if the cable ran east or west. That way you could calculate more easily the error that cable heating introduced into the measurements."] [Jack returns to the Geophone Module near the RTG. He runs using a foot-to-foot stride and, as he gets close, plants both feet in front of himself. The 30 meter run takes about 25 seconds, including a few steps at the beginning to get himself up to speed and a few at the end to stop. His average speed is 4.3 kph. For a long tim

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger. Copy that. (Long Pause) [Jack turns to the east and shields his eyes to find a predetermined point on the East Massif which he will use as a horizon marker so that he can take the east geophone out in the right direction.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Well, it was until I moved it. (Pause) (thinking about throwing the rammer) Do I need my javelin anymore?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: You might.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Yeah, I might.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: One never knows, Geno.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: I think I'll save it until after I drill the core. (Pause) Oh, me oh my. [Cernan - "I called the heat flow rammer a 'javelin' because what I really wanted to do was give it a heave-ho on the Moon and see what it would do."]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Take it easy, Geno. You sound like you're... [Jack picks up geophone 1 by inserting the UHT in the top of the cable reel and lifting it out of the module , and starts running east.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: No, I'm doing fine. (Probably looking up) That Sun is just bright! I ought to put those visors down, I suppose; those other visors. Okay. Let me take a look at my list and see whether I've got everything. (Scanning CDR-19 ) Measured, measured; height, height; you've got all the (thermal) shields; you're coming out south; verify heat flow is level and aligned. It is aligned and gnomon was good; UHT to the LRV LMP seat; and then what do I do? (Turning to CDR-20 ) Let me see. Deep core prep. Jack, I'm going to leave the UHT in the heat flow in case you need it (rather than on the LMP seat).

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Okay. [Cernan - "The checklist pages were made of fairly stiff paper and were about two-and-a-half inches square. They lay flat on your wrist because they were bound with a spiral wire hinge that forced them to bow up. As soon as you turned a page, the hinge put a stress on it and it would lay flat. The tabs that you used to turn the page weren't very large, but even in the gloves it wasn't really hard to get them turned."] [A detail from Apollo 13 training photo 70-HC-83 is a good side view of Jim Lovell's cuff checklist.] 120:19:30 Cernan: Okay. I'm going to go behind a rock over there.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: (Admonishing) Now, now.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: In that depression. Bob, you do want the core in a depression, right?

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger. That's affirmative, Geno. Video Clip ( 2 min 47 sec 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPEG )

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Okay, nobody touch my heat flow. It's the prettiest job I've ever done. Okay, I'm going behind a boulder over here. (Pause) Bob, I've got about 3.85 (psi) and I guess about fifty percent (oxygen). I can't see it too well.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: I copy that, Geno. [Jack reaches the end of the east geophone cable. He is part way down in the swale; the LM is in the background. In looking at the television picture, it appears that the LM is below the ALSEP site and, indeed, at several points in the mission it looks as though the Rover is sitting on high ground when, as is the case here, there is actually no elevation difference. Here, the fact that Jack is down in the swale may contribute to the impression.] [Gene sounds fairly playful now.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: And no flags and no tone; and I'm on intermediate coolant and I feel great.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Likewise; and I'm...

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: ...and LMP is five-six percent.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: What are you, Geno?

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Well. I can't see it. The Sun was...(Pause) I don't know, Jack. I can't...I'm on about...Yeah, about 55 or 54. [Fendell pans away from Jack.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Okay.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Now, this (boulder) ought to shield that thing (the neutron probe) from the doggone (RTG)... 120:20:52 Schmitt: Pressure's 3.85 on the LMP. (Pause) Bob, one comment on getting the geophones within a few degrees of vertical. In this undulating terrain (chuckles), I think they're pretty good; but it's not real easy to tell what vertical is.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Roger, Jack. (Pause) [Schmitt - "Each of the geophones was a cylinder that had a stake on one end. You put the point in the ground and then just stepped on the geophone to push it down into the surface."] [One of the geophones can be seen at the lower left in S72-37259 , just below the thick cable which connects the module to the ALSEP Central Station.] [Training photo 72-H-1412 show Jack deploying a geophone at the Cape. note the cable rell on the UHT in his left hand and the anchor/flag in the right foreground.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Well, this is right in line with the...(It's in a) shallow depression and it's right in line with the RTG, with a rock in the middle. [Frame AS17-136- 20695 from Jack ALSEP pan shows Gene kneeling at the deep core hole. After extracting the core, he will place the neutron probe in the hole and needs to shield the probe from the RTG as much as possible by siting the core hole in a depression or, as he actually did, with a large rock blocking the line-or-sight to the RTG. The boulder in question is immedaitely south of Gene.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay, Geno. As long as you're drilling behind the rock from the RTG, that's great.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: That's where you're going to get it. Let me see what I need. (Reading CDR-20 )"Drill, rack, core bag. Drill at 1 IPS (inch per second)." Okay. Let's go do it right. (Pause) Okay. Let me see, I'm going to put it right in this depression. Right in it.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Yeah, get the middle of that.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: It's a shallow one. If I go over there, I'm not shielded, Jack. Video Clip ( 4 min 04 sec 1.0 Mb RealVideo or 40 Mb MPEG )

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: No, that's good. Get in the middle. Get it in that place.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Right in this little...It's only about a 4-meter (diameter) depression. [Fendell finds Jack again. He is looking toward Gene.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Oh, wait a minute. Oh, you're on the other side of the rock. Okay. [On his way back to the geophone module, Jack stops at a meter-high rock due south of the Rover. He leans on it for a few seconds to examine the minerals and then goes to get the next geophone. The rock appears on the right side of AS17-147- 22549 , taken near Geophone 3, and is in the center of AS17-147- 22584 , taken near the RTG.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, I want to get back here.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: That's good.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Oh, man, go slow. (Long Pause) [The sound of Gene's drilling can be heard. After examining the rock, Jack makes his way to the geophone module, describing the rock to Bob as he runs.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Bob, all of these big boulders around here that I've looked at are the same rock type. (Talking to himself) Ooh. Who pulled over the geophone module? (Pause) Can't imagine. (Pause) Okay. That sounds like the title of a book. (Long Pause) [Jack puts the geophone module upright, picks up geophone 2, and looks west. He is at the top of LMP-23 .] 120:24:23 Cernan: Oh, oh. There it went.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: What happened?

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Oh, I lost my vise. I see it. I see it. [Gene is looking for his wrench, which may have popped off the core stem as a result of tension built up in the wrench while he blocked it with his leg so he could remove the drill.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Hope I took (geophone) number 1 in the right direction. (Pause) Yep. Okay, number 4 will be a little hard to pick up.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Boy, all these little craters are filled with glass. (Probably talking to the errant wrench) Come on back here. I've got to chase this thing over the lunar surface.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: I've seen glass covers. [He means "glass-covered crater bottoms". He is standing on the geophone 1 cable about 10 feet east of the geophone module, sighting across it to the western horizon.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: (To himself) Oh, about out towards there, I guess. (Long Pause) [Jack picks up a flag and heads west, talking as he runs.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: As I was saying, Bob, all these big blocks that I've looked at look like the gabbroic rock that I was talking about: possibly upwards of 50 percent plagioclase rather than 30 (percent) like the mare, but an intermediate gabbro of some kind. And one big block, there, had very-sharply defined, parallel parting planes. I think there is a foliation of minerals that parallel that parting, but I'll have to check it out.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. Copy that, Jack.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Those parting planes (pause as he reaches the end of the geophone line) go through the whole boulder - (the boulder being) on the order of at least 3 meters long - in "outcrop". (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "For various reasons, you sometimes see places in a rock where it's splitting and coming apart. In this case I was saying that I thought the splitting in the rock I'd just examined was produced by the alignment of prismatic habit minerals parallel to that plane; and that's called a foliation. What that implies is some kind of stress during crystallization, either a flow stress as in a volcanic r

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: How is it going, Gene?

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Fine. I'm on my second stem (pair), here. Or I'm starting on it. How are you coming? 120:27:11 Schmitt: Okay. I'm just about ready to pick up the biggie, geophone 4. [Jack goes back to the geophone module, taking long running strides. He covers the 50-meter distance in 33 seconds for an average speed of 5.4 kilometers per hour. He takes about 30 strides, each about 5.5 feet in length. Geophone 4 will be emplaced 90 meters south of the geophone module.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: (Guffawing) Have a good time.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. And Geno, how are you doing? We've been watching Jack traipse back and forth across the Moon.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: I'm getting there, Bob. I'm trying to fit...

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Talk about seven league boots.

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: ...Put stem (pair) number 2 on. RealVideo File by Mick Hyde (18 min 29 sec) [Schmitt - "By now I'm taking longer and longer strides and the running technique is getting to be very much like cross-country skiing. On future missions, either for recreation or for an emergency walkback, you ought to have ski poles available for stabilization. At this point I wasn't breathing hard and I think that, with poles, you could go faster than the Rover can drive (10-12 km/hr on a level surface) without expending much energy. And that way you could greatly extend your driving distance with a Rover. I also t

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: And, Jack, how's the visibility back to the center geophone (meaning geophone 3) (Garbled) [Fendell pans to find Gene, who is northwest of the Rover.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: How's the vis?

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Yeah. Are you...

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: Not bad.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. You're not having to worry about extra photos yet?

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: No; I've been checking it. (Pause) Bob, my biggest problem is that the flags don't anchor.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1201037.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1201037.text: In general, the lines are following the contours. Whoops - whoops - whoops. (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "I don't remember why, but we didn't want the geophone cables to be suspended above the surface as they went across craters and depressions but, rather, wanted them to follow the contours."] Video Clip ( 4 min 01 sec 1.0 Mb RealVideo or 40 Mb MPEG )

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Well, try another one. Doggonit.

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: What's the problem, Geno? It won't screw on?

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Oh, yeah. It's no problem. You know, it's the same problem you always have. You get these threads...You get a little side force on them and, you know, with the helmet and gloves and what have you, you can't...Sometimes they go on easy; sometimes they don't. [Gene starts threading another core stem pair.]

A17A1201037.speaker: Parker
A17A1201037.text: Copy that. (Long Pause)

A17A1201037.speaker: Cernan
A17A1201037.text: Okay. I got this one on now.

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1203005csm.text: Hello, Ron. How's it going up there?

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1203005csm.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [Gene leans on the drill to remove the wrench.]

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1203005csm.text: Boy, do I have a ball of spaghetti here. But the geophones are going in the right direction. I hope you don't have an EMI (electromagnetic interference) problem. Can the geophone lines cross, Bob?

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1203005csm.text: Stand by on that. (Pause) [Gene picks up the drill.]

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1203005csm.text: Okay. Hey, if you see me start to pull over that (geophone) module there...

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1203005csm.text: No, I mean...Oh, I won't hurt it. It's just that it stretches the other geophones tight. [When Jack got to the end of the west geophone line, the cable pulled taut; and, if the geophone module - to which the cables were all attached - had moved, it would have put tension on the remaining cables.]

a17_1203005csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1203005csm.text: Okay. Well, right now we're watching Gene. [Gene attaches the drill and starts drilling.] 120:31:21 Schmitt: Okay. Don't worry about it. I'll watch it. (Pause) The anchors are completely unsuccessful - on the module, anyway. (Pause) [Schmitt - "We had anticipated that if any of the lines got pulled and the module moved, one or more of the geophones would get pulled out. So we equipped the module with an anchor of some sort, to keep it stationary. Obviously, the anchors wouldn't hold in the loose soil."] [Gene has started drilling.] 120:31:47 Parker: That looks pretty good, Geno.

a17_1203301csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1203301csm.text: Houston, America. The mag Lima Lima is on frame number 54 now.

a17_1203301csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1203301csm.text: Oh boy, oh boy! (Tired) Speaking of "boy, oh boy" (meaning Jack), are you a long way off. [Cernan - "As I said earlier, when you stop and take a rest, that's when you have a chance to look around. You've got a second or two to yourself. You take a deep breath, take a rest for a second, and look around, and that's when you begin to enjoy your environment, look at what Jack's doing, look at the beautiful Earth, or notice just how high the mountains are. These are the times you can steal for yourself. But that first "oh boy" here definitely referred to how tired my hands were from working with th

A17A1203615.speaker: Cernan
A17A1203615.text: (On his feet, holding the wrench) Darn it! You know, Bob, one of the problems is I'm working in a small crater; and it's just a little difficult to work on these slopes. Okay. It's on. I'm ready to put the drill in. [Gene hangs the wrench on the rack. His breathing is a bit labored. His heart rate (at 118:00 hours on the chart) is over 140 beats per minute again.]

A17A1203615.speaker: Parker

He has cables inside his suit that are fixed at the center of his chest, run laterally across to his arm pits and then up, over the outside of his shoulders through tubes and, finally, are attached at the center of his back. A17A1205730.speaker: Cernan
A17A1205730.text: Let's see if I can't get a bigger bite. You on one end, and let me stand on the treadle and we might be able to get a bigger bite. See, I can't get a very big bite. That's one of the problems.

A17A1205730.text: Okay. If I do it that way...Get her way down there.

A17A1205730.text: Oh, that's all right. 121:00:59 Cernan: Does it feel like it's loosening up at all? [On this stroke, Jack pushes so hard on the handle that his toes come up about a foot off the ground.] [Schmitt - "I was putting every bit of weight and momentum into it that I could."]

A17A1205730.text: No, go ahead. (Laughter) [Jack loses his balance and spins to the ground; he kicks the rack again on the way down.]

A17A1205730.text: (Both laughing) Okay, okay, okay. [Cernan - "This part - where Jack spins around and falls ass-over teakettle - was the funniest thing in the world."]

Gene is also holding the core, probably to minimize any lateral stress Jack might put on it. During this interval (about 118:20 on the graph ), Jack's heart rate peaks at about 135 beats per minute. A17A1211233.text: We got them three cores; we got the neutron flux down; and we got two heat probes, and an ALSEP. I don't care if we are 30 minutes late. (Pause) [Cernan - "Maybe we were 30 minutes late, but at least we got the job done and we got it done right. I think that was the feeling we had. A feeling of satisfaction. That's what we went up there to do during that period of time and we did it. It was a lot of work, probably more work than people anticipated because we ran into problems in getting the core out, but we got it all done."] [Schmitt - "I was not quite so satisfied as Gene was at this point b

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Bob, did I give you the last cap? [Gene consults his checklist. He is about finished with CDR-22 . Readers who have been following along in the checklists should note that CDR-23 is a duplicate of LMP-25 , the ALSEP photo plan.]

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: That's okay, Gene. We don't really need it. The way they're broken down, there's no problem. The 3-2-3 stands out and the Bravo on the bit end. There's no problem there.

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Hey...

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: What do you need, babe?

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Can you pull that off? [Jack hasn't gotten the LRV sampler attached properly to the UHT. During the following exchange, Jack asks Gene to grab the sampler head and pull it off - with Jack still holding on to the UHT - so that they can get it properly aligned.]

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: (Confirming what Jack wants him to do) Pull this off.

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Yeah. Rotate it 180, there. (Pause) No, no, no, just the...The total thing. That's good. There you go.

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Like that?

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Yeah.

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Okay, and, 17...

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Okay, I have to line it up.

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Go ahead.

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Okay. I'll hold it. You do it.

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: I got it. [Jack returns to the gate.] Video Clip ( 3 min 33 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 35 Mb MPEG )

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Okay. Let me give you a (gravimeter) reading, Bob, before you speak. Wait a minute, let me get it over with. [Gene goes to the rear of the Rover to read the gravimeter. For this reading, he had not taken the instrument off the Rover.]

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Did you punch Grav a second time? That's identical to the first one.

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: It (meaning CDR-22 ) just said to read it. That's what you want, isn't it?

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Yeah, but did you punch Grav after the first reading you gave me there at the ALSEP? Or are you just reading me the same measurements you did before? [Gene was supposed to have punched the Grav button when he was at the Rover getting the treadle. That was on CDR-21 and, in his eagerness to get the core out of the ground, he forgot to do that task. See Gene's further comment below at 121:35:53.]

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Bob, I called them out every time. (Listens) Bob, I'm reading it right here. Everywhere I punched Grav, you've got it written down somewhere.

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Yeah, and I didn't copy your punching Grav, but the one...

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Bob, I did not. When I went to get the treadle and the neutron flux and rammer, I did not punch Grav. [Jack is working at Gene's seat.]

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Okay. So that's the same as the first one. Never mind, thank you. And guys, we're ready for you guys, as you go along here, to do the Geo Prep and press on. As I say, we'll go to Steno and come back from there and do the S.E.P. Over. Any questions about that? (Pause) [The Surface Electrical Properties Experiment (SEP, usually pronounced "Sep") measured variations in the conductivity of near surface materials and gives an indication of the subsurface geologic structure. It consists of an antenna, receiver, and data recorder mounted behind Jack's seat and a transmitter and associated antenna whi

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: We'd also like to know if you have the gnomon, back at the Rover?

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: No, we're just...(Listens to Bob's final question)

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Yes, we do (have the gnomon). ALSEP Deployment Apollo 17 Journal Traverse to Station 1

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: (Reviewing checklist page CDR-21 , which he has completed) Okay, "lay cores in..." (Finding the right page) Okay...

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Can you put that in that sampler tool bag, there?

A17A1211233.speaker: Cernan
A17A1211233.text: Yes, sir. (Pause) We're configuring for geology now, Bob.

A17A1211233.speaker: Parker
A17A1211233.text: Okay, copy that.

A17A1211233.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1211233.text: Bob, right now, (sample bag) 10 Echo is in my suit pocket, I hope.

A17A1212628.speaker: Cernan
A17A1212628.text: (Reviewing checklist page CDR-21 , which he has completed) Okay, "lay cores in..." (Finding the right page) Okay...

A17A1212628.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1212628.text: Can you put that in that sampler tool bag, there?

A17A1212628.speaker: Cernan
A17A1212628.text: Yes, sir. (Pause) We're configuring for geology now, Bob.

A17A1212628.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1212628.text: Bob, right now, (sample bag) 10 Echo is in my suit pocket, I hope.

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1212648csm.text: Okay, Ron. Did you get that mag finished up?

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1212648csm.text: Okay. [They each have a pocket on their right shin and on their left thigh.] 121:26:54 Cernan: Okay. (Reading CDR-24 ) "Mount 20-bag dispenser (from) SCB-1." Let me get at them.

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1212648csm.text: I've got mine on. [The sample bags come in bundles of twenty which are hung from hooks at the bottom of the 70-mm cameras. That way, the bags were always in easy reach. The sample bags have been stowed in Sample Collection Bag (SCB) number one. The SCBs are much larger bags made of laminated Teflon cloth and are each 42 cm high, 22 cm wide, and 15 cm deep. Each of the astronauts will wear one on his PLSS. After a sample is sealed in one of the small, clear Teflon bags, they will put it in one or the other of the SCBs. Gene swings the gate closed; from the perspective of the TV camera, the top

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1212648csm.text: Okay. (Pause) Oh! ("Rats!") This probably goes under the seat, doesn't it? (Pause) Get the camera...(I can't find) where the devil mine is? Excuse me. Oh, I see the gnomon! [Gene goes to his seat, carrying a packet of sample bags. The gnomon is on his seat.]

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1212648csm.text: I put it there so I wouldn't forget it. [The fact that both CDR-24 and LMP-26 have handwritten notes about the gnomon suggests that Jack forgot it more than once during training.] 121:27:31 Cernan: (Laughs) Okay. I tell you, dexterity is the key. Look at those cover gloves. [The cover gloves are dark brown from the impregnating dust. To prepare the gnomon for stowage, Gene grasps the legs which, rather like umbrella stays, collapse onto the central axis. He then puts the gnomon in its stowage sheath behind his seat.]

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1212648csm.text: I guess we can take those off. I don't know whether we ought to or not. [Cernan - "The cover gloves had fingers that were cut out, rather like a golf glove. They went over the regular glove and covered the palms. Because of all of the drilling and such, we just wanted to put a little more protection on our regular gloves. We were only going to use them for the first EVA, because that's where all the manual labor was; the rest was all traverse work. You've seen how hard we worked with those things up to this point; and they were just ripped up and torn up and really battered. Most of the damage

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1212648csm.text: I'm going to leave mine on for a while. I changed my mind. I want to look at my gloves before I take them off. (Pause) [Gene has decided not to discard the cover gloves until, once back in the LM, he's had a chance to examine his suit gloves for wear. Jack is at his own seat, fiddling with his camera.]

a17_1212648csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1212648csm.text: (Consulting CDR-24 ) Okay, where are we? You got your camera, obviously. This is my camera. I'll get the bag dispenser on it. (Pause) It's not a bad day's start. Bob, is the ALSEP working good?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1213027csm.text: Can you still see - see things in Earthshine or is it getting pretty black down there?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Is it?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Yeah. [As a result of problems experienced with John Young's SCB during Apollo 16, the attachment system was re-designed. At various times during Apollo 17, one or the other of the SCBs will come loose, an indication that the re-design was not adequate.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay, you've got to undo the strap...

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Let me get at it.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: You got to loosen that strap and then just put her underneath, and tighten it up again.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: This one here?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: The one on my right. Yeah.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Let me turn around then. I got to get on your...Oh, on your right. Right here.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: I think it is; yeah. That's where it is on yours.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Yeah, I'd like to make sure the other side is all right, though. [Gene adjusts the lower right strap on Jack's PLSS.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Oh, okay. [Jack turns around and presents the left side of his PLSS.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Let me...Yeah, it's all right. Turn around. [Jack presents the right side again.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Let me just get it underneath. I got it so tight now, the Rover...Okay, now. I got it on.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay; that's my last picture off.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay, now, I'll get this hooked. [Gene gets an SCB from the gate and attaches it, top and bottom, to Jack's PLSS.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: That hook's going to be a piece of cake, Jack. (Pause) That ought to keep it; and it's all on and locked. (Consulting his checklist) Okay, you got SCB-2. You got the rammer. You got a cap dispenser. Okay. You can secure SCB-1 (to Gene's PLSS as per LMP-26 ). [As noted previously, Gene has put the hammer in his own shin pocket , rather than mounting the hammer on Jack's PLSS.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Doesn't this go under your...

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Not yet, I don't think. I think it stays there.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: This (long can) does (go under the seat).

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: That does. Yeah. That goes under the seat.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: And this goes here.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Yeah.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Bob, the long can 's going under my seat. [Jack goes to his seat. The long can is about 18 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. Later in the mission, at Station 3, Gene will seal one of the drive tube sections in the long can, protecting it from cabin gases or exposure to the Earth's atmosphere. Note that, in addition to the long can, Jack's camera will be stowed under his seat while he runs back to the LM with the deep core.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay. Copy that, Jack.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: They got a handover, I think.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Handover's complete, guys. [The Moon will set at Goldstone in California in about an hour. Comm will now go thru Honeysuckle Creek near Canberra, Australia.] Video Clip ( 4 min 07 sec 1.0 Mb RealVideo or 41 Mb MPEG )

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay. [Jack returns to the gate.] 121:32:xx Schmitt: (Garbled) which way to unlock those.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay, you can pull it off.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: It's unlocked.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: It's unlocked. There it is.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: It's usually stiff.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay. [They move to the left rear of the Rover. Jack has SCB-1 to attach to the left side of Gene's PLSS.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: For once, I have my camera off. (Pause) [Schmitt - "With my camera off, I could get close enough to Gene to attach the SCB easily. With the camera sticking out a foot or so, you had to work at arm's length."]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Did you get the heat flow pictures, by the way?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: I got most of them. Not all of them. They revised the whole camera (sequence). [That is, Houston had revised the list of photographic tasks.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Hey, Bob, is it going to hurt to leave the UHT in the heat flow electronics?

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Stand by. [Jack's checklist page LMP-22 gave him the option of configuring the LRV Sampler when he went back to the Rover after deploying the LSPE antenna at about 120:10. Had he done the task then, he would have used Gene's UHT, keeping his own for the Geophone deployment. His second option (on LMP-26 was to assemble the Sampler at the start of the Geo Prep, which he did at 121:21:55. Because he was done with his UHT, he used it as the Sampler handle rather than using Gene's.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: (To Gene) Wait a minute. I ought to get that, I guess. (Pause) That's one...(You're) tall.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Here, let me lean down. [Gene bends his knees, keeping his PLSS vertical.] 121:33:00 Schmitt: Two, and the hook's still hooked. Check for sure, here. Those hooks weren't designed for new bags. [The SCB is about the length of Gene's upper arm, has a square cross section six inches on a side, and has sharp creases which will disappear with use. Jack's comment that 'those hooks weren't designed for new bags' indicates that, while they worked well for the well-worn bags used during training, the stiff, fresh bags are harder to secure.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay, Jack...

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay. I think that will ride all right.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: ...they don't want it (the UHT) there (in the heat flow electronics package). If one of you guys can get to it and pull it out.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: I'll get it right now.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay. [Jack goes to the gate; Gene to the heat flow site.]

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Thank you.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Watch the alignment, as you said.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Yeah. (To Bob) I sort of thought you might like it out of there. Let's stay away so I don't get a cable and I don't get dust in the mirror. The alignment is still good. [Gene is no longer talking loudly to Houston when he is at the Rover and only increases volume a little when he moves away from the Rover.] [Schmitt - "Part of this business about talking more loudly to Houston may be psychological distance; but I also notice that, when I'm describing something to them, I get more of an authoritarian tone. Certainly, when we were talking with each other, it was more buddy to buddy and we wouldn

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1213027csm.text: Now, if I can get it out.

a17_1213027csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1213027csm.text: Okay, I'm going back to the LM (as per LMP-27 ).

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Hey, Bob, making 8 to 10 kilometers (per hour), and I'm barely moving. [The terrain around the LM is rather flat and a speed of 10 km/hr - about 10 minutes to the mile - doesn't seem impressive. However, when they get out into rolling terrain, with the potential of finding small, deep craters to jar the Rover just over every ridge, the ride gets a bit more exciting.] [Cernan - "The Rover just didn't move very fast. It wasn't made to go very fast, but it could sure save a lot of energy. You could pack a lot of gear and save a lot of walking time, and it allowed us to cover territory and ground

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Where've you got the SEP, Jack?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Right out over there.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, let me give them a bearing, distance, and range, and some numbers here (at the SEP transmitter).

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Meet you over there.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. (Pause) Ohh! (Long Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Bob, I did see a dense gray rock that's different than the others on my traverse out here. We'll try to find some of that, too.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, Bob, I'm reading 278, 003, and 003 at the SEP site. [The actual range is about 330 meters from the ALSEP and about 140 meters from the LM.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Copy that, Geno. And how about giving me amp-hours and batteries just as long as you're there?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yes, sir, it's coming at you. Amp-hours are 112 and 110; batteries are 92 (degrees) and about 112 (degrees). [Cernan - "The needle width was at least a couple of degrees, so there was a little hesitation here as I decided what figure to give."]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, copy that, Geno.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Motors are all off-scale low.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, okay thank you.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Nav is going to Reset.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Say again there, Gene. You're going to go to Reset, right?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yes, sir; going to Reset.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. (Pause) [Gene is re-initializing the Rover navigation system.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Jack, you can be getting on. You won't need a bomb (seismic charge), and I guess you won't need the LMP camera unless you want it. We'll be deploying the bomb at Steno.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: (Laughing) I thought we were playing it by the checklist, Geno. (Giving the charge to Gene to hold while he climbs on the Rover) Here's the bomb. [Jack will soon regret having ignored Bob's advice about not carrying a charge during the drive. Checklist page LMP-27 calls for Jack to carry a charge, but only because he was to have deployed it near Steno during the planned drive to Emory. According to the original plan, Gene would have stopped the Rover long enough for Jack, without getting out of the Rover, to put the charge on the ground. As Jack will discover, holding the charge will tire his

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, give it to me.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: The "charge". [Schmitt - "During training, Bob liked to use the term 'bomb' and, here, I'm trying to get him to change it."]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I've got it.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, it just happens that the station is at the place we were going to deploy the charge. [Bob is saying again that Jack doesn't need to carry the charge.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, well, we got it off (the transporter on the back of the Rover).

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Do you know which side of Steno he wants us to go, Jack?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Not yet.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, let me fill you in on the plan, guys. We're going to go to the west side of Steno, which is where you would have driven by anyway, and the stop will be at the 340/1.2, which is where you've got the little Delta for EP 6, in your checklist. And we will plan on spending about three-zero minutes there sampling, primarily boulders. [A map of the planned traverse is shown on both LMP-28 and CDR-26 . South is up, on these maps, and the unboxed numbers associated with each traverse segment are a heading and segment length. The boxed numbers associated with the turning points are bearing and ran

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, Geno, west side of Steno, then.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. I got it here (in the checklist). (Pause) Okay...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: You got a good feeling on how to head out of here?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. (Pause) I want to get around the back side - now that I'm down there - on the back side of Trident, and make sure that what I'm looking at is Trident over there. [They are planning to drive into the Sun until they come abeam of the northeast corner of Trident and then will turn south toward Steno. Gene is hoping that, during the first part of the drive, he can clear up his residual doubts about where he's landed. He actually is, of course, about 100 meters north of Poppie rather than West Trident.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, let me try to get on this thing. [This is Jack's first Rover ride of the mission and his first attempt to climb aboard. Ken Glover has produced a video clip of Jack mounting the Rover onboard the 1/6th-g airplane.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. And, 17, just to fill you in a little bit more here. We're looking at a six (hour) plus four-five (minute) EVA. We've given you fifteen minutes to drive to Station 1; thirty minutes at Station 1; and fifteen minutes to drive back to the (spelling the acronym) S.E.P., and then deploying the S.E.P. for two-two minutes. And then a four-zero-minute close-out at six plus four five.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I'm sorry, Bob. After 30 minutes at Station 1, what did you say?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Then we're going to drive back. There's a 15-minute return to the SEP site; and then 22 minutes at the SEP site to deploy the SEP; and then return to the LM and 45 minutes for the close-out.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Understand. (To Jack) Okay, you strapped in?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yes, sir. [The seat belts had been a problem on Apollo 15 because no allowance had been made for the fact that, on the Moon, the suits don't compress as much when the astronauts are seated as they do on Earth. The problem was easily fixed for Apollos 16 and 17.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, we've got to start getting in this Rover facing 90 degrees to the seats, I think. (Pause) I did the same thing.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Did I kick dust?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, we both did.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I tried to knock it all off my feet.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah; that's impossible. [Cernan - "Best way to get in was to face out from the Rover, sit in the seat, get down, and then kick your feet up and then throw them around. Here, Jack probably faced front, then tried to get one leg up and then another leg up. By starting out facing out from the Rover, you also cut down on the amount of dust you scattered on things."] [Schmitt - "What I ended up doing most of the time was standing at the side of the Rover, facing front, and jumping, more or less straight up and over toward the seat; and then rotated my feet up and forward so that I came down in the

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, Jack. Let's see if we can't get around Trident East over here. 121:50:51 Schmitt: Well, I wish I didn't have this charge. Shouldn't have played it by the checklist. I wasn't paying attention. [Jack has finally realized that there is no reason to carry the charge; it could have been left in its transporter on the back of the Rover. He is probably already noticing his hands getting tired from having to keep them closed around the charge against the pressure of the suit. He is probably also becoming aware that the charge is keeping him from using his maps and checklist efficiently.] [NASA p

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: We're on the move, Bob.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, this is Trident, isn't it? So we're starting out...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Well, it's got to be.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. So, you're starting out on the...You really want to head about 29...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: No, no, no.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: No, wait a minute. Where are we?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: We want to go southeast.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: 181... [Jack is misreading the LMP-28 map showing the planned traverse path from the landing site to Emory. Because the traverse is merely being truncated and they think they have landed virtually at the planned point, they plan to follow the checklist and drive east on a heading of 116 (ESE) for 600 meters to get around the east side of Trident and then turn south to a heading of 181 for the drive to the west rim of Steno. The planned bearing and range at the turning point are 296/0.5.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: 17, we'll start out on the same general traverse that you've been on. It's just that we'll stop it sooner.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, we understand.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: We're just getting our bearings, Bob.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: This (possibly Poppie) has got to be Trident East, right here, Jack. See that? That's got to be Trident East. That's the big one.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: On the right or the left?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: On the right.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yeah.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: And Poppie was just over about where...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Watch your...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. I just want to get our bearings here. You can't look to the east. Okay. I've got to...(Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: That's an awful big depression over there, isn't it? (Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: It (the map) says (to) go along this way. Boy, it sure is. [Cernan - "When you're riding and not expending a lot of energy, it's a lot easier to look around and really see what's there."]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Whee! Watch it. Ho - ho - ho - hold it, hold it, hold it!

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Got it, got it, got it (garbled). (Burst of static which clears after a few seconds) Boy, I tell you; I've got to get out (of facing) east. Stand by. [Cernan - "We probably ran smack into a small crater - or maybe a boulder - that we couldn't see facing east and looking right into the Sun. And when I said, 'got it, got it' I meant I had the situation under control. Running into little craters or over little rocks wasn't critical; it was just that we didn't want to run into something big enough to matter. Here, we probably went down in a little crater and came back up. We did that a lot; but we

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Gene, I think...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I'm going to head about one two zero (120 degrees) out of here.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: You've got another hole on your right here.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I got it.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Whoa, whoa. I'm not sure what's the matter. Why don't you go left there?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Go left around this thing.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: And, 17; Houston. For your advice, we're trying to use the low-gain antenna on this traverse also. (Pause) Might try and be good guys and turn it for us when you have to.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Bob.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: That's general reminder number 1. (Static) [On this traverse, Jack and Gene won't often be out of sight of the LM and could communicate through it to Earth. As a general rule, however, NASA prefers to communicate through the low-gain antenna on the Rover, thereby decreasing the frequency and length of communications breaks.] [Cernan - "Pointing the antenna was easy enough when you were parked, but the indicator was really useful when you were driving, particularly when you were driving with the Earth behind you or well off to the side."] [The indicator on the low-gain antenna is described at 1

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Gene, I think we need to head south.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. We've got to go out here southeast. What's that big map look like in relation to Bear Mountain to you?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: You mean the...(Pause) I'm not sure I can get to it. [The traverse maps are clip mounted to the accessory staff mounted on Jack's inboard handhold. There are probably at least two maps, one showing the immediate area of this traverse, the other showing the whole valley. To look at the "big map", Jack would probably have to lean forward and to his left to lift up the local map.] [Schmitt - "With that charge in my hands, I'm not sure I could have reached for anything. And I think the reason my voice is sounding so subdued in this section is that my forearms are starting to get tired and I am mos

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I want...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: It's calling for 116 at 0.6 to (garbled) near the SEP. [The map on CDR-26 shows the first leg of the traverse being a 0.6 kilometer drive on a heading of 116, starting from the spot of his Nav initialization at the SEP site.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I ended up with this charge in my hand. There's a big...What are you headed now, south pretty much?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I think you're getting...That must be Emory over there. See with all the blocks in the wall?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Where you looking? Which way?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Southeast.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Way over there.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. [Cernan - "The helmet didn't turn; so you didn't have a good view. To see to the side, you had to turn your head inside the helmet; but because of the visors, that only gave you a little bit of a view to the side. The only other choice was to turn your body and, because the suit was so stiff, that was very difficult. Consequently, you didn't have a lot of peripheral vision."]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: This is very easily Steno right over here. Let's see, we're between the two big ones...That would be...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: That would be Powell.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: That would be Powell on the right. (Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: You think? Certainly doesn't look like the L&A (Landing and Ascent facility) yet.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: (Chuckling) No, it sure doesn't. [The L&A consisted of a site model suspended over a moveable TV camera on the floor of the facility. The camera moved in response to crew input and provided a view in either the LM simulator windows or, for the Rover missions, on a monitor that was part of an LRV mockup. Dave Scott and Jim Irwin were the first to use the L&A to get a feel for driving the Rover at their landing site. Jim Irwin made the first test drive about a week prior to the Apollo 15 launch and, while local detail wasn't reproduced, the simulations did give Scott and Irwin a feel for the rel

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: How about a range and bearing, guys, I think we can help you.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, it sounds like you're probably just driving by the East Trident or Trident 3. [They are about 200 meters northeast of the rim of East Trident and have not yet learned to judge the sizes of craters.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: You think all that right there is Trident?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: My god, if it is, that's incredible. That's hard to believe.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, there...You're going to go in a hole with your right...No problem.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I can't see the lip too well because of the...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, if that's Trident...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. And, Jack, do you have your camera on...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Boy, I wish they'd caught me with this (charge before I got on the Rover)...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: ...If so, could you give me a frame count some time?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Bob, I got my hands full with this charge.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Oh, okay, forgot about that one. Sorry about that.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Looks like four-five (45 frames).

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, copy that. Thank you. (Long Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Boy, if that's Trident, whoo!

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Hey, you know that is...Don't you suppose that's Trident?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, it sure looks like it, doesn't it?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. We were quite a ways from Trident. [They are now near the east rim of East Trident.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I bet you it is.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: If that's true... We're at 342/0.4. That's about right; we're half a mile (means "kilometer")...That's about right. Boy, what I was looking at (as) Trident isn't anywhere near that big. [East Trident is about 300 meters across while Poppie is about 70m.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, if that's true, then we want to go...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: ...we want to go 181. [As per LMP-28 , they want to be driving south on a heading of 181 degrees.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yes, sir, we're all right now. That's got to be Trident. What we were looking at before...I've got to stop and see what that is. I've got to look at those maps when we get in (the LM after the EVA).

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, it's a triplet all right, with some septum between. (Pause) Well, wish I could take pictures. Take a few, but... 121:56:26 Cernan: Well, let me get a few here. [At this point, Jack may be taking AS17-136- 20727 and Gene may be taking AS17-134- 20390 . During the next few minutes of the drive, Jack will take seven photos , AS17-136- 20728 to 20734 , and Gene will add AS17-134- 20391 and 20392 . In successive frames, individual boulders can sometimes be tracked as Gene and Jack drive toward them. However, on this traverse, Jack takes so few frames that the coverage of the drive is spotty.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, you keep pressing. We can get them coming back. (Pause) (I can) take a few, but it's not continuous. My hands are giving out. I wish I hadn't said "follow the checklist". (Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, we're at 0.5 and 346. And the surface has not really changed except slightly more hummocky and rolling, because of a larger number of irregular depressions or craters. The...Boom! (They've hit a small crater.) The rocks at first glance from the Rover look very much like what we had around the LM. That's the big ones.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: And, 17, you might be...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: There are occasional...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Jack, you might be expecting water flag and a tone in a couple of minutes, to go to Aux.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay. [The main feedwater tank contained about 8.5 pounds of water, and the auxiliary tank 3.4 pounds. They are nearly 5 hours into the EVA and will close the LM hatch at 7 hours 12 minutes, each with about one pound of water remaining. The time they take to use up the main supply depends, of course, both on how quickly they are expending water and on the amount of water they had in the tank to start with. The accompanying table details relevant information about feed water usage derived from the Apollo 17 Mission Report. Crewman/EVA CDR/1 CDR/2 CDR/3 LMP/1 LMP/2 LMP/3 Charge (lbs) 12.19 12.79

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: And CDR('s tone) will be about 5 minutes after that.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I'll get stopped here in a minute, Jack; as soon as I get...(Listens) Okay.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay. I think maybe that might be Steno over there...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I don't think we're too far off.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, there's my...I've got to go to Aux.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Can you reach it?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I hope so. (Pause) [The control is on the bottom of the PLSS and there is a cut-out in the seat so that Jack can reach it.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, Houston, do you see me in Aux?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Stand by. Roger. We see you in Aux.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I'm going to hit some of these (craters) broadside, Jack, and then we won't get any roll angle. (Pause) [Gene has decided that up-and-down motion (pitch) is more acceptable than side-to-side motion (roll).]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, how far have you come?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: (Consulting CDR-26 ) I've got to go about another 0.7 kilometers. I may be coming up on the edge of it. I don't know, I'm on the right bearing. Yeah, we're all right. Steno has got a dimple on the north. Boy, this is a heck of a way to start out our navigation because it's into the cross-Sun here...Not cross-Sun, but (into the) Sun. Now, that's got to be Powell, wouldn't you say?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. Must be. Must be. [The nearest rim of Powell is about 0.5 kilometers southwest of their present location.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Listen, you...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Then that's Steno with all the blocks in it.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Boy, am I glad we didn't land out here! Whew!

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: See this high point up here coming ahead?

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: That should give us our bearings, I hope. (Pause) I can't hold that bomb any longer.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: What are you going to do with it?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I'm going to drop it at my feet.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Okay, it's there. Keep it between your feet. [Gene can see the charge at Jack's feet. Because of the bulk of his suit, the RCU, and the camera, Jack certainly can't see it.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I will. My hands aren't going to be any good for sampling.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, that's Powell, huh? (Long Pause while Jack looks at the map) 121:59:47 Schmitt: Yes. (Pause) Okay, if that's Powell...Quite a ways over there, but I think the thing to do is get up on that little ridge there. [The ridge is shown in AS17-136- 20735 and 20736 .] [All the frames Jack and Gene take during the drive to Station 1 are displayed in the PDF document ( 16 Mb ).]

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Yeah; I think we may end up looking right into Steno when we get up there. Bob, we're at 342/0.9.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. Copy that. 340 and one point...(Stops to listen to Gene)

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Are you reading the low gain, by the way?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. Roger. Beautiful. 340 and 1.2 is where we expect the station to be. (Pause) [This would actually put the station very close to the west base of the Steno "dimple".]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: And it should be up on the top of a little bit of a rise. That you see coming up there. Almost to that rise. You ought to be in the vicinity of some very large boulders.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Houston, (pause as he listens to Bob) there are certainly a lot of big boulders...Whoop!

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Let me take a look into the Sun (east) here. That doesn't look what I thought Steno looked like. There's no dimple there. "One-point-two", he said. All right. This is it over here, though, I guess.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Yeah, Steno ought to be right at your 9 o'clock there, Gene.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: At my 9 o'clock. Yeah. [The nine o'clock position relative to their current direction of travel is east. Steno is actually southeast of them.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Either that or your 3 o'clock. I forgot which one it is.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: (To Bob) How do you know where we are? I think you're probably right, although it doesn't impress me as what I saw in the L&A (Landing and Ascent). [The L&A facilty was housed next to the LM simulator and contained a large, ceiling-mounted model of the landing site . A TV camera on the floor beneath the model moved in response to crew inputs and provided a landing-site view either in the windows of the LM simulator or on a monitor on an LRV mockup.] [Cernan - "This is another reference to simulations where we used the L&A to fly the LM around our landing site to see what these places looked li

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: How much time have we got to drive now, Bob?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, stand by.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I think that's probably Emory up there. That's Steno, I guess.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Yeah. Gene and Jack, we'd like you to...If you're in the vicinity, we think you're just about there. We were planning on you leaving the SEP and getting to this place at about 4 plus 58 (since depressurization) and we're showing about 5 plus 00 right now so you're right on time. And if you're at 340 and 1.2 in that vicinity, you must be at the station or very close to it where you can see. Over.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, it doesn't look real familiar, Bob, as far as Steno's concerned.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I got (my tone and water flag)... 122:02:14 Schmitt: I think they can locate us if we work that block field right there. [They will park about 150 meters short of the Steno rim, at about the 11 o'clock position on the rim relative to the 12 o'clock north that Bob will use in his next transmission. As with Shepard and Mitchell on their climb to Cone Crater on Apollo 14, Gene and Jack won't actually get a look into Steno Crater, but they will sample boulders ejected from the crater. Their stopping place is on the right edge of AS17-136- 20737 . When Jack says "they can locate us", he is no

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Let me get my water.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, on the map, Jack, that you're probably looking at, you're seeing that, with north being 12 o'clock, there are a couple of boulders at about the 09:30 position on Steno. And then there's a couple of more at about the 9 o'clock position on Steno. And we're putting the station right in the midst of all those boulders. Over. [From this, we can estimate that Houston thinks the SEP transmitter is roughly 200 meters west and 300 meters south of its actual location. Bob's remarks have been slightly edited for clarity.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Well, Bob, I don't know. It's hard to follow that that's where we are. I'm not sure. It doesn't look like what I expected Steno to look like.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: No, me neither.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. What's the range and bearing one more time?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I think it would almost be worth...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: I bet that's Emory up on that hill. (Pause; brief static as Gene turns) It's got to be. Yep. [Emory Crater is south of them, about another kilometer.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, well, let's...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: We better park in this boulder field here. Get in this boulder field. 122:03:33 Schmitt: I wish we could have gotten near one of the big ones (that is, near the big boulders Bob has been talking about), but let's do it. We're going to run out of time. 122:03:37 Cernan: Yep. [AS17-136- 20738 and AS17-134- 20393 are taken - in that order - as they maneuver to park at what they will call Station 1, despite the changed location. A labeled detail from the July 2009 LROC image of the landing site shows the location of Station 1.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: That's affirmative, guys...

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: (Garbled under Bob)

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. You want me...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: ... There's no point in deviating around and spending 15 minutes trying to get a particular spot or down to a bigger boulder. You must be in the near vicinity. If you're really worried about it, I guess you might drive a little bit to the east to the rim of the...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay. We got...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: ... crater, unless you're there. Over. Your judgment.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: No, we're okay. We got a good place.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: All right.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I'm parked 180 (facing south as per CDR-27 ).

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Roger. Stand by on that a minute.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: You want us to get off? What do you mean?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. No...

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: What heading?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: ...Okay. I was just wondering about where you were going to park. Go ahead and park 180. There was a question on whether they wanted us to park into the Sun, but don't worry.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I'm heading...

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: 180 is a good heading.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I'm headed 182, 346 (bearing back to the LM), 1.2 (distance driven), 1.1 (range to the SEP transmitter), 110, 108 (amp-hours remaining on each of the two batteries), 100, and 118 (battery temperatures), and off-scale-low on all of the motors.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. I copy that. (Pause) [They are about 150 meters from the Steno rim.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Bob, can we deploy...(Long Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay. (To Bob) You want this charge deployed here?

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: That's affirmative, Jack:

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: I'll deploy it now.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: You can deploy it right now. That's good. (Pause) [There are eight seismic charges in all, differing only in the amount of high explosive each contains and the preset runout time of the mechanical timers. This package, number six, contains 454 grams of explosive. There are three pins which must be pulled to activate the charge and prepare it to act on a fire signal from the LSPE antenna that Jack deployed near the Central Station.] 122:05:25 Cernan: Okay, the fenders are still on, thank goodness.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Beautiful. We'll give you the Taper of the Year award.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Boy, you're going to have to give me the Duster of the Year Award after this.

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Pin 1, (static) 2. Mark, Safe. (Pause) Pin 3. Mark, Safe. (Pause) That will be in the pans, Geno.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Okay. [Jack means that there will be no need to take locator photographs specifically for the charge deployment; the charge will be visible in a pan planned for the end of the station. Note that Jack was supposed to have taken a pan at this point but, for some reason doesn't take it until 122:32:50. Those photos are AS17-136- 20744 to 20776 and show the site, the charge, and the Rover parking orientation.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay, I copy that.

A17A1214627.speaker: Cernan
A17A1214627.text: Bob, you got Mode (static)... [Gene is turning on the TV.]

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Just to confirm that is EP-6, right? (No answer) 17, Houston. Do you read? (Pause)

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: Okay, Bob; we're about 15 meters from a 20-meter (diameter) blocky-rimmed crater. It's about 3 to 4 meters deep. All the blocks on the rim look like the pyroxene/plagioclase gabbro - the vesicular rock - (static) seen at the LM. At least all that I've seen so far. MP3 Audio Clip ( 15 min 40 sec )

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay. I copied that, Jack. And is this crater to the east or west?

A17A1214627.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1214627.text: It's to the northwest of the Rover.

A17A1214627.speaker: Parker
A17A1214627.text: Okay; copy that. [Figure 6-102 from the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report is a planimetric map of Station 1.] Deep Core Apollo 17 Journal Geology Station 1 near Steno Crater

A17A1220706.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1220706.text: The vesicle population varies from about a millimeter to one centimeter. It forms about 15 percent of the rock...10 to 15 (percent). And I've given you grain size for the rocks near the LM and that goes well for this one.

A17A1220706.speaker: Parker
A17A1220706.text: Okay, I copy that, Jack. Very good. [ Fendell pans counter-clockwise past Jack, who is leaning over a two-foot-high boulder west of the Rover.]

A17A1220706.speaker: Schmitt
