a17_1231900csm.text: (Answering Bob) No, I have one sample bag in my pocket that has a rock in it.

a17_1231900csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1231900csm.text: We'll have to take that out when we get in the Rover (meaning the LM), I assume. [Gene joins Jack, who is putting samples from under his seat into SCB-1.]

a17_1231900csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1231900csm.text: Okay. (Pause) Gene, where's that...You want to put that little rock (in SCB-1)?

a17_1231900csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1231900csm.text: Yeah, is it there? [This is the sample Gene collected during the Rover deployment at 117:35:27.]

a17_1231900csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1231900csm.text: Well, what did you do with it?

a17_1231900csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1231900csm.text: It was on the floor on my side.

a17_1232427csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1232427csm.text: Ron, everything's looking great down here. It was a really great day, really busy. We're sorry about that eat period; and it's been real - lot of - lot of things accomplished.

a17_1232427csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1232427csm.text: (Guffaws) You've been thinking of the other kind too long. You've been living in the Command Module too long. (Pause) [Jack is thinking of fecal containment bags. Upon reflection, Jack and Gene both believe that the containment bags Jack is now stowing in the ETB were later put around the SCBs to help with dust control. According to the Lunar Surface Procedures document ( 36 Mb PDF ), the six " sample containment bags " stowed in the MESA are distinct from the six "sample collection bags (SCBs)" stowed on the geopallet. Photos of containment bags in the National Air & Space collection courtesy

a17_1232427csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1232427csm.text: (Joking) That's a pretty good day's workout, you know. I don't think we need an exercise period. [When they are in the Command Module, they have regularly scheduled exercise periods to help counteract the effects of weightlessness.]

a17_1232427csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1232427csm.text: (When) we get back in there, I don't think we have to apologize to anybody. I'm sorry we didn't get out to Station 1. One of the main reasons is, I think, we could have got our navigation bearings a little bit better.

a17_1232427csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1232427csm.text: You know, this is just such an easy site to find out and to identify yourself on and to land in. But, I tell you, all of a sudden there is so many local holes that I can't think big enough.

a17_1233324csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1233324csm.text: Okay, Ron. We're going to drop the up-link here in 1 minute, so see you tomorrow.

a17_1233324csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1233324csm.text: Okay; and Geno, when you're brushing the LCRU, we'd like the blankets (that cover the radiating mirrors) left at 100 percent rather than 65 percent. We'd like them all left open; and it's been a little warm, also.

a17_1233324csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1233324csm.text: [Garble] Voice is going Off. You can call me, but I can't call you. [Laughter.]

a17_1233324csm.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1233324csm.text: 123:34:57 - Ron Evans in America began an 8-hour rest period about 10 minutes ago.

a17_1233324csm.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1233324csm.text: 123:40:17 - America has just gone behind the Moon.

a17_1233457.text: Ron Evans in America began an 8-hour rest period about 10 minutes ago.

a17_1233457.speaker: Cernan
a17_1233457.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, the batteries look pretty good. Bob, the left-hand forward reflector on the batteries is about 10 percent in shade. The others are in the Sun. Is that what you want?

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Okay, we do not bring up the LM ECS canister. Is that correct?

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: That's correct, 17.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Okay. (Pause) [Jack is referring to a replacement lithium hydroxide (LiOH) canister for the cabin Environmental Control System (ECS). The canisters remove carbon dioxide from the cabin air and need to be replaced at intervals through the mission. One replacement is stowed behind the ascent engine cover in the cabin, two others are stowed in the MESA. They will take one up to the cabin at the end of EVA-2 and the other at the end of EVA-3. At the moment, Jack is getting EVA Pallet 1 out of the MESA. Jack remembers that the pallet contains their food for the next 24 hours, along with such things

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: And, Jack, confirm you have the scissors in the ETB.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay, and (garbled)

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: (Laughing and responding to Bob) Yes, sir. Thank you, again.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Fighting the old blanket. (Pause) [Jack is tidying the MESA thermal blankets.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Okay, that pin's green; that pin's green. Both pins are green.

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: Copy that. [The pins are indicators on the PLSS replacement batteries. The fact that they are green indicates that the batteries are fresh.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: But dirty. (Pause)

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Okay, I'll take some stuff up (to the porch). SCB-2, we don't have. Oh, wait a minute. What did we decide to do? ...

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: SCB-2 for the big rock there, Jack.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Put that big rock in the...(Hearing Bob) Oh, okay.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: How's our time, Bob?

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: No problem on time.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: There's a little (dust) in on those (radiating) mirrors, Geno. [Gene is dusting the SEP. Jack has noticed some dust that has gotten under the loose cover.] [Schmitt - "Poor Gene. It was just like when you're doing windows and somebody taps from the other side to point out you missed something."] 123:37:29 Schmitt: Can I sneak in and get a bag?

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Yep. (Pause) [Jack is getting SCB-2 from his seat so that he can take it to the MESA, put the football-sized rock into it, and then carry it and the core-stem bag up to the porch.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: See you later, Rover.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, the SEP blankets are open; it is dusted. Okay, and I verify that the DSEA is Off, and the power's Off.

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: Copy that, Gene; thank you. [The DSEA is the SEP Data Storage Electronics Assembly, which Gene and Jack will remove at the end of EVA-3 and return to Earth for analysis.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay, you want the TGE (put on the ground next to the) right side of the MESA, but in the shade. Okay.

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: That's affirm. (Pause)

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Boy, did it (the TGE ) get covered with dust (because of the lost fender), too. (Long Pause) Bob, no trouble with the TGE and the TV, huh? [ TGE readings could be taken with the instrument on the ground or mounted on the back of the Rover. In the latter case, there had been some concern that movement of the TV camera would spoil the measurements.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Parker
A17A1233604.text: None so we can tell. We'll get another reading here when we see it on the ground here. (Long Pause)

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay, Jack, if I set this here, we'll...(Pause) Jack?

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: What?

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay, I just want to set it here so you don't knock it over.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: What's that?

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: The TGE , right where you left foot is.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Oh, well.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: I'm afraid we'll knock it over if I set it anywhere else. 123:39:24 Schmitt: Well, stand by; I've got a lot of stuff here.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: We should have volunteered to take the big bag in.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Why? You having trouble getting that thing (the football-sized rock) in?

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Oh, it's just (non)standard. (Pause) Yes, I'm having trouble.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Well, here; let me help you.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Hold this big bag, please. [They are trying to transfer the football-sized sample from the big bag to SCB-2. The big bag has the same-sized opening as the SCB but has about twice the length.] [Schmitt - "I couldn't get a grip on the rock to get it out, and I needed to have Gene hold the bag still."]

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Just don't back up if you can help it.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Hold the bag. This big one, this one. No, the other one, the other one; don't.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: I can't (garbled). (Pause) I got it. That's a big rock. (Garbled) fit there is long ways. 123:40:07 Schmitt: Okay, there should be another one in there. Is there?

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Feel it, squeeze it...Hit it. On the bottom. See if there's any in there.

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: (Thinking that he can feel a rock in the bag) Yeah, there is.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay. (Pause) Well, let's get it out. Here, pick it up. We'll get it out. (Pause) Hold the top. (Pause) Shake it. [They've probably turned the big bag over to see if they can shake anything out.]

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Okay. I need the EVA pallet.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay, I'll give you that and then I'll get to work. I've got some work I've got to do for Bob. Ah! Okay, (is) everything on the EVA pallet? [Schmitt - "I don't think I'd actually loaded anything on the pallet. Gene just wanted to make sure nothing had fallen out."]

A17A1233604.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1233604.text: Yeah. Just hand it to me and I'll start unstowing it up there.

A17A1233604.speaker: Cernan
A17A1233604.text: Okay. Man, I forgot I had my visor up. Zowie! See if I can get back in the shade. (Pause) [Schmitt - "Gene must have put his visor up so he could see to dust me while we were standing in the LM shadow at the ladder; and then he stepped out into the sunlight."]

a17_1234017.text: America has just gone behind the Moon.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I need the EVA pallet.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, I'll give you that and then I'll get to work. I've got some work I've got to do for Bob. Ah! Okay, (is) everything on the EVA pallet? [Schmitt - "I don't think I'd actually loaded anything on the pallet. Gene just wanted to make sure nothing had fallen out."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah. Just hand it to me and I'll start unstowing it up there.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Man, I forgot I had my visor up. Zowie! See if I can get back in the shade. (Pause) [Schmitt - "Gene must have put his visor up so he could see to dust me while we were standing in the LM shadow at the ladder; and then he stepped out into the sunlight."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (Handing up the pallet) Got it?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, Bob. I'll try giving them to you one at a time (that is, the items at the bottom of CDR-36 ). LMP's got the EVA pallet. Let me give you a MESA (meaning gravimeter) reading...(correcting himself), or a reading, then I'll tidy the (MESA) blanket.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. The reading is 000, 133, 201 (a nonsense reading), and I can only assume that one of us hit it. I think I've got time to give you another one.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Quickly.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well, that's the way it'll be, because it's already punched. (Pause) Mark it.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Copy that. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, I'm tidying up the MESA blankets. I'm pretty tidy!

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I did that.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, MESA blankets are tidied. Okay. Open TGE . I'll do that (later). (Dust)brush to ladder hook. Final transfer (check, on CDR-37 ), Jack. I'm going to...(Pause) Okay, I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to inventory here. You got the pallet. ETB is here, and you got the core stem bag. SCB-2 is (up) there; SRC-1 is here; big bag is not required. Bob, I think we got everything. The two things on the surface yet are the ETB and the SRC and me.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay, we copy that. But, of course... [A bag can be seen hanging from the ladder hook behind the lefthand side of the bottom rung in AS17-134- 20482 , which will be taken at the end of EVA-3.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Jack, get down (on your belly) a little bit more, and you've got another 2 or 3 inches (to clear at the top of the hatch). 123:58:20 Schmitt: "I can't get any lower, Willie. Me buttons are in the way." [Schmitt - "This a quote from one of Bill Mauldin's more famous World War II cartoons in the 'Up Front' collection. Willie and Joe are down in the mud with bullets going over them and that's the caption."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Keep going. Get your pockets over the sill. There you go. There you are. You're in. Kick off your feet if you can; kick them right there. That's good. That got a lot off. Okay, go on in. You're over to the right...Okay, there you are. You've got all the room you want now.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: That's not as easy as in the K-bird. [Cernan - "We could get about 30 seconds of one-sixth gravity flying in the KC-135 aircraft. That was too short for a lot of things and it had been a problem way back in Gemini . Training underwater was not totally realistic either, but at least it gave you a lot longer duration."] [Schmitt - "We practiced getting in a hatch simulator in the KC-135 but that wasn't a static environment and I think it made it easier. There was just a little bit of motion and I think that helped you get through the hatch. And, of course, our hands weren't tired in the 135 and

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I think I'll give this rock box a quick dusting here.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Your (LM) hoses...We've got to have a better way to store your hoses. [Jack is crawling into the LM and is getting caught up in Gene's LM hoses. They would be to Jack's right as he goes through the hatch, draped over Gene's handcontroller.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yeah, I don't like them there either. (Pause) I saw that when we went out. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (To Jack) You in?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: (Breathing heavily) Whew, boy.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yuh.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Sounds like it. (Pause) (To himself, possibly having missed the first rung and having to jump again) Oh, come on. Get up there. (Pause) Okay, Jack, coming up with the rockbox.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I'm not ready.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well, I've got to...I've got to...

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Can you put it on the porch?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well, I only got one more thing to do and that's just clean up (that is, read) the TGE . Okay. I've got to come up there anyway. (Long Pause) 124:00:08 Cernan: "Godspeed the crew of Apollo 17."

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Who signed it? I forgot to read it.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I'm not going to tell you, but I like the message. (Pause) Probably shouldn't tell you. (Pause, grunting) [Gene isn't absolutely certain, but thinks that the message was written on a piece of tape on the strut. He thinks he may have put the message there himself. Gene and Jack took a number of photos of the official plaque mounted on the ladder strut. One of these shows all but the top two rungs and there is no piece of tape discernible in a 16x20 inch enlargement. Because a good deal of detail on the official plaque can be seen in this image, I conclude that there was no taped message in this

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, that (rock box) ought to stay up there. (Pause) Okay, I can't hand you anything in anyway. I'm going down and clean up the TGE .

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Rog. It should be ready to read by now.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Oh! That last step down again. Okay. Bob, before...Well, let me get this for you. (Long Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Got that, Gene.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: And the cover is up. (Breathing into his microphone as he bends down to reach the TGE ) Cover is up, if I can keep it up. (Pause) If I can keep it up. (Pause) That'll keep it up. (Pause) It's been dusted. And I'll get it to Standby. [Gene is opening the top of the TGE to expose a radiator. The TGE is now sitting in the shade of the LM and will be able to cool during the rest period.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Copy that. And did you dust the radiator?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yes, sir; I dusted that a little earlier. Okay, it is Standby, Bob. Radiator is up.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: And dusted.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Cover is open.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I'm going up to the porch. All I've got down here is ETB, and it's on the LEC. [On the early missions, the Lunar Equipment Conveyor ( LEC ) was a clothesline-like device used to transfer equipment up to the cabin. Using it was a two-man operation. Beginning with Apollo 14, the astronauts carried at least some equipment up the ladder by hand. Finally, the Apollo 16 crew decided that the clothesline LEC was more trouble than it was worth and carried everything but the ETB up by hand. To raise and lower the ETB, they used a simple hook-and-lanyard, but kept the LEC designation. Gene is usin

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I'm ready for you. [Jack has been emptying the EVA pallet, which he will now push out through the hatch, almost certainly with his foot, so that Gene can discard it.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Have you got anything else?

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Negative.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I'm ready for you up here.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Let's see what kind of dusting job I can do on myself. (Long Pause) [The sound of Gene beating on his suit with the dustbrush is audible, unless we are hearing him hit his microphone on his neckring as he strains to look down at what he is doing.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, Jack, coming up.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (Pause, as he makes the long jump, this time unencumbered.) Whee! (Pause, as he climbs to the porch) Okay. [Cernan - "Getting up the ladder was a piece of cake. You pushed up with your legs - just a little spring up - and pulled with your arms."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (I've got to get) a little higher.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I'll get it (the EVA pallet) to you.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I got it.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Watch the (hatch) seal.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, here's an SRC.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay; float her in here. [Gene probably stands the SRC on end to make it easier to grab; then it falls on its side.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Oh, me. Well, I'll get it up for you.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: No. That's all right.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Ah. I think you got the ticket right there.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Ah. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I'll watch that. No sense making it hard. See if I can't stand this one up. (Pause) Okay. (Pause) [Jack is having to bend over as far as he can to grab the equipment as Gene hands it through the hatch. Jack notes that his voice quality suggests that he has his chin bent down so that he can see.] [Cernan - "Even with the hatch open, he couldn't have worked kneeling, because he would have had to have his legs toward the hatch and it would have been hard to reach back and pull things in around his body."] [Schmitt - "As Gene handed the stuff in, I probably put it back on the engine cover, althoug

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Got it?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, and here come the core tubes. (Pause) Boy, let's protect that core tube. Man, that was the turning point today. (Pause) [Cernan - "Once the deep core was finished it really was a turning point. While we were deploying the ALSEP, we had a fixed set of tasks to do; and removing that core was probably the hardest of them. But after it was finished, then we could settle back into an exploratory mode of operations with a lot more control and choice about what we did."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Got it. (Pause) Yeah, we had a lot of turning points. [Schmitt - "From my point of view, the big turning point of the mission didn't come until we'd finished the second EVA. From an operational point of view, which was Gene's perspective, getting the core extracted and the rest of the ALSEP deployed was a major accomplishment; drilling those holes and extracting the core was tough work. But I was frustrated that we were still in the position that, if we had to leave the Moon before we had done another EVA, we wouldn't have had much information about the site. We'd gotten the heat flow experime

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Do you want the LEC in there? You don't, do you?

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Negative, you can leave the LEC outside.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: (Answering Gene) No, just the bag (ETB).

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Where are the scissors , by the way?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: They're in the bag.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I hope they don't come out this time.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Well, I stuck them down in there. I hope they don't.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Yeah, Jack...

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: We'll have to figure out something else if they do.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: ...you guys put the scissors in the ETB.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I think so, Bob.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I'll take a peek down there. If they fell out, they'll be right on top (of the ground surface). Okay. (Pause) Mama me. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Okay, Gene. And you got the SCB number 2 in and the pallet out, right?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Right. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Here it comes, Jack. (Pause) Take that? (Pause) There are no scissors on the ground beneath where the ETB was. So I would say that they're probably in the ETB.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Well, good enough.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: (To Gene) Okay. You got everything, now?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay, let me get out of the way. (Long Pause) [Jack has been working with the hatch door fully open to his right. He now moves to Gene's station on the left side of the cabin, closes the door far enough so that he can move across to his station on the right and then swing the door open as far as possible against his legs.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. (Kicking his boots and shaking the spacecraft) Whoops. That's me dusting. Well, I guess I got about (counting the marks on the gauge) 25, 20, 15, I guess thirteen percent oxygen (and) 3.8 (psi). Okay, babe.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: I copy that. Fifty (sic) percent oxygen, Geno...That's...

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Come on in.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Coming through that hole. (Answering Bob) No; thirteen percent, I think.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: One-five (sic). (Pause) 124:07:08 Schmitt: Okay. Put your "buttons" down. You're great. Now your head up. You're right against the top. Right against the Z-27. Come towards me. Okay, now up. (Pause) [As can be seen in the accompanying diagrams, the plus Z-27 bulkhead separates the front the cabin from the back, and is just forward of the ascent engine cover. The plus Z-27 bulkhead is also the front face of what is called the midstep .] [Cernan - "By this time, I was really tired and it was a lot of trouble to get back in the cabin. It's such a small space; and you've got to twist and turn to g

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Tight fit.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: What am I caught on back there?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: You're just scraping against your PLSS.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I'll just bend. [Schmitt - "While you were arching your back, trying to keep your PLSS from hitting the DSKY, you really had to be careful not to scratch your visor on the back bulkhead any more than absolutely necessary. Gene may have had more trouble getting in than I did, simply because he is a longer person, even though, for the same reason, he didn't have as much trouble getting his back arched. Certainly he was tired - we both were - and it was only prudent for me to help him. You didn't want to bang that DSKY any more than you absolutely had to."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Watch your pockets. Your leg pockets might be part of the problem.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Come on in. Just hug as close as you can. Okay, you're there. (Long Pause) Okay?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yup, let me just get on my feet here. Ohh! Ah. Wait a minute. Got to turn one way or the other. Does this look better?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah. I'd turn towards your right. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well, can't do that.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Try the other way. Get your PLSS back in there towards the circuit breakers.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Move your right...(correcting himself) your left arm.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: (Laughing) Where? Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: There. Okay. Let me make sure there's nothing in that hatch.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Well, there's dust. That's one thing that's in there.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well...Take one quick peek.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: From where I stand, all I can see is dust. [Cernan - "With two guys standing there, relatively immobile and wearing PLSSs, there wasn't a lot of room to bend over to look at the hatch opening for things that might keep you from getting a good seal. So you leaned back to get a look at it. It was important to get a good seal the first time, because otherwise you'd have to go through the whole procedure again."] [Schmitt - "You would probably blow the hatch seal clean if you depressed again, but you certainly didn't want to lose all that pressurization oxygen."]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, it (the hatch seal)'s clear. Hit it. Is that what do we do next?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Pockets...Your pockets (are catching on the hatch door). Okay? [Jack may be kicking the hatch partially shut to get it out of the way. They will actually close and latch the hatch at 124:10:44.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (Reading from the post-EVA cue card, which has the same information as checklist page 3-1 ) "Primary water, Closed. Forward hatch..." Turn our Water (to) Off. (Pause) Do you have to turn the primaries or just the secondary (Auxiliary), Bob?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Primary.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Primary only. (Gene is breathing very heavily) That's why you don't turn your Primary Water off when you go to Aux. [The two feedwater tanks are hooked up in series. The auxiliary tank was added to the PLSS for Apollo 15 and subsequent missions. Apparently, it was easier to add a second tank to the design than to enlarge the existing tank.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. I've got them both Off. Is that all right?

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: That's okay, too.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Well, wait a minute.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Got yours?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: No, I can't quite reach it.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Well, if you can roll to the left, I'll get it for you.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah, I can.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: (Garbled), let me get back here. I've gotten bigger since I've been out there. (Pause) You got to go (that is, turn) more. You got to go more.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yup. There's something keeping me from going more.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Okay, let me see if I can't...(Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: (Garbled) awfully far inboard for what I (garbled).

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Your Primary Water is Off.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. LMP's Water is Off.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Now you're going to have to move way over there, so I can get the hatch. [Closing the hatch is a difficult job in an inflated suit. Gene needs Jack to get back against the right-hand side circuit breaker panel so that he, Gene, can reach down to close the hatch.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah, I have to go back the way I was.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Back up against the circuit breakers.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yup.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Can you see what I'm catching on, upward?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah. You're just hitting the rail over there.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Now. (Pause) See, I can't..."Close and lock forward hatch", huh?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeah. (Pause) Can you do it?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yup. Can't see it. Okay. (Pause) [Cernan - "To get the hatch closed and latched, you had to lean forward and sideways and close it by feel. The instrument panel stuck out about a foot into the cabin and you just couldn't see under it while you were closing the hatch. Then, once I got back up, I could lean back and see it was closed, and as Jack could, too. All of this was necessary because we were really constrained by weight; the LM had to be as lightweight as possible and we couldn't afford a lot of volume in the spacecraft. If we'd had more room and a little bigger hatch, all of this would

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Forward Hatch is Closed...

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Locked?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: ...and Locked. Which one of those dump valves is (open)...That one up on top. I can get that one.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. (Pause) Take it easy. [Gene is reaching up and behind to his right to close the overhead dump valve.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Oh, whew! (Pause) It's Auto, and it's locked.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: You're sure? Is that locked there?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Yes, sir.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: And it is Auto.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. [In the Auto position, the dump valve will open if the cabin pressure exceeds 5.4 psi.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay, I got a tone and I got an H2O flag.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Parker
A17A1235555.text: Roger, Jack; we saw it. [Having turned the PLSS water pump off, they verify that the warning signals are working properly.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, PLSS O2 is not less than 10 percent.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Yeh. Okay... [If the PLSS oxygen supply in either suit was less than ten percent, they would have to do a manual cabin repressurization, watching the suit pressure gauge to make sure the suit maintained positive pressure.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, let's go.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: "If not less (than 10 percent)...manual control repress." Okay. I've got to turn (so that he can get at the valves and circuit breakers and controlling the Environmental Control System).

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Let me get out of your way. Okay. About as far as I can go. Okay. I'll read it to you, when you get there. (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: I think part of our problem is this slope. There's no "purchase"- as my Father used to say - no "purchase".

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, are you ready? Are you ready?

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Wait a minute.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I need you on Cabin Repress (valve) , Auto; and then on (circuit breaker panel) 16 ( CB(16) ) I need you...

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. [Jack will set the cabin repressurization valve so that, when he closes the corresponding circuit breaker, repressurization will begin and, when the cabin is up to 5 psi, the valve will close automatically.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay; Cabin Repress, Auto.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Going Auto.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. ECS Cabin Repress (circuit breaker), Closed.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Stand by for repress.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: I'll try and get cabin...that master. Okay, there's the Master Alarm. (Audible sound of repressurization) Well, I can't (garbled).

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay. [Gene is turning to make sure that the Cabin Warning light has come on.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Cabin is coming up. (Garbled) closed at 1 psi.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Okay.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay. Verify cabin pressure increasing. Press(ure) Reg(ulators) A and B to Cabin.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: Now?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Now.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: A's Cabin; B's Cabin. [The pressure regulators are now set to keep the cabin pressure at 4.8 psi.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, and I want your PLSS O2 Off, when I give you a call. That's when we get greater than 2.5 (psi cabin pressure). (Pause)

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, now. We're at 3. Can you get it? If you can't, I'll reach it for you.

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: It's Off.

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Okay, Cabin Warning Light Off. Verify cabin pressure stable at 4.6. Okay, it's coming up. It's 3.6. And you use the Purge valve to depress. [The EVA ends when the cabin pressure reaches 3.5 psi. Although the PLSS oxygen is off, without intervention, the suits would deflate relatively slowly. To hasten suit deflation, once the cabin pressure is significant, they can open the purge valves.]

A17A1235555.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1235555.text: What's our pressure?

A17A1235555.speaker: Cernan
A17A1235555.text: Cabin pressure is 4. Let me just take a look here at 4.6. Okay. I'm coming down. Suit's coming down. Cabin's up to...Cabin's up to 5, Jack. [The sound of repressurization ends abruptly.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 19 min 55 sec )

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. Post-EVA configuration. White dots out and EVA decals.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay. Checking. [Jack is verifying that the circuit breakers and switches marked with white dots and EVA decals are in the same, powerdown configuration they were in prior to the start of the EVA.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: White dot.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. Give me a chance to turn around and look. Okay. White dots are out; all the white dots. Okay, they're all out here. Boy, does this feel good to get soft suits. Oh, my hands. [Cernan - "Your hands just get so tired and sore, both from the work of squeezing your gloves around things all day and from the constant chafing. I wound up with blisters all over my hands, particularly between the thumb and the forefinger."]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay, they're all out here.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. Okay, on (panel) 16, Suit Fan number 2, Closed.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Suit Fan 2, Closed.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: And Suit Fan Delta-P, Closed.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Closed. [They are turning on the fans and a fan sensor in the Environmental Control System (ECS) Suit Circuit.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: ECS caution and Water Sep(arator) Component light's on.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay, ECS...(Pause) I think it's on. It's hard to see it. [This indicates, as expected, that the Suit Circuit Water Separator is not yet up to speed.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. (Pause) Doff your gloves. Stow on comm panel. Hallelujah! [It is a great relief to get the gloves off.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Cabin's stable, Houston. How's it look to you?

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: Looks good to us, 17. And I'd like you to know you had a 7-hour and 12-minute EVA, from 3.5 (psi) to 3.5 (psi).

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Well, until I get out of this suit, I'm still EVA.

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: Roger. [It is now eight hours and fifteen minutes since they started to get Jack's PLSS on, and it will be another forty-five minutes until they are both out of their suits. Preparations for the next EVA will take even longer, since they will have to start with suit donning.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Oh, doesn't that feel good. Whoo!

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: And I think it's a tremendous job for what we might call a "challenging" EVA.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Bob, that's no pun. It really was. It really was.

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: I know it, men. I know it.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: I tell you, I really wish you guys could have been here with us. You worked as hard at it as we did, if not harder.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Harder, I think. Until today. 124:16:24 Cernan: Ohh! You don't have a tub of hot water I can soak my hands in, do you? (Pause) [Schmitt - "I had been aware from the experience of previous crews that you could get rough or damaged finger tips and that your fingernails could lift right off the quick as a result of constantly reaching in the suit and getting a little bit of grabbing from the rubber bladder. Knowing that, I wore some nylon liners and also kept my fingernails clipped down as far as possible to delay the process. But, ultimately, all my nails were lifted off the quick and I can reme

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Wait until that dust hits the sweat of your hands.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: (Subvocally) Oh, shoot. (Pause) I tell you. [Schmitt - "Other than the times when I was talking to Gene or when Bob had asked a specific question, I don't think I was talking to anyone so much as I was dictating - particularly about the geology, providing a verbal set of field notes that I realized that I or others would be using. So I'm surprised that, even under those circumstances, we had a subconscious avoidance of profanity. Gene would occasionally use his "Manischewitz" as a substitute and I used "Oh, shoot" here and probably used other things on occasion. And I think it was characterist

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Man! Okay, my gloves are off. (Reading) "Doff helmets with visors, lower shades, and stow in BRA ." Well, I guess the first thing is to get this thing off. Boy, let me tell you.

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: Okay. And 17 - or Jack and Gene - I'm going to turn you over to Joe (Allen) now. I'll be back in a while.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, Bob. Thank you for a job well done.

A17A1241414.speaker: Parker
A17A1241414.text: Well, job well done on your side, guys. (Pause)

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: (Subvocally) God Damn. (Pause) Oh, I can't do it. How about getting my glove off? (Pause) Can you handle it?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: (Garbled; pause)

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Thank you. (Pause) 124:18:06 Cernan: Jack, the big one's out of the way. The one (EVA) we really had to get out there on. Boy, look at that visor. No wonder I couldn't see. (Long Pause) Jack, do you read? [They have their visor assemblies ( LEVAs ) off, but still have their helmets on.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Yeah.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, I thought you knocked your thing (the RCU comm switch) to AR or to A or something. (Pause) There's a lot of noise in the background. That's why I was wondering. Need some help? (Long Pause)

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Stow the visors, huh? What is it?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Yeah, stow them in the BRA.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: No, but I mean...Keep the protective visor down?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Keep the protective visor over it, and stow the whole thing in the BRA. (Long Pause) "Verify safety on the dump valve ." I guess I can do that now...

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Again?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: That one's still safe. And that one's still safe.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Smells like gunpowder, just like the boys said.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Oh, it does, doesn't it? (Pause) [They have just removed their helmet and, as did previous crews, notice that the dust in the air smells like burnt gunpowder. There is enough dust in the air to smell, but not enough to see.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, "Descent Water valve, Open." Ohh, boy! I ran out of water out there. I mean the drinking kind. (Pause) [Gene is refering to his in-suit drink bag .] [Cernan - "I ran out late in the EVA, so it wasn't a problem."]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay, what's next?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, "Descent Water Valve, Open." (Pause) [They are opening the descent stage water supply, having turned it off prior to the EVA. This will provide cooling and drinking water until they get out of the suits.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay. Coming Open.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, and then you get your purge valve out.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Not too hard.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Good shot. (Both laugh) If they say anything, just say, "I told you so." (Still laughing) Okay. "Remove your purge valve..."

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: (Laughing)

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: "...and disconnect your OPS hose."

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Yes, sir. (Laughing) If I can. [Twenty years after the event, neither Gene nor Jack remembers what this was about. In 1997, Journal Contributor Brian Lawrence suggested that Jack's purge valve popped out, as a result of residual pressure in the suit, just before Gene's "Good shot." at 124:20:33.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. I tell you, I haven't seen anything...Drilling those holes was a piece of cake until I couldn't get that core tube out. I thought that whole...

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: (Garbled), will you?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: I thought that...

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: I'm glad there were two of us.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: I thought that whole thing was going to break. It was bending about...at about a...(Laughs)

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Well, next time we have to do it...

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Yeah.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Let's see, OPS. That must be this one.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: "Disconnect OPS hose. Connect LM hoses, red to red, blue to blue." I don't want LM (oxygen) hoses yet. I'll just get on water right away. (Pause) Let's put...I'm going to..."(PGA) Diverter valve, horizontal."

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: " Suit Isol(ation Valve) , both." I'm going Suit Flow, get some flow in this cabin. Okay. [They are directing the flow of Suit Circuit oxygen into the cabin via the LM oxygen hoses.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Here, you want me to get it?

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: I tell you, my hands, after working at picking up little things.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: I feel the same way. I think you had the worst of it.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, let's keep as much dust out of those connectors as we can. (Jack laughs) Wise guy.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Okay.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Let's wait on these. Okay, your (PGA) diverter valve horizontal?

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Yep. [By setting the suit diverter valve to the horizontal position, they will direct some of the oxygen flow - once they get the LM hoses hooked up - into the torso, which will help dry the suits.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, and if you can get to the Suit Flow, you can go Suit Flow. In the meantime, get your Fan (and) your Pump, Off.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Fan's Off. Pump's Off. [These are RCU switches for the PLSS oxygen fan and the PLSS LCG water pump. Astronaut Joe Allen joins the conversation as CapCom.]

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Joe, are you still reading us down there?.

A17A1241414.speaker: Allen
A17A1241414.text: Loud and clear, Gene. We're following you close and...

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay. I just wanted to see whether you were there.

A17A1241414.speaker: Allen
A17A1241414.text: Roger. Following you close here.

A17A1241414.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1241414.text: Keep us honest.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: Okay, we're just looking at 5 psi and all the hatches are battened down, and the safeties are on. You can keep a look at the rest of it for us.

A17A1241414.speaker: Allen
A17A1241414.text: Copy that. And we're seeing the same thing.

A17A1241414.speaker: Cernan
A17A1241414.text: (To Jack) Okay, disconnect your PLSS water. Now what I do, Jack, is...(Listens to Allen and then continues) I was going to say put your cover on, but we're going to stow those.

a17_1242248.text: This is Apollo Control at 124 hours, 23 minutes. We've completed a shift handover in Mission Control. Our Flight Director Gene Kranz and his team of flight controllers are replacing the Pete Frank team. Our spacecraft communicator on this shift is astronaut Joe Allen. And aboard Challenger on the lunar surface, Jack Schmitt and Gene Cernan are in the process of getting the Lunar Module reconfigured, ready for their sleep period which the Flight Plan calls for them to begin at 128 hours or about 3½ hours from now. After they complete the reconfiguration of the Lunar Module and get the ca

a17_1242248.speaker: Cernan
a17_1242248.text: (To Allen, having started the procedures on checklist page 3-2 ) Okay, guess we've got to go off the air for a little while. We're both going "O".

a17_1242248.speaker: Allen
a17_1242248.text: Okay. [They are turning their RCU Communications Mode Selector switches to the "O" (Off) position. The accompanying photograph shows the top of the RCU, with the front being up. The Mode Select switch is at the right and has four round cut-outs. The second cut-out from the right is larger than the other three and shows the selected communications mode, in this case "AR". The "O" mode is the next position to the right.]

a17_1242248.speaker: Cernan
a17_1242248.text: And we'll get on our LM comm here, shortly.

a17_1242248.speaker: Allen
a17_1242248.text: Roger. Check back in. [Comm Break. Houston is waiting to re-acquire the Command Module, now on its 19th orbit. They expect that Evans went to sleep during this Farside pass.]

a17_1242248.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1242248.text: (Garbled). Okay, we got to do some more switching, yet.

a17_1242248.speaker: Cernan
a17_1242248.text: Okay. Connect the...Okay. Now in...Audio circuit breakers, Closed. Now, both panels, VHA...(correcting himself) VHF A, Receive; B, Off. Okay. Mode ICS/PTT. [Comm Break]

a17_1243334.text: This is Apollo Control at 124 hours, 37 minutes. The participants for the change of shift press briefing are now on their way to the briefing room in Building 1. That conference should begin shortly. Here in Mission Control, Flight Director Gene status - or Gene Kranz rather has gotten a status from his flight controllers on both vehicles, both Challenger and America and both spacecraft appear to be in very good shape at this time. Aboard Challenger on the lunar surface, Gene Cernan and Jack Schmitt will now be involved in getting out of their space suits, getting the spacecraft cleaned up and

A17A1254644.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1254644.text: Houston, Challenger. We'll both be off the air briefly here as we swing into getting our suits and LCGs (Liquid Cooled Garments) off. The Commander presently has his suit off, and I'll start on mine.

a17_1255201.text: This is Apollo Control. It now appears that the crew aboard Challenger on the lunar surface, Jack Schmitt and Gene Cernan, will be ready to begin the EVA debriefing in about 20 minutes. We're estimating that they'll reach that point in the Flight Plan at about 126 hours, 10 minutes. And the debriefing will run 15 to 20 minutes. Ron Evans aboard America has been asleep now for about an hour and a half. We'll be waking him up at the Ground Elapsed Time of 131 hours, 20 minutes after about 8 hours of rest. America is presently in an orbit, 69.9 by 53.5 nautical miles [129.5 by 99.1 km], on the ba

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, copy that. (Pause) On the outcrops you think you see in the North and South Massifs, do they appear to be linear, horizontal or subhorizontal? Can you see layers, and do you have any feel for the thickness or the attitude or the continuity of them? Can you discuss these outcrops? [Bob is asking if the outcrops line up - hence his use of the word "linear" - and, if they do line up, whether they make a horizontal layer or a slightly tilted (hence "subhorizontal") layer.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Bob, going over (the site) yesterday (during a pre-landing orbit), I thought I could see a structure dipping off to the southeast, apparent dip anyway, on the eastern side of the South Massif. Or northeastern side. We haven't examined them in detail because we were in a rush to get out. We'll put the binoculars (means "monocular") on them and try to examine that question. There's nothing very obvious, any more than you can see on the (overhead) photos, that the ledges were concentrated in the upper portion - (coughs) excuse me - in the upper portion of the Massif's units. [Journal Contributor

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay. Copy that. Here's a short one that I'll ask Jack since he did it. Again I guess we'll have to prove this. (With regard to) the shade portion of the cosmic ray experiment: the question is, and I repeat - I quote - "Are you sure that the detectors, not the decals, were facing out?"

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: I am, Bob; because I said I was sure, and I called you on it.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Roger. I was sure, too, but I had to ask the question.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: I...I under...I know. I understand why it was asked, because I did it wrong at the Cape. But that's why I mentioned it when I deployed it.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Roger. (Pause) Okay, and we can go and recharge the other PLSS whenever you're ready there, guys.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Okay.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, the next question - which calls for a little bit of discussion - is: The layers of lineaments that you remarked on in the Sculptured Hills, can you say anything about them? [Bob is referring to the lineations Gene had described on Bear Mountain after the landing.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Yeah, Bob, I did. I think I said...and I commented (that) I'm not sure whether it was the Sun angle or not...But see, I was not looking at the Sculptured Hills; I was looking back at Bear Mountain, I believe. And, to me it looked like there was some organization that was dipping back to the east, somewhere between, oh, 20 and 25 degrees maybe. And it was very obvious to me. But I'm a little hesitant (to say it isn't a lighting effect) because of some of this Sun-angle stuff. [Cernan - "Because of the low Sun on that first day - and it was a lot better on the second and third days - it wasn't a

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that. I gather we didn't get any 500-millimeters of these lineations, today, right?

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: No, but I think we will. They were on the western side of Bear Mountain back there, and I think I commented that I thought that Bear Mountain is probably what the Sculptured Hills look like. [Schmitt - "Somebody at the USGS - or maybe it was Jim Head - noticed that, in contrast to some of the other hills, they had a knobby appearance and said 'Hey, they look like somebody sculptured them'. So they became the Sculptured Hills."]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that. Is there a scar above the light mantle material? In other words, the slide. Is there a scar above that on the South Massif? Can you see anything up there to indicate that it might have come off of there?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Nothing obvious yet, Bob. [They never did see an obvious scar. In the 100 million years since the slide, impacts and downhill movement of debris have erased and covered the source area on the mountain.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, copy that. On the way back to Station 1, you described a small crater with light material on the bottom. Can you say anything more about that crater? (Long Pause)

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Bob, I don't remember saying that, or...Gene doesn't either.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay. You talked about something that was light. I don't remember; I thought it was a boulder, but the question's about a crater.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: You're right. You're right, there was a large zap pit in a boulder that was very white. It must have been...The crater for the zap must have been 2 centimeters diameter anyway. And it had about that, oh, maybe 3-centimeters worth of crushed minerals around it, that gave it a white - very bright white - appearance.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay. Well that was indeed a small crater, so I guess the question was right. (Pause) Let me change the mode here and ask you three or four simple ALSEP questions again, to verify for various people exactly what happened. Just to make sure that they're clear on it. Jack, when you were laying out the geophone leads, you mentioned and asked me if it was all right if the geophone leads crossed one another, if there was EMI (electromagnetic interference) problems. And so that made people wonder whether or not it was possible the geophone positions were reversed; i.e., geophone 1 was laid out in ge

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: No, that was just a Geophone 4 problem. The geophones are in the right directions.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay. [Schmitt - "The instrumentation identified the signals from each of the geophones by number and, in order to interpret the data, the experimenters had to know where I had deployed each one of them."]

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Geophone 4 fell out of the module and rolled under one of the other lines, or vice versa, I don't know which, and it's crossing one of the other lines. Geophone 1, I think. 126:38:56 Parker: Okay, no problem. When you went to put the LSPE antenna in the heat flow socket, you weren't able to do it at first; was it because of there was a lot of dust in there?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: No, I think it was the same old problem of that piece of aluminum foil or whatever it is going down in the socket and jamming briefly.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that. Did you clear out that foil when you did it, or did you just push it on through?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: I forced it. 126:39:31 Parker: Okay. When you taped the SEP solar cells down, how much of them did you cover with tape?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: We taped the back.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Ah, very good thinking. And, Geno, a question for you on the Rover when you parked it. Do you have any feeling for the roll angle it was parked at the LM? The roll angle.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Yeh, let me look. (Pause) Bob, it's pretty flat. If I had to guess, I'd say zero. And you can bias that by a degree or so, but basically zero.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, is the pitch scale still on it, or did it fall off yet?

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: No. I was going to comment on that. It's still there. [The pitch/roll scale fell off during Apollo 16 but, because a modification of the already-built Apollo 17 indicator would have been difficult and the Apollo 16 crew had had no difficulty in estimating the attitude of their Rover, no change had been made.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, very good. Okay, when you went to Station 1A - we're calling the new Station 1 "Station 1A" - were the blocks there as well-filleted as those near the LM and the ALSEP? Do they all look the same? [Fillets are skirts of soil that pile up at the base of rocks due to small, nearby impacts that splash soil against the sides.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Bob, all the boulders had filleting to a slight degree, but not an extreme amount. I think it no more than what is being caused by the redistribution of the darker, fine-grained regolith.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that. [People in the Backroom are trying to find evidence to support interpretations of the Apollo 15 photography that suggest that only the northern half of the valley was covered by the hypothesized dark-mantling process. If it was a process that occurred late in the history of the valley, then there might have been a difference in the degree of covering of the pre-existing boulders.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Bob, if I had to answer...

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Go ahead.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: ...if I had to answer that question, I'd say yes. Yes, that the boulders are filleted over there about like they are over here. That would be my impression.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: All right. Is there any indication that the fillets are directional, in other words, that the fillets are heavier on one side than the other?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Bob, haven't noticed that.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that. Do you have the feeling that some boulders are more rounded...

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Well that's a good ...(Hearing Bob) That's a good...

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Roger. I agree with you.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: That's a good re...(Hearing Bob) That's a good reminder, Bob. [That is, a good reminder to look for directionality in the filleting.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, do have any feeling that some boulders are more rounded than others? Apparently this looked this way in some of the TV pictures.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Some of the big ones that are just barely exposed above the regolith looked quite well-rounded. Most of those around the craters are subangular. I got the impression that it's just purely a function of how long the same material's been exposed; but some of the big boulders like the one out near the geophones is quite angular in part and quite rounded on other parts. It's quite variable. [Schmitt - "Angular boulders have profiles such that you can draw two lines from any point on the rock and the rock will fill the space between them. Subangular is the case where the tip has been rounded off an

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, do you want to say any more about that boulder (Geophone Rock)? Did it seem to have more or less the same lithology, in addition to the variation in vesicle size that the other rocks in the vicinity of the ALSEP, and the other rocks out at Station 1 had?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: No, it's very comparable to the ones that we saw at Station 1, as a matter of fact.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I copy that.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Both types of rocks were there, both variations. (Pause)

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Do you have a feeling for where the big blocks in the LM/ALSEP area came from? Do you think they were from Camelot, like (garbled) been saying?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Don't have an idea yet; I'm really not sure.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, and as you drove along on the traverse from the SEP to Station 1, did the size of the small craters with blocky rims vary? In other words, what we are looking for here is the variation in the thickness of the dark mantle?

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: I can't answer that one yet, Bob. [The diameter and depth of a crater depend on the impact energy. In places where the regolith is thin, impacts forming relatively small craters would penetrate to bedrock (the subfloor) and dig up blocks.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay. Let me sum up by saying that - I guess as I indicated before - our best guess is that the vesicular crystalline rock - probably gabbro, or I think you've been calling it intermediate basalt or gabbro - forms at least the upper part of the subfloor. I don't think we've been close enough to a large crater rim to say what the deep sections of the subfloor form; but we think that this intermediate gabbro, vesicular rock - at least medium-grained, perhaps coarse-grained rock - forms at least the upper layer of the subfloor. Over. (Pause) [During crater formation, the ejecta blanket can be des

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Yeah, Bob, I think that's pretty safe, right now. Once again, I'm surprised that it's as coarse as it is, that being the upper portion of a plains unit.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Roger.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Say, Bob, driving back from Station 1, where we did some of our circling and what have you, we didn't have time to get off, but we did see down in - I don't remember whether it was in the slopes of some craters, or down on the slope itself - but I'd say several meters down below the mantle where there was what we almost agreed to might be bedrock (on) at least a deeper portion of the subfloor. [Gene is beginning to sound tired again.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Okay, well, I think we'll get to it tomorrow. I think I might just give you a clue to our thinking for tomorrow. But, I don't think we've seen, or done, anything today that is going to make us change very much from the nominal station... (correcting himself) EVA-2 plan. (The next sentence is edited for clarity.) The fact we didn't get to the large boulders at Emory is probably going to mean that Station 5 might be shifted a little bit to the boulders on Camelot. But certainly Station 5 on the subfloor and also Station 10 have assumed a higher priority than they originally had. Other than that

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Okay, Bob. I think that's safe. I suppose somebody's thinking about the possibility of going down to Emory. Maybe you just said that. Going down to Emory late in EVA-3.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: I think at the moment they're thinking primarily about going to Station 10, and not going to Station 1. (Pause) [Station 10 is on the route back to the LM from the more northerly stops planned for EVA-3; Emory Crater, the original Station 1, is well to the south and, therefore, would require a substantial detour.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: Okay, Jack, I've wrested control...

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Some of your experts might...

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: Go ahead.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Some of your experts might think about what they might expect to happen to. What the regolith on a fine-grain pyroclastic would look like.

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: Okay. [Schmitt - "I was asking them to think about the situation of a fine-grained pyroclastic laid down on the subfloor. What sort of regolith would develop in that situation and what would you expect to find? Obviously I was thinking about it, and I wanted the bright guys on the ground to think about it, too. We eventually proved at Shorty that this is what had happened, but we hadn't been there yet and I was asking what might be unique about a regolith developed on a pyroclastic versus a regolith developed on a basalt flow. I don't think I ever got an answer to the question."]

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: We'll tell them. I'll see you tomorrow, guys.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Sleep well, Bob.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Okay, I've just got one question, Bob, before you run off. Did the TGE perform okay with the (TV) camera on?

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: As far as I could tell, Geno, it did. As a matter of fact, I didn't see the gravimeter people afterwards to talk to them. But as far as I could tell, it did. We had one funny reading back at the LM very early when it was on the ground, which I'm at a loss to understand right off. But other than that everything seems to have gone very well. The readings were quite uniform in fact, which is what makes me think they went well.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Okay, well, I'd like to leave it...You know it's a little change in my thinking (but) I'd like to leave it on the Rover if we can, although it's a piece of cake to take off. It's very difficult to lean over that far without losing your balance and take your readings and what have you. So if we can leave it on (the Rover), it would be far better.

A17A1263300.speaker: Parker
A17A1263300.text: Roger. I was noticing that. And I also noticed the only three-ball (three-zero) reading we got was when it was on the ground.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Yeah. (Pause) [This is a reference to the disturbed reading at 123:56:55. Bob remembers that a 000 readout was an explicit indication that the instrument had been disturbed while a measurement was in progress.]

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: Gene and Jack, if you'll get Lunar Surface Checklist to (page) 3-5 , I've got an easy change to read up to you.

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Go ahead.

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: Okay. After the line: "Empty ETB As Follows," change the first line which reads, "B&W Mag Golf In Forward RHSSC" (right-hand side storage compartment) to read, "B&W Mag Hotel In LCG Compartment". And then go into the next column, which begins, "Stow In ETB." Change the second line, which reads: "LMP's Camera With B&W Mag Hotel" to "LMP's Camera With B&W Mag Golf". That's Mag G, ETB. Over. [Frank and Stacey O'Brien have provided a view ( 0.7Mb ) of a RHSSC in a LM simulator taken in 2002 at the Cradle of Aviation Museum. The Right Hand Side Stowage Comparment (RHSSC) is on the lower part of the

A17A1263300.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1263300.text: Got you. Hotel, stow it; and go out with Golf.

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: That's got it. [Gene and Jack had magazines Hotel (or "Helen" as Jack called it when he stowed it under his seat) and Golf ("Gail") out in the ETB at the start of the EVA. During close-out, at 123:31:59 and following, Jack mentioned that he had put Golf in the ETB and Hotel was on the LMP's camera. Jack reported a frame count of 197 on Hotel at 122:50:11 but gives 183 below at 126:58:05 and 126:59:20. It will not be used again. Golf is still unused and will be taken out for EVA-2.] 126:50:08 Allen: And I've got a LEVA-cleaning procedure which maybe you could pencil in there. It's an easy three

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Okay, Joe, we got that. The Commander's PLSS has had its final charge, and we're in the process of working on the LMP's PLSS now. I guess there's no way to verify how much water you've got in there except to go through the procedure.

A17A1263300.speaker: Allen
A17A1263300.text: That's right, Geno. And we think you fellows have earned a good meal now, and maybe you can take the rest of the day off.

A17A1263300.speaker: Cernan
A17A1263300.text: Okay, Joe. Thank you. [Long Comm Break. Details of the final PLSS feedwater recharge are on Surface 3-6 .]

a17_1265412.text: Ron Evans, aboard America, now in his 20th revolution of the Moon, just passed over the landing site a few minutes ago, and appears to be sleeping soundly. Ron has been asleep for about 3 hours now. And telemetry data on America shows the vehicle to be functioning normally, as are all of the scientific instruments with a couple of relatively minor exceptions. The Mapping Camera has not been retracted. It was somewhat slow to retract the last few times that that maneuver was performed and the camera has been left in the extended position, which is the normal operating position for the Mapping C

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Jack, on your mag Hotel, we'd showed you all the way up to a hundred and eighty three at one time on that. Did you miss the "one", this time?

A17A1265920.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1265920.text: I may have clipped it out, Joe. One-eight-three, yes.

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Okay, yeah, you did clip it out, clipped it out cleanly. So thanks for verifying that. [Schmitt - "Joe was just taking a dig at me. I had not clipped the 'one'. He was just sticking one in."] [Comm Break] 127:02:28 Schmitt: (Sounding very congested) Joe, mag Romeo has two-one frames. And I took a few, random, and probably not very good 500-millimeter (pictures) of the North and South Massifs.

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Okay, Jack. Thank you. (Long Pause) [All of the South Massif photos , AS17-144- 21983 to 21989 are badly blurred.] [Frames 21991 to 993 show the North Massif " dark boulder " and its prominent track. As can be seen in Figure 6-15 from the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report , the dark boulder is about 600 meters west and 300 meters north of the Station 6 boulder. The difference in distance from the LM the dark boulder and Station 6 is only about five percent and a comparison of Jack's dark boulder photo from the LM cabin with his picture of the LM from Station 6 gives a good comparison of the

A17A1265920.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1265920.text: And, Joe, verify that you want mag Charlie substituted for Mag Bravo on the CDR's camera.

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Stand by. [Comm Break. These photographs were taken through a lens with a 500mm focal length.]

A17A1265920.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1265920.text: Don't get me wrong. I think it's a good idea, Joe. Don't let everybody work all night on that one.

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Jack, I think the answer to that is "yes". Per the checklist, by the way. That's the way we show it in our checklist here.

A17A1265920.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1265920.text: Roger. We probably have about 100 frames left on Bravo, so we'll just keep track of that.

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Jack, it'll go out later on, Bravo will. Apparently, it's kind of your backup magazine there. (Pause)

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: The reason being, we want to start that EVA-2 with a fresh mag. [Long Comm Break]

A17A1265920.speaker: Cernan
A17A1265920.text: Hey, Joe. Bob told us earlier (that) the sounder looked like it was working. (Long Pause)

A17A1265920.speaker: Allen
A17A1265920.text: Gene and Jack, just a general comment on that. SIM bay's cooking along beautifully. We are getting lunar sounder data. It looks quite interesting. We've only got one or two annoying problems with it, but nothing major...That is, with the SIM bay, not with the sounder. One of them being that we have our usual mapping camera extend problem. And we've just decided to leave it extended and it will serve it right if it gets a little contaminated with an occasional (water/urine) dump. And I guess there's a minor problem with one of the big antennas. It didn't pass its retract check properly, so I gu

A17A1265920.speaker: Cernan
A17A1265920.text: That sounds great; I'm glad to hear that. [Very Long Comm Break] [Cernan - "We were probably eating through this thirty-minute period and I remember that it was almost a relief not to have to talk to the ground or answer questions."] [Schmitt - "I was hoping they would ask more questions during this eat period. It was an opportunity to chat about the geology. I was tired, but I thought it was a waste of time not to talk. We were on 'push-to-talk' so I don't know what Gene and I were talking about at this point. Probably just the mechanics of eating: 'Do you want this? Or, do you want that?' It

a17_1273310.text: This is Apollo Control at 127 hours, 33 minutes. The CSM America has just gone behind the Moon now on the 20th revolution. The spacecraft looking very good when last we had telemetry data on it. And Ron Evans continuing to sleep soundly. He's been asleep now for about 3½ hours. On the lunar surface, Gene Cernan and Jack Schmitt aboard Challenger are eating at this time, and we hope to get them to bed by about 128 hours or about 27 minutes from now.

A17A1275209.speaker: Cernan
A17A1275209.text: Yeah, I'd like to try to get the full amount (of sleep). As I recall, tomorrow's a little bit flexible. If we get out 30 minutes late, it doesn't really hurt us.

A17A1275209.speaker: Allen
A17A1275209.text: Sounds like a good way to proceed. We'll give you the full 8 hours tonight, Geno. And you do have a time pad in there, so it shouldn't hurt a thing. [There is some unallocated time in the flight plan, some "padding" in the schedule.]

A17A1275209.speaker: Cernan
A17A1275209.text: Yeah, the big object tomorrow is to get out, and get back in, and the same thing with the next day. I don't think we're really that time critical either day that we can't go an hour either way. And I think we'd prefer to have the full 8 (hours of rest) tonight.

A17A1275209.speaker: Allen
A17A1275209.text: Roger. We couldn't agree with you more. And if there's any way we can be helping you now, just speak up.

A17A1275209.speaker: Cernan
A17A1275209.text: No, you've been doing fine. We just got a little housecleaning we got to do that's going to take us...I expect we'll be an hour late, Joe. [Long Comm Break] [Cernan - "We still had to set up the hammocks . Our suits were probably already in the back of the cabin, hooked up to hoses to dry out; and there were always a few things to shuffle around: get our foodstuffs stowed, clean the visors, look at the rocks and pack them away, and so on. We were busy almost all the time."] 128:01:56 Schmitt: Hey, Joe.

a17_1275754.text: This is Apollo Control at 127 hours, 58 minutes. And the crew aboard Challenger on the lunar surface are now getting configured to begin their sleep period. Among the things in the checklist that they have done is to turn - turn off the power amplifier which accounts for the somewhat noisier communications that we're getting. This is a normal presleep configuration and we don't expect to be communicating with the crew a great deal in the next hour and of course, none while they're in their sleep period. As you heard in the last exchange between CapCom Joe Allen and Gene Cernan, the crew will p

A17A1281446.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1281446.text: Yeah, but that dissipates in the morning warmth. (Pause) Believe it or not, Joe, I'm going to be off the air briefly. (Pause)

A17A1281446.speaker: Allen
