A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: It's an undulating, hummocky traverse terrain in there, Jack.

A17A1414552.speaker: Evans
A17A1414552.text: Okay; there's 50. Pan Camera to Standby - Stereo - and - Power. Camera to Operate.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: These little craters make it bumpy; but, other than that, it's really smooth sailing!

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: That's right. This is what I sort of expected the dark mantle to look like, rather than what we landed on. Not more than one percent of the surface (is covered with blocks), and that percentage continues right over the rim crest of Horatio down onto the wall until you hit the big blocks.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: What's this depression? That's not...No, we're not to Bronte yet.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: No, I don't have any...No, we're not at Bronte...

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay, 17. And how about an amps and a mobility...(correcting himself) a speed reading.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: I've been pushing anywhere from 9 to 11 clicks, and most of the time that's full out, and amperes are bouncing around 100 apiece.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay, watch these down-Sun craters. They're hard to see.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: I know they are. [Journal Contributor David Harland notes that, although there are occasional comments about visibility, Gene is not having anything like the troubles that John Young had with down-Sun wash-out on the first Apollo 16 traverse. The main difference is that while John was driving almost directly down-Sun and, hence, was getting the full effect of zero phase, Gene is driving in a direction different enough from directly down-Sun to reduce the effect. In detail, during the Apollo 16 traverse to Station 1, the solar azimuth was about 84 degrees and the average bearing to the LM from

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: We're climbing, Jack. Because I've been full bore most of the time, and all I can get out of it is 10 clicks; and when I decelerate, she decelerates in a hurry. What's our next stop here? A sample at 3.9?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Ahhh...(Consulting his checklist) 080/3.9.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Well, I'm sitting on 080 right now and 2.6. I think we've got to add a little bit to that if they're right.

A17A1414552.speaker: Evans
A17A1414552.text: Okay. For the record there, mag Oscar Oscar took three pictures, one with an 80 and two with a 250 lens, and the exposures are now 106, I guess.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Stand by. We'll get a new correction for you guys on that shortly. (Pause) [Houston is using the Camelot and Horatio fixes to re-estimate the location of the SEP transmitter.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay, Bob. The surface is not changing. We see no craters that seem to penetrate into bedrock out in here - that is, with blocky rims - and that's quite a contrast to the area we sampled at Station 1A yesterday. I cannot see in my field-of-view any blocky-rim craters. There are slight craters with fragmental walls and rims, but it looks like instant rock rather than the subfloor material.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Jack, can you see over there to the left - I'll turn a little bit (for a better view) - on the dark area of the South Massif where you get those impressed lineations? See them going from left upward to the right?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah. I see what you mean; right.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: That's what I saw out my window.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah, they go obliquely up the slope.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: They're more like wrinkles, they're linear wrinkles.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah. Crenulations, you might say, in the slope that look something like those I saw from orbit, looking in the shadowed area...or, at the edge of the shadows. [Schmitt - "It was a puzzle, seeing apparent lineations on the slopes of mountains. Some people, as I recall, did some simulations, building models, putting random roughness on the surface, and then dusting them and moving the light around, and they were able to create apparent lineations just with light position. Generally, I think, people don't feel that they represent any underlying structure: it's just an accident of dusting and lig

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Bob, we've seen craters as much as 20 meters - maybe 30 meters - in diameter without blocky rims.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Copy that, (garbled). Thank you.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: The rim block population is not much different than the average for the terrain in here. (Pause) RealAudio Clip ( 5 min 57 sec ) 141:53:02 Cernan: Boy, I'll tell you. If we can't recognize a change in that albedo when we get onto that white mantle, I'm going to be surprised. [AS17-135- 20616 is an excellent picture of the portion of the light mantle draped over the east-facing scarp.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Mark my words. Okay. The light mantle is just what Gene has said, it's...That's it, right now. There are some very bright craters in it. They stand out...Bright-haloed craters scattered over it that seem to be quite a bit brighter than anything we have out here on the dark mantle. See those blocks over there? That's the first different-colored blocks I've seen; they're sort of...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Where are you looking?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Over to the right a little bit.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Darker gray, a little bit. 141:53:41 Schmitt: Watch yourself here. Okay. There's a crater with a big mass of block in the bottom. It looks like it might be a secondary fragment from somewhere. [Schmitt - "Secondary craters, formed by ejecta from other lunar impacts, have a much lower energy and they tend to be more irregular, more elongate, and may have a blob of material in the bottom. The projectiles that form primary impacts hit at about 20 km/s, and that's an explosion. Most of the ejecta leaves the Moon entirely; very little of it falls back on the Moon. At most, the stuff that makes seco

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Do you want to get a photo as we go by?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah. Can you swing a little bit to the right?

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Yep. [Jack's next four pictures , AS17-135- 20623 to 20626 show their approach to the secondary crater.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: That might be worth a...How's our time for traverse, Bob? Do we have time for an (extra) LRV sample?

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: You're doing great, so far. We're looking for that first LRV sample at about 4.2; that's in the light mantle. (Get the sample here) if you can do it quickly; but we weren't planning on it. [They've traveled 2.6 kilometers of straight-line distance in 23 minutes since leaving the SEP. The stops have kept their average speed to a modest 6.8 kph thus far.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Want one here?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah, let's get...

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Target of opportunity there, Jack.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Can you get...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Go ahead.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Swing a little bit to the right now.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Right up across that little ray.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: And I'll try to get a chunk of whatever (formed the crater)...Okay, I want...Keep going; keep going...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Look at that big (garbled)...

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Whoa, whoa, whoa.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Let me get the (Rover power) switch off. 082, 3.0, and 2.6. (Pause) And, Bob, I've been making 10 to 12 clicks coming across the surface; and, as I say, for the most part, that's full bore except where I have to do some rapid changes.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. And, by and large, the back room is interested in you guys pressing on to Station 2.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay, we are. (Pause) (To Jack) Just watch the LCRU.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay, Gene. That's a pretty big rock in there.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. [Jack has collected a piece of rock with the LRV Sampler and is now swinging the head across so that Gene can remove the Dixie cup and seal it. This procedure takes far less time than Jack would take trying to get the Dixie cup off himself.] [Training photo 72-H-1227 shows Jack using the sampler from his Rover seat. He is leaning slightly to his right and has a grip on the accessory staff with his left hand for stability. He probably has turned his head inside the helmet so he can see what he is getting although, as he notes in a 2000 e-mail message: "The sampler was mainly just for coll

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: And, Bob, I think there's...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Hold it. Hold it down further...down.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: It's got quite a bit of dirt in it. (To Bob) I think this is a block from a linear-strewn field of very irregular and jagged rocks that are southwest of a crater that's 10 to 15 meters in diameter. It looks like the material that may have formed the crater, and you can look at some of the pictures and make up your own decision.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Copy that. [This sample, 72135, proved to be a breccia, a probable confirmation that it was a piece of the projectile.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: (To Gene) Can you get it in there? (Pause) Okay. You got it. [Gene is putting the sample in the SCB hanging from the accessory staff.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: No, no. No, I didn't.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: No?

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. The bag (that is, the SCB)'s not open.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Well, okay. Yeah, that's bad.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Can you push it in? Pull down.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. It's down. 26 Echo, Bob. We're on our way.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Copy that...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Go ahead.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: ...And, you got a frame count, Jack?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Oh, yeah. Let me... 141:56:12 Cernan: And I did get my "locator" here.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay. I got mine.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Thank you, Jack...(correcting himself) Gene. [Their "locators" are AS17-135- 20627 and AS17-137- 20895 .]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: And the frame count is 95.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Copy that.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Holy cow! I'd better slow down my picture taking.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Roger, Jack. [AS17-135- 20628 is taken toward the south as Gene turns to get back on course toward Hole-in-the-Wall.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: We're in a little area where the fragment population may be up to 3 percent. It's getting a little more like what we saw around the LM. In fact, I would say it was comparable now.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: I'm going down this slope and up the other side, Jack.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: But nothing like (the block coverage at) Station 1.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Copy that. And the next planned Rover sample will be at a distance of 4.2; so, 080 and 4.2. And it will be in the light mantle if...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. We got it, Bob.

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: ...that disagrees with those numbers. [That is, they want to be sure to get a sample in the light mantle, no matter what the Nav system says about their range and bearing.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay. It's in the first prong of light mantle, as I recall. Is that right?

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Roger; the thumb. [In the overhead pictures, there is a narrow finger of light mantle east of the main mass of the avalanche and separated from it by about a kilometer width of the darker material.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay, Bob. Your heading at 260 looks like it's right on, by the way, from what I see on the skyline. [That is, on the 260 heading, they are pointed right at Hole-in-the-Wall.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Okay. And how's the low-gain antenna holding up?

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Look at that boulder...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: (Responding to Bob) Well, I'm moving it, so I guess you're getting it. [Gene occasionally moves the low-gain antenna to keep it pointed at the Earth.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Yeah, we're getting it. Just checking.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Bob, the blocks I see still seem to be the gabbro, except for that one sample we took, which I hope was what I thought it was... [As noted at 141:55:43, Jack was correct in thinking that the sample was not a piece of gabbro but, rather, was a piece of the projectile.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Gee, it's blocky here.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Watch the...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Ooh, that's a big crater. We got to get around here. 141:57:50 Schmitt: Okay. That must be Bronte.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: My God, is that big! [The diameter of Bronte Crater is about 200 meters, about one third the size of Camelot. AS17-135- 20629 may be Jack's photo of the crater.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: That's bigger than I expected.

A17A1414552.speaker: Evans
A17A1414552.text: Keep losing my maps.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Whoo! I got to go around this thing.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah, yeah. There are some very...

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: I got to go back here. (Static) [Gene is having to make a major detour and, as he maneuvers, doesn't have a hand free to keep the low-gain antenna aimed.] [Cernan - "The low-gain was mounted in front of the control stick at my right hand. Most of the time I could drive and manipulate the low-gain at the same time, reaching across with my left hand to move it, probably not with the greatest of ease, but I do recall being able to do that. But, you know, if you got too many things going and you were making lots of turns you just couldn't sit there twisting that low-gain until you got to some reas

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: (Static clears)...blocks, grayer than the normal gabbro we've seen, that have very large, egg-sized vesicles in them. (Pause) Watch it, you got one on your right there...Here you go.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Yeah. I got them.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay. Don't mind me, Gene.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: No. No problem. That's all right, because some of those down-Suns are hard to see. I want to get off this slope. 141:58:29 Schmitt: I wonder if I took a picture of that block field? (Laughing) I hope I did. Getting to be so automatic that I'm not sure what I'm taking any more. [Jack's next seven pictures are AS17-135- 20630 to 20636 . Frame 20630 is a good photo of Hanover Crater, the sharp-rimmed feature on the lower slopes of the North Massif.]

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: Okay. I'm going to go through this niche on a high point in the saddle here.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Okay. How does it figure, Bob? I think we're just north of Bronte. Does that figure?

A17A1414552.speaker: Parker
A17A1414552.text: Rog. That seems to be about where you should be on the map here. We gather you're circumnavigating a little bit. Comm's dropping out from time to time.

A17A1414552.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1414552.text: Yeah.

A17A1414552.speaker: Cernan
A17A1414552.text: 080, 3.5, and 2.9; and we're on the north side of Bronte. [The traverse started at 141:30:33 and Gene has driven 3.5 km. The range to the SEP transmitter is 2.9 km. Including the stops, Gene's average speed has been 7.4 km/hr and his range rate has been 6.1 km/hr. Because he has been driving directly away from the SEP transmitter most of the time, the difference between his average speed and the range rate is the result of zigs and zags he has taken to get around craters.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 20 min 16 sec ) RealAudio Clip ( 6 min 7 sec ) 141:59:07 Schmitt: And it looks like Bronte has penetrated

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yep. Yep.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: (It's nothing compared with) what we saw around Horatio or in the walls of Horatio and around Camelot. Nothing, also, like we saw yesterday at Station 1. (Pause) Bob, that characteristic little dimple in the bottom of the craters is still with us, and it's invariably glass-lined in the fresh ones.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Very good.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Now, that's not a complete lining. It just seems to be glass agglutinates, if you will, that's holding the fragments in the bottom of the crater together. There's one on the side of an older crater. We're back into about a one percent (block) coverage. I suspect that the reason our block population went up there was because of Bronte.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: An awful lot of these smaller, glass-lined little craters around.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, and you notice, Gene, what I was saying about the little dimple in the bottom?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Watch the fresh ones, and (you'll see that) they all have that little dimple as if that...You see, there's one right there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, right there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Man, you can predict it. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Jack, you know, I think the white mantle is starting right over there. See on your right?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, that's the first...

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: The place you can really see it is where it's reflected off the slopes of the...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yup.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: ...of the (Scarp) cliffs out there, but I think...I hate to say it, but Charlie may be right. [Gene is referring to the difficulty that Charlie Duke and John Young had in detecting albedo changes during the Apollo 16 traverses.] [Cernan - "I don't know what we're going to run into next in the transcript, but I remember that when we drove onto the light mantle, although we talked about being able to see it from a distance, the albedo change was so subtle we really had to convince ourselves that we were there. It wasn't like suddenly going from dark to light, it was just fine-grained, subtle cha

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Well, Geno, one thing that may distinguish it is (that) the bright-halo craters are brighter.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: But I can see it from here...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yup.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: ...on the floor of the valley here.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: On the scarp it really shows up.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Block population is unchanged; still appears to be - where I can see large enough blocks - the gabbro, although there's not as much to look at now in terms of blocks. The surface characteristics have not changed. There are no craters that we see that are bringing up clear (that is, unmistakably) blocky rims. Most of the fresh craters have instant rock around them. (At) craters of the same size that are older and more subdued, that instant rock is apparently broken down. I suspect the small zapping breaks that down fairly quickly.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay, 17. Copy that. You still making about 9 to 11 kilometers?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: No, sir. I've been making from 10 to 12, Bob - mostly 12.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Can you give me a reading on the amps this time, Geno.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Stand by. I've got a little navigating to do.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay; standing by.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay. I'm read...I'm reading...I'm reading 100 - bouncing - around 100 on both of them.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. How about amps and not amp-hours?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: And I'm going up-and-down, hummocky terrain, I think with...(Responding to Bob) Oh, I'm sorry.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Watch your...You got a hole in front of you.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Ohh! There you go. Spun out a little bit.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, let me get up here. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Good vehicle you got here.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. It takes a little getting used to, though.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: I'm not sure I want to go through many of those.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: No. [Jack's traverse pictures indicate that the maps clipped to the Accessory Staff are partially blocking his field-of-view.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay, Bob. I'll give you an amp reading as soon as I can. Just stand by for it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: All right. There's no hurry. No hurry.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Would you believe my camera handle's come off? (Pause) [Although Jack's camera problems are not discussed in the Apollo 17 Mission Report, Pete Conrad and Al Bean experienced similar problems on their missions and Figure 14-45 from the Apollo 12 Mission Report illustrates the situation. With the handle loose, Jack will still be able to take pictures by using his finger to push the button that is just below the lens; however, he is going to have a problem keeping a grip on the camera. Because the bracket with which the camera is affixed to the RCU joins the camera at the top of the handle, a lo

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: The terrain gets a lot more locally hummocky with some well-rounded rims but very large-aspect-ratio craters - which you got to get around in here - in the 4- or 5-meter size. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Charlie, that...(Amazed at his slip of the tongue) "Charlie!" I was thinking of white mantle. That's the white mantle we're coming up on right up here.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. [Gene is still pre-occupied with the problem of detecting the albedo change when they cross it.] [Cernan - "We wanted to know when we were up on the white mantle and we expected it was going to be a very subtle change. Here, we could see it coming; but I distinctly remember that it was very difficult to find a definitive line between the light and the dark mantle."]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: See that on your right?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: That's it, there's not going to be that much difference.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: (Hard bump) Ooh!

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Not going to be that much difference, but...(Warning himself) Look where you're going.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I got to watch I don't lose my camera. It's come loose.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: See, now you can look where we're going to come up on the white mantle. It's dusted with that light...Look at it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: We're only 100 meters from the light mantle.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Well...

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. How about giving us the range and bearing when you get to it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Look at this crater in here. (Responding to Bob) We're coming right up on it now. 142:04:10 Schmitt: Yeah. There certainly is a change in the general albedo, particularly in the craters. The craters are much brighter in their walls than we've seen before. [Jack's next four pictures , AS17-135- 20637 to 20640 are from this part of the traverse. Frames 20637 and 20640 show bright craters.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, that's a...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Although there still is a brown...a light...or a gray dusting over the top of it in here, but it's clearly different - no question about that.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: You can't see the contact as you cross it but we know we're coming into something lighter. You can obviously see it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. We ought to sample the rim of one of these craters when we get our LRV sample, because that's what's distinctly lighter.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: How about a range and bearing, guys?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: We're at 3.8 here, and we can sample that rim...

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy the 3.8.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: (Responding to Bob's request) 083, 4.4, 3.8, and I've been... [Gene's average speed, including stops, is now 7.7 km/hr and the range rate is 6.7 km/hr. The difference indicates that, in making detours around craters, Gene has driven about 15 percent farther than the straight-line distance. This is sometimes called the "wander factor".]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: How about right over there, Geno? Can you get on the rim of that crater?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Right here?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: No, right to the right there...

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Right here. 142:04:53 Schmitt: ...That light stuff. See the big crater here...

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: ...and the light material right on the rim?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. I can get there. But I'm going to have to not give you much of a turn because it's...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: That's all right. I got the pictures. Now, if you can swing to the left a little bit and then back...Whoa. Now, back right. Okay. Hope my camera stays on there. [AS17-135- 20641 and 20642 show their approach to the sample site.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: You like that?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Whoa. Yeah. Whoa, whoa.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay, Bob. We're 083, 4.4, and 3.8; and I've been running about 20 to 25 amps, I think, on both.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Copy that. (Pause) RealAudio Clip ( 7 min 35 sec ) 142:05:31 Cernan: We are in the light mantle. It's not a contrasting light like you might expect, or like we're looking at on the Scarp as the Sun shines on it, but I don't think there's any question.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Beautiful.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. The craters that penetrate into it are definitely different. However, the surface texture is unchanged. There may be fewer blocks. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay; bag 27 Echo, 27 Echo.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy that. And frame count, Jack?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: (Garbled) your bag? We don't want to lose it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: (A little annoyed with Bob's request while they are busy) Stand by.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Hold it up. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. It's in there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Is it in? Okay. Oops, the bags (the SCB on the accessory staff) don't stay open... 142:06:21 Schmitt: Yeah. It will after we get a couple of samples in there. Okay; my "locator".

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: And my "locator". [The "locators" are AS17-135- 20643 and AS17-137- 20896 .]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I hope I don't lose my camera.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: I can't reach it, or I'd help you.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. (Giving Bob the frame count) 110.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy that, Jack. 142:06:39 Schmitt: I guess I didn't do what I wanted to do, and that's get that thing (the camera handle) really cinched down. (Pause) [Jack's next five pictures are AS17-135- 20644 to 20648 .]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Boy, Bob, one of the remarkable things is the Sun-angle difference on that light mantle when you're looking at the slopes of the Scarp versus what we're on. I hate to use a familiar term, but my impression right here is there is more of a raindrop influence than back at the LM, or in the darker mantle.

A17A1415907.speaker: Evans
A17A1415907.text: [Humming]

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Copy that.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. (A little skeptical) Might be.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: I think so.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I think the big thing is, though, that each one of these little craters is much more lightly colored. But we're still not...There's no crater in view that does...(correcting himself) that has a blocky rim. There's fragmental rims based on, almost certainly, instant rock, but no blocky rims.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: You know, one of the reasons those craters look lighter is because of their Sun angle. (That is, the Sun striking the) walls of some of these little craters...It's the same material we're driving on, I'll bet. Yeah, there is instant rock right there, Jack; you're right.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. (Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Oh, boy.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: The fragment population is certainly less than 1 percent in here.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yup.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Right now. When I say fragments, I'm talking about rocks that are greater than a centimeter in (garbled, probably "average diameter").

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: You know, it may be me, Bob; (static) but it also seems to be a little bit more difficult to drive down-Sun in this area.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, I think it is brighter, Geno. I was thinking that a minute ago, but it's hard to make a (judgment)...I think your normal albedo is greater.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Here's some rocks now starting (garbled)...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: And the little craters still have the central pits.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. We're losing your comm a little bit, guys.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: (Garbled)

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, there's a few.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: (Static) (Responding to Bob) Well, we're (pointing) right at you. (Checking the low-gain indicator against the heading indicator) 270.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. There're a few blocks. They still look like the gabbro, though. Hard to tell.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Well, a couple of them looked to me like they had some very light (static) crystals in them. See that?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I'm afraid those are zap pits.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: They could be.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I think I've been fooled by that, too, and that's what I estimated the plagioclase (content) by. [Journal Contributor David Harland notes "Here, Jack is talking about having been fooled, during EVA-1, by the zap-pit halos into thinking there was more plagioclase in the gabbro than there really is. The false lightness in color produced by the zap pits led him to estimate 50 percent plage, rather than 30 percent. He realized his error after EVA-1 when he was able to study a sample in the LM, out of the glare of the Sun."]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Whooo! (Comm clears) I just want to keep you out of those slopes, and I'll tell you, I get you in some...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: That's all right.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: ...(by working at) keeping you out of them. [That is, by trying to avoid going into one crater, Gene gets them in another.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. We're getting a little more blocks in here. Of course, we're approaching the dark mantle again. Now, you can see the difference. You got to look hard for it! But, you see those craters out in there are not white anymore. [A sketch map of the second half of the traverse in shown (identically) on LMP-10 and CDR-10. The planned bearing/range at the turn near Lara is 080/5.5 and at Station 2 near Nansen is 063/7.2. The area below the dashed line that goes through Wagner Crater was mapped, pre-flight as dark mantle, as was the Tortilla Flats area that Gene is about to enter. ]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: I got to get around that slope.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. (Pause) Okay. You still got Hole-in-the-Wall picked out over there, don't you?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, I got it. And, I'm trying to keep comm with them as I'm turning here.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: And, I've been keeping the thing on. I don't know if they're reading us, but I've been moving it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Read you loud and clear, guys.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Looking up on the South Massif, we've got real good views of the block-strewn fields. There seems to be two dominant colorations of the rocks. The light-colored ones (are) very light tan to white, and then there are the blue-gray rocks. There's one major outcrop of blue-gray about a sixth of the way down the slope, (in) the center of the field-of-view we have; and it looks very much like similar blue-gray rocks right at the crest, the highest point from our vantage point. [Schmitt - "Formation of the massifs was part of a dynamic process; and the hard layers represented by the blocks nea

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Bob,...

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay, give me a range and bearing, please.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: ...(do) you want another sample of the dark mantle here? Could you use that?

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Yeah, we want (a range and bearing) as soon as you get into the dark mantle. We're estimating it's (at a range of) something like 4.3 (km), 4.5, somewhere in that vicinity.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: We're there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. We're ready for another (sample), then.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: We're there. (To Gene) Now, let's...If you can...Okay, right over there, and maybe I can get a rock with it (the soil). See that batch of rocks there?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Right here?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Whoa. Yeah. Swing it. Whoa, now swing back over. Little more, little more. Whoa. Little more.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Can you reach it?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Now, if you go forward.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Can you reach it?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Hold it. Right there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay, Bob; 082, 5.0, and 4.3. [The SEP is eight degrees north of east from their position; they have traveled 5.0 kilometers since leaving the LM; and they are now 4.3 kilometers from the Nav initialization point. Gene's average speed is now 7.4 km/hr and the range rate is 6.5 kph. Both LMP-9 and CDR-9 indicate a range for the contact of 4.0 km and a dark mantle sample at 4.2 km.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy that.

A17A1415907.speaker: Evans
A17A1415907.text: [Garble] all right.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: And CDR (Commander) is 3.85 (psi suit pressure) and about 70 percent (oxygen remaining) and no (warning) flags.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Thank you, Geno. (Long Pause)

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I got it (the sample).

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: You got it? Okay.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I got the rock. I got the rock, and there's some dirt in there. Maybe I'd better get a little bit more dirt.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. (Pause) You don't have any trouble getting dirt.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Can you see in there? [Because the Dixie cup is one in a stack, Jack can't see into it without changing his grip on the sampler.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Is there...

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Yeah.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: ...much soil?

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Oh, a little bit...

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Okay. I'll get this soil.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Couple teaspoonsfull. Twenty-eight Echo, Bob.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Say again there, 17.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Twenty-eight Echo.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy that.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: And that's primarily a rock fragment. Jack's getting a soil sample with it.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Copy.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Jack, look at the wrinkles over there on the North Massif. 142:12:34 Schmitt: Yeah. There's no question that there are apparent lineations all over these Massifs, in a variety of directions. Hey, look at how that Scarp goes up the side (of the North Massif) there. There's a distinct change in texture.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay. [The "locators" for this sample are AS17-135- 20649 and AS17-137- 20897 . Both are excellent photos and, among other things, show Hanover Crater and, just to the west (left) of it, the Scarp running up onto the North Massif.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: As a matter of fact, the lineations are not present on the Scarp, that we can see, where it crosses the North Massif. There is no sign of those lineations on there.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Oh, man; yeah. I can see what you're talking about now.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Look over by Hanover.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: It looks like the Scarp overlays the North Massif, doesn't it?

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Yeah. [This observation suggests that the Scarp formed after the mountain was raised.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay. This last (sample) was 29 Echo.

A17A1415907.speaker: Parker
A17A1415907.text: Okay. Copy that. And that's the soil.

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Okay, now I need to get in that bag. (Responding to Bob) That's affirm. (Pause) [Gene tries to put the two folded Dixie cups in the SCB hanging on the accessory staff. Apparently, he has trouble reaching across and gives the samples to Jack to put in the SCB.] RealAudio Clip ( 7 min 19 sec ) 142:13:18 Cernan: Here's another one. You're going to...Don't lose those. [Jack may be in danger of losing the LRV sampler.]

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: Whoooee!

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Oh, boy.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: That really gives me a strange feeling. (Jack laughs heartily).

A17A1415907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1415907.text: Gives me a strange feeling too. (Pause) Those are not intentional.

A17A1415907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1415907.text: I understand.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1421313csm.text: There's the ole Earth. It's about a half Earth now.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: I won't. I'll put it down.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421313csm.text: Okay, Bob, we are rolling.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: Copy that.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: And pray for me, Bob, that I don't lose my camera. Okay. Hanover is quite a ways up the (North Massif) slope. I don't think we'd have gotten to it, as we planned that time. But the appearance you have of the Scarp/North Massif contact is one of the Scarp being smoother textured, less cratered, and certainly less lineated. And I wouldn't be a bit surprised if it's, as Gene says, younger.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: Okay, Jack. Copy that.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: It's not just the slope, it's the materials on the other side of the Scarp, on the west side. (Pause) [That is, the North Massif has lineations east of the Scarp, but not at the Scarp itself.]

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: Okay, I'm going to have to really ease up on pictures. I forgot to give them a frame count. (Static)

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: Yeah. We didn't get a frame count. You want to give us a frame count there, Jack?

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: Well, Bob. The problem is (that) every time I take my hand off, my camera loosens up again.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: Okay; I copy that. And our estimate is that if you continue to go between 50 and 100 meters between frames, we'll make it. 142:15:00 Cernan: (Static clears) Boy, I tell you. Are those Massifs getting to look big now! Holy Smoley! [Somewhere in here, Gene takes AS17-137- 20898 , showing the South Massif and the Scarp. Jack's next next four photos are AS17-135- 20650 to 20653 .]

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: That frame at the LRV sample was about 115.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: Copy that.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421313csm.text: I'll tell you, that Scarp looks nice over there, too, doesn't it?

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1421313csm.text: Ron, is there a difference in the color between the dome and the mare in Aitken, there?

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1421313csm.text: 142:16:49 - We're in contact with America on the 28th revolution.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: Yeah. (Pause) Okay, we're back down in our old friend, the dark mantle. And I think the zero-phase point is not as bright as it was. (We're) passing a small crater, but the block population is still way down there in about - Whoops, watch that one - (the) one percent (range). [Gene is making ten to twelve kilometers per hour on level terrain. However, even "level" terrain has plenty of hummocks formed by the rims of old, subdued craters. In order to maintain speed and get maximum use of their time and supplies of oxygen and cooling water, Gene is driving over blind crests without slowing, keep

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421313csm.text: And, 17, for your benefit, we're showing you with very good net mobility rates here; and things (are) looking quite good. [That is, their average speed is high enough that they will have plenty of time to complete the planned activities at Nansen before moving on. They are currently 4.3 kilometers from the SEP site and have been driving, stops included, for 45 minutes. Their average range rate is 5.7 km/hr.]

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: Thank you. Gene's doing a great job.

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421313csm.text: I'll tell you, it takes all your time to drive, though. You look around, and you're in a hole. (Pause)

a17_1421313csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421313csm.text: Okay here's another small crater (with) instant rock, the same little pit (at the center of the crater) and a spattering of glass holding the pit materials together. None of the glass linings look very coherent, Bob. They mainly just seem to be a sprinkling of glass that's coating (pause) the instant rock.

a17_1421649.text: We're in contact with America on the 28th revolution.

a17_1421649.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421649.text: The craters at about 10 to 15 meters in diameter seem to have somewhat more blocky material in their rims. But they're not clear-cut blocky rim craters. And here's one that's probably 50 meters across that has a fair number of blocks in the bottom. [An impact will penetrate to a depth equal to about one-quarter of the diameter of the crater it produces. Blocks in a 50-meter crater would suggest regolith depth of less than 12 meters.]

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1421741csm.text: You know, you take a look at the central peak of Neper, and on the south and western edge of it, you get the vertical stripes in it or streaking like you get off of the massifs in the landing site area. And then, you look at the area around in the rim - around the rim of Neper, and you get the corncob - I guess - or Sculptured Hill-type of appearance.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421741csm.text: Okay; we're anxiously awaiting them. (Pause) [Hole-in-the-Wall is the juncture between a lobe of the Scarp and the main Scarp face, a geologic equivalent of the web of flesh between a person's thumb and forefinger. Avalanche material overlies both features. Hole-in-the-Wall was spotted in pre-mission photographs as a plausible path up to the top of the 80-m-high Scarp.] [Cernan - "We were concerned about what we were going to find at Hole-in-the-Wall and what path we were going to take to get up the Scarp. I don't remember exactly, but I'm sure we must have looked at the Scarp from orbit."]

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421741csm.text: How about a range and bearing while you're at it?

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421741csm.text: I've been making 10 or 12 clicks (kilometers per hour) most of the time. (Pause; listening to Bob) Okay, 082, 5.6 and 4.9.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421741csm.text: Copy 4.9 on the range. [The average range rate is now 6.3 kph. They are about 0.5 kilometers from Hole-in-the-Wall. The location of Hole-in-the-Wall is shown on a pre-flight map with handwritten feature names. Note the name change from Amundsen to Nansen. The expected view from 1/2 kilometer derived from pre-flight estimates of surface elevations is linked here . The expected views were produced from data extracted from photographs taken from the Apollo 15 Command Module and, despite the low resolution of those photos, these views bear at least some resemblance to what Gene and Jack are seeing

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421741csm.text: And about 20 to 22 amps (the electric current to the Rover wheel motors) most of the time.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1421741csm.text: Okay, we're losing a little bit of low-gain (signal) there, Geno.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421741csm.text: I think you need to tilt it up a little. Probably undershooting the Earth. I don't know.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421741csm.text: Well, our pitch angle (the Rover's up/down orientation) changes all the time. That's the problem. Bob, I have been within 10 to 20 degrees of you the whole time.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421741csm.text: Okay, Bob, we're not in light mantle, I don't think. (Pause) Maybe we are.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1421741csm.text: Now. Okay, went to Standby at - whatever I said now. [Laughter.]

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1421741csm.text: According to my geology map (garbled). I guess we are. Gosh, I was going to say the craters are whiter than they have been. So, we're back in it. And even the zero-phase point's brighter, too. [There is a great deal of glass in the lunar soil and, at the down-Sun or "zero-phase" point, the reflected sunlight can be quite bright - more so here on the light mantle than on the dark mantle.]

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421741csm.text: (Static clears) I think that place where we had those small, blocky craters was within the dark mantle. They're not evident here in the lighter stuff.

a17_1421741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1421741csm.text: Boy, is that (South Massif) getting big. Whoo-ee! (Pause) Hold on. [They're going into a small crater.] MP3 Audio Clip ( 24 min 29 sec )

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Whoooee!

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Oh, boy.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: That really gives me a strange feeling. (Jack laughs heartily).

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Gives me a strange feeling too. (Pause) Those are not intentional.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: I understand.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: I'm not sure I've got enough guts to make them intentional. (Pause) Man, everything's getting to look big the closer you get. (Pause) Hole-in-the-Wall looks more promising, though, Bob. [Up to this point, they haven't been able to see enough detail to tell whether or not Hole-in-the-Wall will be a good place to climb the Scarp.]

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Yeah, I don't think that's going to be any problem.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: (At least not) until we get up and look back. Oh, man, what a trip this is going to be. Golly. (Pause)

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: That Min cooling is just about right, isn't it.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: No, it's just about warm for me.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Yeah.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Bob, is my PLSS cooling working all right?

A17A1421907.speaker: Parker
A17A1421907.text: Rog. It looks like it's working to us.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Okay. [Driving the Rover takes concentration and a fair amount of effort. As indicated in the table at 151:03:03, while they are riding, Gene's metabolic rate is about 10% higher than Jack's.]

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Bob, the rock fragments still look like gabbro. The craters tend to have white walls and white rims, which they don't have in the dark mantled area. The block population is way down, (and covers) one percent (of the surface) or less. However, the bigger craters do have more blocks; but nowhere does that population seem to get above about five percent. And that's on the walls and the rims of the craters, say bigger than 15 meters. There's one probably 20 meters in diameter that has some blocks on it.

A17A1421907.speaker: Evans
A17A1421907.text: Off.

A17A1421907.speaker: Mission Control
A17A1421907.text: 142:24:15 - In lunar orbit Ron Evans is right on the Flight Plan.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: (Glancing at CDR-10 ) Have you seen Nemo (Crater)? I think Nemo is right over there, if I'm not mistaken. (Pause) I don't know. RealAudio Clip ( 7 min 17 sec ) 142:20:49 Schmitt: Nemo will be hard to see. But, yeah, it's probably that one right in there.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Or back here. There's one back here.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Well, it's pretty...Yeah, well...Yeah, that's close to (the) Scarp. It's probably right off your wing there. [Schmitt - "Because of the stiffness of the suits, our field-of-view was pretty much restricted to straight ahead. We could turn our heads a little in the suits and could gesture with our arms, but even then, Gene could really only see a gesture if I made it with my inboard arm."] [Their current position is about 081/5.3. Nemo has a 400 meter diameter They are about 400 meters northwest of the near rim.]

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Okay, I'm going straight ahead and then I'm going to make a left turn (into Hole-in-the-Wall).

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Okay. We're looking at Lara (Crater). Now, Lara...I can see blocks in the northwest rim of Lara. At least, it's rugged terrain; and it looks like blocky terrain. One spot. That's all I see. It looks like it may be a couple hundred meters in average diameter. It starts maybe three-quarters of the way up the wall and goes right up to the rim. [Schmitt - "Lara is almost certainly a crater that pre-dates the avalanche. The avalanche rode over it and, indeed, in the good photographs you can see some subflows (secondary slides) down the slopes into it."]

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Hey, Bob, Hole-in-the-Wall seems to be a...

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Hey, look at that. Look at that crater!!

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Right there? Yeah.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: That central pit goes down about half the depth of the crater, and the crater is a fresh, 3-meter crater. It almost was a cylindrical pit.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Hey, Bob, Hole-in-the-Wall is just a step, headed down to the south or southeast on the Scarp. The Scarp is just about what I think we all expected it to be. It's very rolling and relatively smooth. I don't really see any outcrops (of rock) exposed anywhere out here to the south.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: No. You see, now there's Station 3 area right up there. [The Station 3 stop will be made at the base of the Scarp, just north of Lara, after they finish their activities at Nansen Crater and have driven back down onto the valley floor.]

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Yep.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Looks like maybe that set of...See that bigger crater over there to the right of Lara? That probably is a good place for Station 3.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Yeah, way over there. Okay, we're going to find out something very shortly (about Hole-in-the-Wall).

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: It doesn't look very rocky, Gene.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: No.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: (Garbled)

A17A1421907.speaker: Parker
A17A1421907.text: How about bearing and range, guys?

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Bob, I'll give it to you just as soon as I make my turn. It's not too far - 100 meters.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Are...Are you...Are you going to turn over that or go on closer...

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: No, I'm going right up straight ahead and then go on to the inside of that place.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Yeah. That's more than 100 meters.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Yeah.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: (Giving a bearing and range to the LM) 081 and 5.6.

A17A1421907.speaker: Parker
A17A1421907.text: Copy that.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: There's...Now the craters are getting very, very light colored in their rims and walls.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: You notice when we're in the light mantle looking at the Scarp, at this angle, it loses some of its high albedo (that is, its apparent brightness)?

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Yeah. Yeah. I think we're getting...

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: We've got a long depression to go around.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: ...Your eyes get used to it.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Okay, Jack, we got to watch it because I got to go around a long depression. That's a crater over there.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: On the right; yeah.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: I don't know how I can get over there to...

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: I think...

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: I may have to go up over there. I can't go down that hole. That one's not going to make it.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: What's your pitch?

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: Let's go back here. We can't get there. I'm going to go over here.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: What was your pitch then, Geno?

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: (Static; garbled) primarily. I can't go there.

A17A1421907.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1421907.text: Yeah, I think you're right.

A17A1421907.speaker: Cernan
A17A1421907.text: We'll go up this gentle slope. See what's on top. (Pause) Okay. Let me get my (garbled). (Pause) 142:24:17 Schmitt: (To Houston) We made a turn to the south a little bit at 081 and 5.7. Are you going to try to drive up there?

a17_1422415.text: In lunar orbit Ron Evans is right on the Flight Plan.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1422534csm.text: They're fresher ones. Okays let's see. We're going to Picard and then on up to - Yerkes - Where's Yerkes? There it is. Okay. Let's see where we're aiming at here. Okay. Is it about the time, does it look like?

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. Whatever makes up the light mantle is - at least, the instant rock that it forms - is much lighter than anything we see (elsewhere). Those fragments probably are 30 percent lighter than any fragments we see out on the dark mantle. And that's around the fresh craters. But it is not blocky. (Pause)

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob, are you still reading?

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Roger. Read you loud and clear.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay, I just wanted to make sure my antenna's working.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1422534csm.text: Started it. Picard X.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Roger.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: We're doing a little zig-zag navigation. I literally came up a slope at about a heading of 240 (WSW). We couldn't get through the actual turn to the south because there is a big crater right at the foot of it. So we're just making our way through some relatively local undulating slopes that get pretty steep, but it seems to be no problem.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, I think we're in good shape. Bob, I can't ...There are not any blocks big enough to really make a statement about what the (underlying) rock is. But it really doesn't look like gabbro anymore.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. Copy that.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: It doesn't have that...

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: And a reminder that eventually you're going to have to turn to the south a little bit to pick up the final thing...at Station 2. [Gene's average heading during the drive from Hole-in-the-Wall to Nansen will be about 225.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: We're not on top of that Scarp, yet. We're still in the Hole-in-the-Wall rim.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. Copy that.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob, as far as lineations in the soil or on the surface that are observable at this range (that is, close at hand), I don't see any. I think there may be a finer raindrop pattern on the light mantle than maybe there was out on the dark. But that's an awfully hard judgment to make.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1422534csm.text: Sure hope that color difference shows up in - on Picard.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1422534csm.text: 142:28:48 - Ron Evans performing infrared, ultraviolet, laser altimeter experiments.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. Copy that.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: How you doing, Geno?

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Doing fine. Bob, we've slowed down (to) between about 5 to 8 - maybe 5 to 10 - clicks most of the time. I'm going to head right up there, I think. Get around this crater.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Pretty healthy roll we're going to have here.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, I'm going to head more straight up the hill. Once I get up on top, I'll be all right. I'm going to head down in this hole and then up that way.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, I think...

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: I don't mind pitch, but I sure don't like roll.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: I don't either. (Pause)

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Now I'm going to head straight up...I'm going to head straight up that slope right there. Okay. (Long Pause) RealAudio Clip ( 7 min 53 sec ) 142:28:49 Schmitt: Bob, It looks like maybe the large fragments in here are still crystalline. They have white zap pits on them. But they do not yet really resemble the gabbros. ["Zap pits" are small craters blasted into the surfaces of rocks by sand-grain-sized impactors. On the gabbros, Jack noted white halos of fractured minerals created around the craters.]
Ron Evans performing infrared, ultraviolet, laser altimeter experiments.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay, Jack. Copy that. Give us a hack when you get up on top of the Scarp there.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Let me tell you, Bob, I've got to go cross-slope some of the time because the Rover is really working to go uphill now. [The Rover is designed to handle loose slopes of up to 25 degrees. Steeper slopes can be handled by driving cross slope.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: All right.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: But we're almost there.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: As I look up the Scarp to the west, there are some big blocks scattered around on our horizon; but, again, I would guess that we're not dealing with more than 2 or 3 percent total coverage of blocks in here, if that. 142:29:45 Cernan: Well, I think, for the most part - for the most part - we're on top.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, we're...we're on top.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob, we're at 7.8...Correction: 078, 7.2, and 6.2.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Copy that. [Since starting the drive up Hole-in-the-Wall, they've driven about 600 meters in 5 minutes for a net speed of 7 kph. They've climbed about 80 meters up from the valley floor. Jack's photo at the crest is AS17-135- 20665 .]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Now, Jack, where was Nansen (Crater) with respect to those (boulder) tracks up there (on South Massif)?

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Well, they never really had any good tracks pinned down, I don't think. You'll be able to see Nansen, I think, soon as you get over this hill. [From the LM, Gene and Jack had seen tracks made long ago by boulders as they tumbled downhill from outcrops high on both the North and South Massifs. Some of the North Massif tracks were visible in the pre-mission photography taken from orbit during Apollo 15.] [Cernan - "As I recall, from orbit you really had to look for the tracks. If you could find one of the very big boulders you could trace the tracks on the slopes of the massifs. On the surface t

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Boy, I tell you, when we look back (into the valley toward the LM), that's going to be quite a sight if we can see into that Sun. We have been coming uphill! Well, I'd say this is the last straw to the top. And is she working! Come on, baby. (Pause)

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. I think you bear...

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: I'm going to try to get over along (means "to") the base of the massif now.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah. Head towards that track area there, anyway. (To Bob) There are a lot of boulder tracks coming down from the blue-gray rocks, Bob. We'll see whether or not we're going to get to those tracks at Nansen, or we might want to move over to the tracks and see if we can find the boulder that made them. [By sampling boulders that are clearly identified with boulder tracks, they can be sure of sampling rocks derived from outcrops high on the mountain.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay; if they're in the vicinity, it might be a nice idea. 142:31:02 Schmitt: But there's no question where those tracks come from. [Jack's next six photos , taken during the drive toward Nansen, are AS17-135- 20666 to 20671 .]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: And we gather you're slowing down to about 5 clicks now, coming up this last rise.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah. I'm back up to about 7 to 10 now, Bob. The slowdown is because that's about all it will take!

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob, I have the impression that there is a dipping (meaning "not horizontal") zone of blue-gray outcrops or block concentrations up there on the Massif that trends from the high point just beneath the Earth cross-slope; and probably the apparent dip is - oh, I don't know - 10 or 15 degrees (down) to the east. It looks like those outcrops may match up along that trend. [From a position at the base of the Scarp, it will be impossible to prove whether these were true outcrops of bedrock or just concentrations of partially buried boulders. However, given the steepness of the slopes on the upper mo

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Jack, I'm going to head right along this ridge because I think that's the depression we were talking about.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yep, that's Nansen down there. >i>[Although they have finished climbing the scarp, they still can't see the base of the South Massif. There is a trench-like depression at the base of the mountain and they will need to get closer before they will be able to see the planned Station 2 location.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Where are you looking? Right there?

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: I think, right below...

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: I think you're right. I think that's it. Let me get over here, and then I'll head a little bit to the south.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, we're a little more west, I think, than we intended to be.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, I think you're right. (Pause)

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob...(Trying to read the instruments) What is it? 078 and 6.5? (Pause)

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: Bob, I've had an impression, and I can't prove it yet, that we're dealing with more heterogeneous rock. Possibly there are breccias in here. But it's awfully hard to tell right now. They're very light-colored rocks, I think even lighter colored than the gabbros. [Lunar breccias are rocks made up of fragments of other rocks, and even soils, welded together during large impact events.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. We'll soon find out.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: I'm afraid those...I think we can follow those (boulder) tracks. The pictures, maybe... [Jack means that they can visually follow the tracks from the boulders up to the source outcrop.]

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1422534csm.text: Okay. It's about now. Change to 5.6. Getting out into the mare.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1422534csm.text: Yeah, I think we can see some of those coming down.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1422534csm.text: I think the ones from the big outcrop of blue-gray rock, though, are the ones going into Nansen.

a17_1422534csm.speaker: Cernan

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Boy, look at all the dust without that fender (meaning "with the replacement fender on"). I hate to think of what it would have been like with that (replacement) fender gone. [Gene can see how much dust the front wheels are throwing up under the fender and is thinking what it would be like driving without the replacement.]

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: Yeah. (Pause) There's a good-sized block, sort of blue-gray.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Looking up there, Jack, I ought to get some 500s looking right up that hill, but...

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: Well, you may want to do that out a ways (from the Massif). [Gene is talking about getting pictures with the 500-mm camera; Jack is suggesting that they would get a better view from a position farther to the north.]

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Some of that stuff is mantled, or buried, in the massif material. Some of (the rocks) just seems to be laying on it, of course.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: Yeah. Well, I think it has to do with how long it's been there. You'll tend to get the downslope movements forming uphill fillets, and that's what a lot of it looks like. [Out on the valley floor, fillets are formed exclusively by ejecta from local impacts splashing against the sides of rocks and building up skirts of soil. On steep slopes, downhill movement of regolith can also contribute to fillet formation.]

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Most of it is uphill fillets. Most of it is pretty sharp. (To Bob) But my guess, from back at the LM, that those blocks on the massif were much more angular, I think, is a good guess because that's what they look like to me here.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt

a17_1423729csm.text: Okay. High Gain...

a17_1423729csm.text: Jimmeny Christmas! Listen, if the Earth goes behind it, we're changing Station 2. (Laughter)

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: Gonna be nip and tuck, pardon the expression. [The North and South Massifs are 2000m and 2300m tall, respectively. a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: Okay. As we get closer, actually, we're out of the block area. And that blocky region of 5 percent may have been just associated with that crater. I still see no lineations, although...

a17_1423729csm.text: Look at these wrinkles (on the Massif), though, Jack...

a17_1423729csm.text: Yeah. I was talking about the mantle.

a17_1423729csm.text: Oh.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: But you're right about on the Massif.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: The same wrinkled lineations we saw sloping uphill to the west on the eastern half of the Massif are still very evident at this Sun angle (and, therefore, may be real and not an optical illusion). 142:39:51 Parker: Okay, 17; And we're estimating that you should be there within...

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: (To Gene) Come back up!

[During mission planning, it was assumed that, should the Rover fail at any point during the traverse, the astronauts could walk back to the LM at an average speed of 2.7 km/hr, using cooling water and oxygen about 25 percent faster than they would have during normal activities (1290 BTU/hr rather than 1000 BTU/hr). a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1423729csm.text: Okay. Beautiful. (Pause)

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Well...

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: We're getting close.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: I'll give them their 5 minutes. We'll make it by then.

a17_1423729csm.text: Bob, the boulder tracks are really just chains of small craters, for the most part. (Pause)

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1423729csm.text: Okay; copy that. That's interesting.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: I don't think they can tilt the television camera high enough to see the top of the Massif. (Pause) Jack, we're on the edge here, but I don't know. Is that the...Well, let me go up here.

a17_1423729csm.text: No, you're doing great.

a17_1423729csm.text: See, there's Nansen off to my right now.

a17_1423729csm.text: Rog. We see them.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Yeah, I just want to make sure that I'm not driving down a hole here...which I am, but...I don't want to drive down(into) Nansen.

a17_1423729csm.text: Going down here very slowly.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1423729csm.text: I think (a) station (pause) just about anywhere near the big blocks...

a17_1423729csm.text: Yeah, that's where I'm going to put it.

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Schmitt

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: That's where I'm going to put it. (Pause)

a17_1423729csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1423729csm.text: Okay, Jack, I'm going to do a 180 (degree turn) and park the Rover at 045. [Gene will park the Rover pointing northeast. The checklist pages describing the stop at Nansen are LMP-11 , LMP-12 , and LMP-13 . Gene has identical pages. Generally, the items listed for the Apollo 17 geology stops are generic tasks which leave plenty of room for real-time decisions by the crew and the Backroom.]

A17A1430419.text: Okay. It's back on. [Something has come loose, possibly Gene's pack of sample bags. Fendell pans away to look at some nearby boulders and small craters at maximum zoom.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Cernan
A17A1430419.text: Okay, Bob. I missed that. I didn't give it to you; but I think...Well the next bag I take out, you can check the num(ber)...Well, wait a minute, I'll do it for you.

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: No. That's okay. I suspect it's 498.

A17A1430419.speaker: Cernan
A17A1430419.text: (Not having heard Bob yet) I'm almost positive it was 498.

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Okay. We'll put that down.

A17A1430419.speaker: Cernan
A17A1430419.text: Yeah, I did, too. (Pause)

A17A1430419.speaker: Evans
A17A1430419.text: That's the last of the - you know, it's kind of associated with its own little thing. It doesn't look like it's a ray. It doesn't look like a ray, in other words, it doesn't thin out in different parts of it, like a ray does.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: Okay, Bob, looking at the blocks directly down-Sun, the gray-matrix breccias seem to be fragments, or schlerin anyway (elongated fragments with vague boundaries, usually elongated by either compression or shearing), within the white-matrix breccias.

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Okay. I copy that. [Schmitt - "I think one reason you hear the word 'Okay' so much is that we were using it as a trigger for the VOX, the voice-activated communications circuit, so that you don't cut out your first real word. I don't think it's something we talked about; it just developed."] [A quick check of the transcripts from the other Apollo missions indicates that all of the astronauts frequently used "Okay" and most often at that start of utterances.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: And I got a couple pictures down-Sun to show that texture. [These are AS17-138- 21036 and 21037 .]

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Okay. And one thing we'd like to do would be to sample a variety of blocks, in terms of looking at differences in the blocks...from block to block.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: Rog. We're going to do that. We're going after a lighter-colored block, now. (To Gene) Are you going up there?

A17A1430419.speaker: Cernan
A17A1430419.text: Yeah. [Gene is about to climb the slope to Boulder 2.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Okay; and if you're going up the Massif, why don't we try and get the rake sample up there now. When you finish these rocks. [Fendell returns to them.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Evans
A17A1430419.text: Now.

A17A1430419.speaker: Cernan
A17A1430419.text: Hey, Jack...Jack, don't come up here unless you bring the rake. It's a long trip. No sense coming up here twice. I can go get this sample. I'd get the rake, if I were you. Don't walk back up twice.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: Well, I don't...(Contemplative mumble) I'm not sure they're going to gain anything by coming up to the top (higher than the Rover). Okay. [Jack starts for the Rover; Gene, visible in the gap, starts climbing the slope to the southeast.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: You're not going to gain a thing, Bob.

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Standby.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: You're still on the talus. (Pause) You guys...Oh, well. (He decides not to waste time arguing) The rims of the small craters in the talus are softer than the normal terrain. My foot goes in maybe 10 centimeters where normally it only goes in a centimeter. [Jack reaches the Rover.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: Okay. As long as it's above the break of the slope, Jack, we don't have to get very far up the slope.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: (Testy) That's right!! [Jack mounts the scoop on the gate, takes the rake.]

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
A17A1430419.text: And, Jack, since you're back at the Rover, how about giving us a Grav reading before you leave.

A17A1430419.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1430419.text: Because I'm late sampling, that's why. But I'll do it anyway. Video Clip ( 3 min 21 sec 0.9 Mb RealVideo or 33 Mb MPEG )

A17A1430419.speaker: Parker
