A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Oh, man! That is dusty.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Yeah, let me disconnect yours; you disconnect mine. It's easier with the...

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: I think I can get...What did you say?

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: ...OPS hoses.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Oh, yeah.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Or whatever it said.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Yeah.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Disconnect OPS hose.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Is that what it said?

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Yeah. (Pause) Maneuver my fingers in here a little bit better. (Pause)

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: They are all showing a little bit of stickiness.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Glad we're in this (means "doing this") in pairs.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: (Laughing) Well, just everything's, you know, harder to...

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Okay. There, you're disconnected.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: PGA diverter valve, horizontal.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Okay. Horizontal. [With the diverter valve in the horizontal position, air is flowing into the suit cavity. During the EVA, they had it in the vertical position and only got flow into the helmet. Flow into the torso helps dry the suit by keeping some flow going despite the fact that they have their helmets and gloves off.]

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: (Now on Surface 5-2 ) And Suit Isol(ation Valves) , both to Suit Flow.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: All right...We don't have the LM hoses on. So don't...Put mine to Suit Flow to get some air in here.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Yeah. Start filtering the dust. [Schmitt - "We were setting up the LM oxygen flow and, even though we weren't connected to the LM hoses, the system would start to filter dust out of the air."]

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: PLSS pump, Off; and fan, Off.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Okay.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Man, that's hot. Feel that. [Gene may be talking about his RCU because that is where the switches for the pump and fan are located. See the discussion at 148:25:00.]

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: (It was) out in the Sun.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Yeah.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: Pump's Off. Fan's Off.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Okay.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: "Disconnect PLSS H2O from PGA." Okay. [The PGA or "Pressure Garment Assembly" is the combination of suit, PLSS, and visor assembly.]

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: And connect LM water. That's what we want.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: (Garbled). The P(ressure) and O(xygen) flags.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Yeah. (Garbled) LM water hose, here. 148:23:04 Schmitt: I'm sorry that's so complex, there.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Oh, that's perfectly fine.

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: But it was easier to start.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: It had to be. (The dust) smells like someone's been firing a carbine in here. (Pause)

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Why don't you stay there and push in that...

A17A1481224.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1481224.text: I will

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: ...pump breaker...When you get it. (Pause)

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Hey, Little Joe? Are you there?

A17A1481224.speaker: Allen
A17A1481224.text: 17, this is Houston. And...

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Little Joe, are you there?

A17A1481224.speaker: Allen
A17A1481224.text: Roger. How do you read Houston? Over.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Joe, we're reading you loud and clear. We're on the left-hand column (of the post-EVA card) and we're both going PLSS mode to O, and we'll be off the air for a skosh. [They are still on the left-hand column of Surface 5-2 . "Skosh" means "a little bit".]

A17A1481224.speaker: Allen
A17A1481224.text: Roger, Geno. I've been following you real close, and you two are mighty smooth. Boy, was that nice today.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Thank you. 148:24:59 Schmitt: (To Gene) Feel how hot that is.

A17A1481224.speaker: Cernan
A17A1481224.text: Yeah, the whole thing. [Comm Break] [After turning off the PLSS by going to Mode O, they hook up the LM comm circuit before recharging the PLSS oxygen tanks and then doffing the backpacks. Because of the short interval between Gene's comment about "going PLSS Mode to O" and Jack's remark about a hot piece of equipment, the most likely candidate, again, would seem to be the chest-mounted RCU . An alternate interpretation comes from Apollo 15 when, at 148:39:34, Scott and Irwin noticed that the EVA-2 SRC was hot. For Apollo 17, I think it is far more likely that the "hot" object is an RCU than t

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Geno, we hear you on that and we'll be watching it. (Long Pause) [The nominal cabin pressure is 5.0 psi and Gene's question is whether or not there is some valve open that should be closed. Eventually, they will trace the increased pressure to a slow leak in Pressure Regulator A. There will be more discussion of this leak through the evening and into Day 3.]

A17A1483400.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1483400.text: Joe, we're about 2 minutes into the CDR's (PLSS) O2 charge.

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Thank you. [Comm Break. Jack does not sound as congested as he did after EVA-1.]

A17A1483400.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1483400.text: Joe, LMP has 96 percent on his (oxygen) gauge.

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Thank you, Jack. We copy that. (Long Pause)

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Geno, with regard to your observation made to us a few moments ago, I guess we will ask for the Cabin Return (Valve) to the Auto position and your Suit (Gas) Diverter (Valve) to Cabin, please. We are about two-tenths of a psi from Cabin Relief. Over. [They are resetting the Suit Gas Diverter valve so that oxygen can flow from the suit circuit into the cabin. Frank O'Brien has provdied a photo of the upper part of the forward surface of the ECS ( 628k ) in the LM simulator at the Cradle of Aviation Museum. The suit gas diverter valve is at the upper right in its own recess.]

A17A1483400.speaker: Cernan
A17A1483400.text: Okay, we're getting that now. (Long Pause) [If the cabin pressure exceeds 5.83 psi, a relief valve will dump the excess out of the spacecraft. As long as the valve works, there is no danger to the crew or the LM but, obviously, they would rather not waste oxygen.]

A17A1483400.speaker: Cernan
A17A1483400.text: Joe, CDR is reading 94 percent on the O2 charge.

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Thank you. [Long Comm Break.] [Having finished Gene's PLSS recharge, they are disconnecting and removing the RCUs and OPSs and then the PLSSs. These activities are listed on Surface 5-3 . Before stowing the OPSs, they will perform OPS checkouts and report the source pressures. The checkout procedures are stenciled on the OPS cover, as can be seen in training photo KSC-72PC-347 . The procedures can also be found in Section 4.2.1 in Volume 2 of the A15-17 EMU Handbook .]

A17A1483400.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1483400.text: Okay, Joe. LMP's OPS pressure is 6300 (psi).

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Copy, 6100. [Comm Break. Next they will change the PLSS batteries and LiOH canisters. These activities are listed in the right-hand column of Surface 5-3 .]

A17A1483400.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1483400.text: Say, Joe, our cabin pressure is rising even higher, now. About 5.7.

A17A1483400.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1483400.text: Joe, we had the commander's hoses stowed, but in Suit Flow. That might have done it. Is that right?

A17A1483400.speaker: Allen
A17A1483400.text: Sounds very plausible, Jack. We'll look at it a little more here. [Long Comm Break. Jack is speculating that oxygen from the Suit Circuit is being added to the cabin through Gene's hose without returning to the Suit Circuit. However, it is normal procedure to have both Suit Isolation Valves ( 628k ) in Suit Flow at this point. The Cabin Gas Return Valve is currently in the Egress position and no oxygen would be flowing from the cabin to the suit circuit through that valve; cabin gas should be flowing back into the suit circuit through the return hoses; and, finally, with pressure regulators A

A17A1493215.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1493215.text: Okay, Joe. We'll be at your beck and call.

A17A1493215.speaker: Allen
A17A1493215.text: I'll only smile at that. [Very Long Comm Break. Jack's sinuses sound a little clogged. During this period they are probably cleaning the zippers and other fittings on Gene's suit as per checklist page 5-5 . Once they are done, they will stow the suit on the engine cover, neck ring aft, and will put the suit legs in jettison bags to try to control the dust. Once that is done, they will reconnect the air hoses to the suit to help dry it out.]

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Joe. You don't want me to go on the Verb... You're not going to give us an update, huh?

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: No update required. That was just to prevent an overflow. And then I'm ready for the quick changes in the Lunar Surface Checklist when you are. (Long Pause) [Cernan - "I think our computer-based inertial navigation system was the state-of-the art. It ended up in 747's flying across the Pond (usually the Atlantic Ocean). We'd write the software for the different missions and it would take hours and hours in the simulator to wring out all the bugs in it before you would have a level of confidence in it that it could be declared operational. It's obsolete equipment today but, as far as I know, th

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Joe, go ahead.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay. Begin by putting the Demand Reg Bravo to Cabin position and leave the Demand Reg Alpha in the Cabin position where it now is. And I'll continue on with the changes in the checklist here. Page 5-6 , left-hand side, where it reads "Configure ETB." The fourth line down that starts out "Four B&W mags," they should read, "Hotel, India, Juliett, and Romeo in LCG compartment." Then going up to the right-hand side under "Stow in ETB," change the line "One B&W mag Romeo" to read "One B&W mag Kilo." Over.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Joe. I changed the mags in the "Empty" from Kilo to Romeo and the mag in "Stow" from Romeo to Kilo.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, that sounds like the thing to do. And a note on your demand regulators. We're showing that the demand regulator Alpha has good integrity and we're now in the process of checking demand regulator Bravo. I've got a couple of fairly quick questions here when you're ready for those.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Joe. Go ahead with your questions; and integrity is certainly what we need around here, right? (Pause)

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay. Jack, a question for you to begin with. Is your gold (electroplated) visor sticking halfway down? Apparently, that's based on a discussion earlier. Over. (Pause)

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Yeah. Apparently his visor is sticking. (Pause) (To Jack) Which one?

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: The gold visor? No, he said his sunshade is sticking halfway down, but his gold visor's not. [Schmitt - "I was working a lot with my gold visor halfway down, just so I could see better. And they got confused when Gene or I made a comment some other place that the sunshade wouldn't come all the way down."]

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, that answers the question. We couldn't tell from the TV whether it was the visor or the sunshade. That's fine. We also heard some discussion about possible wear in the seats of the suits when you were dusting each other off. We want to know if you could see any hint of the aluminum layers showing through in the suits. Over. [Joe is referring to comments made at 147:55:56 when Gene was dusting Jack's PLSS.]

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: No, Joe. Not to worry. It's just a few scars on the PLSS thermal blanket in back where you probably rub the seat when you get in. Nothing on the suits.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Geno. Now two real quick geology questions that will help us do the planning for your EVA tomorrow. The first one has to do with Station 4. And you called out some material on the rim (of) the crater at Station 4 which looked like "bedded spatter". And we're wondering if that resembled things that you'd seen in Hawaii? Over.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Hey, Joe, I think they misheard. I think I may have said "shattered" and you might have thought "spattered". No, I didn't - neither one of us - intended to leave that impression. The big rock we sampled looked like intensely-shattered gabbro, such as we've had around the LM. Probably more significantly, the rocks - one of which Gene picked up - (were) the fine-grained, coarsely-vesicular basalts. And we didn't have any time to really examine the interrelationships of those rock types there, but those were the two fragment types we saw. [The phrase that Jack used at 145:25:00 to describe the St

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Jack. That's quite clear to us now. Also a question about Station 4...

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Joe...Joe.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, go ahead.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: The bottom of that crater, now, had material that was extremely disorganized in its aspect and, really, we didn't have time to examine it in detail in order to decide why it was disorganized. It did not necessarily look (in texture) like the boulder that we sampled at the rim. [At 145:23:48, Jack described the rocks in the bottom of the crater in the following words: "The central peak, if you will, or central mound, is very blocky and jagged. And the impression I have of the other mounds in the bottom is that they look like slump masses that may have come off the side."]

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Jack. Understand that. A question about the boulder you sampled at the rim. Would you compare the basalt in this boulder - which you may have called a gabbro, I'm not sure, in any case a basalt - to samples which you collected at Camelot and at ALSEP. Over.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Well, my impression was that they were the same rock types. [Jack sounds like his sinuses may be a bit clogged.]

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Okay, that's our impression, too. Thank you. That's it for us on the questions. And for information, we're showing your cabin pressure is holding fairly steady even with both those demand regs on.

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Okay. Keep watching it for us, would you, and let us know. I expect one of them is probably leaking pretty slow.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Yeah; no worry about that, Gene. We're looking at it real close.

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: How's (Command Module) America looking to you?

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: It is just as clean as a whistle.

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: It may not be when we get back there, judging from the looks of us. (Pause) That's good to hear, though. It's a good bird. So is this one. (Pause) 150:40:20 Schmitt: Joe, is there any...You got any more debriefing questions?

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Negative, Jack. And we're interested that you move right along so we can get you turned in there and get some rest.

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: We're moving. We're eating now, and we feel the same way, I think. (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "Almost certainly, I was surprised - and I think I recall it now - that they didn't want to ask more questions about EVA-2. More than likely, there were lots of questions; but the Flight Director was saying 'We've got to get them back on the timeline and get them to sleep.' We did a lot of geology debriefing when we got home but, unfortunately, we can't find the tapes or a transcript. I sat with Lee Silver and probably Muhlberger and Swann and others and recorded a lot of extra debrief."] [A raw transcri

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Troops, enjoy your meal there. And at your convenience, you can go ahead with the (PLSS) feedwater recharge. We want you to hold off on the oxygen recharge until we watch these regs for about another 10 minutes. And give us a mark if you do start the water recharge, please. Over.

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: And if there are any ways we can cut corners on the time here, it'll be helping us, because we're still looking at being down a couple of hours nearly.

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Okay, Joe. We're working at it as fast as we can. (Pause) Best place in the world to make it up is tomorrow night. [Schmitt - "After EVA-3, you were getting ready to go home, you'd done what you'd come to do so why worry about getting your full eight-hour rest period? You don't need eight hours of rest anyway; five was plenty, I think, for both of us. Plus, we were going to spend three days in orbit after rendezvous, so there wasn't going to be any hurry. So I think Gene was just trying to discourage them from even thinking about shortening the EVA."]

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Right, Geno, and, actually, we're going to pick up a good one shortly, because we're coming up to a pad in the timeline. So, as long as we don't waste too much time, we're doing pretty well. [That is, there is an hour's worth of unallocated time in the schedule. This is the item on Surface 5-7 called "MCC-H Conference"]

A17A1503200.speaker: Cernan
A17A1503200.text: Okay; be assured we're not. There's just a certain amount of housekeeping we have to do. But, very seriously, day after tomorrow is a very short day, and I think we ought to look at making up any time. I'm a hold-faster on sleep periods but tomorrow('s rest period) is the one that I think is flexible.

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Roger. We hear you. [Cernan - "We had five and a half hours to get prepared from the time we woke up to the time of lift-off and that was an enormous amount of time. We could have pushed the third night's sleep back and gotten up an hour later. And, if we did shorten the sleep, once we got back in the Command Module we could make it up."] [As things will turn out, they will have a 7-hour rest period after a full, 7-hour, 15-minute EVA.] [Cernan - "I've said that I thought sleeping on the Moon was a big waste of time. We needed physical rest, we needed to get out of our suits, but I really wish

A17A1503200.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1503200.text: Hey, Joe. This is Jack. We're eating here. Won't be too long at it, but if you've got any significant news or anything, why don't you give it to us? (Long Pause)

A17A1503200.speaker: Allen
A17A1503200.text: Jack, I don't know if it's significant news, but at least I know you'll be interested. Both your demand regs look good now. We show no evidence of a leak there and it may have been that just recycling them reseated them and solved whatever problem we had. You can go ahead with the O2 (top-off) recharge on the PLSS and the water recharge at your convenience. And let me poll the room here for other news items. Over. [Comm Break]

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: Joe, this is Jack. Do you know where specifically they're seeing the hot spots west of Copernicus?

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Jack, I don't have it on the page in front of me here. We're going to check into it and I'll get back to you in a second. [Comm Break]

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Jack, this is Houston. With regard to your questions on the hot spots, apparently they've not yet indexed these warmer sources that they're detecting to the CSM ephemeris, and so they don't know exactly what they correspond to as far as the surface features themselves go. So I can't help you on that right now. [Houston knows the times at which the hot spots were seen from the Command Module instruments; but geographical identification will require knowing exactly where the spacecraft was in its orbit at each of the observation times.] 150:59:14 Schmitt: Okay, Joe. Just curious. [Comm Break]

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Gene and Jack, TELMU handed me some numbers which I think you will be interested in. From the EVA-2 EMU summary, the elapsed EVA time was 7 hours plus 37 minutes plus 22 seconds for a new outdoor record under international rules. The rest of the sheet looks free from problems in a comforting way. Let's see, average metabolic rates: for you, Geno, 855 (BTU per hour); and, Jack, you're running at around 920. And that's relative to pre-mission (estimated) averages of around 850. And you have a grand total EVA time now of 14 hours 49 minutes and 35 seconds. [The previous single EVA records had bee

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: Very interesting numbers, Joe. Do you have any idea how the metabolic rate compared to yesterday?

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Good question. Let me ask on that one. (Pause) Yesterday you were running at 1045 and 1090. So you're down considerably from your work rates of yesterday, which is good news. Maybe you're learning how to do it more easily or something like that. [Schmitt - "Because we spent at least a couple of hours on the Rover on this second EVA, clearly we didn't stress ourselves as much as during the first day. And we were more familiarized, so there was less emotional stress than on the first EVA, if there had been any at all. And I'll tell you, I never remember feeling anxious about anything except abou

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: Yeah, but we spent a lot of time riding today and a lot of time working yesterday.

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: That's true. I guess that's not taken into consideration of the average here. It's certainly true. We can ask for the metabolic rate of the Rover. I bet that is pretty impressive for today. [Schmitt - "Joe was joking here. He was going to ask how hard the Rover worked. That's the way Joe thinks."] [The energy saved by riding the Rover is shown dramatically by the following table of activity averages. The table is derived from the Apollo 17 Mission Report.] Average Metabolic Rate (BTU/hr) Activity Gene's Average Jack's Average Riding 479 447 Geology Stations 1036 1189 ALSEP Deployment 1129 1104

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: Well, don't get me wrong. Driving that Rover is soft; but, I'll tell you, it keeps your attention.

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: I'm sure it does.

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: It keeps the passenger's attention, too!

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: I'm sure it does. We noted some comments when you were rolling along today; and reading between the lines from time to time. (Pause)

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: Actually, Joe, for good long spans of the run up to Station 2, except when we had to pick our way up the Hole-in-the-Wall, I was running full bore at anywhere from, I guess, what'd I say, 10 to 12 to 15 clicks. I didn't hit 15 going up (to Station 2) very much. Coming down I did, but it's really a "standby for a turn and watch where you're going" type of run. Because the small craters, of course, are the ones that can really jolt you. But the trouble is, you can never see what's just over the next ridge, and the next ridge may be 20 meters away and you just can't see it until you're there, and

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Roger, Gene. We copy that. [At 10 kilometers per hour, they would cover 20 meters in 7 seconds. Note Gene's statement of 15 kph versus his claim of 17 1/2 or 18 kph at 144:21:31.]

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: Joe, that des...

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Go ahead.

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: That description fits the geology up in there (on the Scarp), because we weren't seeing blocky rimmed craters and otherwise you would have been able to tell more easily about the old versus new craters, which would be the ones you could either go through or not go through, respectively.

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Roger. (Pause) [The avalanche that produced the light mantle had covered the Scarp with fine material - to a depth estimated to be 20 m at the base of the South Massif - and, unlike out on the valley floor, there were very few blocks of any size near the rims of even the freshest craters. Therefore, when they were approaching a crater, unless they could actually see the interior, there was no ready way to distinguish the deep, fresh craters - which they wanted to drive around - from the shallow, aged craters they could usually drive through.]

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: That's a super machine to drive though, Joe, I'll tell you. If you had enough time you could really learn to take it all the way. But you don't really do that, just the second time around.

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: Geno, was it spraying dirt at you today? Could you notice that you still missed the real fender and that the patched fender wasn't quite doing what maybe it could?

A17A1505652.speaker: Cernan
A17A1505652.text: No, sir, I don't think we missed it at all.

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: Fact is, we're recommending a design change, Joe.

A17A1505652.speaker: Allen
A17A1505652.text: That'll be for next year's models.

A17A1505652.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1505652.text: That's right. [Long Comm Break as they finish eating, get the debris out of the way, and refill their in-suit drink bags .]

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: (Sounding quite stuffy) Hey, Joe; Challenger.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Go ahead.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: (Have) they succeeded in leveling the gravimeter (the LSG), yet? (Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Jack, we'll check it, update our information on that. My understanding at the moment is that they've not; but they're thinking that the unit's just too cold and they're in the process of warming it up by dumping heat into it by running some of the equipment around it and in it, and they've by no means given up hope for that unit.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: I figure that means that my fooling around with it didn't help 'em.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Apparently, it didn't do too much for them, but what it did do was convince them that it's probably somehow locked up because its temperature's not right yet. And they're not worrying about whether it's level or not level now. They're confident that it's been set up okay, and now they're just biding their time to bring that temperature up. We'll get some more words to you sometime tomorrow on it as you make your traditional visit to the ALSEP site again, probably. How are you coming along with your sleep prep?

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: We're just about there, Joe. We picked up some time somewhere in here. Couldn't be much more than an hour behind.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: No, that's just about right. You're looking pretty good on that. [Deke Slayton joins the conversation.]

A17A1521612.speaker: Slayton
A17A1521612.text: If you get to sleep in the next 5 minutes, you're one hour behind.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Yes, sir; I'm putting my hammock up now, as a matter of fact. [They are now on Surface 5-8 . The rest period was scheduled to start at 151:25.] [Schmitt - "Gene got his hammock up first and got in it, then I put mine up and got in it. There wasn't much spare space. The suits were on the engine cover under Gene's hammock and, as I recall, the helmets and visor assemblies were way at the back, sort of under the suits."]

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: What's he (Slayton) doing up so late?

A17A1521612.speaker: Slayton
A17A1521612.text: Well, somebody's got to sit up and keep you guys honest. (Pause) I think we're getting more sleep down here than you are. (Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: (Garbled).

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: I might add that not only do we have to stay up late, we have to get up mighty early to keep you honest, too.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: Okay; you going to let us sleep 8 hours or what? 152:19:03 Allen: That's affirm, Jack. We're looking good on the time, and not only will you get, we hope, 8 hours of good sleep, but you'll have a full EVA tomorrow. So, it's not costing us anything there.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Okay, Joe; I'll buy that. (Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Sounds great, Joe. I fully expect it won't be much longer now. (Long Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Might add, also, that there are a lot of us looking forward to that third EVA tomorrow. It's going to be the last one on the lunar surface for some time.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: I tell you, if it's anywhere near what the first two were like, we're looking forward to it, also. (Long Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: And, Gene, just for rough planning purposes, we'll start to figure your sleep period starting around 152:30. And we'll be looking at your getting up around 8 hours from that time.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Gene and Jack, we're still marveling at the beautiful television pictures that we're getting from your TV camera there. It's fun, in fact, to watch the tracks that you're leaving behind in the lunar soil, both footprints and Rover tracks. And some of us are down here now reflecting on what sort of mark or track will - someday - disturb the tracks that you leave behind there tomorrow.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: That's an interesting thought, Joe, but I think we all know that somewhere, someday, someone will be here to disturb those tracks.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: No doubt about it, Geno.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: Don't be too pessimistic, Joe. I think it's going to happen.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Oh, there's no doubt about that. But it's fun to think about what sort of device will ultimately disturb your tracks.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: Well, that device may look something like your little boy.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Ah; he'd make short work of them. (Long Pause) [Joe's son, David Christopher Allen, was a very active four year old at the time of the mission.]

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Joe, I'll tell you it's also a pretty philosophical thought to think that you're riding around out here on what is really undisturbed everything, you know. If there was someone here, way back when sometime, they didn't leave much sign of their whereabouts, but that's an interesting thought, too, as you drive around and all of a sudden cross your own Rover tracks and figure out those are the only ones that have maybe have ever been here.

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Very true.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: And with that, I'm rolling out my hammock. (Long Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Okay, Joe. I'm waving goodnight to you. I'm rolling up my overhead (Rendezvous) window cover. (Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Okay, Gene and Jack. We'll say good night to you from down here, unless there's some other way we can help you.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: No, sir. If there is, we'll give you a call, though. (Long Pause)

A17A1521612.speaker: Allen
A17A1521612.text: Just want to end by saying what a terrific job you did today, and we're really looking forward to tomorrow. Have a good 8-hours rest.

A17A1521612.speaker: Cernan
A17A1521612.text: Thank you, Joe.

A17A1521612.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1521612.text: Tomorrow we answer all the unanswered questions. Right? 152:24:15 Allen: If not more. [Cernan - "It was easy to get philosophical. I've said before that I've always felt that sleep was one of the greatest wastes of the short time we had on the Moon. You're only there for 75 hours and you sure don't want to waste twenty four of it sleeping or resting. You'd like to be doing something that would allow you to go further in learning and exploring. And, yet, you had to rest if you were going to take advantage of your physical and mental capabilities the next day. Each EVA you became more tired and

a17_1544022csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1544022csm.text: Good morning, America. How are you? [Long pause.]

a17_1544022csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1544022csm.text: Hey, Houston. This is the Command Module Pilot of the United States spaceship America, and we're ready to participate in another day's activity.

a17_1544022csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1544022csm.text: Glad to hear it, Ron. Good morning.

a17_1544022csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1544022csm.text: I slept with my lightweight headset on last night so didn't have to have that cap on. Is the fidelity of this thing any good at all?

a17_1544022csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1544022csm.text: Pretty good, Ron. Pretty good. And as you start your morning's activities, you can be aware that we were watching the spacecraft through the night and, as Flight puts it, everything is swinging. [Pause.]

a17_1544626csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1544626csm.text: We start work early around here.

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545234csm.text: You know, I'd just be kind of curious how the - how the old heart rate compares to those sleep tests that we did preflight? Is it about the same when I'm soundly asleep or is it lower or what, you know?

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545234csm.text: Stand by, Ron, and I'll ask the men on the left.

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545234csm.text: Okay. You know, maybe they'll have that information.

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545234csm.text: Rog. They think maybe 5 minutes. And we'll be back to you.

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545234csm.text: Okay. No problem. Curiosity more than anything. [Long pause.]

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545234csm.text: I didn't get quite as much sleep last night. I took a bath and changed my underwear, and all those good deal things, huh. Probably only got - oh, maybe 7 hours at the most. Probably closer to 6½ of good sleep

a17_1545234csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545234csm.text: I'll give you the rest of that in just a jiffy when I get it all squared away.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545821csm.text: America, this is Houston.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Go ahead.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545821csm.text: Roger, Ron. Apparently in your preflight data base they show you with a rate of in the low 60's or high 50's, that's a sleeping rate. And we're showing you now, during your sleep periods, of heart rates of about 10 beats lower per minute. And with heart rates that show less variation than the preflight data shows. [Pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Ah ha, okay. Well, thank you much. The heart does slow down a little bit up here, then.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545821csm.text: Apparently so. They - they assured me however, that it would not be approaching zero. So you can relax there.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: [Laughter.] Okay. [Pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545821csm.text: And, Ron, in the meantime, Gordo's arrived here and - I'll turn the console over to him. Be talking to you later perhaps.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, Joe. Hey, we thank you much. Appreciate it.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Allen
a17_1545821csm.text: Enjoyed it. Have a good day. We'll all be watching you close.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, Ron. Good morning and go ahead.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, Houston; America. Here's my medical log.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: I disposed of my day off [laughter]. Okay, Gordo. Glad to have you aboard with us. Okay. PRD, 15041; and the sleep, I mentioned, probably about 6½ or 7 good hours. I took a Seconal last night, and I had four cans of fluid.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, here's the old chow for day 6.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Scrambled eggs, bacon squares, peaches, cinnamon toasted bread cubes, orange juice, cocoa with potassium and a vitamin pill. Okay. Lobster bisque, all the peanut butter, all the jelly, three pieces of bread, citrus beverage, a tea, a chocolate bar, and a package of pecans. And I had a beef steak, butterscotch pudding, and an orange drink. [Pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Yeah, Ron. You're loud and clear. [Pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, got that.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: And I think that was it. [Pause.] Hey, today I get sausage, grits, fruit cocktail, orange beverage, and coffee. [Long pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: And, Gordo, if you have one of these preflight, not preflight - but, what do you call it - geology summaries of EVA-2, like you had yesterday. I thought that was great.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1545821csm.text: Okay, Ron. I just picked it up. Let me read it over and then I'll give you a summary.

a17_1545821csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1545821csm.text: Oh, okay. Sure; no problem.

a17_1550840csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1550840csm.text: Hello, Ron. I'll give you a little summary here of the EVA. It's going to be a little rambling, because I haven't had time to organize it, but it was a very interesting night last night on that second EVA.

a17_1550840csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1550840csm.text: Traverse lay over terrain of extraordinary geologic diversity and yielded a far greater variety of information than ever obtained on any other lunar traverse. Systematic descriptions and samples of four of the six main units of the area, massif, subfloor, the light mantle, and the dark mantle were obtained. In addition, detailed descriptions were given of a variety of craters, including exciting discoveries at the crater Shorty, and descriptions of the Lee-Lincoln Scarp and lineaments in the hilly terrain. The South Massif is composed of two main varieties of breccia; blue-gray and tan-gray bl

a17_1550840csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1550840csm.text: Okay. They're going to take the antenna away from us, Ron. I'll have to finish this next time around. Spacecraft's looking good, we'll see you in about 45 minutes or so.

a17_1550840csm.speaker: Mission Control
a17_1550840csm.text: This is Apollo Control at 155 hours, 11 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Even though there are some 4 minutes and 25 seconds remaining to actual disappearance of the spacecraft America behind the Moon, the network has taken down the uplink to the spacecraft so, for all practical purposes, we have had Loss of Signal to Ron Evans aboard the spacecraft America. We'll see him again in about 48 minutes. Meanwhile the crew of Lunar Module Challenger is still asleep at Taurus-Littrow. To reiterate the new wake-up time for the Challenger crew, it's Ground Elapsed Time of 160 hours, 25 minutes with the sta

a17_1550840csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1550840csm.text: Okay. Mighty fine Gordo. Thank you.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Houston, this is America. See you tried to come in there.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. I'm just finishing up my fruit cocktail.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. While you're munching there, let me give you a few status reports here. First of all, your RCS is hooking right along there, 4 percent above the Flight Plan line; however, we have some plans for that 4 percent, which I'll go over with you later. On the oxygen, you've gained a little on it, since I was last on anyway. O 2 tank 1 is a little low, but it's balanced by tank 3 being a - a little high, and tank 2 is right on the redline, so I think they all balance out to be - not on the redline, on the Flight Plan line. And they all three balance out to be right on the Flight Plan line, as cl

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Very good. [Pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, while you're - I've got some words on - on your orbit here, which won't require anything - writing down anything - but for some reason you're missing the mascons or something, and your orbit's not degrading like we expected it to. It's not degrading down into a circular orbit. It's - I think it's staying just about the way it was, and so we're looking ahead to plane change, and we're - we're thinking about an extra maneuver prior to plane change - about 1 hour prior to plane change on the back side. There was some discussion here about what to call that maneuver. Somebody wanted to call

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: How about "mascon adjust?"

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Anyway, what the maneuver's going to be - whatever we call it - is about 11-foot-per-second RCS burn, 1 hour prior to plane change so that'll be on the back side. And, that'll just about use up your RCS overage and put you back on the Flight Plan line. That will adjust the height when you get around to the plane change, and then the plane change will be a little bigger than originally planned, showing about 365 feet per second, SPS, of course. And, looking at the consumables, that will put you down right - right on the rescue redline on SPS, so we're still in good shape - consumablewise. Furth

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: No, it sounds like you all thought it out. I appreciate your letting me know about that. I think - Is the time line worked out good enough in there to work in a P41? I guess it does - an hour before, huh?

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Yeah, well - we'll make it. I haven't looked at it myself, but we are - FAO has - and I haven't...

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Yeah, okay.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: ...heard exactly what needs to be changed, if anything. Okay, on the SIM bay. Basically there's nothing new to report. And all the people down here appreciate your timely operation of the SIM bay, and it's responsible for really maximizing the data return. In general, we're pretty happy. The problems that we're have - having with it are ones that have already been mentioned to you. On the - on the HF antenna retract problem that we have, if we have it, here's the plan. We're - Well, first of all, the consensus on that is that we really think the antennas are retracting okay. That it's a malfun

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Yeah, that sounds like - sounds like a good plan to me.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, we got one request from EECOM here. Can you turn the H 2 Tank 2 Fans, Off, please?

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: H 2 Tank 2 Fans are Off now.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. And when you get between courses on breakfast there, I have some pencil work for you in the way of Flight Plan updates. Not too much, really. [Long pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. Contrary to the way I eat breakfast on the ground, I always end up leaving my orange juice to last. I guess that's because you llke to eat the hot things first.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Rog.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: That's good. Flip the page - flip two pages and copy the next sounder PAD, which is for 158:40. T-start is 158:49:35 and stop time is 158...

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Wait a minute; wait a minute. I'm not with you.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. I got it [chuckle].

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. T-start...

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Go ahead, now, very sorry.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, that's correct. Now at - that same page - 158:13, after "Pan Camera - On," add a line that says, "V/H Override - High Altitude." [Pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, at 158:13, "V/H Override to High Altitude."

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, and at 158...

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: I think it's still in High Altitude from yesterday. Yes, it is.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. 158:21 is another, "Verify all Command Module VHF, Off." [Long pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, 158:21, "Verify all VHF, Off," and I know what that means.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, and the next two are easy. Next page, at 159:01. Just draw a line through "Mapping Camera, Retract," and at 159:05...

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, I got it.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: ...draw a line through "Mapping Camera Laser Altim - Laser Altimeter Cover, Closed."

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, got it.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, I think we're caught up. We're ready for High Gain, Auto.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, I'll go back to where we are in the old Flight Plan. Okay, you have Auto.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay. I don't think this lightweight headset's quite as good as the - the other one, and I'm going to change as soon as I get a chance here.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay.

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1560312csm.text: Okay, VHF A is Off, B is Off, Receive Only, B Data is Off, Beacon is Off, Ranging is Off. That's all [chuckle].

a17_1560312csm.speaker: Fullerton

A17A1602504.text: I figured the Gold Team might do that. You know, I've woke up to a lot of pleasant thoughts, but never to an Aggie before. (Pause) Hey, Gordo, don't forget I'm a Boilermaker. A17A1603452.text: That's affirm. Okay; start with Rev 38. Time is 162:22:52. Rev 39 is 164:21:24; 166:19:55; 168:18:27; 170:16:59; 172:15:31. That should have been rev 43 (the last one), and read back starting with rev 38.

A17A1603452.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1603452.text: (Read back much quicker) Okay; rev 38: 162:22:52; 164:21:24; 166:19:55; 168:18:27; 170:16:59; 172:15:31. And what is our present rev?

A17A1603452.speaker: Fullerton
A17A1603452.text: That's a good question. Let's see here. (Pause) We're working on rev 37. (Pause) Ron just went by you about ten minutes ago on rev 37. [The crew first entered lunar orbit by firing the Command Module engines over the lunar Farside. Evans has completed a bit more than half of the current revolution. Gene and Jack are about to start eating breakfast. Forty-five minutes are allotted in the flight plan for each of the meals.] [Long Comm Break.]

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1604329csm.text: Just of interest to you, Ron. We are really pleased with the way that our visual display and that worked out last night during the orbital science visual. Farouk was able to feed me the questions, and I was able to get them to you. If you have any comments one way or another, if you don't want us to do it on rev 40 or not, let us know. We plan right now on rev 40 for those orbital science visuals to do the same thing going - It's the visuals through landing site down through D-Caldera, and we're going to run the same operation, since it went so smoothly down here. We hope it went that way for

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1604329csm.text: Okay; thank you. What's the date today?

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1604329csm.text: It's Wednesday - let's see - Wednesday, the 13th of December.

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1604329csm.text: Right now, it's about 1:35 in the afternoon (Central Standard Time). (Pause)

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1604329csm.text: Okay; just took a quick peek up there. I can't really see too much of the North American continent. South America looks pretty good. And it might be my eyeballs rather than the clouds up there, but it looks like most of the clouds are up into the north-central part of the southeastern United States.

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1604329csm.text: I have a satellite picture here, and that's about the way it looks. [A Starry Night view of Earth from Taurus-Littrow at 1335 CST on December 13, 1972 ( 18k ) shows South America dominating the sunlight portion of Earth with Antarctica on the left and the southeastern U.S. on the right. This image is, of course, cloudless.] [Schmitt - "I remember that Gene was looking at the Earth through the rendezvous window. You couldn't see it out the front unless you got down and most of the time we were standing. The suits were on the engine cover, so you'd just stand and lean. In one-sixth g it was no b

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1604329csm.text: Good show. We're prepared to do it on this next rev, and I guess you might say even though it isn't that way in the Flight Plan, we'll probably just stand by right straight through on rev 40 where you - you pick up at the landing site and go right through D-Caldera. We'll be just standing by for that whole rev - that rev - whole piece - about 12 minutes, or so.

a17_1604329csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1604329csm.text: Well, it's sunny and pleasant in the valley of Taurus-Littrow. (Pause) And, Gordo, what is our Sun (elevation) angle going out today?

a17_1605207csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1605207csm.text: Okay. Looked like she worked. We're going 0.2 of a degree per second, now.

a17_1605747csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1605747csm.text: Ron, just a little information for you. One of those highlights of your day. When you come around AOS on this next pass, they'll be - White Sands will be standing by in a countdown on an Aero - Aerobee rocket for a UV calibration shot, and if that one doesn't go, they've got one for tomorrow, same way.

a17_1610425csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1610425csm.text: Is it starting to look pretty good on your High Gain Antenna scale down there, to switched to High Gain yet? [Pause.]

a17_1611036csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1611036csm.text: Ron, we're about ready to lose you, and at 161:30 you have a maneuver. We want to make sure that gets started on time because of Sun problems on the camera.

a17_1615728csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1615728csm.text: America, Houston. Don't want to interrupt your eat period, but just would like a word from you on how the SIM bay configuration went. Did the UV cover come open? We're standing by on that Aerobee launch.

a17_1615728csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1615728csm.text: Okay, Houston. This is the LMP from Challenger. How do you read?

a17_1615728csm.speaker: Fullerton
a17_1615728csm.text: Jack, you are loud and clear. [Very Long Comm Break. By the end of this break, they are both in their suits. While Jack does the battery management, Gene may be getting unneeded items stowed and out of the way.]

a17_1620135csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1620135csm.text: Okay, frame number 110 of mag Oscar Oscar was taken from window 1 off toward Lomonosov. You could really see the swirls in Marginis. They're - Trying to compare them with the same type of swirls back there in Arabia.

a17_1620135csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1620135csm.text: These are the swirls looking off across the - Marginis toward Lomonosov and - let's see, what's that other sea? Big - big crater just to the northwest of the Neper?

a17_1620135csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1620135csm.text: Well, yes. The swirls in that one crater seem to be in Marginis, and I hope that's Marginis. I want to look at my map here in a minute and look for sure: but they seem to be emanating essentially radial from that bright crater - going out across the mare.

a17_1621226csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1621226csm.text: You know, I'm looking north of - along Crisium. Okay, yeah; there's Picard and Peirce. And you get the - same - same pattern that looks kind of like a swirl. Looks the same - same type of albedo as a - as a swirl with light places and dark places. The only difference being that you can definitely tell that these are ejecta from Proclus because the pattern is somewhat radial, you know, from Proclus itself. And then you've got the same thing, there's a crater up on the north - north rim...

a17_1622139csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1622139csm.text: You know, I'm looking out of window 2 now, and you can definitely get three different color textures on the thing. You've got the - that light tan of Serenitatis, and then you've got the - an annulus ring that stops somewhere in about the middle of the two ridge systems that go around. And then you come down south in the landing site area and the two dark things change - Ah, I can't quite see it anymore. The landing site is a darker - more of a gray, and it go - goes on - goes on up - There's a subdued crater; there's kind of a - The rilles go on up there, and then there's a filled-in crater j

a17_1622139csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1622139csm.text: Frame 110 and 111 were taken, just now, out of mag Oscar Oscar - one of the landing site, and one north of the landing site, trying to get the color distinction between the three of them there.

a17_1622741csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1622741csm.text: Ron, do you have your Flight Plan handy? I've got an update and stuff like that. I don't want to interrupt eating. If you don't have it, we'll get it after the eat period.

a17_1622741csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1622741csm.text: (Watching telemetry on the batteries) Okay. We've got that. We're ready for Power Amp, Off, and PCM (Pulse Code Modulation), Low (bit rate). [Comm Break. Next, they will report their PRD readings, as per Surface 6-1 .]

a17_1622741csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1622741csm.text: Okay, 113, 114, and 115 were taken on the western edge of Serenitatis. I'll get unwound from the cord here in a little bit and I'll [laughter]. You know if we design another spacecraft, we got to have something with a - so you don't have to be tied up to this crazy cord.

a17_1622741csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1622741csm.text: Bob, CDR's PRD (Personal Radiation Dosimeter) is 17043. 17043.

a17_1624106csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1624106csm.text: I'm sorry, Bob, (for not having noticed the change in CapCom). [Long Comm Break. They have just finished the left-hand column of Surface 6-2 . First, they will get Jack into his PLSS and then Gene into his.]

a17_1624912csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1624912csm.text: I don't mean barber pole. I mean gray [laughter]. Well, whatever it was, it changed.

a17_1624912csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1624912csm.text: Bob, CDR is starting on with the PLSS donning. (Pause)

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1625223csm.text: The - Since we're having a little trouble with that, why don't I put the Track Extend switch to Off on that one?

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1625223csm.text: Challenger, Houston. We've lost downlink from you guys. We've got a very weak signal. You might check your configuration up there, please. (Pause) Challenger, Houston in the blind. We've lost downlink from you. Please check your comm configuration. Over.

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1625223csm.text: Okay. That, or he may want to skip one of the 60-second exposures in there somewhere, you know.

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1625223csm.text: Ron, our film record down here indicates you've got three more frames on there than you need for the zodiacal light, or do we have a bad number somewhere?

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1625223csm.text: (Static clears) Okay, Challenger. We have you back loud and clear.

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1625223csm.text: Okay, Houston. That's...(Listens) Okay. It looks like I might have hit the Yaw knob on the steerable (antenna) with the PLSS.

a17_1625223csm.speaker: Parker
a17_1625223csm.text: Okay. Copy that. (Long Pause) [Cernan - "He had a signal strength meter and control knobs for pitch and yaw so that he could tweak up the signal. He must have hit one of the knobs."]

a17_1625915csm.speaker: Evans
a17_1625915csm.text: Okay, Charlie 3 and Bravo 3 are On. Alpha 3, and Bravo 3 are Off. It should have been Charlie 3 and Dog 3 are On.

a17_1630407csm.speaker: Overmyer
a17_1630407csm.text: Roger, Ron. We're probably going to lose you early here. You're looking good as you go around the horn. We went around the room, and everything's - all systems are Go. Just a reminder on this next back side that there is no recording so there will be no DSE recording of voice on this back side.

a17_1630407csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1630407csm.text: Okay. (On) your PLSS comm, Audio breaker, Closed. Okay, PLSS PTT Main right, verify, and go Mode (switch) A.

a17_1630407csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1630407csm.text: Okay, I got you. You'll get the tones (on), vent flag, press flag, and O flag.

a17_1630407csm.speaker: Cernan
a17_1630407csm.text: Call Houston and give them your O2 reading.

a17_1630407csm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_1630407csm.text: Okay, Houston. This is the LMP on Mode A and my oxygen is nine-four (that is, 94 percent).

a17_163xxxxcsm.speaker: Schmitt
a17_163xxxxcsm.text: Okay, Houston. This is the LMP on Mode A and my oxygen is nine-four (that is, 94 percent).

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. I got all mine down.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: You all set?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Well, I got my left hand. Got the left hand. Now, let's see what I can do with the right hand. (Pause) 163:20:49 Schmitt: Almost tempted to take those cover gloves off today. [The cover gloves are fingerless and are worn to protect the suit glove. Gene and Jack had planned to discard the cover gloves at the end of the first EVA but, because the cover gloves were getting worn, it seemed prudent to leave them on and postpone damage to the suit gloves for as long as possible.] 163:20:53 Cernan: I might take a look at that, too. I hate to argue with success, but I need that dexterity today. (Pause

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Gene, you dropped out there right in the middle. (No answer; Long Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Challenger, Houston. You dropped out there. (Long Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, Bob. How do you read now?

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Loud and clear, Gene.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, I hit the VOX switch on my audio panel.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: You did!? 163:22:20 Cernan: Yeah, when I picked up my glove. Okay, Bob, the only thing I said - a little point of interest - I wore the RTV off the...Not all of it, but right through to bare metal on the hammer sometime in the previous 2 days. No problem; it just interests me. [ Details from two photos of Gene taken late in EVA-3 shows, AS17-134- 20478 and 479 , show an area on the hammer handle where the RTV has worn off. ] [Cernan - "I used the hammer so much that, in some spots on the handle, I literally wore off the RTV coating. You can surmise anything you want from that: I was squeezing

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Okay, copy that. And copy that you still have you cover gloves on today, right?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Yes, sir! I'll tell you, we have become very respectful of the dust.

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Copy that.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Oh, yeah, cover gloves, yeah...We've also got the wrist dust covers on, too.

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Roger. Strike a blow for Mason jar rings.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: And what's left of the cover gloves. [Mason jars are a brand of canning jars with rubber rings to provide the necessary airtight seal. Bob is saying that protection of the wrist seals is valuable.] [Like the RTV coating on the hammer handle, Gene's cover gloves are very worn. He and Jack will discard their cover gloves during the Rover preps on this EVA, at 163:48:11 .]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, Jack, you on?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: I'm on.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: And locked?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: And locked.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Well, I got my thing on; I want to make sure I'm locked again. (Pause) Yeah, I am. I took it off again. Well, I was. Talking and you just do things...Okay. (Reading cue card, same as Surface 6-6 ) "Don EV gloves...(skipping forward in the checklist) Cover (wrist rings)..." Okay. PGA biting? No. Okay. "LCG cold as required", and then "LCG Pump (circuit breaker), Open". I guess you can open it. (Pause) And disconnect the LM...

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay. LCG pump.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: ...Water hose.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: And I got a tone but that's because I turned my oxygen on briefly. [Here, Jack is putting a little pressure in his suit to keep it from collapsing around him because of breathe-down. Gene will put a little pressure in his suit at 163:24:54. The Apollo 12 crew had noted this problem in their post-mission technical debriefing and suggested this fix. Gene and Jack will fully inflate the suits for the pressure integrity check at 163:26:46.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, Pump (breaker)'s Open. (I'll) turn around here and help you.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: You can take the water off.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Water's off. Or the pump's off. Okay, your (LM) water (hose)'s off. [Next, Jack will connect Gene's PLSS water hose.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Stick that (LM water hose) there for a minute. (Pause) Okay, hang on. Okay, you're in and locked. Locked over nicely. Okay. [And, then, Gene connects Jack's PLSS water hose.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. (Pause) You're off. I'll lay that (LM water hose) there. Where's your (PLSS) water? Here it is way over here. (Long Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Hold on. (Pause) Okay. And it locked, and your (dust) cover's on. I got to zap my PGA. Wait a minute, I'm biting here.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay. Well, let me try to stow this (LM water hose). (Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. (Pause) "Verify your PLSS (feed)water's Min when you get a chance."

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, that's verified. Did that a minute ago.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: And mine's verified and your (PLSS LCG) pump on.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, Pump's going On.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Mine On. "Pressure Reg(ulators) A and B to Egress."

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, they are Egress.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, pressure integrity check. (Pause) Ready? [They are now at the top of the right-hand column of Surface 6-6 .]

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Let me (garbled).

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. (Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Awful lot of line there, isn't there?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Uh-huh. [Schmitt - "There were some gold-colored, yard-long lines connected to the utility lights and, since the clamps were outside on the fender, the lines may have been dangling. Or, I could have been referring to the LM hoses."]

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Don't know exactly what to do with it. (Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: (Garbled)

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay. All right. You happy?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Yep. " Pressure Regs A (and) B , to Egress."

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: They are Egress.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. Put your PLSS O2 water (means oxygen)...

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: No.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: ...On, now. Mark it.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: PLSS O2, On?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: PLSS O2, On. Right?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, it's on.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, and mine's on. We'll wait till it builds us up. Press flag should clear at 3.1 to 3.4 (psi), O2 flag'll clear at 3.7 to 4.0. (Pause) Okay, I'm coming up (in pressure). (Pause) Hope the old suit integrity is just as good as it has been. I don't see why not. (Long Pause) [Schmitt - "I will always be surprised that the suits held up as well as they did to the abuse we gave them. Just think about what we were doing and the dust environment we exposed them to. We tried to clean the bearings and plug the holes (that is, the connectors) and things like that; and they really did well, just like

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Coming up?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Yep. (Pause) About 3.5 now.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Yeah, me too. (Pause) Okay, let me know when you are up.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: I think I'm up; I'm 3.8. [Next, they will turn off the flow of oxygen into the suits so they can check for pressure integrity.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, let's see if we can't get the...(Pause) Want me to get yours? I can.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: I got it

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: (Turning off his oxygen for the integrity check) Okay, mine's Off.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Mine's Off.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Mark it. We wanted decay for 1 minute.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, I started at 3.83 (psi).

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. That's about exactly where I was. (Pause) Another 45 seconds to go.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: So far, it looks as tight as it was yesterday. (Long Pause) Another 30 seconds. (Pause)

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Maybe lunar dust is a good sealant. (Pause) [After getting out of their suits the night before, they cleaned and lubricated the zippers, seals and connectors as best they could. Under the conditions, it is not surprising that they weren't able to get everything completely clean. Consequently, there was still some dust in the connectors and mixed in with the lubricant. Jack is marveling that the suits aren't leaking more than they are.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Houston, CDR (garbled) 3.82 to (misreading) 2.70.

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Understand 3.70.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, LMP was (3.)83 to 70.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, Jack. You can get your O2 on.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: It's on.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. Can you move to the left - a little bit to your left? I got to get in front here. [Schmitt - "Gene was going to lean down to get the hatch . I was facing him and he wanted me to lean toward the rear of the spacecraft to maximize the room he'd have to get down. It was tough to get down there and get a hold of the hatch."] [Cernan - "Once we had the suits up to 3.8, we moved around like tin soldiers (meaning very stiffly). 'You move a little bit, and I'll move a little bit.' From this point on, where you've got two people with the pressurized suits and the PLSSs on and the hoses on, a guy

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: Okay, you're Go from here...

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, let me turn this (cue card) over. [They are in the middle of the right-hand column of Surface 6-6 .]

A17A1631953.speaker: Parker
A17A1631953.text: 17, you copy Go.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, stand by. (Pause) Okay, Heck of a time to have to turn the checklist over. Okay, we've got a Go for depress. On (circuit breaker panel)16, Cabin Repress (breaker), Open, and Cabin Repress Valve , Closed.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay. [Jack is still facing Gene. The Cabin Repress valve is on his left and the circuit breaker panel is on the wall behind him.]

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: (You need to get) the breaker open and the valve closed.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, stand by. Can you give me a little room to...

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Let me...Okay, how's that? [Jack needs to turn around to get the circuit breaker and Gene is probably leaning back to give him room to get around.] [Cernan - "I can see in my mind Jack turning a little bit so that he could see the circuit breaker panel, and then his PLSS is hitting me right smack in the face."]

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay. (Pause) Okay, Repress (circuit breaker) is Open.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay. Now, why don't you face the wall over there and move in as close (to it as you can) and I'll get the overhead valve.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Wait a minute, I've got to close the ( ECS ) Repress valve. You got it all right. Okay, it's Closed and I'll get where I was yesterday.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: How's that? (Pause) [Cernan - "Jack is getting as far over on his side (and as far forward) as he can, so that I can get back and up to get the overhead valve."] [Training photo KSC-72PC-540 shows the overhead valve at the upper right.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: We'll find out in a minute.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: I've got to get my PLSS... [Gene is now turning to his right, putting his PLSS against the circuit breaker panel on the left wall so that he can reach up with his right arm.] [Cernan - "The shoulder bearing really restricted your movements and I may have even been up on my tiptoes to get high enough. If we had been in a round room or a square room it might have been different. But we were in a room with all kinds of shapes and corners in our way. And we, ourselves, were very bulky and non-conforming shapes."]

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Can you get it?

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Well...

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, wait a minute.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: I can turn with my back to the wall and you might have a little more...

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Well, I think...I feel like I'm hooked on something. Wait. I can't turn either way. Stay where you are. (Pause) There. Okay. (Pause; straining to reach) Okay, the safety (pin on the overhead valve is pulled)...Oh, boy, I'm glad I'm not an inch shorter. Okay, coming down, Jack. You ready?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Go ahead, to 3.5 (psi).

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay, it's Open.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, 4.5 - 4 - Stand by. Mark.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Auto.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, at 3.5.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Can you read the checklist?

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Okay, I can. Okay. Open, Auto. 3.5. Cuff checklist...(Realizing his error) Ah. (Chuckles) (I mean that the) cuff gauge does not drop below 4.6. It hasn't.

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Mine's good.

A17A1631953.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1631953.text: Have to put your (left?) hand down. I can't read it (the cue card).

A17A1631953.speaker: Cernan
A17A1631953.text: Okay.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: I guess the next thing is to open the hatch, huh?

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Yup. (Pause)

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: I've got to get down out of 5 (psi suit pressure), too, here before I can turn too well and open the hatch. I'm going to let it come down a little bit this time so I don't get down there unnecessarily. [Cernan - "At five psi you might just as well have been in a block of concrete. Going down to 3.7 or 3.8 gave me a lot of flexibility that I didn't have at 5 to get down and open the hatch. When you went down to open the hatch, you're literally straining against the suit. So I didn't want to get down until my suit was down. And, also, there was no point in getting down to get it until the cabin

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Yeah. It's got a ways to go yet. (Pause) About point three now. (Pause) Point two.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: I've got a tone and it's (a) water tone (because he hasn't yet turned on his PLSS feedwater). Okay, I'm going to go after that hatch. (Pause) Can you slip to the right as far as you can? (Pause)

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Got it.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Got to hold it (open) until the pressure decreases.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: (looking out his window) All sorts of junk going out there. Ice. (Pause) [Schmitt - "One of the big issues for any kind of permanent lunar habitat is going to be dust control. And it just occurred to me that the design of the air/dust lock ought to be such that, when you depress to go out on an EVA, the air currents remove the dust you brought in the last time. Never thought of that before, and I've been dealing with this - along with a lot of other people - for a long time. I ought to patent that idea."]

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Okay, now. Okay. It's partially open. [Cernan - "Once I was able to open the hatch against whatever residual pressure there was, if I didn't hold it open the pressure would slam it shut again. So I had to hold it open until the cabin relieved totally."]

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Okay, get your (sublimator feed)water if you can.

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: Okay, Jack. We'd like you to close Reg(ulator) A, please.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Oh, close Reg A, huh?

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: That's affirm. [The regulators are normally set in the Egress position during EVA's. Evidently, Houston is having second thoughts about this regulator, which was the one that experienced the slow leak before the rest period.]

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Okay, stand by. That's not an easy task (because the valve's behind me). (Long Pause) Reg A is Closed. Gene, can you get my (PLSS feed)water?

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Yeah. (Long Pause)

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Did you get in there?

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Okay, it's Open.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Okay. LMP's water is Open. You got yours?

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Yeah, I got mine.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: (Burps) Excuse me.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Well, let's see.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Okay, you got it open, so I need to turn around. See if I can back in and (get) out of the way of the door.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Say, Bob. What did you see in Reg A?

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: Stand by, Gene. We're seeing high suit pressures, stand by.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: High suit pressure? [Bob meant to say "high suit-loop pressures" and, hence, the confusion.]

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: Okay, and...

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Yeah, I'm seeing about...

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: Challenger, Gene, you're Go to go out, and once you get out, maybe Jack can turn around and work on those a bit better. We're seeing, I guess, the suit loop's a little high in pressure.

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Okay.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Okay, I'm looking at about 4.7 on the suit loop right now.

A17A1633344.speaker: Parker
A17A1633344.text: Okay; we copy that.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Okay, Jack. (Pause) [Gene is starting to turn around so that he can get down, put his feet out through the hatch and back out of the spacecraft.]

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: There you go. (Long Pause) (Garbled). (Pause) Okay, turn. (Long Pause)

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Okay. What does it look like to you?

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Well, you're doing great; keep down. Just a little hang-up on the DSKY.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: I gotta get my arm down there. 163:38:13 Schmitt: You need to go to your left a little to clear the purse and your harness. There we go. [Schmitt - "There was a little bag called the 'purse' where we stowed the purge valves between EVA's."] [The purse is hanging under Panel 5, directly in front of where Gene stands.]

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Jack, you see this? This is one of those cards that...

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Yeah, I saw that, Gene.

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: I'll put it right there. (Garbled).

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
A17A1633344.text: Can you come forward just a little?

A17A1633344.speaker: Cernan
A17A1633344.text: Forward?

A17A1633344.speaker: Schmitt
